en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Entrance to the Abhidhamma:
An Introduction to the Work.
Having bowed my head to the Tathāgata, the unsurpassed Buddha of infinite compassion and wisdom, and to the Dhamma and the assembly of the virtuous, I—
of incomparable prowess— [shall speak] upon the stone named Paṇḍukambala.
Seated upon the stainless, cool surface of the King of Devas,
the God of Gods— worshipped by the gods themselves—
taught the Dhamma in the world of the gods while surrounded by the divine assembly.
Therefore, for the sake of proficiency in the most excellent Piṭaka of the monks,
I shall set forth this *Abhidhammāvatāra*, which is sweet and increases the intellect;
it is the unsurpassed bolt for opening the door of delusion.
For the bhikkhus entering the great city of the Abhidhamma,
crossing over the great ocean of the Abhidhamma so difficult to cross— crossing,
as it were, the ocean of sea-monsters that is so very hard to traverse.
I shall briefly explain the unsurpassed manual of the Abhidhamma bhikkhus;
listen to it with concentrated minds. Chapter One.
The Exposition of Consciousness: "Consciousness, mental factors, matter, and Nibbāna—
thus the Peerless One taught the Dhamma in four ways, revealing the Four Noble Truths."

In this context, "consciousness" (*citta*) means that which cognizes objects. What, then, is its etymological meaning? It is said: it is called "consciousness" because it thinks by way of encompassing all things; or it is called "consciousness" because it accumulates one's own continuity.
It is consciousness because it makes various distinctions, or because of its own variegated nature.
[The term *citta*] is also used for a designation, for consciousness, and for a variegated painting.
The conventional designation "mind" (citta) should be understood here by the wise as referring to consciousness (viññāṇa).

That [consciousness], moreover, is of one kind insofar as it possesses an object; it is of two kinds according to whether it is with result (savipāka) or without result (avipāka). Among these, that which is with result is the wholesome (kusala) and the unwholesome (akusala); that which is without result is the indeterminate (abyākata). It is of three kinds according to the classification of its types: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
Now, what is the etymological meaning of the term "wholesome" (kusala)?
It is called *kusala* because it flows away from what is vile,
or because of the cutting away of the weeds (*kusa*), or because it is to be gathered by means of the weed;
this word *kusala* is used in the sense of skillful, health, and blamelessness.
It is seen here as having desirable ripening, blamelessness, and so forth.
Therefore, the wholesome (kusala) has the characteristic of blamelessness and desirable ripening; its function is the destruction of the unwholesome; its manifestation is purification.

Alternatively, because it is the opposite of the blameworthy, the wholesome has the characteristic of blamelessness; its function is the state of purification; its manifestation is desirable ripening.

It has appropriate attention as its proximate cause. Unwholesome [kamma] is characterized by being blameworthy and having an undesirable ripening. Indeterminate [kamma] is characterized by being the opposite of both, or else it is that which does not admit of ripening.
In this context, wholesome consciousness is of twenty-one kinds. This is fourfold according to plane: sense-sphere, fine-material-sphere, immaterial-sphere, and supramundane.
Among these, sense-sphere wholesome consciousness is of one kind according to plane; it is twofold according to the distinction between those with a physical basis and those without a physical basis.
It is threefold according to the division of inferior, medium, and superior; it is eightfold according to the division of joy, equanimity, knowledge, and effort.
That is to say: one accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, unprompted; one prompted;
one accompanied by joy, dissociated from knowledge, unprompted; one prompted; and one accompanied by equanimity...
One consciousness associated with knowledge and unprompted, one prompted, one accompanied by equanimity and dissociated from knowledge and unprompted,
and one prompted— these eight types together are called the wholesome sense-sphere consciousness.
In brief, there are two kinds of sense-sphere [consciousness], according to the basis of defilements.
Defilement is indeed craving and lust; the basis is the cycle of the three planes.
Defilement-desire desires, and the basis is desired;
thus this twofold desire is established for you in the two types of agents.
Furthermore, that region where both these two kinds of sensual pleasure (kāma) prevail by way of the attainment of success—
that region belongs to the four [classes of] beings and indeed to the six [classes of] devas.
However, by way of human beings alone, it is of eleven kinds. Herein,
that which belongs to the past of the sense-sphere is designated as "sense-sphere" (kāmāvacara),
because it is distinguished by its objects, like the domain of a weapon (sasatthāvacara).
The form-existence itself is "form"; thus it is designated as "kāma" (desire), having elided the latter member of the compound.
And because this mind always ranges within that desire, [it is called "kāmacchanda"].
"Thus it was spoken by the Destroyer of Desire as 'belonging to the sense-sphere' (kāmāvacara).
Or, because it causes rebirth-linking to proceed within the existence of desire, it is called 'belonging to the sense-sphere';
or, in that context, it is called 'included' (pariyāpanna)."
This eightfold consciousness, known as sense-sphere consciousness, proceeds by way of the ten bases of meritorious action:
giving, virtue, meditation, the dedication of merit, ... [the rest of the verse] ... [Note: The provided text fragment ends here.]
Service, teaching, and rejoicing;
association with those of right view, and timely hospitality—
thus should the classification of the bases of merit be understood.
Giving is included within the act of giving itself, as are the transfer of merit and rejoicing in merit;
likewise, within the merit consisting of virtue, are service and honoring;
and within the merit consisting of meditation, are teaching, listening, right view, and directness.
Again, there are exactly three [categories], as well as the ten meritorious deeds (puññakiriyā).
All the merits of the recollections (anussati), praise, and the three refuges are included within the rectification of views (diṭṭhijukamma); of this there is no doubt.
The first is the act of relinquishing, and the subsequent three are volitions;
thus there is merit consisting of giving. In this same way, it should be illustrated for the remaining [types of giving].
Now, the sequence of the arising of these eight kinds of sense-sphere wholesome consciousness should be understood as follows.
For when, having encountered the excellence of the recipient of the gift and so forth, or some other cause for joy, one is exceedingly delighted and—
preceded by right view occurring in the form of "there is what is given" and so on— performs meritorious deeds such as giving even without being urged by others,
then for him there arises the first [jhāna], which is accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, and unprompted (asaṅkhārika).

A great wholesome consciousness arises. However, when one—joyful and exceedingly joyful—performs the action having placed right view foremost and being encouraged by others, then that very same consciousness of his becomes "prompted" (*sasaṅkhārika*).
In this context, "prompting" (*saṅkhāra*) is a designation for the prior application of oneself or another. But when [one acts] for the sake of one's kinsmen...

When children who have gained familiarity through witnessing the practice see the bhikkhus, they become joyful and impulsively give whatever is in their hands or pay homage; at that moment, their third consciousness arises.
But when they say, "Give, noble ladies! Pay homage! and, thus encouraged by their kinsmen, give what is in their hands—
Or they pay homage; at that time, their fourth consciousness arises.

However, when—due to the absence of the excellence of the gift, the recipient, and so forth, or due to the absence of other causes for joy—they are devoid of joy in all four modes, then the remaining four arise accompanied by equanimity. Thus, according to the distinction of joy, equanimity, knowledge, and application:
The eightfold wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere should be understood.
Furthermore, one should explain that these same types of consciousness become numerous through the ten meritorious deeds and so forth.
One should designate seventeen thousand two hundred and eighty types of sense-sphere merit. That, in turn,
brings about the attainment of existence and enjoyments in the happy destinies of the sense sphere according to its correspondence.

As for the others, the wholesome consciousness of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara-kusala-citta) is of one kind when considered by way of its physical basis; it is of two kinds because it arises in two types of existence;
it is of three kinds according to the division into inferior, medium, and superior; it is of four kinds according to the division of the modes of progress (paṭipadā), etc.;

and it is of five kinds according to the association with the factors of jhāna. That is to say: it is that which has abandoned sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.

The first is associated with initial application, sustained application, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind; the second is dissociated from initial application and associated with sustained application, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind;
the third is dissociated from both initial and sustained application and associated with rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind;

the fourth is dissociated from initial application, sustained application, and rapture, and associated with happiness and one-pointedness of mind; [the fifth] is dissociated from initial application, sustained application, rapture, and happiness, and associated with equanimity and one-pointedness of mind.
"Fivefold" refers to this fivefold wholesome consciousness pertaining to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*).
Furthermore, it is of many kinds according to its occurrence upon objects such as the earth-kasina and so forth, as appropriate.
All of this, however, proceeds by means of the merit of fine-material-sphere meditation and produces rebirth in the fine-material sphere accordingly.
...it exists. Thus, first, the fine-material-sphere wholesome [consciousness] is to be understood.
As for the remaining two, the immaterial-sphere wholesome consciousness is, first of all, of one kind according to the distinction of its association with equanimous feeling;

it is of two kinds according to the distinction between having a physical basis and lacking a physical basis; it is of three kinds according to the distinction of inferior, medium, and superior; and [it is further distinguished] by the distinction of its object.
It is fourfold. The space disclosed by the kasiṇa, the consciousness occurring therein, the disappearance of that [consciousness], and the base of nothingness—this is its fourfold object.
It is fourfold according to the division of these objects in their respective order.
That is to say: through the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, through the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and through non-attention to perceptions of diversity...

The fourfold wholesome consciousness of the formless sphere (*arūpāvacara-kusala-citta*) consists of: that accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana-saññā*), that accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana-saññā*), that accompanied by the perception of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana-saññā*), and that accompanied by the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana-saññā*).
All of these proceed from the merit of formless-sphere meditation and, according to their respective nature, bring about rebirth in the formless realms.
Thus should the wholesome consciousness of the formless sphere be understood.

As for the other—the supramundane wholesome consciousness—it is of one kind by way of having Nibbāna as its object; it is of two kinds by way of the distinction between those with fixed and unfixed bases;
it is of three kinds by way of being attainable through the three doors of liberation; and it is of four kinds by way of the distinction of association with the four paths.
Namely: the stream-entry path-consciousness, which effects the abandoning of the fetters of identity-view, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances;

the once-returning path-consciousness, which effects the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion; the non-returning path-consciousness, which effects the complete abandoning of sensual lust and ill-will;
and the arahant path-consciousness, which effects the abandoning of lust for the fine-material realm, lust for the immaterial realm, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance.
This is what is called the fourfold supramundane wholesome consciousness.
Each of these, moreover, is fivefold according to the distinction of the combination of jhāna factors; thus, there are twenty types in total.

All of this proceeds from the merit of supramundane development and brings about the four noble persons through the arising of the fruit corresponding to the path. In this way, supramundane wholesomeness is to be understood.
In the sense-sphere there are eight, and five in the fine-material sphere;
four in the immaterial sphere, and likewise four in the unsurpassed. Thus, there are twenty-one wholesome states. Being mindful, one should avoid both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Whatever wholesome [teaching] was spoken by the Sage, the Master, pertaining to the four planes— both that which is wholesome and that which is wholesome through the wholesome— I have recited it all.
As for the unwholesome (*akusala*), from the perspective of its plane (*bhūmi*), it is of one kind, being exclusively of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).

It is twofold according to whether its object is fixed or unfixed, and according to whether it has one root or two roots, and according to whether it produces rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) or does not produce it. Furthermore, it is threefold by way of its roots: through association with the three feelings (*vedanā*), it is rooted in greed (*lobha*), rooted in hatred (*dosa*), and rooted in delusion (*moha*).
Among these, that which is rooted in greed is further divided by way of association with joy (*somanassa*), equanimity (*upekkhā*), and wrong view (*diṭṭhi*).
It is of eight kinds. Namely: one unprompted consciousness accompanied by joy and associated with views;
one prompted consciousness [of the same type]; one unprompted consciousness accompanied by joy and dissociated from views; one prompted consciousness [of the same type];
one unprompted consciousness accompanied by equanimity and associated with views; one prompted consciousness [of the same type]; one unprompted consciousness accompanied by equanimity...
One type is dissociated from views and unprompted, and one is prompted. For when,
having placed wrong view at the forefront in such a manner as "there is no danger in sensual pleasures," one enjoys sensual pleasures simply out of joy and satisfaction,
or assents to the idea that sights are auspicious and so forth as being essential, [this occurs] by means of a naturally intense [consciousness] that is not incited.
When it is prompted by a weak mind, then for him the first unwholesome thought arises; but when it is prompted by a dull [but still active] mind, then the second.

When, however, without being preoccupied with wrong view, he merely engages in sexual intercourse out of sheer joy and satisfaction, or covets another's prosperity, or carries off another's goods—doing so with a naturally sharp [impulse]—then [the third arises].
When it is prompted by a moderately encouraged mind, then the third arises. When it is prompted by a weakly encouraged mind, then the fourth arises.

However, when—due to the non-attainment of sense pleasures or the absence of other causes for joy—they are devoid of joy across all four modes of apprehension, then the remaining four arise accompanied by equanimity.
Thus, greed-rooted consciousness should be understood as eightfold, according to the distinctions of joy, equanimity, view, and application.
As for hate-rooted consciousness, it is of one kind because its object is invariably accompanied by aversion;

it is twofold, however, according to the distinction between being without effort and with effort—namely, that which is accompanied by displeasure and associated with repulsion, being either without effort or with effort. Furthermore, regarding this [hate-rooted consciousness] in acts such as killing living beings...
Its arising should be understood as occurring at the time of sharp and intense activity.
That which has delusion as its root is also twofold due to its association with doubt and restlessness:

that accompanied by equanimity and associated with doubt, and that accompanied by equanimity and associated with restlessness. Its occurrence should be understood at the times of indecision and distraction.

Thus, first of all, the twelvefold unwholesome consciousness should be understood. All of this, according to its respective nature, brings about rebirth in the states of misery, and even in the happy destinies, it produces various forms of suffering.
Eight [types] arise by way of the root of greed, two by way of the root of hatred, and two by way of the root of delusion; thus they are of twelve kinds.
"By means of non-evil, [I have removed] evil from evils"—this which was spoken regarding the evil mind has been fully set forth by me through the abandonment of evil from evils.
Furthermore, the other, the indeterminate, is of one kind because it is devoid of karmic fruition; it is of two kinds according to the distinction of birth: resultant consciousness (*vipākacitta*).
Regarding "functional consciousness": therein, resultant consciousness is fourfold according to the division of planes—sense-sphere, fine-material-sphere, immaterial-sphere, and supramundane.
Therein, sense-sphere resultant consciousness is twofold: wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant.
Wholesome-resultant consciousness is twofold: with root-cause and without root-cause.
Therein, resultant consciousness with roots is eightfold, according to the distinctions of joy, equanimity, knowledge, and effort, just like its own corresponding wholesome consciousness.
That is to say: accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, without prompting; with prompting; accompanied by joy, dissociated from knowledge, without prompting;
with prompting; and accompanied by equanimity, associated with knowledge, without prompting; [with prompting].
With effort, accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from knowledge, without effort, and with effort—this eightfold [consciousness] is called "root-cause resultant.
However, unlike the wholesome [consciousness], which operates upon six types of objects by way of giving and so forth, this does not do so. This...
For it proceeds only toward the six objects included within limited (paritta) phenomena, by way of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, death, and the registration consciousness.

And although there is no difference in the associated states, it should be understood that resultant consciousness is effortless, like the reflection of a face on the surface of a mirror, whereas wholesome consciousness is energetic, like the face itself. Now, the locus of the ripening of these [wholesome states] is—
This should be understood. For these [kamma-formations] ripen by becoming the rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, the death-moment, and the object-at-the-time-of-death.
These are the rebirth-linkings for sense-sphere deities and humans who possess either two roots or three roots.
Then, having become a functioning consciousness (pavatti), it remains as such for the duration of the life-span;
likewise, when the object is powerful, it becomes a registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa).
Then, at the time of death, having become a death-consciousness (cuti), it proceeds into the next existence.
Thus, one should explain that they ripen in four locations:
within wholesome states belonging to their own plane, together with the great resultants (mahāvipāka), excluding the [great] faultless states;
and as the door of action and the action itself, which constitute the basis for meritorious deeds.
Because they are not produced by intimation, because their nature is non-resultant, and because they do not continue in a series,
resultant states are not equal to meritorious deeds.
Furthermore, because their objects are limited, they are exclusively so.
Compassion and sympathetic joy never arise toward them.
Likewise, the three abstinences do not arise in them;
for the Teacher declared that the five training precepts are wholesome only for those [who possess these qualities].
Likewise, one should determine here that [the factors] do not exist by way of predominance (*adhipati*), because desire and the rest,
having been made the primary burden, do not arise [again]. Furthermore,
the classification into "without effort" (*asaṅkhāra*) and "with effort" (*sasaṅkhāra*) is based on merit (*puñña*).
The wise person should understand the knowable both by way of conditions and among the results (vipāka).
Because the results of meritorious deeds— such as those that are inferior and so forth— are taught by the proponent of merit,
it is explained that the results themselves are "inferior" and so on.
These eight types of consciousness are exclusively based on a physical base;
they arise in the sense-sphere world, but do not arise elsewhere.
Thus, firstly, the resultant consciousness with roots should be understood.
Rootless resultant consciousness, however, is devoid of roots such as non-greed; it includes eye-consciousness accompanied by equanimity,
ear-consciousness accompanied by equanimity, nose-consciousness accompanied by equanimity, tongue-consciousness accompanied by equanimity, body-consciousness accompanied by pleasure,
and rootless mind-element-receiving consciousness accompanied by equanimity, as well as [mind-consciousness-element-receiving consciousness] accompanied by joy.
The rootless investigating consciousness of the mind-element accompanied by equanimity, and the rootless investigating consciousness of the mind-element accompanied by equanimity—
these eight types are called rootless resultant consciousness. Furthermore,
these eight types are of one kind in terms of having a fixed physical basis, and of two kinds in terms of having fixed or non-fixed objects.
Therein, the fivefold consciousness has a determined object, while the remaining three have undetermined objects. It is threefold by way of association with pleasant, joyful, and equanimous feeling.
Therein, body-consciousness is accompanied by pleasure; investigating consciousness is associated with both joy and equanimity, depending on its two locations;
and the remainder is associated with equanimity.

It is fivefold by way of having a visible object as its domain, an audible object as its domain, a tangible object as its domain, a domain consisting of the visible, audible, and tangible, and a domain consisting of the visible, audible, tangible, and cognizable.
Therein, eye-consciousness has a visible object as its domain; ear-consciousness has an audible object as its domain;

the triad of nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness has a tangible object as its domain; mind-element and the [two] receiving consciousnesses have a domain consisting of the visible, audible, and tangible; and [the investigating consciousnesses] have a domain consisting of the visible, audible, tangible, and cognizable.

"And the two mental-consciousness elements. Thus, from the standpoint of their bases (*vatthu*), they are sixfold. How so? For eye-consciousness, the eye alone is the base; likewise, for ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness, the ear, nose, tongue, and body are the bases respectively; and for the remaining three [mental consciousnesses], the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) alone is the base.

From the standpoint of their objects (*ārammaṇa*), they are sevenfold. How so? Eye-consciousness has only visible form as its object; likewise, [the others] have sound, odor, flavor, and tangible objects as their respective objects.

In successive order, there are the ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousnesses; the mind-element has the five objects beginning with visible form as its domain; and the remaining two mind-consciousness-elements have all six objects as their domain.

All that resultants of rootless consciousness, however, are eightfold according to their functional roles (*kicca*). How so? Eye-consciousness has the function of seeing; the rest have the functions of hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, receiving, investigating, and registration.
Among these, consciousness that occurs by way of the eye, or consciousness that is dependent upon the eye, is called "eye-consciousness."
The same applies to ear-consciousness and the others. Therein, eye-consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing visible forms dependent on the eye;

its function is to have mere visible form as its object; it is manifested as being directed toward visible form; and its proximate cause is the subsidence of the functional mind-element that had visible form as its object.
Likewise, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness have the characteristics of cognizing sounds and so forth dependent on the ear and so forth.
The [five] sense-cognitions have as their characteristic the tasting of the objects consisting of mere sound and so forth; they are manifested as being directed toward sound and so forth;
and they have the subsiding of the functional mind-element (kiriyamanodhātu) regarding those objects of sound and so forth as their proximate cause.

However, the reception by the mind-element has the characteristic of cognizing visible forms and so forth immediately after eye-consciousness and the rest; it has the function of receiving visible forms and so forth; and it is manifested as such [receptive] being.
It is the proximate cause for the disappearance of eye-consciousness and the rest.

The remaining two rootless mind-consciousness elements, however, should be understood as having the characteristic of cognizing the six kinds of objects, the function of investigating and so forth, the manifestation of being such [in their respective ways], and the heart-base as their proximate cause. Among these, the first occurs only with respect to desirable objects.
Because it exists during the course of existence (*pavatti*), it accomplishes the function of investigation (*santīraṇa*) at the five sense-doors while being associated with joy;
thus, having stood at the five doors, it ripens. However, when there is a powerful object at any of the six doors, it ripens as a registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*).

The second type, however, being associated with equanimity because it exists during the course of existence toward objects that are neither-desirable-nor-undesirable, [functions] by way of investigation, registration, rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), and death (*cuti*).

Through its occurrence, it ripens in five places. How so? First, in the human world, at the moment of seizing rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), it ripens as the rebirth-linking consciousness for those such as the congenitally blind, the congenitally deaf, the congenitally dull-witted, the congenitally insane, the eunuchs, the hermaphrodites, and the neuter.

Once the rebirth-linking has passed, during the course of existence (*pavatti*), it ripens as the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) for as long as the lifespan lasts. Furthermore, it ripens as the investigating consciousness (*santīraṇa*) within the cognitive process of the five desirable or neutral sense objects.
Having been a sacrifice, having become a registration-moment at the six doors with a powerful object, and having become the death-moment at the time of death—it ripens in these five places.
Thus, first of all, the rootless resultant consciousnesses are to be understood.
There are sixteen resultants of sense-sphere merit.
That should be illustrated by way of merit rooted in three causes.

Now, the fine-material-sphere resultant consciousnesses are discussed. They are of one kind in terms of having a fixed physical basis; they are of five kinds according to the distinction of association with the factors of jhāna. How so?

The first is associated with initial application, sustained application, zest, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind; [the second] is associated with sustained application, zest, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind.
The second [jhāna], associated with rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind; the third, associated with happiness and one-pointedness of mind;

and the fourth, associated with equanimity and one-pointedness of mind—these five fine-material-sphere resultant consciousnesses function as rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death in the process of rebirth.
Now the resultant consciousnesses of the immaterial sphere are discussed. Like their respective wholesome counterparts, they are fourfold according to the distinction of their objects.

How so? The four resultant consciousnesses of the immaterial sphere are: that accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite space, that accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite consciousness, that accompanied by the perception of the base of nothingness, and that accompanied by the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Having been made to follow after the wholesome, why would it be classified as "exalted" (mahaggata),
since— like sense-sphere merit— it does not have an unequal fruit?
For this [consciousness] is in every respect identical to its own wholesome states.
Just as the shadow of elephants and other such beings resembles those very elephants and so forth,
even so is the sense-sphere merit of a being who has not fallen away from jhāna and is destined for existence, which does not result in experience in subsequent lives.
And because the fruit arises immediately after the wholesome itself,
this [wholesome category] was made to follow the wholesome for the purpose of making this known; furthermore,
it is for the sake of showing the sequence of the path and the distinction between the inferior and so forth.
And here, by one who discerns, it should be understood that this very distinction applies to the absence of predominance as well as to the attainment of jhāna;
all the rest is considered equal to the remaining wholesome [states].
In this way, the resultant consciousnesses of the fine-material and immaterial spheres are to be understood.
Now follow the supramundane resultant consciousnesses. Because they are the fruits of consciousness associated with the four paths, they are of four kinds. How so?

They are: the path-and-fruit consciousness of stream-entry, the path-and-fruit consciousness of once-returning, the path-and-fruit consciousness of non-returning, and [the path-and-fruit consciousness of arahantship].

The consciousness of the path and fruit of arahantship. Thus, in this context, each [type of supramundane consciousness] is fivefold according to the combination of jhāna factors, and furthermore, it is twofold according to its occurrence as a path-process, a fruition-process, or an attainment. In this way, the supramundane wholesome and resultant consciousnesses are to be understood.
They are called "void," "signless," and likewise "desireless."
These three names are obtained for the fruit immediately following the path, but not for the subsequent fruits of practice;
those names are obtained only by way of insight (vipassanā).
But the supramundane fruits possess only the dominant condition;
there is no resultant or dominant condition, except for those that are untainted (anāsava).
By virtue of its own nature as the path, the path is called "the path."
The fruit is called "the path" by depending upon the path.
Thus should the supramundane resultant states be understood.
Now, the seven unwholesome resultants are stated: eye-consciousness accompanied by equanimity, which is an unwholesome resultant; [and so forth].
Ear-consciousness accompanied by equanimity, nose-consciousness accompanied by equanimity,

tongue-consciousness accompanied by equanimity, body-consciousness accompanied by pain, mind-element-receiving consciousness accompanied by equanimity and rootless, and investigating mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity and rootless—
these are the seven unwholesome resultant consciousnesses.
In this context, however, when unwholesome karma has been accumulated by means of any of the eleven types of unwholesome consciousness accompanied by equanimity and rootless,
the mind-consciousness element— taking as its object any one of the three signs, namely, the kamma, the sign of the kamma, or the sign of the destination—
arises as rebirth-linking in the four woeful states. Once the moment of rebirth-linking has passed, from that point onward, it occurs during the second mental moment.
To the extent of its lifespan, it matures as the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*); as the investigation (*santīraṇa*) for the fivefold sense-consciousness process having an undesirable or neutral object;
as the registration (*tadārammaṇa*) in the six doors when the object is powerful; and at the time of death, as the death-consciousness (*cuti*).
Thus, it matures in five ways. For those wholesome-resultant rootless consciousnesses have wholesome kamma as their condition.
These are the conditions for unwholesome kamma. This is the distinction between these [two sets] and those [other types].
These function within a range that is undesirable, desirable, or neutral;
those are associated with the triad of pleasure and so forth, while these are associated with pain and equanimity.
Thus, there are eight types of wholesome resultant consciousness of the sense sphere accompanied by roots, and eight types without roots;

five types of fine-material-sphere resultant consciousness according to the distinction of jhāna factors and their association; four types of immaterial-sphere resultant consciousness according to the distinction of objects;

four types of supramundane resultant consciousness according to the distinction of the path-associated consciousness and its fruit; and seven types of unwholesome resultant consciousness according to the distinction of eye-consciousness and so forth.
The resultant consciousness should be understood as being of thirty-six kinds.
Thus, the Sugata, honored for his teaching on the results [of karma],
spoke skillfully regarding those states that have results and those that are resultless.
Furthermore, the functional-inefficient (kiriyābyākata) consciousness is of one kind in terms of being non-resultant; it is of two kinds in terms of being limited (paritta) or sublime (mahaggata);

and it is of three kinds according to the distinction of the planes of the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere. Among these, the sense-sphere consciousness is of two kinds: with root-cause (sahetuka) and without root-cause (ahetuka).
Therein, that with root-cause is of one kind, arising only in an Arahant. It is divided by joy, equanimity, knowledge, and application, just like the wholesome consciousness of the sense-sphere.
It is eightfold. Namely: accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, unprompted; prompted;

accompanied by joy, dissociated from knowledge, unprompted; prompted; accompanied by equanimity, associated with knowledge, unprompted; prompted; accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from knowledge, unprompted.
"Volitional" (*sasaṅkhārika*) refers to these eight root-cause functional consciousnesses (*sa-hetuka-kiriya-citta*).

These, moreover, arise only in those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), according to their respective suitability through acts such as giving and so forth. Thus should the root-cause functional consciousnesses be understood.
As for the rootless functional consciousness (*a-hetuka-kiriya-citta*), it is threefold: the functional rootless mind-element accompanied by equanimity and the adverting consciousness.

The mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy with functional roots, which is the consciousness arising as laughter; and the determining consciousness accompanied by equanimity with functional roots.

Therein, the functional root mind-element accompanied by equanimity, depending on the heart-base, [arises] at the eye-door in relation to objects that are desirable, desirable-neutral, undesirable, or undesirable-neutral.
When any one of the sense-faculties is struck by a visible-form object, it arises by apprehending that respective object;
acting as a precursor to eye-consciousness through the mode of adverting, it turns back the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
This same method applies to the ear-door and the others as well. However, the other two rootless mind-consciousness elements (manoviññāṇadhātu) are of two kinds: common and uncommon.
Therein, the uncommon functional mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy arises, having the function of producing a smile, for one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) alone;
it occurs at the six doors with respect to the six inferior objects and has a fixed basis.
The common rootless mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity, however, has the characteristic of cognizing the six kinds of objects.
It manifests as suchness; it is common to all sentient beings possessing minds within the three realms of existence, and there is no one with a mind to whom it does not arise.
When arising, however, it arises in the five sense-doors and the mind-door performing the functions of determining (*voṭṭhabbana*) and adverting (*āvajjana*).
Even the six types of uncommon knowledge take only that object which has been grasped by this [advertence].
They grasp [objects]. Because they are capable of grasping all objects, they should be understood as having the omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) as their range.
These are the three rootless functional consciousnesses (ahetuka-kiriyacitta).
Standing here, the laughing consciousnesses (hasanacitta) are to be examined. There are thirteen laughing consciousnesses. From the wholesome side, there are four...
Ordinary worldlings laugh by means of these eight consciousnesses—namely, the four unwholesome states accompanied by joy;
however, those in training (sekkhā) laugh by means of six: the four wholesome states and the two unwholesome states dissociated from views and accompanied by joy.
Those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) laugh by means of the five functional states accompanied by joy.
There are eight consciousnesses associated with joy, both wholesome and unwholesome;
and five from the functional class—thus there are thirteen consciousnesses accompanied by laughter.
Among these, worldlings laugh with eight types of consciousness.
The six are for those in training and those beyond training, but the five are accompanied by laughter.

Now follow the functional consciousnesses of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara-kiriyacitta*): the first is associated with initial application (*vitakka*), sustained application (*vicāra*), rapture (*pīti*), happiness (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*);
the second is associated with sustained application, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind; [the third] is associated with rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind.

The third is associated with pleasure and one-pointedness of mind; the fourth is associated with equanimity and one-pointedness of mind; and the fifth is associated with equanimity and one-pointedness of mind—these are the five functional consciousnesses of the fine-material sphere.

Now, the functional consciousnesses of the immaterial sphere are described: that accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite space, and that accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite consciousness.

Accompanied by the perception of the base of nothingness, and accompanied by the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—these are the four functional consciousnesses of the formless sphere (*arūpāvacara*).
These functional consciousnesses of the fine-material and formless spheres, however, resemble their respective wholesome (*kusala*) counterparts of those same planes.

The only difference is that these functional consciousnesses arise only in those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), whereas the wholesome ones arise in trainees (*sekha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*).

Furthermore, these [signs] arise for those whose taints are exhausted by way of the mode of development (*bhāvanākāra*); however, those for trainees (*sekha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*) arise by way of the power of merit from development (*bhāvanāpuñña*).
This alone is the distinction between these and those.
But that which was produced during the time of being a worldling—
The attainments of the fine-material and immaterial realms belong to a bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted.
As long as that bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted does not actually enter them, those attainments remain merely wholesome; however, once he has entered them, they become functional.

Thus, it should be understood that there are twenty types of functional consciousness (kiriyacitta) according to their planes: eightfold with respect to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), being divided by way of joy and so forth;

threefold without root-cause (ahetuka), being divided by way of the two elements—the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu); fivefold in the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), being divided by way of the association with jhāna factors;
and fourfold in the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara), being divided by way of the object. Thus, the functional consciousness is to be known as twentyfold by way of plane.
There are eleven types of functional consciousness in the sense sphere, five in the fine-material sphere, and four in the immaterial sphere;
thus, all the functional consciousnesses amount to twenty.
But why does supramundane functional consciousness not exist?
Indeed, because the path consists of a single moment of consciousness,
there is no [distinction between] action and non-action. That Victor who taught the distinction between the attainment of action and non-action spoke of the mind as both active and inactive.
For one who delights in the performance or non-performance of what is beneficial and what is harmful,
the performance and non-performance [of actions] has been fully explained by me.
To this extent, there are twenty-one kinds of wholesome [states], twelve kinds of unwholesome, and thirty-six kinds of resultant [states].
The mind introduced at the beginning as "the twentyfold functional consciousness" has thus been explained by way of a method consisting of eighty-nine divisions.
Twenty-one types of merit, twelve unwholesome states,
thirty-six resultants, and twenty functional consciousnesses.
All ninety-eight types of consciousness-arising have been succinctly explained by the Great Seer,
having categorized eight as supramundane.
These are found in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka for those monks who desire proficiency.
Therefore, this should be mastered and reflected upon again and again.
Those who cross over this world and the world beyond by means of the *Abhidhammāvatāra*— they cross over the great ocean of the Abhidhamma.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Exposition of Consciousness," in the *Abhidhammāvatāra*. 2.
The Second Chapter.
The Exposition of Mental Factors: Those mental factors which were indicated by me immediately after [the exposition of] consciousness—
I shall now provide their detailed analysis hereafter.

In this context, *cetasikas* are those associated with consciousness (*citta-sampayutta*) or those existing within consciousness. Like consciousness itself, they are of one kind insofar as they possess an object (*sārammaṇa*).

They are of two kinds according to whether they have a result (*savipāka*) or no result (*avipāka*). They are of three kinds according to the division into wholesome (*kusala*), unwholesome (*akusala*), and indeterminate (*abyākata*). They are of four kinds according to the division into the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth.
Among these, those associated with sense-sphere consciousness are the sense-sphere *cetasikas*. Of these, [those] associated with the first great wholesome sense-sphere consciousness...
Thus, twenty-nine factors invariably arise together with their own characteristics. They are as follows:

contact, feeling, perception, volition, applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, one-pointedness of mind, faith, mindfulness, energy, wisdom, the life-faculty, non-greed, non-hatred, moral shame, moral dread, serenity of body, serenity of mind, lightness of body, lightness of mind, and malleability of body.
Mental pliancy, bodily wieldiness, mental wieldiness, bodily proficiency, mental proficiency, bodily rectitude, and mental rectitude.
Furthermore, zeal, resolve, equanimity, and attention—these four are factors that must necessarily be included.
With these four, there are thirty-three. Furthermore, compassion, appreciative joy, and abstention from bodily misconduct...
Abstention from verbal misconduct and abstention from wrong livelihood—these five are indeterminate (*aniyata*). These, moreover, arise only occasionally.

Among these, at the time of cultivation by way of compassion (*karuṇā*) and appreciative joy (*muditā*), either the preliminary stage of compassion or the preliminary stage of appreciative joy arises;
they do not arise simultaneously. However, when [one acts] with this mind through wrong action and so forth...
When one abstains, then right action and the other factors are fulfilled;

thus, a single abstinence arises together with compassion (*karuṇā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*), yet they do not arise simultaneously with one another. Therefore, among these, when combined with any one [of the two], there are exactly thirty-four mental states.
Together with the initial wholesome mind, thirty-three are considered determinate (*niyata*).
With compassion and sympathetic joy, these become thirty-four.
But why were loving-kindness (*mettā*) and equanimity (*upekkhā*) not included here among the "included states" (*yevāpanaka-dhamma*) by the Teacher, the King of Dharma?
Since loving-kindness is included by non-ill will, and equanimity is included by mental neutrality,
therefore both [the former two] are not separately mentioned.
Why were the "concomitant" states not mentioned by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun?
All of these are indeed similar [to those already mentioned], yet they are not extracted in the canonical text (pāḷi).
Because some are indefinite, because others do not belong to a specific category,
and because some are weak, they have therefore not been stated in the canonical text.
Zeal, resolve, sympathetic joy, and mental attention;
equanimity, compassion, and the threefold abstinence;
by these, all merits are either fixed or unfixed.
These other factors were not mentioned by the Best of Sages.
But why was contact alone proclaimed first here?
It is because it is the first impact of the mind upon its object, so it is said.
Having touched by means of contact, one feels by means of feeling;
one perceives by means of perception, and one intends by means of volition.
And because they are powerful conditions, they indeed [function] for those that are co-nascent.
Contact was mentioned first; therefore, it was spoken of here by the Great Seer.
All this is not the cause [of the mind], but rather because those things born of mind arise simultaneously with the mind itself, through their state of co-arising and so forth.
But there is no such thing as "this arose first" or "this arose later";
even when the conditions are equally powerful, no reason [for such a distinction] is seen.
Furthermore, it was mentioned first according to the sequence of the teaching.
However, it should be understood in this way by the wise, not in detail.

This sequence of what precedes and follows need not be sought after; rather, one who understands the phenomena (dhammas) themselves should discern them through the meaning of the words, their characteristics, and so forth.

However, since these phenomena become clear and easy to understand when their etymological meanings, characteristics, and so forth are explained, I shall therefore set forth their etymologies, characteristics, and other attributes.
They are as follows: it touches, thus it is contact (*phassa*). This contact has the characteristic of touching;
its function is impingement; it is manifested as the meeting of the three; and it is manifested as feeling in the sense of being its fruit.
Alternatively, its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) is the object that has come into range. For although this is an immaterial phenomenon, it occurs solely in the mode of touching objects;
it should be regarded as like the meeting of two rams.

One who possesses a beautiful mind (*mano*) is "well-minded" (*sumana*); the state of being well-minded is "mental joy" (*somanassa*); mental joy itself as feeling is "feeling of mental joy" (*somanassavedanā*).
Feeling has the characteristic of being felt; its function is the experiencing of a desirable aspect, like a king tasting the flavor of fine food;
it is manifested as mental relish and has tranquility as its proximate cause.
Perception is so called because it perceives an object distinguished by blue and other qualities; it has the characteristic of perceiving and the function of making recognition possible.
It has the function of making a determination according to the sign as it was grasped, like a carpenter’s mark; its manifestation is the act of insistence based on that sign;
its proximate cause is the object as it presents itself.
It is called *cetanā* because it intends; the meaning is that it directs itself together with the associated states toward the object.

It has the characteristic of volition; its function is striving; it is manifested as the act of coordinating; it accomplishes its own task and the tasks of others, like an eldest pupil, a master builder, and so forth.

It is called *vitakka* because it "thinks upon" (*vitakketi*) the object, or else the act of thinking upon is *vitakka*. This [mental factor] has the characteristic of directing the mind onto the object; its function is striking and threshing [the mind]; it is manifested as leading the mind toward the object.
It is *vicāra* because the mind moves about (*vicarati*) upon the object; or rather, *vicāra* is the act of moving about. What is meant is "moving along" (*anusañcaraṇa*).
It has the characteristic of rubbing against the object, the function of engaging with its co-nascent states therein, and it is manifested as the continuous binding of the mind.

It is *pīti* because it gladdens (*pinayati*). It has the characteristic of endearing, the function of refreshing the body and mind—or alternatively, the function of pervading—and it is manifested as rapture (*odagga*).
One-pointedness of mind is *cittekaggatā*. This is a name for concentration (*samādhi*). Its characteristic is non-distraction, or its characteristic is non-diffusion;
its function is to bind together co-nascent states, like water binding bath-powder;
it is manifested as tranquility, and it has happiness specifically as its proximate cause.
It is called *saddhā* because by means of it one has faith, or because one oneself has faith, or because its nature is merely that of having faith.
Furthermore, this *saddhā* has the characteristic of believing; its function is to clarify, like a water-clearing gem; it is manifested as the absence of turbidity;
and its proximate cause is an object worthy of faith.

It is *sati* because they remember by means of it, or it itself remembers, or because it is merely a remembering. Its characteristic is non-forgetting; its function is non-confusion; it is manifested as protection;

its proximate cause is firm perception. The state of being a hero is *viriya*. Or, the action of heroes is *viriya*. It has the characteristic of exertion; its function is to support co-nascent states; it is manifested as the state of non-collapse; its proximate cause is a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).

It understands, thus it is wisdom (*paññā*). This wisdom has the characteristic of discerning; its function is to illuminate the object, like a lamp; its manifestation is non-delusion, like a guide through a forest.
Life (*jīvita*) is so called because the states associated with it live by means of it. It has the characteristic of maintaining those states that are inseparable from itself;
its function is to cause them to proceed; its manifestation is the establishing of those very states; its proximate cause is the states that are to be sustained.
And although it exists only at the very moment of their existence,
it protects those phenomena— just as water protects lotuses and the like— and it protects the phenomena arising from their respective conditions, just as a nurse protects a child;
it proceeds solely through its connection with the phenomena that have already set themselves in motion, like a pilot, and not after their dissolution.
It does not cause [the mind] to proceed because of the absence of both itself and those things that ought to be proceeded toward;
nor does it establish [the mind] at the moment of dissolution, because it is itself dissolving, like the oil in a lamp wick as it is being consumed.
They are not deluded by it, nor is it itself deluded, or rather, non-delusion alone is the continuum—this is *alobha* (non-greed). It [functions] toward the object...
Non-greed has the characteristic of the mind’s lack of attachment, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf; its function is non-clinging, like a monk who has renounced possessions;
it is manifested as the state of not adhering, like a man who has fallen into filth.
Because of it, beings do not hate, or it itself does not hate, or it is simply the absence of hatred—thus it is non-hatred (*adosa*). It has the characteristic of the absence of ferocity.
Or, it has non-opposition as its characteristic, like a compliant friend; its function is the removal of resentment, or its function is the removal of fever, like sandalwood;
it is manifested as gentleness, like the full moon.

It is called *hirī* because one feels shame (*hiriyati*) on account of bodily misconduct and so forth; this is a synonym for modesty. *Ottappa* is that by which one feels dread (*ottappati*) on account of those very same things.
This is a designation for the dread of evil. In this context, *hirī* has the characteristic of disgust toward evil, while *ottappa* has the characteristic of fear [of its consequences].
Both have the function of not committing evil; their manifestation is shrinking back from evil; and they are grounded in self-respect and respect for others.
These mental states should be regarded as guardians of the world.
Tranquillization of the body is bodily serenity (*kāyapassaddhi*). Tranquillization of the mind is mental serenity (*cittapassaddhi*).
Here, "body" refers to the three aggregates beginning with feeling. Both of these, taken together, have the characteristic of the subsiding of disturbances in body and mind;

their function is the crushing of disturbances in body and mind; they are manifested as the state of non-trembling and coolness in body and mind; they have body and mind as their proximate cause; [they are] of body and mind...
It should be understood that they are the opposites of the defilements such as restlessness and lack of tranquility.
Lightness of body is bodily lightness (*kāyalahutā*); lightness of mind is mental lightness (*cittalahutā*). Their characteristic is the subsiding of heaviness in body and mind;
their function is the crushing out of heaviness in body and mind; their manifestation is the non-sluggishness of body and mind; and their proximate cause is body and mind.
It should be understood as being the antidote to the defilements such as stiffness and torpor, which cause heaviness of body and mind.
Softness of body is bodily pliancy (*kāyamudutā*); softness of mind is mental pliancy (*cittamudutā*). Its characteristic is the subsiding of rigidity in body and mind;
its function is the crushing of rigidity in body and mind; it is manifested as non-resistance; and its proximate cause is body and mind.
It should be understood as being the antidote to defilements such as views and conceit that cause rigidity of body and mind.
Bodily wieldiness is the state of bodily adaptability; mental wieldiness is the state of mental adaptability.
Its characteristic is the subsiding of the unwieldiness of body and mind; its function is the crushing out of the unwieldiness of body and mind. Of body and mind...

It should be understood as having the accomplishment of making an object its characteristic manifestation, the body and mind as its proximate cause, and being the antidote to the remaining hindrances and defilements that cause unworkability in the body and mind.

The state of bodily proficiency is bodily lightness (*kāyapāguññatā*); the state of mental proficiency is mental lightness (*cittapāguññatā*). It is characterized by the non-ailing nature of the body and mind;
its function is to crush the ailment of the body and mind; it is manifested as freedom from danger; and it has the body and mind as its proximate cause.
It should be understood as being the antidote to the defilements such as lack of faith, which cause the state of sickness in body and mind.

Rectitude of the body is *kāyujujatā*; rectitude of the mind is *cittujujatā*. It is characterized by the absence of crookedness in body and mind, or it is characterized by straightforwardness in body and mind;
its function is to crush crookedness in body and mind, and it is manifested as the absence of deviousness.
It should be understood as having body and mind as its proximate cause, and as being the antidote to defilements such as deceit, fraud, and crookedness which produce distortion in body and mind.

"Zeal" (*chanda*) is a designation for the desire to act. Therefore, zeal has the characteristic of the desire to act; its function is the seeking of an object; it is manifested as the state of needing an object; and that very [object] is its proximate cause.

Adhimokkha (resoluteness) is the act of resolving. It has the characteristic of reaching a conclusion; its function is non-wavering; it is manifested as certainty; its proximate cause is the thing to be concluded upon. It should be regarded as like a city gate-post because of its immovability with respect to the object.

Tatramajjhattatā (equanimity regarding formations) is the state of neutrality toward various phenomena. It has the characteristic of keeping the mind and mental factors in balance; its function is to prevent deficiency or excess, or its function is to sever partiality; it is manifested as the state of neutrality.
*Manasikāra* is making (kāra) of the mind (*manas*), it is the act of attending to the mind. It is also called *manasikāra* because it makes the mind different from the previous state of mind.

This [mental factor] is of three kinds: that which leads to the object (*ārammaṇa-paṭipādaka*), that which leads to the cognitive process (*vīthi-paṭipādaka*), and that which leads to the impulsion (*javana-paṭipādaka*).
Among these, that which leads to the object is the making of the mind; it has the characteristic of recollecting (*sāraṇa*) the object for the associated states.

Its essence is fettering; its manifestation is the state of being directed toward an object; its proximate cause is the object; it is included within the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha);

and because it directs the associated states toward the object, it should be regarded as like a charioteer. "Directing across the path" is a designation for five-door adverting consciousness (*pañcadvārāvajjana*);
"directing toward impulsion" is a designation for mind-door adverting consciousness (*manodvārāvajjana*); these two are not intended here.

Compassion (*karuṇā*) is so called because, when there is suffering in others, it causes the hearts of the virtuous to tremble (*karoti*); or alternatively, it is compassion because it "wishes to remove" (*kināti*) or "destroys" (*vināseti*) the suffering of others.
Its characteristic is the manifestation in the mode of removing the suffering of others; its function is the inability to endure the suffering of others;
its proximate cause is non-cruelty; and its foundation is the perception of the helplessness of those overwhelmed by suffering.

It is called *muditā* because beings rejoice through it, or because one rejoices oneself. Its characteristic is gladdening; its function is non-enviousness; it is manifested as the dispelling of discontent;

and its proximate cause is seeing the prosperity of beings. Some, however, maintain that loving-kindness (*mettā*) and equanimity (*upekkhā*) are also not restricted [to specific objects], but that should not be accepted.
For in terms of meaning, loving-kindness is simply non-hatred (*adosa*), and equanimity is simply the equanimity of neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).
Abstaining from bodily misconduct is "abstention from bodily misconduct. The same method applies to the other two as well.

From the perspective of their characteristics and so forth, however, these three abstentions have the characteristic of not transgressing the bases such as bodily misconduct; they have the function of contracting away from the bases such as bodily misconduct;
they are manifested as non-performance; and they have faith, moral shame, moral dread, fewness of wishes, and other such qualities as their proximate cause.
Some, however, maintain that each one of these is a fixed (niyata) abstinence (*virati*).
Thus, it should be understood that by means of the first great wholesome consciousness of the sense-sphere, these thirty-three or thirty-four states enter into association.
And just as with the first, so too with the second consciousness; for the only difference here is the presence of volitional effort (*sasaṅkhārabhāva*).
Furthermore, by the third [jhāna], with the exception of non-delusion (*amoha*) due to dissociation from knowledge, the remaining thirty-two or thirty-three [factors] are to be understood.
Likewise, by the fourth as well, the only distinction is the mere presence of volitional effort (*sasaṅkhārabhāva*);

however, among those mentioned in the first [jhāna], with the exception of joy (*pīti*), the remainder associate with the fifth. And here, in the place of mental pleasure (*somanassa*), there is equanimous feeling (*upekkhā-vedanā*).
[The jhāna] has entered. It, moreover, is characterized by the experience of what is desirable, undesirable, and their opposites;
its function is the cutting off of partiality. And just as with the fifth [jhāna], so it is with the sixth; there is only the distinction of being "with effort" (*sasaṅkhāra*).
With the seventh, however, excluding wisdom (*paññā*), there are either thirty-one or thirty-two factors; likewise with the eighth.
The only distinction lies in the degree of volitional effort (*saṅkhāra*). Thus, first, the wholesome mental factors of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) are to be understood.
In consciousnesses associated with equanimity (*upekkhā*), neither pain, pleasure, nor joy arise;
rather, the five—compassion, sympathetic joy, and so forth—arise separately.
As for the remaining [factors], those associated with fine-material-sphere consciousness are fine-material-sphere.

Among these, first, those associated with the first consciousness should be understood as the remainder, excluding the three abstinences, from among those mentioned in relation to the first sense-sphere consciousness.

However, the abstinences arise only in wholesome sense-sphere consciousness and supramundane consciousness, not in others. By the second [consciousness], they are the same, excluding applied thought (*vitakka*).
With the second [jhāna], there are thirty-two or thirty-three. With the third, excluding sustained thought (*vicāra*), there are thirty-one or thirty-two.
With the fourth, further excluding rapture (*pīti*), there are thirty or thirty-one. With the fifth, further excluding compassion (*karuṇā*) and gladness (*muditā*), there are thirty;
here, equanimity (*upekkhā*) has taken the place of joy (*somanassa*). Thus should the wholesome mental factors of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara-kusala-cetasika*) be understood.

Those associated with immaterial-sphere consciousness are the immaterial-sphere [consciousnesses]; they, however, are to be understood by the method explained for the fifth type of fine-material-sphere consciousness. The distinction here, however, is the state of being immaterial-sphere.

Those associated with supramundane consciousness are the supramundane [consciousnesses]; they, moreover, are to be understood by the same method explained for the first fine-material-sphere consciousness in the context of the path-consciousness of the first jhāna, and likewise for the various types of path-consciousness beginning with that of the second jhāna, according to the method explained for the second fine-material-sphere consciousness and so forth.

They should be understood. Furthermore, the distinction here lies in the absence of compassion (*karuṇā*) and appreciative joy (*muditā*), their state of being invariably associated with abstinence (*virati*), and their supramundane (*lokuttara*) nature.
Thus, first, the mental factors associated with wholesome consciousness (*kusalacitta*) should be understood.

As for unwholesome mental factors (*akusala-cetasika*), they are of one kind according to plane, being exclusively of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*). Among them, those associated with the first unwholesome consciousness rooted in greed (*lobha*)—
Thus, there are nineteen factors consisting of fifteen that are fixed as to their nature and four that are included among the "ye-vā-panaka" (or-whatever-other) factors.
There are six that are unfixed and included among the "ye-vā-panaka" factors; thus, all together they amount to twenty-five. They are as follows:
contact, mental joy, perception, volition, initial application, sustained application, zest, one-pointedness of mind, energy, life-faculty, lack of moral shame, and lack of moral dread.
Greed, delusion, and wrong view—these three are included as they appear in their own right, making fifteen.

Desire, resolve, restlessness, and attention—these four are included as "invariably associated" (niyata-yevāpanaka); these, moreover, are invariably present in the ten successive types of consciousness.
Pride, envy, avarice, worry, sloth, and torpor—these six alone are "non-invariably associated" (aniyata-yevāpanaka).
Thus all the evaṃyevāpanaka states, both the fixed and the unfixed—ten in total—are explained among the evil thoughts by the Tathāgata, who has destroyed evil.
Therein, "contact" (phassa) is contact co-arising with unwholesome consciousness. This same method applies to the remaining [factors] as well. One who does not feel shame is "shameless" (ahirika).
The state of one who is shameless is *ahirika*. *Ottappa* is that by which one feels dread (*ottappati*) regarding bodily misconduct and so forth; the absence of such dread is *anottappa*.
Therein, *ahirika* is characterized by a lack of disgust toward bodily misconduct and the like, or by a lack of shame.
*Anottappa* is characterized by a lack of trepidation regarding those same things, or by a lack of fear of blame.
Lobha (greed) is so called because by means of it one becomes greedy, or because one is oneself greedy, or because it is the mere state of being greedy.

Its characteristic is the grasping of an object, like the smearing of a monkey; its function is clinging, like a piece of meat thrown into a hot pan; its manifestation is non-relinquishment, like the stain of oil and collyrium;
and its proximate cause is the perception of gratification in things that lead to fettering.
It is called delusion (*moha*) because by means of it beings are deluded, or because it itself is deluded, or because it is merely the state of being deluded.
It has the characteristic of blindness of the mind, or the characteristic of non-knowing; its function is the failure to penetrate, or its function is the obscuring of the true nature of the object;
it is manifested as darkness, and its proximate cause is improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*).
It is wrong view because one sees wrongly by means of it, or because one sees wrongly oneself, or because it is merely the act of seeing wrongly.
It has the characteristic of irrational insistence; its function is misapprehension; it is manifested as wrong adherence; and its proximate cause is the desire not to see the Noble Ones and so forth.
Agitation is restlessness (*uddhacca*). Its characteristic is lack of tranquility, like water stirred by the impact of the wind;
its function is instability, like a banner or flag fluttering in the wind; its manifestation is wavering, like ashes tossed up by the impact of stones;
and its proximate cause is improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*).

It conceives, thus it is conceit (*māna*). Its characteristic is puffing up; its function is grasping; its manifestation is the desire for prominence; its proximate cause is greed dissociated from views. It envies, thus it is envy (*issā*).

Its characteristic is resentment toward the success of others; its function is lack of delight in that very thing; its manifestation is turning away from that; its proximate cause is the success of others.
The state of being stingy is stinginess (*macchariya*). It has the characteristic of hiding one’s own acquisitions; its function is the inability to endure others sharing those very acquisitions;

it is manifested as contraction; and its proximate cause is one’s own acquisitions. That which is badly done is *kukata*; the state of that is worry (*kukkucca*). It has the characteristic of remorse; its function is grieving over what has been done and left undone; it is manifested as regret; and its proximate cause is what has been done and left undone.
Sloth is sluggishness (*thinatā*); torpor is drowsiness (*middhatā*). The meaning is a lack of exertion, a sinking down, and a failure of capability.
Sloth and torpor constitute *thīnamiddha*. Therein, sloth has the characteristic of lack of exertion; its function is the dispelling of energy; it is manifested as a state of sinking.
Torpor has the characteristic of unwieldiness; its function is shrouding; it is manifested as sluggishness.
Both have unwise attention as their proximate cause. The remaining [hindrances] are to be understood in the manner already stated for the wholesome [states].
In this context, however, wrong intention, wrong effort, and wrong concentration are the specific factors for initial application (vitakka), energy (vīriya), and concentration (samādhi) respectively.
Thus, it should be understood that these nineteen mental factors associate with the first unwholesome consciousness.

And just as they do with the first, so too with the second. Furthermore, the state of being accompanied by volitional effort (sasaṅkhāra-bhāva) here refers to the necessary presence of sloth and torpor (thinamiddha).
And this is the distinction. By the third [statement], among those mentioned in the first, one should understand the remaining eighteen, excluding *diṭṭhi* (wrong view).

However, *māna* (conceit) here is indeterminate, as it does not arise together with *diṭṭhi*. By the fourth [statement], among those mentioned in the second, one should understand the remainder, excluding *diṭṭhi*.
And here too, *māna* is indeterminate. By the fifth [statement], among those mentioned in the first...
Excluding *pīti*, the remaining factors enter into association. However, in this case, *upekkhā* (equanimity) has taken the place of *somanassa* (joy).

The sixth [jhāna] is also exactly like what was stated for the fifth; the distinction lies in the presence of volitional effort (*sasaṅkhāratā*) and the fixed presence of *thīnamiddha* (sloth and torpor).
By means of the seventh [jhāna], one should understand the remaining factors from those stated for the fifth, excluding *diṭṭhi* (wrong view). As for *māna* (conceit), it is present here...
Indeterminate. Among those stated in the sixth [chapter] by the eighth [section], with the exception of wrong view, the remainder should be understood. Here too, conceit (māna) is indeterminate.
Thus should the mental factors rooted in greed be understood.
Regarding the two types of states rooted in hatred that are accompanied by displeasure and associated with aversion: first, in the case of the unprompted [state].
Thirteen [mental factors] are associated, fixed, and included by their own nature. Namely:
contact, mental pain-feeling, perception, volition, one-pointedness of mind, applied thought, sustained thought, energy, life-faculty, lack of moral shame, lack of moral dread, hatred, and delusion.
These thirteen states, together with the four—desire and so forth—which are fixed and included, become seventeen when envy, avarice, and worry are added.
With one of the three indeterminate [mental factors], there are eighteen; yet even these three do not arise together.
In this context, "dumano" means one who has a corrupted mind; the state of being such is "domanassa," which is a designation for the feeling of displeasure (*domanassavedanā*).

That which is accompanied by this is "domanassasahagata" (accompanied by displeasure). It has the characteristic of experiencing an undesirable object, and its function is the enjoyment of an undesirable aspect.
It has mental affliction as its manifestation and the heart-base as its proximate cause.
It is called *dosa* because it corrupts by means of itself, or it is itself corrupted, or it is merely the act of corrupting.
Its characteristic is ferocity, like a struck venomous snake; its function is to spread, like the application of poison; or its function is to burn its own support, like a forest fire.
It has the appearance of an enemy who has found an opportunity; its proximate cause is a basis for resentment (*āghātavatthu*). The remaining factors are of the types already described below.
Thus, it should be understood that these seventeen or eighteen [mental states] associate with the ninth [factor].

And just as they associate with the ninth, so too with the tenth; however, the distinction here is the presence of volitional effort (*sasaṅkhāratā*) and the arising of sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*).
In the two types of consciousness rooted in delusion, first, those associated with the eleventh type—the consciousness associated with doubt—thirteen factors are mentioned by their specific names:
contact, equanimity-feeling, perception, volition, applied thought, sustained thought, energy, life-faculty, mental stability, lack of moral shame, lack of moral dread, delusion, and doubt;
and two factors, restlessness and attention, are included as fixed adjuncts (*yevāpanaka*). Together with these...
Together they make fifteen.
Among them, one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*) is merely the persistence of the process [of consciousness]. Doubt (*vicikicchā*): it is called doubt because the remedy (*cikicchā*) has departed;

or, it is doubt because one suffers (*kicchati*) and is wearied while investigating its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). It has the characteristic of uncertainty, the function of wavering, and is manifested as indecisiveness.
They have improper attention as their proximate cause. The rest are exactly as described by the method already stated.
In the twelfth [type], that which is associated with restlessness, it is mentioned in its own form;
among those associated with doubt mentioned previously, doubt is omitted, while restlessness is mentioned in its own form. Therefore, there are only thirteen. This is because of the absence of doubt.
In this context, resolve arises; with that, there are fourteen. Because of the occurrence of resolve, concentration becomes powerful.
Resolve and attention are two factors included among the mental concomitants (*yevāpanaka*); together with these, there are exactly fifteen.
Thus, firstly, the unwholesome mental factors are to be understood.
Now the indeterminate (abyākata) states are discussed. The indeterminate are twofold, distinguished as resultant (vipāka) and functional (kiriya).

Among these, the resultants are fourfold according to plane, just like the wholesome: the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara), and the supramundane (lokuttara).
Among those, the sense-sphere resultants are twofold by way of being with root-cause (sahetuka) and without root-cause (ahetuka). Among these, those associated with the resultant with root-cause...
They are with roots (*sahetuka*). They are similar to those associated with wholesome states of the sense-sphere that possess roots.

However, compassion (*karuṇā*) and appreciative joy (*muditā*), being indeterminate (*aniyata*), do not arise among the resultants because their objects are sentient beings. Furthermore, because the resultants of the sense-sphere have exclusively limited objects, the abstinences (*virati*) are not found here, as they are exclusively wholesome.
In the *Vibhaṅga*, it is stated: "The five training precepts (*sikkhāpada*) are exclusively wholesome."
For it has been said: "In this way, the mental factors of the sense-sphere resultant consciousness accompanied by roots should be understood.
There are thirty-three [factors] in the first two [types of consciousness];
thirty-two in the next two; thirty-two in the fifth; and thirty-one in those beyond that."

Those associated with rootless consciousness (ahetuka-citta), however, are themselves rootless. Among them, first, those associated with eye-consciousness consist of six factors mentioned by their own specific names—contact (phassa), equanimous feeling (upekkhā-vedanā), perception (saññā), volition (cetanā), life-faculty (jīvita), and mental stability (cittaṭṭhiti)—and seven when attention (manasikāra) is added.
Those associated with ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness likewise consist of exactly seven mental factors. Among these, regarding those associated with body-consciousness:

However, in the place of equanimity (*upekkhā*), pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*) has entered. It is characterized by bodily gratification and has the function of refreshing; the rest is exactly as previously stated.
