Why did the Teacher declare that there is only equanimity in the four types of consciousness—eye-consciousness and the rest—even when they are associated with desirable objects?
One should explain that, because of the derived material form (upādārūpa) dependent upon the primary material form (upādāyarūpa),
there is a lack of strength for impact and friction,
as if it were a heap of cotton or a tuft of wool surpassing the sensitive organ (pasāda).

Because there is the impact upon beings by means of a real form, resulting in pleasure and so forth, it should be understood that body-consciousness is associated with pleasure and the rest. Those associated with the mind-element (manodhātu) are six as they appear in their own form together with eye-consciousness;
they are eight when accompanied by initial application (vitakka) and sustained application (vicāra); and [nine] when accompanied by resolve (adhimokkha) and attention (manasikāra).
In two types of resultant consciousness (yevāpanaka), there are ten mental factors. Likewise, in the mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity, there are ten.
In that accompanied by joy, there is an increase in the factor of rapture (*pīti*) and a change in the feeling; this is the distinction. Therefore, in this case, there are eleven factors.
Thus, the rootless resultant mental factors of the sense-sphere should be understood.

However, those associated with fine-material-sphere resultant consciousness are fine-material-sphere; those associated with immaterial-sphere resultant consciousness are immaterial-sphere. All of these are exactly similar to the mental factors associated with their own respective wholesome consciousnesses.
Those associated with supramundane resultant consciousness are supramundane.

All of these are similar to those very same supramundane resultant consciousnesses and similar to the mental factors associated with wholesome consciousness. Thus should the mental factors of the fine-material-sphere, immaterial-sphere, and supramundane resultant types be understood.
The unwholesome-resultant mental factors (akusalavipākacetasika) are those associated with unwholesome-resultant consciousness.

These are similar to the mental factors described in the case of wholesome-resultant rootless consciousnesses, such as eye-consciousness and the rest. However, in body-consciousness, painful feeling (dukkhavedanā) is included;
its characteristic is physical affliction. The remaining factors are exactly as previously stated. Thus, the thirty-six mental factors associated with resultant consciousness should be understood.

Furthermore, functional-indeterminate (kiriyābyākatā) mental factors are threefold according to their plane: belonging to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), and the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara).
Among these, those of the sense sphere are twofold, being either with root-cause (sahetuka) or without root-cause (ahetuka).

Of these, those associated with functional consciousness accompanied by root-causes are "with root-cause"; they are identical to the eight types of sense-sphere wholesome consciousness associated with root-causes, with the exception of the three abstinences (virati).
In those states that are indeterminate and associated with the attainment of cessation, only compassion (*karuṇā*) and gladness (*muditā*) arise.

Those associated with rootless functional consciousness (*ahetuka-kiriya-citta*) are themselves rootless; they are identical to those associated with the wholesome and resultant rootless mind-element (*manodhātu*) and mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*).

However, in the two types of mind-consciousness-element, the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*) is additional. Because of the presence of the faculty of energy, concentration (*samādhi*) here reaches the stage of a power (*bala*).
There are twelve mental factors associated with the consciousness arising from a smile, together with joy (*pīti*). This is the distinction here.
However, those associated with functional consciousness of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) belong to the fine-material sphere;

those associated with functional consciousness of the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*) belong to the immaterial sphere. All of these are identical to those associated with their respective wholesome consciousnesses of the same plane. Thus, there are twenty.
And the mental factors associated with functional consciousness (kiriyacitta) should be understood.

Up to this point, the mental factors associated with the eighty-nine types of consciousness—distinguished by the divisions of wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional—have been explained. [This includes those] associated with the wholesome and unwholesome, as well as the resultant and functional...
But the mental factors associated with the heart have all been well explained by me,
as they were explained by the Sugata, the Great Sage.
He who understands this subtle [teaching] possesses supreme wisdom in every respect regarding the system of the Abhidhamma,
which is difficult to approach.
It unfolds in the exceedingly profound state.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Exposition of Mental Factors," in the *Abhidhammāvatāra*.
3. The Third Chapter:
Exposition of the Analysis of Mental Factors.
All mental factors have been declared by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.
By virtue of the commonality of their names alone, there are fifty-two of them.

Namely: contact, feeling, perception, volition, initial application, sustained application, rapture, one-pointedness of mind, energy, life-faculty, desire, resolve, attention, equanimity, faith, mindfulness, moral shame, moral dread, and non-greed.
Non-hatred, non-delusion, the six pairs beginning with bodily tranquility, the three abstinences, compassion, sympathetic joy,
greed, hatred, delusion, restlessness, conceit, wrong view, envy, avarice, worry, sloth, torpor, doubt, lack of moral shame, and lack of moral dread—
these are the fifty-four [factors] in the sense-sphere; fifteen are found in the fine-material sphere.
These consist of twelve types of form and forty types free from taints.
In brief, there are one hundred and twenty-one classes of consciousness in total;
having extracted the arising of each from among these, they are treated individually.
But hereafter I shall explain the phenomena beginning with contact,
for the sake of the proficiency of the bhikkhus regarding the mind and mental factors:
one-pointedness, attention, life-faculty, and the pentad of contact.
These eight are inseparable, arising together and perishing together:
contact, feeling, perception, volition, the life-faculty,
one-pointedness, and attention— these are common to all consciousness.
Initial application (vitakka) is declared to arise in fifty-five types of consciousness;
its occurrence in sixty-six types of consciousness is certain, there is no doubt.
Rapture (pīti) arises in fifty-one types of consciousness, and pleasure (sukha) in sixty-three.
Equanimity occurs in fifty-five consciousnesses, while suffering exists in three.
However, the faculty of mental joy occurs in sixty-two consciousnesses;
the faculty of physical pain occurs in one, and likewise the faculty of physical pleasure occurs in one.
The Leader spoke of energy in one hundred and five types of consciousness;
he declared the faculty of concentration in one hundred and four types of consciousness.
This is excluding all rootless consciousnesses as well as those with a single root.
In one hundred and one types of consciousness, the arising of desire is indicated—
excluding the ten types of consciousness and that associated with doubt.
In one hundred and ten types of consciousness, resolve is proclaimed.
Faith, mindfulness, moral shame, moral dread,
non-greed, non-hatred, and equanimity— these six pairs of factors, totaling nineteen,
invariably arise in ninety-one types of consciousness.
In rootless consciousnesses and in unwholesome consciousnesses, wisdom does not arise.
Wisdom arises at all times in seventy-nine types of consciousness;
in twenty-eight types of consciousness, compassion and gladness may arise.
In the forty-six types of consciousness— namely, those of the sense-sphere merit and all those that transcend the world—
the threefold abstinence, faith, mindfulness, moral shame, moral dread, and also the triad beginning with non-greed are present.
The pairs, equanimity, compassion, and sympathetic joy,
as well as the three abstinences— all these twenty-five [factors] are both wholesome and indeterminate, and are thus explained by way of the wholesome.
Shamelessness, lack of moral dread, delusion, and restlessness—
these arise with certainty in the twelve unwholesome states of consciousness.
Greed, hatred, and delusion, conceit, wrong view, and doubt.
Lethargy, restlessness, and worry, Stiffness, and also stinginess, Shamelessness,
lack of moral dread, Envy, and dejection—
These are declared to be exclusively unwholesome by the Great Seer.
Greed is specified among the eight [unwholesome roots]; it is stated to exist in four of the views.
Pride arises in those [views] free from wrong view; hatred arises in only two.
Envy, avarice, and worry arise in two [of the unwholesome roots], but not together.
Doubt, however, occurs in one [aggregate]; sloth and torpor, in five.
Contact, feeling, perception, volition, life-faculty, mind, applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, energy, and concentration.
Volition, resolve, and attention— these fourteen [mental factors] are wholesome,
unwholesome, and also indeterminate. In twenty-nine types of consciousness,
the jhāna is considered to consist of five factors.
One should point out thirty-seven factors associated with the four jhānas.
Elevenfold consciousness is declared to have three factors;
thirty-fourfold consciousness is declared to have two factors.
One should not enumerate the jhāna factors in those states that are by nature without applied thought;
one should not enumerate the path factors in all rootless consciousnesses.
A wise person should declare the three faculties in sixteen types of consciousness.
The Victor declared that in one [consciousness] there are four,
and in five [types of consciousness] there are thirteen pure faculties; in seven and twelve types of consciousness there are seven,
and in those with one less and in the forty-eight, there are eight.
The Leader has declared that among the forty-four types of consciousness, there is a group of nine;
in this same way, the association with the faculties should be understood by one who discerns.
Herein, eighteen are rootless and do not possess the factors of the Path.
The factors of jhāna do not exist in the two and five types of consciousness.
One consciousness has two path-factors, seven have three path-factors,
and in forty types of consciousness, that path is fourfold.
In fifteen types of consciousness, the path is considered five-factored;
in thirty-two types of consciousness, it is said to be seven-factored as well.
Indeed, in eight types of consciousness, the path is considered eight-factored.
In this way, one should extract the path-factors from all types of consciousness.
One should illuminate two powers in two types of consciousness, three in one,
four in eleven, and six in twelve.
There are seventy-nine powers and sixteen indeed that are weak;
thus the mind should be understood as both powerful and weak.
The factors of jhāna, the factors of the path, the powers, and the faculties—
Indeed, whatever [states] arise in whichever minds,
all of those have been extracted by me and stated therein in brief.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Exposition of Mental Factors," in the *Abhidhammāvatāra*. Chapter Four.
The Exposition of the Singlefold, etc.
Hereafter I shall explain the method beginning with the singlefold,
for the increase of the intelligence of those bhikkhus who are versed in the Abhidhamma.
All consciousness is of one kind by virtue of its nature as cognizing;
and consciousness is of two kinds by way of being rootless or with roots.
Indeed, in the sense-sphere, there are fifteen [types]: ten that are wholesome, unwholesome, or resultants, and five that are resultant.
All eighteen rootless states of consciousness are called "kriyā" (functional).
The remaining seventy-one types of consciousness were designated as "sahetuka" (with roots) by the Great Sage,
the Knower of Suchness, who teaches the doctrine of causes.
Based on having a basis (*savatthuka*) and being without a basis (*avatthuka*), as well as by way of both together;
all the aforementioned types of mental states are thus threefold.
All [the results] of sensual desire, and fifteen also in the realm of form (*rūpa*);
The first path, the arising of cold, the mind-element, and functional [consciousness],
as well as the two types of mental grief—
these forty-three types of consciousness do not arise without a physical basis; they are invariably accompanied by a physical basis.
The resultant consciousnesses of the formless realm are exclusively without a physical basis (avatthuka).
The remaining forty-two types of consciousness may be either with or without a physical basis.
A single type of consciousness has one object, while another has five objects.
And with the six objects—thus it may also be threefold.
There are two and five consciousnesses, and the eight supramundane ones;
all these are "exalted," except for the mind of direct knowledge (abhiññā).
Forty-three [consciousnesses] are to be understood as having each one object;
therein, the triad of mind-elements is said to have five objects.
The remaining forty-three are considered to have six objects.
And likewise, consciousness is threefold according to the wholesome,
unwholesome, and so forth. It is fourfold— being without cause, with one cause, with two causes, and with three causes—
and thus should it be understood by the discerning person.
Eighteen rootless states were also pointed out by me below;
that associated with doubt and restlessness was declared to have one root.
Furthermore, in the sense-sphere, there are twelve types through merit, fruition, and functional [states].
The tenfold unwholesome consciousnesses, together with the twenty-two twofold-rooted [wholesome consciousnesses], constitute the sense-sphere wholesome consciousness.
Furthermore, there are twelve kinds in the sense sphere consisting of merit, fruition, and functional;
all sublime consciousness, as well as the immeasurable, are threefold-rooted.

Furthermore, that consciousness is of four kinds according to whether it produces or does not produce intimation (viññatti) of the material body or the vocal path. Among these, there are twelve unwholesome types,
and the wholesome types belong to the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu).
Likewise, ten courses of action in the sense-sphere,
and two mental [courses] consisting of direct knowledge, give rise to material forms,
fashion the postures, and produce intimation— these thirty-two are mental.
The wholesome and the functional states, those with exalted minds,
the eight types of consciousness free from taints, and the twenty-six types of consciousness—
these give rise to material forms and fashion the postures of movement.
They do not reach the state of fruition; these are fixed as having two functions.
Excluding the ten consciousnesses, there are nineteen [types of consciousness] that are resultant in the two planes, as well as the functional mind-element.
They give rise to material forms, but do not produce the other two;
furthermore, the two sets of fivefold consciousnesses, as well as the resultant [consciousnesses] among the formless,
and the rebirth-linking consciousness and the death-consciousness of all except the Arahant.
They do not perform their three functions; these are the sixteen mental states.
According to the divisions of one, two, three, four, and five factors, the One with the Five Pure Eyes declared that consciousness is fivefold.
All wholesome and unwholesome states of consciousness, the great functional states,
the sublime functional states, and the four resultant minds—
these fifty-five in total were taught by the Teacher who is free from conceptual proliferation.
Precisely because of the place of javana, they are restricted to a single location.
Furthermore, the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousnesses— likewise in seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting,
and standing (touching)— occur in successive order.
The triad of mind-elements— consisting of the element of mind in its place, adverting, and receiving—
these sixty-eight have reached the state of being single-based.
Furthermore, two types of consciousness are declared to be double-based.
Investigation associated with joy may occur at the five sense-doors.
When there is a strong object at the six doors, there likewise occurs registration; in the five sense-doors, this is called "registration" (voṭṭhabba).
In all instances at the mind-door, there occurs adverting;
this is called the "two-staged" process, consisting of two types of consciousness.
Furthermore, by way of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death;
Those nine great resultant [consciousnesses] are considered to have nine stations:
eight great sense-sphere resultants [occur] by way of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and object-presentation; and the [remaining] one by way of death.
One should point out that there are eight fourfold types of consciousness:
two accompanied by equanimity, which are wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant;
and five investigating consciousnesses, which occur at the five sense doors and in the six-door process.
It becomes the object of registration when the object is powerful. Furthermore,
by way of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and the moment of death,
this twofold "five-door-cognizing consciousness" has been described.
The mind has five functions and two [types]; four functions and eight [types];
three functions and nine [types]; two [types] have two functions each; the rest have one function each. These are:
the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), adverting (āvajjana), seeing (dassana), and receiving (sampaṭicchana).
Investigation, determining, and the impulsion that is seventh—
this is sixfold according to the classification of the six types of consciousness,
but sevenfold according to the classification of the seven elements of consciousness.
The mind is eightfold: by way of the sixfold division of objects with a single object, and by way of the sixfold division of objects with fivefold objects.
Among these, the two sets of fivefold consciousness each have a single respective domain.
Two [consciousnesses] have visible form as their object; two each have sound and so forth as their domain.
All sublime consciousness, excluding the five direct knowledges, and all supramundane consciousness—each of these has a single object.
This group of six should be understood by the discerning as having a single object;
the triad of mind-elements (manodhātu) would have five objects.
There are forty sense-sphere consciousnesses (kāmāvacara-citta), and likewise one [supramundane].
And all the direct knowledges have the six sense objects as their domain. Thus,
within the seven consciousness elements, consciousness is ninefold when the last one is divided into three according to its wholesome, unwholesome, and other qualities.
By way of merit and demerit, and by way of the distinction between resultant and functional [consciousness],
the division of the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) is of seventy-six kinds.
By dividing the mind-element (manodhātu) into two according to the distinction between resultant and functional, [the total becomes seventy-eight].
The mind becomes ninefold through those previously mentioned,
and tenfold by dividing the two elements into three; furthermore,
the wise one should explain that the mind becomes elevenfold.
Having analyzed the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) in four ways according to its wholesome,
unwholesome, and other aspects, speak of it as established in twelve ways.
Consciousness exists in fourteen ways according to the distinction of fourteen bases.
By way of rebirth-linking and the life-continuum, of death and adverting,
of the five [sense-cognitions] such as seeing, of the receiving consciousness,
of investigation, and of determining and the impulsions.
Likewise, by way of the different stages of the mind that takes that as its object,
one should explain that consciousness thus becomes fourteenfold.
Furthermore, it proceeds according to the diversity of planes and individuals.
Furthermore, one should discern that this mind becomes manifold.
In this regard, the wise and skillful bhikkhu who is proficient in the method of the singlefold and so forth—
But for one who has entered into the Abhidhamma, the meanings are as clear as an *āmalaka* fruit held in the palm of the hand.
Thus ends the section titled "The Exposition of the Singlefold, etc. in the *Abhidhammāvatāra*.
The Fourth Chapter. 5.
The Fifth Chapter:
An Exposition of the Grounds, the Individuals, and the Arising of Consciousness.
Henceforth I shall explain the method that increases intelligence:
the arising of the stages of consciousness according to individuals,
including both gods and humans, as well as the three planes of misery.
Five destinies have been pointed out, yet by the Teacher, three existences were taught.
There are exactly thirty planes therein, and in those [planes] there are exactly thirty types of persons;
indeed, all persons whatsoever are born within these planes.
According to the types of rebirth-linking consciousnesses, there are nineteen;
and this rebirth-linking is declared to be of two kinds:
those without consciousness and those with consciousness. Among these, the rebirth-linking of non-percipient beings is without consciousness.
The remaining ones should be known as "with consciousness," and they number nineteen.
By way of rebirth-linking alone, there are twenty types of persons;
however, because the present context concerns consciousness, those without consciousness have not been mentioned here.
There may be three kinds of persons: those who hold to no cause, those who hold to a double cause, and the noble ones, who are eightfold;
thus all together are said to be eleven. Now, from the classification of all these persons:
Understand from me as I speak of the arising of consciousnesses within the planes.
"Tell me, how many consciousnesses arise within the thirty planes?
"Indeed, there are exactly fourteen consciousnesses in all the planes."
Twenty consciousnesses always exist only in the sense-sphere existence (kāma-bhava);
five exist only in the fine-material existence (rūpa-bhava), and four only in the immaterial existence (arūpa-bhava).
Indeed, eighteen [consciousnesses] belong only to the sense-sphere and fine-material existences.
There are forty-two types of consciousness even within the three realms of existence.
However, setting aside all those that belong to the four planes of the mundane path,
there are only thirteen types of consciousness that pertain to the twenty-six planes.
Furthermore, excluding the four formless planes,
twenty-six types of consciousness arise in six planes.
Excluding five planes, [these arise] for the gods of the Pure Abodes.
Five types of consciousness arise in twenty-five planes.
There are two others in twenty-five planes,
excluding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the four planes of the base of mastery.
Two types of consciousness arise in the twenty-four planes, excluding the woeful planes:
[the consciousnesses of] nothingness and neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Excluding the woeful planes, there are three formless planes.
However, there are only two types of consciousness in twenty-three planes.
Excluding eight planes— the formless realms and the woeful states—
there are eleven kinds of consciousness in twenty-two planes.
Excluding the nine planes— the Pure Abodes and the woeful states—
among the remaining twenty-one planes, only four [types of consciousness] arise constantly.
On seventeen of those planes, only one type of consciousness arises.
Excluding the Pure Abodes, the woeful planes, and the formless planes,
beings are born in only twelve [realms] among the eleven planes;
for all the remaining planes are exalted (mahaggata).
By way of the sense-sphere devas and humans,
eight types of consciousness arise constantly across the seven planes. One [type],
which is the ripening of the fifth jhāna, arises in the six planes.
However, there are four types of consciousness in each of the three planes.
There are four types of consciousness in each individual plane;
this should be explained by way of the resultant states of the formless realm.
In the sense-sphere, there are wholesome and unwholesome [consciousnesses], their results which are rootless,
and the two types of adverting consciousness.
There are exactly seventy-three mental states that arise even in the four miserable states,
such as the hells; the remaining fifty-two never arise at all.
In the sense-sphere, for gods and humans, there are nine matured [resultants] that are sublime;
they do not arise, yet they constantly arise eighty times from the heart.
In the sense-sphere, there are eight great matured [resultants], and also the two types of mental grief.
Likewise, the triad of nose-consciousness and so forth are results born of demerit;
there are no immaterial-sphere results in the fine-material sphere.
Together with these consciousnesses, there are the three paths and two fruits.
The four associated with views, as well as that associated with doubt—
these four lower ripened states are not found among the Suddhāvāsa deities.
However, the remaining fifty-one types of consciousness are found there.
All those belonging to the fine-material sphere, the resultants of the sense-sphere,
the path accompanied by grief and so forth, the functional consciousnesses, and the two rootless types—
these forty-three types of consciousness do not exist on the plane of the immaterial sphere.
In this way, one should analyze the arising of consciousness by means of the planes themselves,
and likewise by means of the eleven types of persons. [One should also analyze] the wholesome and unwholesome states in the sense-sphere realm.
Their results are rootless,
as are the two types of adverting; thus,
there are exactly thirty-seven types of consciousness.
For a being born without root-cause (ahetuka), [results] arise in five planes;
the remaining fifty-two do not arise at any time.
Regarding those stated for the one without root-cause, the two-rooted results of the sense-sphere (kāma) [arise].
For those with two roots, forty [types of consciousness] arise, and likewise one for each.
All are sublime, and all are also without taints;
they are associated with three roots, are resultant, and in the sense-sphere, there are nine that are also functional.
For a being of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) who possesses a three-root rebirth-linking (*tihetuka-paṭisandhi*), forty-eight [mental states] do not arise;
for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), fifty-four mental states arise.
For those with two roots, forty have been stated, and likewise one for the single root.
Four are associated with knowledge; these are the resultant states in the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu).
In the fine-material and immaterial spheres, there are fifty-four meritorious mental states.
Thirty-five [defilements] arise in the worldling,
but they do not arise in the embodied one who is a stream-enterer among gods or humans.
One should designate that for him, through the cultivation of wisdom, these thoughts arise.
It should be shown that ninety minds do not arise for one who has entered the stream, excluding the first fruit;
for one who is a once-returner, there would be [the remaining] fruits of his own.
One should designate that those consciousnesses which were stated for the stream-enterer—
excluding the two types of aversion— and omitting the second fruit,
arise for the being who is a non-returner.
How many types of consciousness arise for an Arahant in the sense-sphere?
Forty-four; indeed, forty-four may arise for an Arahant in the sense-sphere.
For each of the four individuals standing on the path, there is their own respective [consciousness].
The path-consciousness may belong to them, for they [the noble ones] possess only a single moment of consciousness.
One should designate that for an ordinary person, within the three levels of the first jhāna alone,
exactly thirty-five types of consciousness arise.
In the case of the nose and so forth, the triad of consciousnesses consists of seven unwholesome [states],
as well as the great resultants and the resultants belonging to the higher planes of jhāna. Furthermore,
the formless-sphere resultants and the two types of mental grief are also [resultants].
The eighteen functional consciousnesses and the eight supramundane consciousnesses—
these fifty-four types of consciousness, which arise in the bodies of worldlings who have attained the first jhāna,
are not found [in those who have reached the higher stages].
Thirty-one moments of consciousness arise there for the stream-enterer;
for the worldling, among those mentioned, excluding the five unwholesome [states].
For the once-returner, having set aside the first fruit therein;
Thirty-one [minds] arise, including its own fruit.
For the non-returner, excluding the second fruit,
thirty-one likewise arise through their own fruition-consciousness.
Consciousness of the eye and ear, the two types of receiving born of merit, the two types of investigating, and the functional consciousnesses—these are twenty.
The fruit of Arhatship is the result; it arises from the first jhāna.
Twenty-seven types of consciousness arise in an Arahant.
In the planes of the second jhāna, they arise as only three in an ordinary person (puthujjana),
but thirty-six in one who has matured the second and third jhānas.
Among those stated for the worldling, having excluded the fivefold set of demerit,
there are thirty-two for the stream-enterer together with his own fruit.
Among those stated for the stream-enterer, having set aside the first fruit;
With thirty-two fruition-consciousnesses, there are [thirty-two] for one who is a once-returner himself.
Among those stated for once-returners, excluding the second fruit,
there are indeed thirty-two for him by means of the non-returner fruit.
For an Arahant, there are exactly three [kinds of rebirth]; for oneself, twenty-eight [are possible] through the fruit of the second and third jhānas.
Among the gods of the limited-splendor and other realms in the three planes, [these results occur].
Thirty-five [minds] arise as the fruition of the fourth jhāna.
Among those, thirty-one minds arise for the stream-enterer (sotāpanna);
likewise for the once-returner (sakadāgāmin) and the non-returner (anāgāmin).
For one whose taints are exhausted, twenty-seven mental states occur right there;
likewise, all the mental states occur in the Vehapphala realm as well.
In the stages of the Suddhāvāsa heavens, there are exactly thirty-one types of consciousness.
One should explain that for a non-returner (anāgāmika), these [thirty-two] exist.
For an arahant, however, there are twenty-seven mental states right there.
Thus should the minds among those possessing form be understood by one who is discerning.
One should designate that twenty-four types of consciousness arise for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) in the plane of the first immaterial attainment (*paṭhamāruppabhūmi*).
For a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), the same applies there, with the exception of the fivefold meritorious consciousness.
There, twenty minds arise for the once-returner, including his own fruit; likewise for the non-returner as well.
Twenty minds arise, excluding each preceding fruit.
For one whose taints are destroyed, there are fifteen mental states right there;
for an ordinary person, there are twenty-three mental states in the second immaterial plane. Having stated this, one should analyze them.
Here, for the three types of trainees (sekha), there are nineteen kinds of consciousness.
However, in the second immaterial plane, there are fourteen kinds of consciousness:
twelve functional (kiriya) and one resultant (vipāka); but for the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), it is the fruit [of Arahantship].
It should be explained that for an ordinary person (puthujjana) on the plane of the third immaterial state, twenty-two types of consciousness arise.
For a stream-enterer (sotāpanna), eighteen types of consciousness indeed arise.
For the once-returner, those [twenty-nine] arise, excluding the first fruit.
For those described as once-returners, excluding the second fruit;
eighteen consciousnesses indeed arise for the non-returner.
One should designate that thirteen consciousnesses arise for a being whose taints are exhausted in the third immaterial plane;
twenty-one consciousnesses [arise] in the fourth immaterial plane.
One should designate that they arise for an ordinary person (puthujjana).
One should reveal seventeen for a stream-enterer (sotāpanna);
for a once-returner (sakadāgāmin), those [remain] excluding the first fruit.
Among the states of those who have attained the fruit of once-returning— excluding the second fruit—
there are seventeen mental states for the non-returner. However,
in the fourth immaterial plane, there are only twelve types of consciousness.
Having said, "They are born for the Arahant," one should explain as follows:
Above the lower formless Brahmās,
both those skilled in the formless realm and those performing functional (kriyā) states arise.
Those who are formless in the higher [realms] are born only in the formless states, while those in the lower [realms] are born in the lower ones,
it is said, because they have seen the danger [of the higher realms].
Excluding the first path, there are three types of wholesome supramundane [attainments].
The meritorious and non-meritorious karmas of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), likewise ten;
the four meritorious karmas of the formless sphere (ārūpya), all their results (pāka) which are unsurpassed;
the result of the first formless attainment, and the nine functional (kiriya) karmas of the sense sphere.
All immaterial functional states as well— these forty-three mental states arise in the plane of the first immaterial realm. And all kamma-resultant states of the sense sphere,
as well as all sublime and exalted [resultants] of the fine-material sphere;
The arising of consciousness is the mind-element (manodhātu), as well as the two types of mental grief.
Three resultant states are the initial path; likewise, above that, there are the four formless attainments.
Forty-six [states] are absent here in the plane of the first formless attainment.
But among the states already mentioned,
excluding the first three immaterial attainments (āruppa) and their own respective resultants,
these forty-four arise in the plane of the second immaterial attainment.
In the same way, the remaining two dyads should be understood, excluding each successive lower stage.
The four [types of consciousness] within their respective spheres, as well as the four untainted [consciousnesses],
are all results of kamma (vipāka) in the four immaterial planes.
With a mind of determination, there are eight great functional [consciousnesses] regarding sense-sphere objects, and four of the formless [spheres]; thus there would be thirteen functionals.
These arise in one whose taints are destroyed on the plane of the first formless attainment.
There are exactly twelve functional states in the second immaterial plane;
there are eleven functional states in the third immaterial plane;
and it should be known that there are ten functional states in the fourth immaterial plane.
Furthermore, there are nineteen types of consciousness for an Arahant:
all the functional (kiriya) states of Arahantship, excluding the two types of adverting consciousness.
There are also [nineteen] for those established in the four fruits and for worldlings (puthujjana) possessing triple-rootedness.
One should explain that there are thirteen types of consciousness:
four associated with knowledge, nine great resultants,
and those which are form-sphere and formless-sphere resultants— these indeed constitute the thirteen.
In the four who stand in the fruit-stages and in worldlings possessing two roots,
four types of consciousness devoid of knowledge arise as results alone.
[This applies] to all three types of worldlings and to the four types of noble beings.
Indeed, there are seventeen types of consciousness belonging to all seven [planes].
These seventeen consist of two and five types of consciousness, as well as the three mind-elements (manodhātu),
the investigating consciousnesses (santīraṇa), and the determining consciousness (voṭṭhabbana).
For the three who have attained the fruits [of stream-entry, once-returning, and non-returning], for the triple-rooted worldling,
and for all four types of exalted [consciousness], there are only nine wholesome states.
For the three types of worldlings and for the first three noble ones:
One should point out that thirteen types of consciousness arise:
the eight meritorious consciousnesses of the sense sphere, those demeritorious states that are devoid of wrong view,
and the four associated with restlessness— thus there are thirteen.
In the case of the two lower fruit-attainers, as well as in all worldlings,
only two types of consciousness associated with mental grief arise.
However, in the case of the three other worldlings, five types indeed arise.
There are four [consciousnesses] associated with views, as well as that associated with doubt.
For each of the four who stand on the path, there is its own respective path-consciousness;
having stated that for them there can be only one at a time, one should analyze it.
By way of states of existence, types of persons,
and for the sake of proficiency among monks, the arising of consciousness has been explained by me.
Thus, all this consciousness is [classified] according to the distinctions of planes and persons.
"And he becomes manifold as well"—this should be understood by one who discerns.
It is possible for a discerning person to know the divisions by following what has been stated;
however, fearing excessive length in the text, I have presented this in brief.
Having examined what precedes and follows, having reflected again and again,
and having scrutinized the meaning, it should be grasped by one who is discerning.
And this *Abhidhammāvatāra*, which is of excellent essence—
Better than that is the person who always reflects upon and recites this lamp for dispelling the darkness of delusion;
passion and hatred do not long remain with such a person.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Arising of Consciousness by Way of Plane and Person," in the *Abhidhammāvatāra*. Chapter Six.
The Exposition of the Classification of Objects:
Next, I shall show the objects of these consciousnesses;
for without them, their occurrence is impossible.
Form, sound, odor, taste, tangible object, and mental phenomena—
these six they call the objects of experience, according to those skilled in the six objects.
Therein, derived from the primary elements, visible form arises from four sources.
Visible and impinging, it is designated as having form as its object.
Sound is indeed taught to be of two kinds:
that which arises from the mind and that which arises from the four [great] elements. Only sound with consciousness is produced by the mind.
That sound which is without consciousness is produced by the seasons;
this sound is of two kinds.
It has become the objective field of sound.
It "goes" (gacchanto) because it is borne along (dharīyati), or else because it indicates (sūcanato);
this [object], which arises from four sources, is considered the objective field of odor.
That which tastes and causes tasting is designated as "taste" (rasa);
it is of fourfold origination and is named the object of taste.
That which is touched is the "tangible" (phoṭṭhabba), consisting of earth, fire, and air.
Tangible object is composed of the four [great] elements; it is considered to have tangible objects as its objective support.

Having set aside all name-and-form—that is, the pentad beginning with visible form—and the characteristics, there is that which is known as the objective support consisting of conceptualized phenomena (paññatti-dhamma).
Objects of consciousness are obtained as follows:
three are found in the sense-sphere plane, three in the fine-material plane, and one—the mental object—in the immaterial plane.
Those which, due to their momentariness, substantiality, or minuteness, do not come within the range of the senses;
Those [consciousnesses] for which visible forms and so forth are said to be the objects take those very phenomena as their object.
They must indeed be excluded from being the domain of one another;
for those who do not experience them through the other senses, the mind alone is their domain.
And because it was stated by the Teacher, "He experiences that," the objects of the divine eye and other such knowledges are indeed visible forms and so forth;
for visible forms and the rest are the objective spheres of the divine eye and other knowledges.
Nor is it tenable to say that those [objects] have not even come into the range [of the senses].
How can that which has a visible form as its object become that which has mental phenomena (dhamma) as its object?
If this were so, how could there be any fixed rule for these [objects]?
All this objective field has been declared to be sixfold;
it is considered manifold by way of the triad of limited objects and so forth.
All [resultants] of sensual desire, as well as both types of functional states, are likewise included.
Twenty-five [consciousnesses] have exclusively limited objects.
Furthermore, the fivefold desirable and so forth— visible forms, sounds, and the rest—
are the respective objective spheres of the five pairs of consciousnesses in their proper order.
All five [objects] beginning with visible form are the domain of the three mind-elements (manodhātu);
however, for these thirteen [consciousnesses], only the aggregate of material form (rūpakkhandha) is their object.
It is neither non-material, nor a conceptual designation (paññatti), nor past, nor future.
And while making an object, the range is present.
These thirteen types of consciousness arise in the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu);
four in the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), and none at all in the immaterial sphere (arūpa).
The eight great resultants, the three investigating consciousnesses,
and the six types of limited objects such as visible forms are the spheres of the six doors.
The six limited objects, beginning with visible form, are the spheres of the smile-producing consciousness.
Arising at the five doors, and pertaining to the three times at the mind door—
these six types of consciousness are fixed as the second immaterial consciousness and the fourth immaterial consciousness; they have the sublime as their object.
Because it has Nibbāna as its object and is exclusively non-differentiated,
the domain of the eight types of taintless consciousness is indeed immeasurable.
And the four [types of consciousness] lacking knowledge, as well as those from sense-sphere merit;
There are also four from the functional class and twelve unwholesome states.
These have limited objects and also have exalted spheres;
because their objects are concepts, they are indeed not to be classified [as mundane or supramundane].
Four are associated with knowledge, both by way of merit and by way of action;
likewise, two types of direct knowledge, as well as the application of energy.
The range of these eleven is threefold.
Because they have concepts as their objects, these [remaining] states are also not to be described [as either pleasant or painful].
Indeed, those consciousnesses which remain after what has been stated should be understood by the discerning person as having objects that are not to be described.
The triad of limited objects is completed.
Furthermore, the second immaterial consciousness and the fourth immaterial mind—
these six types may have exclusively past objects.
For the five pairs of consciousnesses and for the three mind-elements (manodhātu), the present objects—
consisting of the five [sensory] phenomena beginning with visible form— are their domain.
So too are the eight great resultant states of the sense-sphere and the three investigating consciousnesses.
The mind arising from laughter—these twelve are mental states.
They may have past objects, or have the present and future as their domain;
they are wholesome or unwholesome in the sense-sphere, while nine are functional.
The two types of consciousness consisting of direct knowledge (abhiññā-mānasa) may have the past and so forth as their object;
even at the time of the designation "peaceful" (santa-paññatti), these are not to be described [as such].
However, all the remaining [types of consciousness] exist even in the realms of form and formlessness.
They are indeed not to be described by such terms as "having a past object" and so forth.
In terms of desire, there are five activities, and in terms of form, the fifth activity;
for these six classes of consciousness, there is no sphere that is not their range.
Tell me, how many types of consciousness are able to take as their object Nibbāna, the fruit, the path, and both the form and the formless? [The answer is:
Four are associated with knowledge.
From merit and likewise from action;
both from direct knowledge and the heart,
as well as from action and from determining.
They are able to take as their object the eleven types of consciousness, as well as nibbāna, the fruit, the path, and both the fine-material and immaterial realms.
Now, among all these states of consciousness, tell me: how many types of consciousness do they possess?
They are able to make the path to the fruit of arahantship their domain.
Now hear from me about six types of consciousness among all states of mind that are able to make the path to the fruit of arahantship their domain.
Four [consciousnesses] associated with knowledge, the functional determining consciousness,
the functional direct-knowledge consciousness, the mind-element, and the six [sense-sphere consciousnesses] are capable of their respective objects.
Four [consciousnesses] associated with knowledge, the direct-knowledge consciousness, and [the consciousness] from merit;
They are able to take as their range of experience the fruit and the path of Arahantship.
Why is it that ordinary worldlings or those in training are unable to know the path-consciousness or the fruition-mind of an Arahant?
The worldling does not know the mind of the stream-enterer; the stream-enterer does not know [the mind of the once-returner].
The mind of a once-returner is not known by a once-returner;
the mind of a non-returner is not known by a non-returner;
the mind of an arahant is not known by an arahant.
The lower one does not know the higher ones at all,
but the higher ones know the lower ones and the mind of the one below.
Whatever state [belongs] to whatever state...
However, there is an object;
having extracted each one from that,
I shall explain them hereafter.
A wholesome object [is the condition] for [states] in the sense-sphere,
for both wholesome and unwholesome [states], for the mind of direct knowledge, and for the wholesome functional [mind].
Likewise, it is the condition for the resultant of the sense-sphere and for the functional of the sense-sphere.
Of these aggregates, however, there may be six objects.
The meritorious deeds of the fine-material sphere, excluding those that ripen in the sense-sphere,
are indeed the objects of the [remaining] five aggregates.
Also for the wholesome states of the formless realm, for the wholesome states of the three planes,
for the functional states of the three planes, and likewise for the unwholesome states. Furthermore,
for the two types of resultants of the formless realm, and for the fourth jhāna;
Of these eighty-four [types of consciousness],
the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) exists for the unshackled merit, for that which belongs to the sense-sphere,
and for the wholesome and functional [consciousness] of the fifth [form-sphere].
The object of the four groups is always present;
likewise for the unwholesome, as well as for the wholesome and functional [states] of the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere, and similarly for the unwholesome.
The resultants of the sense sphere are stated as the objects of six groups;
in the sense sphere, they are the objects of wholesome and functional states belonging to the sense sphere,
as well as those of the fine-material sphere.
The object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) exists for the results (pāka) of the sense-sphere,
likewise for the unwholesome (akusala), and for the six groups [of consciousness].
In the form realm (rūpa), there is also the resultant object from the sense-sphere.
From the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), from the wholesome (kusala) and the functional (kiriya),
and from the demeritorious (apuñña)— this is the range for the five aggregates.
This same principle is held to apply to the immaterial-sphere results (arūpāvacara-vipāka).

Furthermore, the fruition of the supramundane (apariyāpanna) becomes the object of wholesome functional consciousness (kusalakiriya), as well as of [wholesome consciousness] pertaining to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).
This functional consciousness (kriyacitta) [arises] in the sense-sphere (kāma) and also from that which pertains to the sense-sphere.
For the wholesome and the functional [consciousness] of the fine-material sphere,
for the resultant of the sense-sphere, and likewise for the unwholesome—
these six groups have the object-condition.
The functional consciousness regarding form has the five aggregates as its object, even though it lacks the ripening of kamma. However,
the functional consciousness in the formless realm has those same five aggregates as its object.
The form produced by the four [causes] and designated as the object of form is indeed the range of the immaterial and of functional consciousness,
as well as of the six types of sense-sphere wholesome merit and likewise of wholesome [consciousness].
For a consciousness possessing two kinds of direct knowledge (abhiññā), for a consciousness with kamma-resultant or functional nature pertaining to the sense-sphere,
these six groups serve as object-conditions (ārammaṇa-paccaya).
However, [consciousness] having Nibbāna as its object arises from the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere.
For both types of wholesome [states]— those pertaining to the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere—
as well as for the functional [wholesome], for the unshackled (i.e., supramundane), and for the wholesome fruit: these six groups have the object-condition.
All that is of various kinds has a concept as its object,
as does the merit of the three planes, and likewise the unwholesome;
as do the resultant of the fine-material and immaterial planes, and the functional of the three planes.
Of the nine groups [of consciousness], there is the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya).
However, two have visible form as their object; two each have faith and the other [faculties] as their domain;
and three types of consciousness-arising are considered to have five objects.
Herein, among the forty-five sense-sphere consciousnesses, these are considered to have six objects.
This is the sequence of objects for sense-sphere consciousnesses, excluding the five direct knowledges (abhiññā),
as well as the form-sphere, formless-sphere, and taintless (anāsava) consciousnesses.
All these states of consciousness have mental phenomena as their objective field.
The first wholesome immaterial state, the second immaterial consciousness,
and the resultant and functional wholesome [immaterial states] may have [the preceding immaterial states] as their object.
This is the result of the first immaterial attainment; it is not the object of the second immaterial consciousness, nor of a wholesome result, nor of a functional [consciousness].
However, the first functional consciousness is the object of the second immaterial consciousness.
It is not the object of merit nor of its result;
rather, it is the object of the first functional consciousness and of the second formless-sphere functional consciousness.
Thus should it be understood by the discerning one.
For an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) and for one in training (*sekkha*), the immaterial object is twofold:

and likewise for the eight limited (paritta) consciousnesses in the unhappy destinies (duggati).
In the course of existence (pavatta), conditions exist; they do not exist at rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).
In the sense-sphere happy realms, they exist in the aforementioned manner;
likewise for the sixteen types of resultants (vipāka) in both the course of existence and at rebirth-linking.
In the form realm, meritorious formations are conditions for the five resultant consciousnesses at rebirth-linking on the fine-material plane.
Non-meritorious formations are conditions for two types [of resultant consciousness] at rebirth-linking in the miserable destinies within the sense realm.
But for consciousness alone, there are conditions at rebirth-linking.
However, for the six [bases], they exist only during the course of existence, not at rebirth-linking;
even for the seven [bases], they exist only during the course of existence, not at rebirth-linking.
In the sense-sphere happy realms, for those seven [types of beings],
as well as for those four types of consciousness in the fine-material realm, during the course of existence these conditions exist, but they do not exist at rebirth-linking.

Conditions exist in the course of existence, but they do not exist at rebirth-linking. And that [rebirth-linking] occurs upon the apprehension of undesirable forms and so forth in the sense-sphere existence;
however, undesirable forms and so forth do not exist in the Brahma-world.
Likewise, the immovable formation occurs in the formless sphere during the course of existence and at rebirth-linking for the four resultant consciousnesses.
Thus, firstly, regarding these states of existence, in both their rebirth-linking and their course of existence:
And just as conditions exist, so should they be understood by one who discerns them.
This same method is to be known regarding the sources (*yoni*) and so forth;
herein, this is merely a demonstration of the general outline, beginning from the very start.
In general, the formation of merit produces rebirth-linking in both types of existence;
having given, it generates all its fruition.
Likewise, it should be understood among the four modes of birth, such as the egg-born and the rest.
Among the many gods and humans, and likewise in the two destinies;
similarly, in the stations of consciousness characterized by diversity of body and so forth;
and likewise in the fourfold abode of beings as previously described.
Thus, the formation of merit is a condition for twenty-one kinds of results in the various states of existence as appropriate, and it functions in two ways.
In the realm of sense-desire, the formation of demerit [is a condition] in all four modes of birth.
In the three realms of existence, in one [of the four] stations of consciousness,
and in one of the abodes of beings,
that condition arises in two ways.
In the course of existence and at rebirth-linking, there are seven resultant consciousnesses;
likewise, there is the immovable formation in a single-form existence.
It is a condition in two ways for one kind of birth and also for one kind of destiny;
likewise for the three stations of consciousness and for the fourfold abodes of beings;
it is a condition in two ways for the four resultant consciousnesses.
By way of rebirth-linking and the course of existence alone,
formations are to be understood according to how they arise and what their conditions are within the realms of existence.
However, there is no transmigration of material or immaterial phenomena.
If there is no passing over, how could there be rebirth-linking?
There is no passing over of consciousness from a past existence to this one;
therefore, in the absence of a cause, its manifestation is not found.
Having obtained conditions, mere form and non-form arise; thus,
while arising and having indeed obtained conditions,
it is conventionally called "passing on to another existence."
There is no being, no life-principle, nor even a self to be found.
Having made this clear, I shall now properly demonstrate the process of rebirth-linking;
understand it well, for it is difficult to comprehend.
In his past existence, as he was indeed approaching death,
it was like a green palm leaf cast into the heat;
while his body was withering away and his faculty of sight and the others were lost.
When the physical sensitivity and other faculties abide merely within the heart-base,
at that very moment the consciousness is supported by its base;
and there is also karma— either meritorious or demeritorious— that was previously cultivated.
It proceeds by taking as its object either kamma or the sign of kamma;
thus proceeding, that consciousness has obtained its condition.
However, when the danger in the sense-object is concealed by ignorance, [craving arises].
Craving inclines one toward formations, while those born together propel one.
Yet, though being carried away by craving, one does not do so by the power of the continuity [of existence];
rather, it is like grasping a rope from this shore.
This [consciousness] proceeds by transcending the matrix (mātikā); it abandons its former support (nissaya),
and having either clung to another support or being produced from kamma,
it continues to proceed through conditions such as the object (ārammaṇa).
The former is the passing away here, while the latter is the rebirth-linking.
Yet this [rebirth] has not come here from the former existence,
nor has it appeared without a cause such as karma and the like.
And herein, regarding the arising of this consciousness from a previous existence without coming here [from that state],
there are examples such as echoes, lamps, and seals, which occur through the causes of past existences.
Just as [sounds] arise elsewhere upon arriving due to causes such as sound,
so too should consciousness be understood by one who discerns:
through the continuity of the stream, there is neither identity nor difference.
If there were a continuity of the stream [of being], there would necessarily be identity;
milk could never give rise to curd.
Furthermore, if there were absolute difference, [the same would follow].
A man who is the owner of milk would not thereby become the owner of curd.
Therefore, in this matter, neither absolute identity nor difference should be accepted by a wise person who understands the conventional usage.
But surely, if there is manifestation without transmigration,
then those aggregates that arose during this human existence—
because they have ceased here due to karma being the cause of their fruit— [would not exist].
Because it would follow that [the fruit] comes from another, and because of what has been done here by him;
because the fruit would be one thing arising from another action—
therefore, this entire arrangement is not at all correct.
Here it is said:
That which is the fruit within the continuum belongs neither to another nor from another;
the conditioning of seeds is the proof of this meaning.
Furthermore, the fruit occurring within a single continuum does not arise from another [continuum],
nor does it arise from something other than that [same continuum].
The conditioning of seeds is the proof of this point.
When seeds have been treated with honey and such substances,
at first the seed’s continuum receives those conditions;
however, in the course of time, its fruit-taste becomes sweet.
For those seeds, or even the volitional formations themselves, do not reach the place where the fruit arises; this case should be understood in the same way.
[This applies] to knowledge, spells, medicinal herbs, and so forth, employed during childhood.
This [kamma] should be illustrated as yielding fruit at the time of its maturation.
Even so, that kamma—whether it still exists or has ceased—is a condition for the fruit. Or else, it is that which no longer exists.
If it exists, then at the moment of its occurrence,
it must be accompanied by its result (vipāka) and by faith as its cause.
Alternatively, if it does not exist, it would be a condition for that which has already ceased.
[If it were so,] before and after the moment of its occurrence, it would have a permanent fruit.
It is said in reply:
Kamma is a condition by way of having been performed (kaṭattā); therefore, it does not have a permanent fruit.
Acts such as those of guaranteeing and so forth should be understood as illustrations.
That act is indeed "kamma by way of having been performed" (kaṭattā), yet it is a condition for the fruit;
however, there is no existence of that [act], because of its non-existence.
This is the *Abhidhammāvatāra*, which elucidates the ultimate truth;
it should be heard by listeners, for it increases their joy and wisdom.
Thus ends the section titled "The Exposition of Merit, Ripening, and Conditions" in the *Abhidhammāvatāra*.
The Ninth Chapter. 10.
The Tenth Chapter:
Exposition of the Analysis of Matter.
That matter which was described at the beginning as being born immediately after consciousness—
I shall now provide a concise analysis of it.
It is called "matter" (rūpa) because it is "disintegrated" (ruppati), or likewise, because it "disintegrates" (rūpayati).
Having transcended both the realms of form and formlessness, the one of beautiful form spoke of form. That form is twofold, distinguished by way of the primary elements and derived matter;
the great elements are fourfold, while derived matter consists of twenty-four types.
The earth element, water,
fire, and likewise air;
these four are the great primary elements (mahābhūta).
They were taught by Mahābhūta.
Or, because they have become great (*mahantā pātubhūtā*), they are called "Great Elements" (*mahābhūta*);
or, because of their deceptive nature, they are designated as "Great Elements" despite being unreal (*abhūta*).
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and the [visible] form;
sound, odor, flavor, the female faculty, male faculty, and vitality.
The bases, the nutriments, and the two types of intimation—bodily and vocal.
Space and the triad of lightness and so forth of matter,
accumulation, continuity-matter, decay, and impermanence—
these twenty-four are called derived [matter].
"Depending upon the great elements (mahābhūtāni),
that which proceeds without being released from them is called derived form (upādārūpa)," so said he whose mind was free from grasping (nirupādāna).
Earth exists because of its spreading out, and wind exists because of its blowing.
Fire heats up forms; water performs its function of cohesion.
Now I shall explain the characteristics and other qualities of these forms;
for when the characteristics and so forth are known, the true nature of phenomena becomes clear.
The commonality or the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) is considered the characteristic (lakkhaṇa) of phenomena;
its function (kicca) or its fulfillment is explained as the essence (rasa).
Alternatively, the fruit (phala) is the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna), or it is the manner of presentation (upaṭṭhānanaya).
That which is the proximate cause is designated as the "proximate basis" (*padatthāna*).
In this context, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness; its function is to provide a foundation, and it is manifested as receiving.
The water element has the characteristic of trickling; its function is to intensify, and it is manifested as cohesion. The fire element has the characteristic of heat...
The fire element has the characteristic of heating; its function is maturing; it is manifested as the provision of softness. Or alternatively, the air element has the characteristic of distending;
its function is moving; it is manifested as conveying. And here, it should be understood that each one has the remaining three primary elements as its proximate cause.
It is called "eye" (*cakkhu*) because it sees (*cakkhati*); the meaning is that it makes visible form known.
Therein, the eye is said to be twofold, distinguished by its nature as wisdom and as flesh.
Of these, the eye consisting of wisdom is fivefold: namely, the Buddha-eye, the Dhamma-eye, the Samanta-cakkhu (Universal Eye), the Knowledge-eye, and the Divine-eye.
Understand from me their distinction according to their sequence:
the knowledge of inclinations and latent tendencies, and the higher and lower degrees of the faculties—
this is designated as the Buddha-eye by the Sage, the Eye of the World.
Knowledge in the three lower paths is designated as the "Dhamma-eye";
that which is to be known is the "Universal Eye," while all-knowing knowledge (*sabbaññutā*) is the "Eye of Wisdom.
That which is recorded as "the eye arose" is the eye of wisdom.
The wisdom born of the mind of direct knowledge is called the divine eye.
The fleshly eye is also twofold: by way of its physical basis and its sensitivity.
Herein, the physical basis is that which is situated within the eye-socket.
Below by the bones of the eye-sockets, above by the bones of the eyebrows,
on both sides by the temples, and internally by the brain;
externally, it is delimited by the eyelashes.
Bound together by sinews, it is called a mass of flesh.
And this entire world, like the petal of a lotus—
broad, vast, and blue— is thus perceived by the eye.
That which is called "eye" is not that [visible object]; it is said to be its "base.
However, this is explained as the eye together with its constituent parts (sasambhāra-cakkhu). These are:
color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence.
And also the four elements,
the configuration of the arising of existence,
and likewise the vitalities.
The physical eye and the sensitivity of the eye—
these are the fourteen requisites;
thus it is in detail.
And there are also four elements:
color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence,
as well as shape and origin.
These ten have four modes of origination;
thus they become forty.
The eye, the body-faculty, the [mental] state, and life itself—
There are forty material qualities, yet there are indeed four [types]. By means of these material qualities, when they are gathered together,
this is declared by the wise to be the "eye as an aggregate of requisites."
Whatever is here attached is a slight obstruction;
however, the sensitivity of the four primary elements is born of kamma.
This is declared by the five eyes to be the "sensitivity-eye."
This [eye] is in the middle of that eye which, together with its constituent parts,
is entirely surrounded by a white circle,
or situated in the middle of a black circle within the visible orb.
Supported by the four elements whose functions include cohesion and so forth,
and further assisted by temperature, consciousness,
and other factors, that life-force performs its protection.
Surrounded by forms such as color, fragrance, and taste,
it serves as the basis and the door for eye-consciousness and the rest;
it remains with a size equal to the head of a louse.
For this has been said:
“The clarity of the eye by which one perceives forms—
this is limited and subtle, comparable to the head of a louse.”
The same method should be understood by the discerning person regarding the ear and the other [senses] as well;
I shall explain hereafter only the specific differences.

It is called the "ear" (*sota*) because it hears; it is located in that region covered with fine, reddish-brown hair, shaped like a finger-ring, and [occupied by] the aforementioned types [of elements].

Supported by the primary elements, sustained by the conditions of temperature, consciousness, and nutriment, and maintained by the life-faculty, it remains performing its function as the basis and door for ear-consciousness and the rest.

It is called "nose" (*ghāna*) because it smells (*ghāyati*); it exists within the cavity of the nose, which consists of various constituent parts, in a location shaped like a goat’s hoof, appearing in the manner previously described.

It tastes, thus it is the tongue (*jivhā*); or, it calls forth life, thus it is the tongue. That [tongue-sensitivity] remains in the region above the middle of the tongue together with its physical basis, having the shape of the tip of a lotus petal, in the manner already described.

The body (*kāya*) is the arrival (*āya*) of despicable impurities. However, throughout this entire body, wherever there is derived matter (*upādinnaka-rūpa*), the body-sensitivity remains everywhere in the aforementioned manner, like oil on a cotton cloth.
Now, I shall explain their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth: the characteristic of the sensitivity of the element originated by kamma rooted in the desire to see.
The eye has the function of impinging upon visible forms; it is manifested as the basis for eye-consciousness; its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to see.

The ear has the characteristic of sensitivity derived from the primary elements originated by kamma rooted in the desire to hear; it has the function of impinging upon sounds; it is manifested as the basis for ear-consciousness; its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to hear.

The nose has the characteristic of being a translucent matter originated by kamma rooted in the desire to smell; its function is to seize odors; it is manifested as the support for nose-consciousness; its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to smell.

The tongue has the characteristic of being a translucent matter originated by kamma rooted in the desire to taste; its function is to seize flavors; it is manifested as the support for tongue-consciousness; its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to taste.

The body has the characteristic of being a translucent element (pasāda) originated by kamma rooted in the desire to touch. Its function is to reach out toward tangible objects. It is manifested as the state of being the support for body-consciousness. Its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to touch.
However, some say:
"But the eye is the translucent element of those primary elements in which fire is predominant."
But for those who hold that space, wind, water, and fire are predominant, the remaining [elements] are secondary.
They should be told this: "Bring a sutta," for they will certainly not find even a single sutta [to support their view].
If there were a distinction among the primary elements, how could there be clarity?
For clarity is demonstrated as belonging to equal primary elements.
Therefore, it belongs entirely to the four supporting primary elements.
But having set aside the conceptualization of distinctions among these,
the distinction between the types of faith should be understood by way of the distinction in their actions;
for there is no distinction among them based on a distinction in their constituent elements.
Thus, among these, the eye and the ear grasp what has not reached them, while the remaining triad, beginning with the nose, grasps what has reached them.
"Rūpa" means that which "rūpaya-ti" (is affected); the meaning is that by undergoing a change of color, it manifests its state as being within the heart-base.
Furthermore, that [visible form] has the characteristic of impinging upon the eye; its function is to serve as the objective domain for eye-consciousness;
it is manifested as the range of that same consciousness; and its proximate cause is the four great elements.

And just as this is so, so too are all derived forms. Regarding sound: it is called "sound" (*sadda*) because it resounds (*sadayati*). It has the characteristic of impinging upon the ear; its function is to serve as the objective domain for ear-consciousness; it is manifested as the range of that same consciousness.
It is called *rasa* because it is tasted (*rasanti*) by that [tongue]; its characteristic is impinging upon the tongue; its function is being the objective field for tongue-consciousness;

its manifestation is being the range of that same consciousness. It is called *gandha* because it scents (*gandhayati*) and indicates itself; its characteristic is impinging upon the nose; its function is being the objective field for nose-consciousness; its manifestation is being the range of that same consciousness. The female faculty (*itthindriya*)— [...]* *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "Itthindriyanti". The translation reflects the available portion.*
This female state is born of kamma, originating from rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi);
as for these female characteristics and so forth, they are not themselves the faculty.
However, it is precisely by depending on the female faculty that the female characteristics and so forth arise.
These arise only during the course of existence, not at the moment of rebirth-linking.
Furthermore, that [sex] is not cognizable by eye-consciousness; it is cognizable only by mind-consciousness.
The female sex organ and so forth may or may not be cognizable by eye-consciousness.
This same method should be understood for the remaining male faculties as well;
however, both of these arise during the course of existence (pavatti) among those of the first aeon.
It should be understood that they "arise" (samuṭṭhāti) [in this way], whereas subsequently they arise at rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).
Even while in the course of existence, having arisen, one revolves within that very course.
By great unwholesome karma, the male faculty perishes;
by great wholesome karma alone, the male faculty is born.
By weak unwholesome karma alone, the female gender-sign perishes;
indeed, by weak merit alone, the female state arises.
Even for one with both sexual organs, there may be but a single faculty.
This being so, there would be an absence of the second gender.
Yet, why should there not be an absence? That [absence] is not the cause of the gender;
for it is the mind of lust, accompanied by karma, that is the cause.

Now, the characteristics and other attributes of both these [faculties] are stated. Therein, the female-faculty has the characteristic of the female state; its function is to manifest as "female"; it is manifested as the cause for the female sex, marks, gestures, and behavior.

The male-faculty has the characteristic of the male state; its function is to manifest as "male"; it is manifested as the cause for the male sex, marks, gestures, and behavior. As for "life" (jīvita):
Regarding what should be said here in the exposition of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), one should state it according to the very method already explained for immaterial life.

Its characteristics and so forth should be understood as follows: the life-faculty has the characteristic of maintaining co-nascent material phenomena; its function is to cause their occurrence; its manifestation is the stabilization of those very phenomena; and its proximate cause is the primary elements that are to be maintained.
“Basis” (vatthu) refers to the heart-basis (hadayavatthu).
That which, depending upon it, the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu) function within the fivefold plane of existence— that is called the “basis.”

The heart-base has the characteristic of being the support for the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element; its function is to serve as their foundation, and it is manifested as that which upholds them.
As for "nutriment": edible food is nutriment. It is called nutriment because it brings in (āharati) material form consisting of the eightfold nutritive essence.
That nutritive essence by which beings are sustained, and wherever those beings dwell—
This, however, is called "edible food" (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra).
It consists of the physical basis such as food and drink, which sustains the fire born of karma;
yet it alone is not able to preserve life.
Oja (nutritive essence) is able to preserve [the body] but cannot take it away;
the digester is able to take it away but cannot preserve it; both together are able to do so.

Furthermore, from the perspective of its characteristics and so forth, edible food should be understood as having the characteristic of nutritive essence (*ojā*), the function of bringing about material form, the manifestation of support, and the proximate cause of being swallowed after being made into morsels.

In the exposition of bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*), it is called "intimation" (*viññatti*) because, for those who make their own state known by means of the body, that state is made known through this [action] which is apprehended following the apprehension of the body; or alternatively, it is called "intimation" because it is itself made known following the apprehension of the body.
Furthermore, as it is said, "Restraint by body is good, restraint by speech is good," the body itself—reckoned as the *copana* (the moving force)—is the intimation.

Bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*). It is called bodily intimation because it is an intimation by means of the body, both because it causes the manifestation of one's intention through the movement of the body and because it is itself cognizable as such.
In that regard, [it arises] together with the co-nascent wind-element born of mind.
The cause for the movement of matter is its transformation into a single mode.
This is called bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti), and it is considered the "body-door" (kāyadvāra).
In that regard, it is established by volition (cetanā) through the influence of merit and demerit.
"Bodily action" has been defined by the Teacher who seeks our welfare;
however, its actual occurrence also arises through the door of speech.
Having obtained support within the cognitive process of a single adverting moment, [it proceeds].
By the six preceding consciousnesses, [the body] is moved by matter originated from the air element.
But by the seventh consciousness, matter originated from the air element—
conjoined with intimation— moves the co-nascent matter by means of itself.
In the exposition of verbal intimation, however, it is said:
“The condition for the arising of consciousness, In the striking of what is clung-to,
That which is the single alteration of mode— This [is the function] of the earth element.”
Vocal intimation is to be understood as being dependent upon sound;
it is designated as the "vocal door" by the scion of the Sakyan clan.
There is no sound born of mind that exists apart from the impact of intimation.
Indeed, sound arises together with the impact of the elements.
Because it makes known and because it is to be known, it may be called "intimation" (viññatti);
its occurrence depends on two types of agents.
The two modes of intimation are not like the eight types of matter born of mind;
rather, because they are modifications of what is born of mind, they are called "born of mind.
Among these, bodily intimation has the function of manifesting one's intention, and its manifestation is the state of being the cause for the movement of the body.
