They have the air element produced by mind as their proximate cause. Likewise, vocal intimation has the function of manifesting intention;
it is manifested as the causal state of the sound of speech, and it has the earth element produced by mind as its proximate cause.
It is called "space" (ākāsa) because it does not obstruct; however, it is the opening between material forms.
That which is the delimitation of material phenomena is called "space. It has the characteristic of delimiting matter;

its function is to reveal the boundaries of matter; it is manifested as the limit of matter, or alternatively, as the state of non-contact and the state of gaps and apertures; its proximate cause is delimited matter. (In the description of the three qualities of matter, such as lightness, etc.—)
In the same manner as explained above regarding the lightness and other qualities of matter,
the three transformations of matter should be understood by the discerning one. Furthermore, regarding the sequence and the occurrence of these three:
A healthy, supple hide, or refined gold as an illustration,
cannot perform its function by means of the triad of lightness and so forth; rather,
it is the triad of nutriment itself that performs it, and from that, the triad of agility arises.

In this context, the lightness of matter has the characteristic of non-slowness; its function is the removal of heaviness from material phenomena; it is manifested as quick transformation; and its proximate cause is light matter.

Furthermore, the malleability of matter has the characteristic of non-stiffness; its function is the removal of stiffness from material phenomena; it is manifested as non-resistance to all activities; and its proximate cause is malleable matter.

The wieldiness of matter has the characteristic of adaptability suitable for bodily action; its function is the removal of unwieldiness; it is manifested as the state of non-weakness; and its proximate cause is the matter that possesses wieldiness. Moreover, these three [characteristics] do not mutually exclude one another.
In the description of accumulation and continuity:
"That which is called 'accumulation' is the heaping up of material phenomena."
The continuous succession of these [moments] is called "continuity" (santati).
In terms of their actual meaning, both of these are explained as the "matter of birth" (jātirūpa);
they are stated either because of the diversity of their modes or according to the needs of those to be trained.

As for its characteristics and so forth: accumulation (*upacaya*) has the characteristic of piling up matter; its function is to cause matter to emerge from the past; it is manifested as the act of bestowing [upon the future] or as the state of fullness;

its proximate cause is accumulated matter. Continuity (*santati*) has the characteristic of occurrence; its function is to bind [phenomena] together in succession; it is manifested as non-interruption; its proximate cause is matter that is bound in succession.
In the description of aging (*jarā*): aging is the process of growing old.
This so-called aging is twofold: manifest and unmanifest.
It is manifest among material phenomena and unmanifest among immaterial phenomena.

The aging of matter has the characteristic of the maturation of matter; its function is to lead [matter] toward decline; its manifestation is the non-disappearance of individual essences despite the disappearance of their specific qualities, like the state of ripeness in rice; its proximate cause is matter that is undergoing maturation.

The impermanence of material form should be understood as having the characteristic of disintegration, the function of sagging, the manifestation of destruction and decay, and the proximate cause of material form that is being disintegrated.
Thus should the twenty-four derived material phenomena be understood.
There are four primary elements and twenty-four derived forms.
Indeed, all twenty-eight material phenomena exist.
However, for the sake of non-confusion regarding these material phenomena,
this [section] treats their combination, their origination, their derived nature, and their conditioned nature.
I shall briefly explain the objection, the resolution, and the method beginning with the singlefold, as well as this miscellaneous section; listen to it.
Therein, "comprehensive inclusion" means that all this matter, by way of comprehensive inclusion, consists of the earth element, the water element, and the fire element.
The air element, the eye base, and so forth... including aging and impermanence, constitute twenty-eight kinds;
there is no materiality other than these. However, some who propound the existence of torpor maintain that "there is such a thing as torpor-materiality.
They cite [the verses]: "Surely you are a Sage, a Perfectly Awakened One; for you, there are no hindrances," and "the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor and the hindrance of ignorance..."
Furthermore, because of the expression "associated with the hindrances" (*nīvaraṇasampayutta*), and because it contradicts such scriptural passages as those in the *Mahāpakaraṇa-ṭṭhāna* stating,

"Dependent on a state that is a hindrance, a state that is a hindrance arises by way of non-prenascence condition," and likewise in the formless realm: "Dependent on the hindrance of sensual desire, there arise the hindrances of sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-worry, and ignorance."
And it should be rejected that "sleep is formless. However, even in the formless realm, the arising of this sleep is established by the textual authority;
therefore, a wise person should understand that its conclusion is reached here, and that it is indeed formless.

Others say: "There are twenty-nine material qualities together with the material quality of strength (bala-rūpa), thirty together with the material quality of production (sambhava-rūpa), thirty-one together with the material quality of birth (jāti-rūpa), and thirty-two together with the material quality of disease (roga-rūpa).
These [views] must also be rejected by demonstrating that each of these [additional qualities] is not distinct from those already mentioned.
When the air element (vāyodhātu) is included, the material quality of strength is already included; it is nothing other than that.

There is no such thing as "nutriment-produced matter" (bala-rūpa) as a separate category. The "matter produced by cohesion" (āpo-dhātu-sambhava-rūpa) is included under the "matter of birth" (jāti-rūpa), which consists of integration (upacaya) and continuity (santati).

The "matter of disease" (roga-rūpa) is comprised of aging (jaratā), impermanence (aniccatā), and so forth; there is no other matter called "disease. Therefore, there are only twenty-eight kinds of matter.
Thus they should be understood when taken together.
Regarding "origination" (*samuṭṭhāna*): there are four origins of matter—temperature, consciousness, nutriment, and kamma.
Kamma, temperature, consciousness, and nutriment are the causes of matter;
it is from these alone that material phenomena arise, and not from anything else.
Therefore, there are indeed eleven things that arise from a single origination:
the eight faculties, the physical basis, and the two types of intimation.
The eight faculties and the physical basis are exclusively born of kamma.
The Great Sage has stated that the two kinds of intimation (viññatti) are born of consciousness alone.
Sound is originated by both consciousness and physical temperature (utu).
The triad of lightness and so forth (lahutādi) is produced by physical temperature, nutriment, and consciousness.
Color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence,
as well as the four primary elements—
continuity, integration, and space.
There are eleven fourfold existences.
Eleven arise from one;
two arise from two; three arise from three.
Four and eleven are directly known;
two are not produced by anything.
Twenty material phenomena arise through kamma, while seventeen arise through consciousness.
By way of the primary elements there are ten and five; by way of nutriment, fourteen.
All these together, by way of the classification of origination, are sixty-six;
and with aging and impermanence, they become sixty-eight.
Aging and impermanence are not produced by anything;
for if they too were born, they would be subject to ripening and dissolution, since that is the nature of what is born.
But if that were so, then even those [aging and impermanence] would have no ripening or dissolution.
It ripens or it breaks apart, yet it does not break apart, for that [entity] does not exist.
Because of the ripening and breaking apart of what has been born, these two do not arise.
This might be understood in some cases, for there is indeed the term "accumulation of matter" (*rūpassupacayo*).
Just as it has been illustrated by the statement, "birth, it is born," so too does ripening indeed ripen, and likewise, disintegration indeed disintegrates. However, birth itself is not born;
this should be understood by one who possesses discernment.
When a phenomenon is arising, its "origination" (nibbatti) is proclaimed.
In that context, just as there may be a birth of certain phenomena themselves,
so too is the conventional expression of their causal condition and the designation of their production used.
In that same way, they indeed obtain [their results]; from the differentiation of their ripening, those [results] are obtained:
the conventional designation of being conditioned by them, and the conventional expression of their production.
Thus, both of these also arise from karma and so forth.
They never at any time receive that designation based on their ripening and breaking apart.
Why? Because of the absence of productive conditions;
however, it is obtained by birth at the moment of its manifestation and arising.
Because of the conventional usage of the term "personality-factors" (khandhas) and the designation for their arising,
one therefore undergoes birth, but not the other two [states].
It should not be said that "one ages," nor that "those two [factors] perish."
If you think: "Because of the absence of conditions at the moment of experiencing [the result], this aging-and-death is impermanent and conditioned;
and because it is stated that 'this is born,' therefore it must be so."
And yet it should not be said so, for that is a teaching by way of a method (pariyāyadesanā);
rather, it is because of aging and death that impermanent phenomena are likewise called "impermanent" and "conditioned," just as the case with the intangible communications (viññatti).
If it is thus, then because it is entirely unarisen, one might think it does not exist at all, like a sky-flower, or that it is permanent and unconditioned like space.
But why is it neither of these two? Because its existence is dependent upon a support.
Because earth and the other elements exist as the supporting bases,
therefore that triad does not exist like a flower in the sky; yet,
because it is obtained through the absence of earth and the others, it exists.
Therefore, that triad is not eternal like Nibbāna. Regarding the term "produced" (*nipphanna*):

here, eighteen types of material phenomena—namely, the four great elements; eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, visible form, sound, odor, flavor, femininity, masculinity, life-faculty, physical nutriment, and the heart-base—are called "produced. The remaining ten are called "unproduced" (*anipphanna*).
The eighteen [types of] derived matter and the remaining non-derived matter—
if they were non-derived, they would be unconditioned. Furthermore,
because of their being modifications of those very same material phenomena, they would be unconditioned.
"How indeed could they be both produced and conditioned?"—
in this way, it should be understood as "produced and conditioned.
Regarding the "refutation of the objection" here:
The female state, the male state, life, and physical birth,
as well as the sensitivity of the body— these are described as having all [eight] bases.
But such being the case, there would be the fault of confusion among the phenomena (dhammas).
The unity of the eye and the body-sensitivity arises.
But in the ultimate sense, one thing does not exist within another;
therefore, the body-faculty is not confused with the sensitivity of the eye.
But because they occur through mutual inseparability,
it is impossible for one who knows the [proper] occasion to state a separate location for them;
wherever there is an unclung-to continuum, there that [continuity] exists.
"There is clarity of the body"—thus it has been stated.
Even by way of its characteristics and so forth, it has attained diversity;
the shadow of the five-colored banners has become a metaphor for it.
Therefore, the wise person who understands the conventions should know that there is indeed no mutual confusion among phenomena.
In this way, the state of being produced or unproduced, as well as the objection and its resolution, are to be understood.
"It is not of one kind, etc."— because it is mundane, because it is not a cause, and because it is conditioned, that [consciousness] is subject to taints;
all matter is of one kind, because its occurrence is dependent on conditions.
Internal and external, as well as faculties and non-faculties;
subtle and gross, and twofold from the perspective of being clung-to and so forth.
The five beginning with the eye-base are indeed internal.
The remaining twenty-three types are called "external.
Furthermore, there are eight faculties, beginning with the eye-faculty and ear-faculty;
the remaining twenty types of matter are declared to be non-faculties.
The eye-base and so forth, the nine, and tangibility itself—
these twelve kinds of matter are declared to be gross.
The remaining sixteen kinds of matter, however, are subtle.
But that which is born of kamma is either clung-to (upādinna) or not-clung-to (anupādinna);
thus it is twofold.

Furthermore, there is a division into visible-with-resistance (sanidassana-sappaṭigha), invisible-with-resistance (anidassana-sappaṭigha), and invisible-without-resistance (anidassana-appaṭigha); and another division into that born of kamma, that not born of kamma, that born of both, and that born of neither.
And it is threefold. Therein, the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) is visible and impinging;
the remaining eleven kinds of gross matter are invisible and impinging; the remaining sixteen kinds of subtle matter are invisible and non-impinging.

That which is born from kamma is "kamma-born" (*kammaja*); the eight faculties and the physical basis (*vatthu*) are kamma-born; that which is born from other conditions is "non-kamma-born" (*akammaja*).
Nothing has arisen from anything; there is nothing born of karma, nor is there anything not born of karma, [regarding] aging and impermanence. Thus it is threefold.
Furthermore, it is classified according to the seen, the heard, the sensed, and the cognized; and by way of the door and the basis:
that which is a door but not a basis, that which is a basis but not a door, that which is neither door nor basis, and that which is both door and faculty.
It is fourfold according to its divisions: as being a door but not a faculty, as being a faculty but not a door, as being neither a door nor a faculty;
and likewise according to its divisions: as being both a basis and a faculty, as being a faculty but not a basis, as being a basis but not a faculty, and as being neither a faculty nor a basis.
In this context, "seen" refers to the sense-sphere of visible form; "heard" refers to the sense-sphere of sound;

"sensed" refers to the triad of sense-spheres consisting of odors, tastes, and tangibles; and "cognized" refers to the remaining five beginning with the eye-sphere, as well as the sixteen kinds of subtle matter.

The pentad beginning with the eye-sphere serves both as the door and as the physical basis (*vatthu*); the two types of intimation serve only as doors and not as bases; and the heart-basis serves only as a base.
[The female faculty] is a door, but not a base; the rest of all material form is neither a door nor a base.

In the third tetrad, those that are faculties but not doors are the female faculty (*itthindriya*), the male faculty (*purisindriya*), and the life faculty (*jīvitindriya*). For these are indeed faculties, but not doors.
The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated in the immediately preceding tetrad. In the fourth tetrad, [the first] three terms...
This was stated with reference to the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*); the rest is exactly as previously explained. Thus, it should be understood that there are four kinds.
Furthermore, according to the classification of those born from one, two, three, four, or five sources: [there is] that which is both a door-faculty and a base;
that which is a door but neither a faculty nor a base; that which is a base but neither a faculty nor a door; and that which is a faculty but...
It is fivefold according to its classification as follows: not a basis, not a door; neither faculty nor basis nor door.
Therein:
Eight faculties, the basis, and the two types of intimation;
Elevenfold material form is called "single-born" (ekajaṇti).
Sound alone is called "twice-born" (dvija); the triad beginning with lightness is "thrice-born" (tija);
the remaining elevenfold [form] is declared to be "four-born" (catujaṇti).
Aging and impermanence, moreover, do not arise from anywhere;
the pentad beginning with the eye is the door, the faculty, and the basis.
The pair of intimation-acts is the door, but neither a faculty nor a basis.
The heart-base is a base only; it is neither a door nor a faculty.

The female, male, and life faculties are faculties only, being neither bases nor doors. The remaining material phenomena are neither faculties, nor bases, nor doors. Thus, it should be understood as fivefold.

Furthermore, it is sixfold according to the classification of being born of kamma, mind, temperature, nutriment, or spontaneous birth, and by way of being cognizable by eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness.

Therein, the eight faculties and the [heart-]base are born only of kamma; the two kinds of intimation are born only of consciousness; sound is born of temperature and consciousness; the triad of lightness and so forth is born only of temperature, consciousness, and nutriment;
the remaining elevenfold [materiality] is called "born of all four"; and decay and impermanence are not born from anything at all.
In the second hexad, that which is cognizable by the eye is the visible base (rūpāyatana) cognizable by eye-consciousness... [and so on].

That which is cognizable by the body is the sense base of the tangible; that which is cognizable by the mind consists of the remaining five [bases], the sixteen subtle material phenomena, and the coarse material phenomena—thus it is twenty-one-fold. In this way, it is sixfold.

Furthermore, when divided according to whether they have a physical basis (*savatthu*) or do not have a physical basis (*avatthu*), it is sevenfold: that which is cognizable by the eye, that which is cognizable by the ear, nose, tongue, and body, that which is cognizable by the mind-element (*manodhātu*), and that which is cognizable by the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*).

In this context, the five bases beginning with the eye, together with the heart-base, constitute six bases; the remaining twenty-two kinds of material phenomena are called non-bases. This second septad is thus explained. In this way, there are seven kinds.

Furthermore, by way of the distinction between the seven doors and the non-door, there are eight kinds. In that regard, the five doors beginning with the eye-door, together with the door of bodily intimation and the door of verbal intimation, constitute seven doors; the remainder is the non-door. Thus, there are eight kinds.
Furthermore, by way of the distinction between the eight faculties and the non-faculty, there are nine kinds.
Furthermore, it should be understood as tenfold through the division into *navakamma* (newly formed) and *jātakamma* (born-together);
as elevenfold through the division by way of the sense bases (*āyatana*);
and as manifold through the division of the occurrence of material groups (*rūpakalāpa*) within the various states of existence (*bhava*).

Henceforth I shall explain the arising of material phenomena in the two realms of existence— of sense-sphere and fine-materiality— both in the process of rebirth-linking and in the course of existence.
[This applies] among the gods, excluding those of the earth-dwelling class, as well as in the Niraya hell and in the Nijjhāmataṇhika hell.
One should determine that the first three modes of birth do not exist [there].
In the remaining three destinations, as well as among the deities of the earth,
it should be understood by the discerning one that all four modes of birth occur.
At the moment of rebirth-linking for a being born from a womb,
thirty material phenomena arise in that embodied being according to its own nature.
For those not born from a womb and for those born from eggs, twenty arise.
Furthermore, there are material phenomena which, by way of the physical bases of the body,
become eleven here through the inclusion of both those already mentioned and those not yet mentioned.
This same method should be understood for all the decads as well.
When the pure octad of material phenomena arises together with life,
it is declared to be called the "life-nonad.
This life-nonad may be unified with the body-sensitivity.
That is called the "body decad"; thus it is summarized.
This same method should be understood when combined with the [heart-]base and the [mental] state, as well as by joining the eye and the other [senses];
thus the wise should know the seven decads.
For beings of spontaneous birth, for those reborn among humans, and for the gods of the sense-sphere,
there are always seventy material phenomena:
the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the physical basis (the heart-base).
For "and existence" refers to the seven decads;
however, for the material Brahmās, it is by way of the decads of the eye and ear bases.
There are also three decads, and the nonad of vital force.
Furthermore, by way of the four groups of material phenomena,
there are indeed thirty-nine material qualities.
The arising of non-percipient beings is illustrated by the life-nonad alone.
But in the case of a eunuch who is devoid of congenital blindness and deafness,
there is [the possession of] the body and tongue faculties. Regarding the base, from the minimum up to the maximum,
within the range of the maximum, it is according to suitability.
Furthermore, the arising of material phenomena in living beings should be understood by one who discerns them through the influence of fully developed material qualities.
There are twenty-seven material phenomena in the bodies of those belonging to the sense-sphere realm.
They exist because two elements occur together in one place:
the nose, the tongue, and the body, as well as two elements [of odour and taste].
However, for the material Brahmās, the five [sensory] forms do not exist.
In the realm of desire there are four continuities; in the realm of form, three continuities;
in the non-percipient beings, two continuities; and externally, one continuity.
However, for all living beings, when material form is being produced:
First, it arises from kamma alone; of this there is no doubt.
However, at the moment of rebirth-linking for beings who take conception in a womb, they arise precisely upon the arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness.
Just as thirty material phenomena arise at its arising,
so too thirty and thirty arise at its duration and dissolution.
All these material phenomena are designated as the aggregate of matter.
Impermanent, unstable, and insubstantial, it is nothing but a mere mass of suffering.
Having seen form as a disease, as a tumor, as alien, and as subject to disintegration,
one should see form as suffering and thus cause desire for form to fade away.
This [work] was undertaken by that monk who desires the welfare of others and who wishes to go forth into the Abhidhamma Piṭaka as fully mastered by the General of the Dhamma.
However, it should be studied thoroughly and correctly.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Analysis of Matter," in the *Abhidhammāvatāra*.
11. The Eleventh Chapter:
The Exposition of Nibbāna Nibbāna, which was indicated at the very beginning immediately after form (rūpa), [is now explained].
Now, the method for its analysis has arrived.
Therefore, to demonstrate that which is difficult to perform and difficult to understand,
I shall hereafter explain its analysis according to my ability.
In this context, regarding *nibbāna*: "binding" (*vāna*) refers to craving (*taṇhā*), because it binds one to existence and non-existence.
Because it has emerged from that binding, it is called *nibbāna*—the deathless, the unconditioned, the supreme bliss. For it has been said:
"That which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation—that is *nibbāna*."
And that through the attainment of which there comes to be the destruction of all defilements—
that has been pointed out as "Nibbāna" by one skilled in Nibbāna. Furthermore,

this which is called Nibbāna should be understood as having the characteristic of peace, the essence of deathlessness (or the essence of providing consolation), and the manifestation of signlessness (or the manifestation of escape).
Here it may be asked: "Does not Nibbāna, as a single entity with its own intrinsic nature, exist in the ultimate sense?
For like the self of the heretics and like a hare's horn, it is unapprehendable. No;

for to those who seek welfare and investigate with the eye of wisdom, it is apprehendable through practice corresponding to that [investigation]. Indeed, that which ordinary worldlings do not apprehend is said to be "non-existent."
It should not be said so. If it is argued that when the Venerable Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, was asked by his companion,
"What, friend, is Nibbāna?", he replied, "That which, friend, is the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred,
and the destruction of delusion," and thus showed only the destruction of lust and the other defilements, therefore Nibbāna is merely the destruction of lust and the rest— this is not so.
Why? Because it would entail the fault that even for Arahantship there is merely the destruction of lust and the other defilements. How so?

Immediately after the question regarding Nibbāna, when asked, "What, friend, is Arahantship?", [the answer] stated only the destruction of lust and the others: "That, friend, which is the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion.
Therefore, according to your view, even for the fruit of Arahantship, [there is only the destruction of lust and the rest].
It would be a mere exhaustion; however, it is not logical that the unsurpassed supramundane fruit-consciousness should result in a mere exhaustion of lusts.
Therefore, do not speak thus based on the shadow of the literal expression; rather, the meaning of both these suttas must be investigated.

However, that Dhamma by the attainment of which there is the destruction of lust and the other defilements, although it is itself undestroyed, is spoken of by way of a metaphorical designation for "destruction" as "the destruction of lust and the others is Nibbāna.
It should be understood that this is stated by way of a metaphor for the fruit, just as in such expressions as "the tipusa is fever" or "sugar is phlegm," and so forth. [This refers to] Arahantship.

However, it is called "destruction" (khaya) because it arises at the end [of the defilements]. If Nibbāna were merely the destruction of lust and the other defilements, then all foolish worldlings would have attained Nibbāna and realized cessation.
Furthermore, there would be the fault of falling into the error of a plurality of Nibbānas;
for if that were so, since the destructions of lust and the rest are many, Nibbāna would likewise be many.

There would be multiplicity, and Nibbāna would possess the characteristics of the conditioned; because it possesses the characteristics of the conditioned, it would be included within the conditioned;
and because it is included within the conditioned, Nibbāna would be impermanent and suffering.
Furthermore—if cessation were Nibbāna—what [function] would the change-of-lineage, purification, path, and fruition consciousnesses have?
"Now, do you speak of an object? 'Speak it, friend,' [he said]. 'I speak of the very destruction of lust and the other defilements.
But do lust and the others perish at the moment of the lineage-consciousness (gotrabhu) and so forth, or will they perish, or have they already perished?

What do you mean here by saying, 'I speak of destruction only when they have already perished'? Speak well after having reflected thoroughly, friend; if you say that destruction occurs only when they have already perished,"

"It is not established that the *gotrabhū*-consciousness and the others have Nibbāna as their object. What is the reason? At the moment of the *gotrabhū*, lust and the other defilements will be exhausted;
likewise at the moment of purification (*vodāna*); at the moment of the Path (*magga*), they are being exhausted, but are not yet exhausted; at the moment of the Fruit (*phala*), they are exhausted.
This being so, according to your opinion, only the Fruit has exhaustion as its object, and not the others; however, for the others..."

"What object do you say it has? [He would reply: "Certainly, not seeing an object, he will be left speechless. Furthermore, the destruction of the defilements (kilesakkhaya) is performed by the virtuous;
the meaning is that it is brought about through practice corresponding to the individual's capacity.
But Nibbāna is not made by anyone, nor is it produced; therefore, Nibbāna is unowned (amata) and unconditioned (asaṅkhata). That which is unmade—
Because he knows thus, the noble disciple is called "one who is grateful. And this has been said:
"The man who is faithless, ungrateful, and a breaker of the bond..."
“Having deprived [the defilements] of their opportunity and having vomited them out—he is indeed the supreme person.
Furthermore, because it was spoken of by the Blessed One as “escape” (*nissaraṇa*); for “escape” is the name for *nibbāna*.
As it is said: "Monks, there are these three things that are difficult to penetrate. What are the three things that are difficult to penetrate?
They are the three elements of escape (*nissaraṇadhātu*). This is the escape from sensual pleasures, namely, renunciation (*nekkhamma*).
This is the escape from forms, namely, the formless (*arūpa*). And whatever has come to be, is conditioned, and is dependently arisen—of that, cessation is the escape."

For it is said, “there is an escape. If, because of the fault of non-existence, that Nibbāna spoken of in such a way were non-existent, then the first jhāna and the base of infinite space would also have to be non-existent. Therefore, it is improper to attribute the fault of exhaustion to the inexhaustible Nibbāna; indeed, Nibbāna is not exhaustion. And [it is said]:
“There is an escape in the world, well-polished by my wisdom,” and, “Bhikkhus, there is the unborn, the unbecome...”

Because it has been stated by the Lord of Dhamma, the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Enlightened One, in numerous Suttantas—by way of the ultimate meaning—that "it is unmade and unconditioned," one must reach the conclusion here that "there exists a single phenomenon called Nibbāna.
Furthermore, having cited the phrase "Which phenomena are immeasurable? from the *Paritta-ttika*, [the Buddha] said: "The four paths that are not included [within the realms of existence]..."

Since it has been stated that "the four fruits of recluseship and Nibbāna—these phenomena are immeasurable," how could it be logical for the destruction of lust and the other defilements to be immeasurable?
Therefore, Nibbāna indeed exists as a single intrinsic nature (sabhāva) in the ultimate sense.
Yet, like the "primordial matter" (pakati) of the Prakṛtivādins, like the "self" (attā) of the heretics, and like a hare's horn, it is not found [as a substantial entity].
Now, if it is argued that *nibbāna* is a mere designation (*paññattimatta*), that too is incorrect. Why?

Because the mind and mental factors that have *nibbāna* as their object cannot be said to have an inexpressible object. How so? In the triad concerning limited objects, having cited the phrase, "Which states have immeasurable objects?
[the text states]: "The four paths that are not included [in the mundane world] and the four fruits of recluseship—these states..."

For it is said: "They have immeasurable objects. If, however, their object were a conceptual designation (*paññatti*), then having immeasurable objects would not be tenable; they would instead fall into the category of having indeterminate objects.
"The fine-material-sphere triplets and quadruples of jhānas—whether wholesome, resultant, or functional—and the resultant of the fourth jhāna, and the base of infinite space..."
For it has been said: “The base of nothingness, in its aspect as wholesome, as result, and as functional, these states have objects that are not to be described”;

therefore, Nibbāna is not a mere conceptual construct (paññatti). And since the status of being a conceptual construct is not tenable for Nibbāna, it is therefore permanent because it serves as the object-condition for the paths and fruits, and because it is devoid of arising and so forth; it is [permanent] because it lacks the intrinsic nature of material form (rūpa).
It should be accepted that there exists a state called Nibbāna, which is formless and, due to the absence of conceptual proliferation (*papañca*), is free from proliferation.
It is absolute, infinite, peaceful, deathless, and luminous;
it is sublime, a refuge, secure, a shelter, a cave, and the ultimate goal.
The auspicious, subtle, and true, the destruction of suffering, free from taints;
the further shore so difficult to see, Nibbāna, which is invisible;
the destruction of craving, the permanent island, free from affliction and calamity.
The storeless and formless, the deathless state,
the imperishable; dispassion, cessation, liberation,
and indeed deliverance— it is by these names that Nibbāna is described.
Having understood this, as well as Nibbāna and its imperishability,
and the means for its attainment, the wise person should always act accordingly.
This [work] generates faith and wisdom regarding the Tathāgata’s teaching and destroys delusion.
Whoever understands this [work], which produces confidence through the arising of wisdom,
which is rich in meaning and phrasing, most sweet, and which astounds those who know the essence—
such a person has reached the ultimate goal in the profound and subtle Abhidhamma Piṭaka.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of Nibbāna," in the *Abhidhammāvatāra*. Chapter Twelve.
The Exposition of Descriptions (Paññatti-niddesa).
Here it is asked: "Is the knowable only this much, or is there something else as well? There is indeed that which is called a "description" (paññatti).
It is called a "description" both because it is to be described and because it describes. Therefore it was said: "That which of those..."
“Of those phenomena, it is a reckoning, a designation, a description, a conventional term, a name, a naming, a denomination, a linguistic expression, a phrasing, and a verbal utterance.
In this context, it is called a *saṅkhā* because it is reckoned; the meaning is that it is spoken of.
How is it spoken of? It is spoken of in many ways as “I,” “mine,” “another,” “another’s,” “bed,” “chair,” and so forth.

It is a formation (*saṅkhā*). It is designated (*samaññāyati*) as "designation" (*samaññā*). It is made known (*paññapīyati*) as "description" (*paññatti*). It is expressed (*voharīyati*) as "convention" (*vohāra*). How is it expressed?
As "I," "mine," "another," "another's," "bed," and "chair. Thus, it is called a "description" (*paññatti*) because it is to be described in such a way.
For indeed, by depending upon and relying on the phenomena of form and so forth, [the notion] "I" arises. This is the cause.

Having established that those phenomena such as form (rūpa) possess arising and passing away, this "I"—which is neither of such a nature but is established merely by worldly convention—is what is called and designated; this is the meaning of "conceptualization" (paññatti).
Now, in order to reveal conceptualization by way of its designating function, he says: "name, naming," and so forth. Therein, "name" (nāma) means:
One designates each respective phenomenon (dhamma) as "this is such-and-such a name"; therefore, it is called a designation (paññatti).
"Name-action" (nāmakamma) and so forth are synonyms for that very [designation]. This is what is called a designation by way of making known. Furthermore, this [designation] is threefold:
designation by way of kind (tajjā-paññatti), designation by way of dependence (upādā-paññatti), and designation by way of comparison (upanidhā-paññatti). Among these, designation by way of kind...

Designations by name (*nāma-paññatti*) proceed according to such methods as "eye," "ear," "visible form," "sound," "earth," "fire," "air," and so forth. Designation by derived matter (*upādā-paññatti*), however, is twofold:

by way of a collection (*samūha*) and not by way of a collection. Among these, what is called "designation by a collection" is spoken of by taking the name of one or many among material and immaterial phenomena, and referring to them as a collective whole. How so? Such as the various distinctions of "bear," "hyena," "jar," "cloth," and so on. This is...

This is called a collective designation (*samūha-paññatti*). Non-collective designations (*asamūha-paññatti*), however, are divided into those based on direction, space, time, signs, non-existence, cessation, and so forth.
When it illuminates an existing ultimate reality (*paramattha*), it is then called an "existent designation" (*vijjamāna-paññatti*).
When it illuminates a mere name—whether it refers to a collective or a non-collective—that does not exist, it is then called a "non-existent designation" (*avijjamāna-paññatti*).

...is so called. Both of these types, moreover, are cognized by the mind-door impulsion consciousness (*manodvāra-javana-viññāṇa*) which has previously grasped the conventional designation (*saṅketa*) immediately following the ear-door impulsion.
It is that [designation] by which something is made known through the mind-door impulsion consciousness that has previously grasped the conventional designation. With reference to this, it is said:

"Designation of the existent (*vijjamāna-paññatti*), designation of the non-existent (*avijjamāna-paññatti*), designation of the non-existent by means of the existent (*vijjamānena avijjamāna-paññatti*), [and designation of the existent by means of the non-existent]."
“The sixfold method is stated as: designation of what exists, designation of what exists by means of what exists, and designation of what does not exist by means of what does not exist.
In this context, the making known of form and so forth, which exist in the ultimate sense, is “designation of what exists.
Likewise, the making known of things such as woman and man, which do not exist [ultimately], is “designation of what does not exist. However, setting aside the etymological meaning...

The designation of things such as a fifth truth—which are not apprehended in any way—or of things such as the "primordial person" (pakati-purisa) imagined by the non-Buddhist sectarians, is likewise a designation of what does not exist.

A designation of the non-existent by means of the existent is that which occurs in such modes as "one possessing the three knowledges" (tevijja), "one possessing the six direct knowledges" (chaḷabhiñña), and so forth.
A designation of the non-existent by means of the non-existent is that which occurs in such cases as "the sound of a woman," "the sound of a man," and so forth.
The designation of what exists (*vijjamāna-paññatti*). Such [designations] as “eye-consciousness,” “ear-consciousness,” and so forth, are designations of what exists by means of what exists.
Such [designations] as “a kṣatriya youth,” “a brahmin youth,” “a novice monk youth,” and so forth, are called designations of what does not exist by means of what does not exist.
These six types of designations thus mentioned are also included herein. This is what is called “designation based on dependence” (*upādā-paññatti*).

Designation by comparison (*upanidhā-paññatti*) is also a sub-classification of this very [designation]. It occurs in such ways as, “The short is designated in comparison with the long,” or “The long is designated in comparison with the short,” and also in such expressions as, “Human kingship is miserable when compared with celestial happiness.

Therefore, it should be understood as “designation” (*paññatti*) both because it is that which is to be designated and because it is the act of designating. The section on synonyms (*samaññā*) is concluded.
In the ultimate sense, there is only designation; a third alternative does not exist.
One who is skilled in these two points is unshakable by the doctrines of others.
Thus ends the "Exposition of Designation" in the *Abhidhammāvatāra*.
The Twelfth Chapter. 13.
The Thirteenth Chapter:
The Exposition of Penetrating the Agent.
Here it is said: Although the phenomena (dhammas) such as the wholesome and so forth have been pointed out, their agent—the self (attā)—has not been pointed out.
For if that agent and experiencer, the self, were non-existent, there would be an absence of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena;
and in their absence, there would be an absence of their results (vipāka), which exist in dependence upon them. Therefore, [the teaching] of wholesome and other phenomena...
"Is it pointless? To this it is said: This teaching is not pointless; indeed, it is meaningful.
If, due to the absence of an agent, there were an absence of wholesome states and so forth, then there would also be an absence of that "self" which you have postulated. Why is that?
Because, for you, there is no agent other than that self. If you argue that even in the absence of an agent, the self exists as the doer—so it is.
The existence of wholesome states and so forth must be admitted even in the absence of an agent;

why then do you insist on that [agent] there while seeing a contradiction here? Furthermore, just as in the world the production of sprouts and the like is seen to occur in dependence on earth, water, fire, air, and so on, even in the absence of a creator, so too the production of these wholesome and other phenomena should be understood to occur through the completeness of causes and conditions.

Furthermore, if it is argued that there exists, in the ultimate sense, a self (attā)—imagined by that wisdom—which is permanent, eternal, and the agent of wholesome states and so forth, we shall first examine that.
Is that agent and experiencer, the self, conscious or rather unconscious? What follows from this?
If it were unconscious, it would be like a wall, a tree, or a stone.
For him, there would be an absence of being an agent or an experiencer. If he is conscious, he must be either other than volition or non-other than it.

If he were non-other, then upon the destruction of volition, the self itself would be destroyed. If you ask why, it is because of his non-difference from volition. Or perhaps your intention is this: "But the self is not destroyed because it is eternal; [only] volition..."
"Does it not perish? It is said: When the self does not perish, volition (*cetanā*) also does not perish. If one asks why, it is because volition is not other than the self.
Since volition and the self are not distinct, it is illogical to say that perishing occurs only for volition and not for the self.
Furthermore, since there is no specific reason for the destruction of volition alone, let the self itself perish.
Let the volition stand aside. Now, if you argue that when the volition perishes, the self does not perish, then the self must be something other than the volition.
If, upon the destruction of one thing (the volition), another thing (the self) does not itself perish, then your own admission—that "the self is not other than the volition"—is undermined.
Furthermore, if the self and the volition were non-different, then there would be no non-destruction of the self [when the volition perishes].
Let there be the destruction of volition as well. If it does not so happen, then your proposition is abandoned.
Or, if it should be the opposite of what has been stated, let the self perish and let volition remain. But if you say, "It is not so"?
Then abandon the position of non-difference. If, however, you do not abandon it, you are one whose proposition is abandoned.
Now, if your intention is this: "This self of mine is not non-different from volition, but rather it is indeed different," then it is said in reply:
Here, moreover, difference is of two kinds—difference produced by characteristic and difference produced by location.
In that regard, do you assert that the self of volition is different by way of its characteristic, or is it different by way of its location?

"I speak of difference as determined by characteristic. For just as visible form, taste, smell, and so forth, though existing in the same location, are different by way of their characteristics, so too consciousness and self, though existing in the same location, are different by way of their characteristics;
therefore, I speak of difference as determined by characteristic. To this it is said: "Just as, for example, of fire..."
When a raw lump of clay is being burned, with the destruction of its raw color, there occurs the destruction of its taste and other qualities;

in the same way, if consciousness were destroyed, the self (attā) itself would also be destroyed. If you ask why, it is because [the self] would occupy the same spatial location as the visible form, taste, and so on. Now, if your view should be this: "Even though they occupy the same location, there is no destruction of the self, but only of the consciousness..."
"Does destruction occur? To this it is said: Even through the destruction of the self, there is indeed destruction of volition (*cetanā*).
If one asks why, it is because they are inseparable (*avinibbhoga*), just like color-form (*rūpa*) and taste (*rasa*).

Now, since they share the same status of being a single entity and are inseparable, for what reason does destruction occur only for volition and not for the self? If you say that there is no distinguishing cause, then [your position falls].
"Let the self perish by means of the volition; let the volition remain.

Now, if it is argued that when the volition perishes, the self does not perish because there is no single locus for both, and if one asks, "In that case, what is the fault?"—then as for what you have said, namely, that just as form, taste, smell, and so forth, though existing in a single location, are distinct by way of their characteristics, so too [are] volition and the self in a single location...
Is it that even for those things currently existing, there is otherness by way of their characteristics? That [position] is untenable; thus your admission is inferior.
Now, if—just as with color, taste, and so forth—despite having an identical location, the self does not perish when consciousness perishes, then you are defeated by your own admission.
Or else, if it were the opposite of what has been stated, let your self perish and let consciousness remain. And so it is.
If you say it does not exist, then there is no partiality [of selfhood] at all.

Or, if you claim that there is a difference produced by a change of location, then when the consciousness-self is different, its distinctness would follow as in the case of a pot, a cloth, a cart, a house, and so forth.
Without consciousness, your self would not be non-distinct; it would be as different [from itself] as a cloth is from a pot.
It might be so. For is a pot one thing and a cloth another? If it is asked, "What fault is there in this being so?

[the answer is: One is not released from the fault previously stated, namely, that "the self is insentient. Therefore, it should be understood that in the ultimate sense (paramattha), there is no self whatsoever that is either an agent or an experiencer.
If this is so, then why did the Blessed One say:
"This person runs from this world to the next world"?
"He both acts and experiences;
pleasure and pain are self-made," and:
"A being has entered into saṃsāra."
"Suffering is his great terror;
there is a mother, there is a father, and there are beings who undergo rebirth. Thus it is said.
“The five aggregates are indeed the burden,
and the person is the bearer of the burden;
the taking up of the burden is suffering in the world.”
And: "The laying down of the burden is happiness.
For whatever a person does by way of body, speech, or mind—
"For that indeed belongs to him, and taking that with him, he goes"— and: "For one [person],
by means of one eon..."
"A heap of a person's bones,
a pile as large as a mountain—
so it was said by the Great Seer."
The man who lacks faith, who is ungrateful,
who severs the bond of continuity— he has destroyed his own opportunity and vomited up his hope.
“He indeed is the supreme person”—thus it was said.
This was indeed spoken by the Blessed One, but by way of conventional designation (*sammuti*), not in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*). For has this not also been said by the Blessed One:
“Why do you conceive of a ‘being,’ Māra? Is this a speculative view (*diṭṭhigata*) of yours?”
“This is merely a heap of pure formations; herein no being is found.
And: “Just as, through the combination of parts, there comes to be the designation ‘chariot’;”
"Thus, while the aggregates exist, there is the conventional designation 'a being'.
Therefore, one should not rely on mere words alone, nor should one be one who grasps with stubborn delusion; rather, one should attend upon a teacher of the lineage.
The intended meaning of the scriptural passages must be understood, and one should apply oneself to those passages. Two truths were spoken by the Blessed One:
"the conventional truth and the ultimate truth. Therefore, both the conventional and ultimate truths must be known without confusion.
Having known them thus without confusion, [one realizes that] there is no agent or experiencer who is permanent or eternal.
Having investigated that "self" does not exist in the ultimate sense, and having observed the occurrence of phenomena through the assemblage of conditions,
a wise son of good family who desires the welfare [of beings] should practice for the making of an end to suffering.
He who constantly contemplates this text to the utmost—
Through gradual practice, supreme wisdom reaches its full expansion for him—
wisdom that transcends the intellect, brings forth excellence, destroys doubt, and produces what is dear.
The intelligence of that bhikkhu who always recites and hears this [treatise] blossoms here.
Thus ends the section titled "The Exposition on the Penetration of the Agent" in the *Abhidhammāvatāra*.
The Fourteenth Chapter: The Exposition of the Development of Concentration Belonging to the Fine-Material Sphere. The Thirteenth Chapter. The Fourteenth Chapter.
The Exposition of the Development of Concentration Belonging to the Fine-Material Sphere.
Honoring the Sugata, who is the way of development,
the way of welfare, and the way of happiness,
I shall hereafter explain the supreme method.
Listen to this sweet commentary on its meaning.
One who desires to attain for themselves the supreme vision and knowledge of the Dhamma among human beings must first purify their virtue.
For one whose conduct is dubious, who is immoral and devoid of virtue, there is no meditative absorption (jhāna), much less the Path; therefore, one should purify one's virtue (sīla).
Virtue is considered to be twofold, by way of what is to be practiced and what is to be avoided.
That virtue, moreover— unbroken, untorn, unblemished, and unstained—
is what should be practiced by one who desires welfare and seeks the bliss of seclusion.
Indeed, for monks, this virtue is the unsurpassed ornament.
Virtue is a jewel, a secure refuge, a protection, a shelter, and the ultimate resort;
it is a sublime wish-fulfilling gem and the unsurpassed vehicle.
Virtue is cool water that washes away the stains of the defilements.
It is the root of all virtues, the destroyer of the power of faults,
the ladder for ascending to the third heaven, the most supreme staircase,
and the secure path for entering the city of Nibbāna.
Therefore, that virtue which is perfectly pure and possesses a twofold characteristic should be practiced by a bhikkhu who desires his own welfare and cherishes virtue.
Furthermore, while established in this perfectly pure virtue, [the following] should be performed here:
The cutting off of impediments, and the ten impediments:
“Residence, family, gain,
the group, and the task as the fifth;”
"Travel, relatives, illness, books,
and psychic power— these are the ten obstacles.
Having brought about the severance of all these ten kinds of obstacles, [one should proceed].
One should approach him who bestows the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna)—one who is dear, venerable, and inspiring; who gives counsel and is patient with what is said;
who speaks of the profound and does not urge one toward what is inappropriate.
Having approached such a benefactor, endowed with these and other virtues—
a spiritual friend who, at the proper time, bestows a meditation subject—
one should receive that meditation subject after first performing the proper duties toward him.
Having understood that person's temperament as well, it should be given to that bhikkhu. Furthermore,
this temperament is considered to be sixfold, according to the influence of lust, hatred, and delusion, and according to the influence of faith, wisdom, and thought.
By way of their divisions, these amount to sixty-four;
since there is no purpose for them here, they have not been shown by me.
Here, there are only the ten foulness subjects (asubha) as well as mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati).
These eleven are favorable to one of lustful temperament:
the four immeasurables and these eight colored kasiṇas.
And these eight are always favorable to one of hateful temperament.

This single practice of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna) is indicated as being suitable for one whose temperament is characterized by delusion (moha-carita) and for one whose temperament is characterized by discursive thought (vitakka-carita). However,
the preceding group of six recollections (anussati) is for a person whose temperament is characterized by faith (saddhā-carita).
Associated with the approach to death, dependent on mindfulness and nutriment,
perception is the discernment of the elements and the natural disposition of a person;
these four, moreover, are explained as being favorable.
The four formless attainments and the remaining kasiṇas are described as being favorable to all temperaments because they are entirely opposed [to their respective opposites]. All of this, moreover,
is due to their state of absolute opposition.
The wise should understand that all these meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) have been stated according to their suitability. They are described as being forty in number:
namely, ten kasiṇas, ten foulness-subjects (asubha), and ten recollections (anussati).
The four immeasurables, the four formless [attainments],
the analysis of the four elements, and perception as nutriment:
among these meditation subjects, how many bring about access concentration?
But having set aside mindfulness of breathing directed toward the body,
even though it is not lost, the remaining eleven recollections, the perception of loathsomeness,
and the analysis of the four elements— these thirteen are said to lead to access concentration; the rest lead to absorption.
In this context, the ten kasiṇas and mindfulness of breathing lead to absorption;
these possess four jhānas.
Herein, the ten foulness subjects and likewise mindfulness directed to the body [possess one jhāna].
These eleven states may belong to the first jhāna.
The three beginning with the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) carry three jhānas each;
the four formless attainments (āruppa) are considered to belong to the fourth jhāna.
The twofold transcendence of the bases, objects,
and factors occurs in the formless realms through the transcendence of the objective field, while in the fine-material realm,
it is the transcendence of the jhāna factors. Herein, the ten kasiṇas are indeed to be expanded.
And the remaining [meditations], such as the foul (asubha) and so forth,
do not increase. Herein, there are ten kasiṇas, ten foul objects,
mindfulness of breathing, and likewise mindfulness directed to the body.
The counterpart signs (paṭibhāganimitta) indeed become the objects of meditation;
the remaining [objects] would have the counterpart sign as their object.
The ten kinds of foulness (asubha), the perception of food (āhārasaññā), and mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati);
Among the gods, these twelve never occur at all.
These same twelve, together with mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasati*),
making thirteen, are not found in the Brahma-world.
Except for the four formless [attainments], there is nothing among the formless states;
in the world of humans, all [meditative attainments] proceed without a doubt.
Excluding the fourth kasiṇa, as well as the kasiṇas and the foulness meditations (asubha), [the remaining ones proceed].
These nineteen are to be grasped by what is seen alone;
even regarding the body, the five layers of skin are to be grasped by what is seen.
It is explained that everything else here is to be grasped by what is heard.
Mindfulness of breathing is here illustrated by what is touched;
herein, it is grasped as the air kasiṇa through what is seen and touched.
The remaining eighteen [meditation subjects] are to be grasped by means of hearing alone.
The equanimity and the immeasurables, as well as these five formless attainments—these thirty-five remaining factors should be taken from the beginning;
it is declared that they do not exist [in the first jhāna].
The rest, numbering thirty-five, are to be taken from the beginning.
Among these subjects of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna), excluding the space-kasiṇa,
there are nine kasiṇas which serve as conditions for the formless attainments (arūpa).
All ten kasiṇas, however, serve as conditions for the direct knowledges (abhiññā).
The three divine abodes also become the lower members of the tetrad;
for the lower immaterial state is the basis for each successive higher one,
and likewise the fourth immaterial state is the basis for cessation— thus it is explained.
Moreover, all these forty types may serve as conditions for the bliss of insight and for excellence in existence.
Having taken up a meditation subject in the presence of a teacher,
It should be told to Vassa at the very moment he has arrived.
But when a bhikkhu who has learned it wishes to go elsewhere,
he too should tell it to him in a manner that is neither too brief nor too detailed.
Having taken up a meditation subject that is well-suited for the mind,
and which is always free from the eighteen faults,
one should dwell in a suitable monastery outside the village.
Neither too far nor too near, in a peaceful place endowed with the five factors.
If there is even a minor impediment that must be severed:
long hair, nails, and body hair should be trimmed by one who is discerning.
The robe-cloth should be dyed if it has become soiled;
if there is dirt on the bowl, it must indeed be thoroughly boiled.
Afterward, by that monk whose impediments have been severed, [the bowl should be used].
Dwelling at ease in a secluded place,
one should avoid blue, yellow, white, and red clay;
instead, using soft, dawn-colored clay that is pleasing to the mind.
The wise person who desires to attain the kasiṇa-jhānas that ought to be practiced should do so in a secluded dwelling, or elsewhere of a similar kind—
whether in a concealed place, on a mountain slope, or within a cave.
Either a portable [seat] should be made, or one that remains fixed in place.
When making a portable one, on all four legs,
one should likewise use leather, bamboo, cloth, or even leaves.
Having bound it, it should be made according to the measure of the clay;
having spread it out upon the ground, one must indeed inspect it.
Having struck the circle standing there on the ground with a wooden stake,
Having bound it with creepers, one should fashion a circular rim (*kaṇṇika*) of equal size.
In width and measurement, it should be two spans (*vidatthi*) and four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*);
it is proper to make it round, for a square shape is incorrect.
Having made the kasiṇa-maṇḍala as smooth as the surface of a drum,
and having swept that place, the wise one, having bathed,
returns. Within the distance of a hand’s reach from that kasiṇa-maṇḍala—
In a well-appointed place, with a seat properly spread out,
sitting there on a high seat four vitathis wide,
with the body held erect and mindfulness directed toward the front.
Having seen the danger in sensual pleasures and having seen renunciation as security,
and having generated supreme joy and gladness toward the Triple Gem:
“I shall surely be a partaker through this practice.”
"Of the bliss of solitude"— having thus made the highest effort,
one should open the eyes with an even gaze,
skillfully grasp the sign, and develop it again and again.
One should not look at the color, nor should one observe the marks;
rather, without abandoning the color, one should fix the mind with a one-pointed state of mind upon the object of designation by means of its prominent features.
“‘Earth, earth’— having said this, the wise one should meditate. ‘Earth, the supporter,
the ground, the bearer of wealth, and the sustainer of wealth’—
thus, among the names for earth, it is even permissible to recite just one.”
Opening [the eyes] and closing them, he should advert again and again until the acquired sign arises.
For him who thus cultivates it with a one-pointed mind, [the sign will arise].
But when, having closed his eyes, the yogi reflects and the object comes into focus just as it was at the time of opening them,
then that is called the "learning sign" (uggaha-nimitta), which has arisen.
But once the sign has arisen, from that time forth,
the wise yogi who understands must not sit in that place again; rather,
having entered his own dwelling place, he should remain there.
While sitting there, he should develop [meditation] as he pleases.
However, for the purpose of avoiding elaboration (papañca) when washing his feet,
he should have one or two sandals with single soles.
If his young tree of concentration should perish due to some unsuitable condition,
he should go to that place where it was, take it up again, and—
sitting comfortably on a seat— it should be developed by him over and over again.
One should attend to it and even apply reasoning to it.
But if, having abandoned that sign, the mind runs outward, one should restrain it and fix the consciousness upon the sign.
Wherever that one rich in asceticism wishes to sit,
there day and night his mind attends upon him.
As that practitioner proceeds in this way, step by step...
They suppress all five hindrances as well;
the mind becomes concentrated through access concentration,
and the counterpart sign arises for the practitioner.
What indeed is this distinction between this [present state] and the former?
It is like a polished mirror-disk drawn forth from its case,
or like the full orb of the moon emerged from the clouds.
That counterpart sign is like a crane against a rain-cloud;
that acquired sign has emerged as if bursting through it,
and having become even purer than that, it stands forth for him.
It possesses the shape of the body, yet it does not possess its color;
it is merely a counterpart image, born of wisdom and consisting of mental development.
When the sign consisting of mental development has arisen as a counterpart image, [it is]...
The five hindrances are indeed suppressed;
the defilements have settled down for the bhikkhu who is engaged in yoga;
and his mind is indeed concentrated through access concentration.
However, by means of two aspects, the mind becomes concentrated:
at the moment of access and upon the acquisition of that concentration.
Likewise, through the abandoning of the hindrances, it is so at the moment of access.
But at the moment of acquisition through the manifestation of the factors—
what, then, is the difference between the two kinds of concentration?
It is that the factors have become firm by means of the moment of access.
The factors of absorption arise with firm strength;
therefore, that absorption-consciousness continues even for a day.
Having further developed that sign by means of that very cross-legged posture,
If he is able to attain absorption (appanā) through that beautiful sign,
well and good; if he is not able to do so,
then that sign must be abandoned by the yogi.
Like the womb of a universal monarch,
it is as difficult to obtain as a jewel.
It must be constantly guarded by one who is heedful and possessed of mindfulness.
For one who guards the sign, no loss of what has been gained occurs.
When there is no guarding, whatever is gained perishes again and again;

therefore, it must be guarded. This is the method for guarding it: nimittaṃ rakkhato laddhaṃ, parihāni na vijjati. ārakkhaṇe asantamhi, laddhaṃ laddhaṃ vinassati; rakkhitabbaṃ hi tasmā taṃ, tatrāyaṃ rakkhaṇāvidhi.
The dwelling, the pasture, the talk, the person, the food, the climate, and the posture—these seven that are unsuitable one should avoid.
One should cultivate the seven that are suitable; for practicing in this way, [one attains success].
In no long time at all, absorption arises for the bhikkhu.
Even for one practicing in this way who does not yet attain absorption,
the wise one should properly master the skill of absorption.
"For this tenfold skill in absorption (appanā) here has been omitted by me,
fearing the expansion of the text. Thus, for one who accomplishes it in this way,
there is indeed skill in absorption.
When the sign has been acquired, absorption proceeds.
Even for one practicing in this way, if it does not proceed,
the wise person should not abandon the practice, but should indeed exert effort.
Therefore, the wise one, observing the mode of the mind’s activity,
should repeatedly apply evenness of energy;
even when the mind falls into slight laxity, he should uplift it.
Having restrained excessive exertion, one should cause [the mind] to proceed with evenness.
Having freed the mind from states of lethargy and agitation,
one should direct it toward the counterpart sign.
Furthermore, for one who thus directs [the mind] toward the sign, absorption will indeed succeed right now.
Having interrupted the life-continuum, the earth-kasiṇa likewise—
Taking that very same object, the mind-door adverting consciousness arises in the mind-door of the yogi; then,
with respect to that same object, four or five impulsion consciousnesses arise.
But at the end, there is one belonging to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*);
however, reasoning and the others become more powerful than the others.
Those [factors] of the mind in absorption (*appanā*) arise from the preliminary (*parikamma*) and access (*upacāra*) stages.
They are called preliminary stages (*parikamma*) and access concentrations (*upacāra*).
Because they are in conformity with absorption (*appanā*), they are also called "conformities" (*anuloma*);
and that which is the very last among these is called the "change-of-lineage" (*gotrabhū*).
By the phrase "the grasping of what has been grasped" here,
the preliminary and access [concentrations] are indicated as the second, that access concentration as the third,
conformity as the fourth, and the change-of-lineage as the fifth; absorption is seen as the sixth.
First is access concentration, second is conformity,
third is seen as change-of-lineage, and fourth is called absorption;
it absorbs at the fourth or the fifth, but not beyond that.
In the sixth or even the seventh [moment], absorption (appanā) does not yet arise;
this is because the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is still near, and thus the mind remains directed toward the impulsion (javana).
Having received the service of the preceding moments, it reaches the sixth or even the seventh.
Regarding this, the Abhidhamma master Godatta said:
"Just as some man running might fall headlong over a precipice,"
One who wishes to stand at the edge is simply unable to stand there; even so,
when the mind reaches the sixth or the seventh [jhāna], it cannot remain.
"It is not possible" means it is impossible to enter [absorption]; this should be understood by one who possesses discernment.
However, this absorption lasts for only a single moment of consciousness;
thereafter, there is a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga)—thus it is fully explained.
Then, having interrupted the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), there arises the adverting consciousness (āvajjana) caused by reflection;
from that follows the mind reflecting upon the jhāna.
Then come sensual desire (kāmacchanda), ill will (byāpāda), sloth and torpor (thinamiddha), and restlessness (uddhacca).
Regret and doubt— these five have been abandoned.
This jhāna is five-factored, being associated with applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness.
But for one who is greedy for various objects and under the sway of sensual desire,
the mind wanders here and there like a monkey in the forest.
[Therefore,] one should indeed concentrate the mind upon a single object alone.
“Concentration is said to be the antidote to sensual desire,” because it possesses the nature of gladness and is cool by its very essence.
Therefore, “rapture is declared to be the antidote to ill will.”
Because it functions with a wide diffusion and because it proceeds toward renunciation and so forth,
"Applied thought (vitakka) is the antidote to sloth and torpor (thinamiddha)" is thus praised.
Because its own nature is exceedingly tranquil, [it overcomes] the state of being unpeaceful.
“Pleasure is the antidote to the pair of restlessness and remorse.
Because it conforms to the intellect, “sustained application (vicāra) is characterized by continued investigation; it is shown to be the antidote to doubt.”
That jhāna is dissociated from the five factors and conjoined with the five factors;
it is auspicious, excellent in three ways, and endowed with ten characteristics.
Thus is the first [jhāna] attained by that yogin.
By one who desires that jhāna to endure for a very long time,
it should be entered after having completely purified all evil states.
For one who enters it thus, its duration will indeed be very long.
A bhikkhu who desires the full development of the cultivation of the mind should, in due order, expand that counterpart sign.
There are two stages for this expansion: access (upacāra) and absorption (appanā).
Or, having reached even the access stage (upacāra), it is appropriate to expand that [meditation object].
But once absorption (appanā) is reached, this is the method for expanding therein:
just as a farmer delimits the area to be plowed according to its location, so too should one proceed.
In this very way, the yogin, having delimited it again and again by two finger-breadths,
three finger-breadths, and so forth, should expand it as he desires.
Even when the first jhāna has been attained, it should be expanded through its five aspects.
That practitioner of austerity must be one who has mastery over what has been well-practiced.
Mastery over five things has been declared: in advertence, in attainment, in the three determinations, in emergence, and in reviewing.
Having adverted and resolved, having attained again and again,
having emerged and reflected, one who dwells [in mastery] accomplishes five things.
One who, while not yet masterful in the first, seeks the second—
The yogi may fall from both the first and the second [jhanas].
If perceptions and mental attentions accompanied by sensual desire still wander,
then for that practitioner of negligence, his jhana is partaking of decline.
When mindfulness is established in that state, and peace follows its natural course,
the meditation of the dull-witted yogi becomes "partaking of stability.
If perceptions accompanied by lack of reflection continue to operate through mental attention, [the mind remains unstable].
For one who is diligent, that jhāna may partake of distinction.
If perceptions associated with disenchantment and acts of attention proceed,
it is explained that the jhāna partakes of penetration.
Therefore, one who has mastery over these five well-practiced [attainments],
having emerged from the first jhāna by way of proficiency according to the prescribed method,
[should proceed]; for this attainment is proximate to the unwholesome and coarse.
"Because of the coarseness of those who subsist on mere conjecture,
this [first jhāna] is therefore weak in its factors. Having seen such dangers in the first [jhāna],
the wise yogin should then contemplate the second jhāna as peaceful.
Having brought his attachment to an end, he should again undertake the sequence of development for the sake of attaining the second jhāna from within the first jhāna. Then,
when he has emerged from the first jhāna according to the proper method,
For the yogi who is mindful and clearly comprehending while reviewing the factors of jhāna,
the coarse modes of reasoning indeed persist; however,
for him, the remaining three factors remain truly peaceful.
For the abandoning of the coarse factors and for the acquisition of the peaceful factors, that very same sign is for that yogi at that time.
Furthermore, as he practices with the mind, thinking "earth, earth," thus...
"Now the second jhāna will arise"— thinking thus,
the bhavaṅga is interrupted, and the earth-kasiṇa itself is made the object in the mind-door of the yogin.
The consciousness of adverting arises first toward that object;
thereafter, indeed, four or five impulsion-moments arise.
At the very end, however, there is also a single consciousness of registration following those impulsion-minds.
It belongs to the fine-material sphere and is the mind of the second jhāna.
It is associated with serene confidence, equanimity, rapture, and bliss, as well as one-pointedness; thus, this jhāna possesses three factors.
One should discern the remainder exactly according to the method explained above.
Thus, while lacking two factors, it is endowed with three;
this jhāna is excellent in three ways and possessed of ten characteristics.
The second [jhāna] is attained by the bhikkhu consisting of development.
When the second jhāna has been attained, through the five modes and having become one who has mastery over what is well-practiced, he is mindful even in the second [jhāna].
Therefore, having emerged from the first jhāna which is well-mastered,
this second attainment is called "near to the movement of thought" because it is dear to his mind due to its rapture, which gladdens the heart.
But because of the grossness of rapture (*pīti*), this [third jhāna] is weak in factors compared to that.
Having seen the danger therein, and seeing the peace in the third,
one should then completely eliminate attachment to the second jhāna.
The sequence of development should be performed for the sake of the third attainment;
then, when he has emerged from that second jhāna and is reviewing the factors of jhāna while being mindful and clearly comprehending:
It appears as coarse when one attends to it as "yellow," but as peaceful when one attends to it as "pleasure" and so forth. At that time, for that yogin,
that very same sign serves both for the abandoning of the coarse factors and for the attainment of the peaceful factors.
“‘Earth, earth’—thus again by means of the mind, as he practices;
now the third jhāna will arise for him.
Having interrupted the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), [he focuses] upon the earth-kasiṇa.
Taking that very same object as its support, in the mind-door of the yogi, there arises the mind of adverting (āvajjana); thereafter,
four or five impulsion moments (javana) arise with respect to that same object.
But at the conclusion, one of those impulsion-minds becomes a fine-material-sphere consciousness, possessing the third jhāna,
endowed with mindfulness, clear comprehension, and bliss.
Connected with one-pointedness, the third is considered to have two factors.
One should observe the remainder according to the method already stated below:
thus, it is deficient by one factor but endowed with two factors.
The jhāna, which is beautiful in three ways and endowed with ten characteristics,
is attained by the bhikkhu through the power of meditation.
When the third jhāna has been attained, it is characterized by five aspects.
But having become a master of what has been well-practiced, by means of mindfulness therein,
one emerges again from that third jhāna which is well-familiarized.
For this attainment proceeds with the nearness of the fault of attachment to rapture.
If there is even a slight mental preoccupation here,
thinking "this is happiness," then because of this abundance of happiness, this [jhāna] becomes weak in its factors.
Having thus seen the danger in the third jhāna, once again—
Having seen the fourth [jhāna] as peaceful with the mind, the yogi,
having exhausted attachment, should again perform the sequence of development for the sake of attaining the fourth jhāna within the third jhāna.
Then, when he has emerged from that third jhāna and is mindful and clearly comprehending while reviewing the factors of the jhāna,
that mental pleasure appears to him as gross; consequently, he [seeks] beyond that.
Equanimity is his peace, as is the one-pointedness of mind.
This is for the abandoning of the gross factor and for the attainment of the peaceful factor;
for that very sign is indeed [the object], namely, "earth, earth."
"By means of the mind alone, again and again for the yogi,
this fourth jhāna will arise. Then,
having interrupted the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), [he attends] likewise to the earth-kasiṇa.
Taking that very same object as its support, the mind-door adverting consciousness arises in the mind-door of the yogi; thereafter,
four or five impulsion consciousnesses arise with respect to that same object.
But at the conclusion, one of those impulsion-consciousnesses becomes a fine-material-sphere mind belonging to the fourth jhāna.
It is devoid of one factor and joined with two factors.
This fourth jhāna, moreover, is said to have two factors.
Thus, possessing three kinds of excellence and endowed with ten characteristics,
it is attained by a bhikkhu through the practice of meditation.
Because pleasure does not arise through equanimity, nor is there repeated cultivation [of it],
and because the impulsion-moments (javana) impel accompanied only by equanimity,
