therefore the fourth jhāna is declared to be accompanied by equanimity.
This indeed is the distinction here; the rest, however, follows the method already stated.
That which was the second jhāna in the fourfold system has been divided into two, and having done so, it is made the second and third in the fivefold system.
The third [is] the fourth here, and the fourth is the fifth;
the first is indeed the first—this is the distinction here.
Thus far has it been stated by me, neither too briefly nor too elaborately.
This cultivation of the fine-material sphere is not overly extensive.
Whom would it not delight with its exceedingly sweet and excellent words?
It is to be experienced as generating a clarity of understanding that is most sharp and lucid.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Development of Rūpāvacara Samādhi," in the Abhidhammāvatāra. Chapter Fifteen.
The Exposition of the Development of Concentration in the Formless Realm: By one who has transcended form and the formless, who experiences form, the formless, and so forth,
whatever formless merits there are have indeed been brought forth together with form.
Now I shall briefly explain to them,
for the benefit of the practicing monks, the supreme method of meditation.
"While form indeed exists, there may be the taking up of sticks and so forth."
"Furthermore, there are many afflictions, such as eye diseases and the like.
Having seen the danger in form, with a mind weary of form,
one practices the formless for the sake of transcending it.
Having become disillusioned even with those universal forms, he,
being confident and desiring to depart like a boar struck by a spear,
becomes one who has mastered his skill in the fourth jhāna.
Emerging from the fourth jhāna according to the prescribed method,
the wise one again makes this mind take form as its object,
accompanied by proximate joy, because of the liberation that is gross and peaceful.
Having thus seen the danger therein in its entirety,
and having completely exhausted all attachment even to the first formless attainment as peaceful, he—
whether extending to the limits of the world-system or as far as he desires— [perceives it].
Having spread it out to that extent, and whatever space has been covered by it—
whether one calls it "space" or "the infinite"— it is indeed space.
For it is while performing [the meditation] with the mind that one is said to "open" [the eyes]. Indeed,
while opening [the eyes], one does not contract that kasiṇa.
That yogi does not extract [the object] from the skull, as one might [extract] a cake.
Rather, he neither adverts to it nor looks at it;
for by neither adverting to nor looking at it, he indeed ejects it by name.
The space cleared by the kasiṇa is indeed that sign;
he adverts to it again and again with the thought, "This is space.
As he adverts in this way, indeed...
And even when one has been struck by a blow,
the five hindrances are completely suppressed for him.
He cultivates and develops that sign again and again;
for that yogin of tranquil mind who performs this very practice,
his consciousness then reaches the first formless state in space.
Here too, in the earlier portion, three or four impulsions are indeed associated with equanimity;
the fourth or even the fifth is a mind belonging to the formless realm.
Furthermore, one who desires to develop the second immaterial attainment,
having attained mastery over the mind of the first immaterial attainment, [should consider it] as the adversary to the neighboring fine-material-sphere jhāna.
"Like the second formless consciousness, it is not peaceful"—
having seen such disadvantages in the mind of the first formless attainment,
one exhausts attachment to it; yet, regarding the second as peaceful, [one proceeds].
Having pervaded that space, while the mind is still active,
one should thus perform much mental work regarding that consciousness itself:
one should perform the act of adverting, as well as the application of reasoning.
“Endless,” “endless”— thus should one fix it in the mind. As the mind investigates that sign,
the yogi’s consciousness becomes concentrated through access concentration.
He cultivates and develops that sign again and again;
as he does so, his mind is possessed of mindfulness.
With consciousness touching space, his mind enters the second formless attainment.
The method by which absorption (appanā) occurs therein is exactly as previously described.
"This space is infinite"—thus it is that very space;
the consciousness that proceeds having pervaded it is called "consciousness" (viññāṇañca).
Even by way of mental attention, the infinite is thus illuminated;
indeed, this should be called "infinite consciousness.
Then, by one desiring to develop the mind of the third formless attainment:
Having become master of what has been well-practiced,

one regards the third immaterial-sphere consciousness as the enemy of the proximate first immaterial-sphere consciousness within the mind of the second immaterial sphere, and likewise as not peaceful.
Having seen such danger in the second formless state of mind,
and having exhausted attachment to it, one should regard the third as peaceful.
Having thus attended to it with the mind, it should then be further cultivated by the mind.
The non-existence of the consciousness of the first immaterial realm is its emptiness. Yet, having mentally set aside that space-consciousness, one should again [contemplate] it as "it is not,
it is not" by means of the wind-element, or as "empty, empty."
For indeed, that which is to be adverted to and that which is to be performed even by the mind must be struck with reasoning again and again by the wise one.
As he thus investigates that very sign, his mind—
Mindfulness stands even more firm, and the mind becomes concentrated.
One cultivates and develops that sign again and again;
as he does this, his mind is endowed with mindfulness.
Having pervaded on all sides the space cleared by the kasiṇa,
[one contemplates] the non-existence and absence of the occurring consciousness of the third immaterial state. This is the consciousness of the third immaterial attainment.
Yogis attain that [state];
here, the method for absorption (appanā) is the same as that which has been described.
Having dwelt perceiving the consciousness that has gone into space with the eye of the second formless attainment, and having [contemplated] it as "there is not,
there is not," and so forth; when that preliminary mental application has disappeared—
He dwells observing only the mere disappearance of that [object].
Just as someone, having seen a gathering of a community somewhere,
perceives that place as being truly empty once the community has departed.
Furthermore, one who desires to develop the fourth formless attainment should first become master over the well-practiced third formless attainment. Then,
regarding the mind of the second formless attainment as an adversary to the mind of the third formless attainment—
"Only the fourth immaterial state is peaceful," and "it is not peaceful"—
having thus seen the danger in the mind of the third immaterial state,
and having exhausted attachment to it, one regards the fourth as peaceful.
Having thus brought it to mind, the wise one again right there makes this mind proceed by taking non-existence as its object,
repeatedly thinking: "This consciousness is peaceful, truly peaceful."
There is that which is to be adverted to and that which is to be performed even by the mind.
As the mind thus investigates that very sign,
mindfulness stands more firmly and the mind becomes concentrated.
He cultivates and develops that sign again and again;
as he does so, his mind is endowed with mindfulness.
And regarding the four aggregates comprised within the third formless attainment—
The fourth immaterial consciousness: that indeed the yogi attains.
Herein, the method for absorption is similar to the method explained above;
however, this distinction should also be understood by the discerning one.
“Ah, how peaceful indeed!”— thus does the attainment appear;
yet that which will remain making even mere non-existence its domain is seen through insight as “peaceful” precisely because of its peaceful object.
If attention is equanimous, how can there be transcendence?
Because of the desire not to fall [into error], there is indeed transcendence;
the improper application of thought, "I shall enter this," does not exist.
For by making that peaceful state subtle through the mind,
one reaches the sublime state of non-perception, which is yet a form of weakness.
And then there is the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
He exists by means of that perception;
it is not merely perception alone,
but rather it is of such a kind.
In the same way, O venerable ones, the subtle feelings and so forth here are like the oil for greasing the bowl and the water on the path.
This meaning should be proclaimed for the sake of awakening to the fourth formless attainment.
Because it neither performs the function of clear perception,
this fourth immaterial attainment— arising from the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception"—
is designated as "neither-perception. It is incapable of performing the function of clear perception.
Just as the fire element performs its function of burning in warm water,
yet it exists there in a subtle state because only its residual formations remain;
so too, that perception is called "neither-perception."
For having successively transcended these—
form, space, and consciousness which is the absence of that [space]—
And it is said: "By way of transcending the object, these four also come to be;
yet the discerning do not admit a transcending of factors for them."
In this context, each subsequent simile is more excellent than the preceding one;
therein they should be understood as such.
"The silk garment from the palace roof. Thus,
this method for the formless attainments has been shown in brief by me,
who sees clearly and sees with affection.
But that bhikkhu who knows this most essential method for the attainment of the meditative absorptions of the fine-material and immaterial realms,
and who is skilled in those absorptions of the fine-material and immaterial realms—
Having overcome it, he goes from the realm of form to the formless existence.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Development of Concentration in the Formless Realm," in the *Abhidhammāvatāra*.
16. The Sixteenth Chapter:
The Exposition of Direct Knowledge (Abhiññā).
Hereafter, I shall provide the subsequent [exposition] which brings about the purification of wisdom.
This is merely a demonstration of the gateway to the five higher knowledges (abhiññā).
Having produced both the form and formless attainments, as well as the eight [liberations];
The mundane higher knowledges should also be developed by one who is discerning.
Even within the fourth jhāna alone, by one who is mindful and has mastery over well-practiced concentration;
It is fitting for the yogi to apply himself to the higher knowledges (abhiññā).
For monks, these higher knowledges are unsurpassed;
indeed, they are called an ornament, a refuge, and a teacher.
When the direct knowledges have been produced by the bhikkhu practitioner,
his cultivation of concentration will then have reached its consummation.
[This includes] the divine eye and ear, and the knowledge of others' minds through psychic power.
"Knowledge of past lives"— these may be the five direct knowledges (*pañcābhijñā*).
By means of the fourteen methods, such as the conformity with the kasiṇas (*kasiṇānuloma*), one who desires to attain the direct knowledges must discipline the mind.
When the mind is concentrated, pure, cleansed, stainless,
free from defilements, supple, wieldy, and steadfast;
when the mind is thus endowed with these eight factors, it is capable of the various modes of psychic power.
If he directs his mind toward it, the transformation of supernormal power is accomplished. Then,
having entered the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge,
and having emerged from it, he can manifest either a hundred or a thousand forms, according to his wish.
Having formed the mental resolve, "May I be pure,
may I be pure," he then enters the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā).
Emerging from that, he resolves once again.
With a mind accompanied by resolve,
that yogi indeed becomes one among a hundred;
this same method applies to a thousand and so forth.
The consciousness of the foundational jhāna may have the sign as its object;

however, the preliminary-work consciousnesses here have various objects, while those of the actual attainment have mindfulness as their object. That consciousness which is the resolve upon that [attainment] likewise has mindfulness alone as its object.
Like the previously mentioned absorption consciousness, it arises immediately after the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū).
That single mind, belonging to the fourth jhāna, is born there;
the remaining details are the same as before, being merely a distinction in the preliminary work (parikamma).
The knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (iddhividha-ñāṇa) and the divine ear (dibbasota): how should these be developed therein?
One should enter the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā-pādaka-jjhāna), and then, from that state, [proceed].
Having emerged from the preliminary work with a sense-sphere consciousness,
the sound— whether loud or subtle— must be adverted to.
Then, as he attends to the sign of that very sound:
"Then, this divine ear will arise for him.
Having made some particular sound its object,
once that [sound] has arisen and ceased, there arises again the adverting of the mind-door.
For javanas indeed arise—four or five of them;
while among these, there are three or four preceding thoughts.
Those named preparation (parikamma), access (upacāra), conformity (anuloma), and change-of-lineage (gotrabhū);
The fourth or even the fifth consciousness is said to be the mind of absorption (appanā).
However, that knowledge which is co-nascent with the mind of absorption—
experts in hearing call that knowledge the divine ear (dibbasota).
While establishing firmness, that knowledge [arises] for the yogi through the mind:
"I hear a sound occurring within this [space]," [measuring] more than a finger-breadth or two finger-breadths.
A vidatthi, a ratana, likewise;
a village, a district, and then up to the world-system (cakkavāḷa), and beyond that.
Having thus delimited [the range], he should expand it in due order.
This one who has attained direct knowledge, by means of the base object,
hears all sounds that have reached the space touched [by his ear].
Hearing even a single word, he is able to discern it clearly.
This is the knowledge of the divine ear (dibbasotañāṇa).
But how is the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) to be developed?
This knowledge is refined by means of the divine eye itself.
Having increased the light, therefore, with the divine eye,
one sees the blood that is circulating in dependence upon the heart.
Having seen what is to be understood by another,
the mind of the bhikkhu becomes endowed with joy.
It may be red when [the mind] is associated with rapture; but when the mind is associated with mental grief, it is black;
when the mind is accompanied by equanimity, it may be like sesame oil.
Therefore, having seen the blood in the heart of another being,
one should develop that knowledge of the penetration of minds until it has reached firmness.
When that [knowledge] has thus become firm, then, according to the proper sequence:
The mind itself cognizes, even without the seeing of blood.
It cognizes every state of mind belonging to the sense sphere, as well as the mental states of the fine-material and immaterial spheres—
distinguishing them all according to their classifications such as "with lust" and so forth.
Knowledge of the minds of others (cetopariyañāṇa).
The recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussati) is what is to be performed by means of the knowledge of past lives;
it should be accomplished by a beginner bhikkhu who desires to master it.
The jhānas are four, according to their successive attainments.
These are the jhānas that serve as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā).
Having emerged from them, the bhikkhu must indeed avoid the very last posture, which is sitting.
From that time forth, however, everything—
both what was done during the day and at night— must be brought to mind in reverse order.
In this same reverse order, it should be done on the second and third days as well.
Day by day, week by week, month by month, and likewise year by year,
as long as there is a connection in this present existence,
so too must that bhikkhu review what was done in his previous existence.
When one has thoroughly reflected thus upon the mind-and-body (nāmarūpa) that had arisen at the moment of death, then,
making that very same mind-and-body at the moment of death the object [of attention], [the subsequent rebirth-linking consciousness arises].
At that time, mental attention arises at the mind-door.
When the adverting consciousness has ceased,
having taken that same object, four or five impulsion-consciousnesses occur.
The remainder should be understood by the wise according to the method already stated.
However, while the preceding stages are called "preliminary" (parikamma) and so forth,
the final consciousness is absorption (appanā), belonging to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara).
The knowledge associated with that mind, and the mindfulness associated with it,
is designated as the recollection of past lives. This is the knowledge of the recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa*).
A bhikkhu who wishes to see forms with the divine eye should first master the jhāna based on a kasiṇa object as a foundation for direct knowledge,
making it capable of being directed toward that goal; or else, he should do so with the fire-kasiṇa.
Whether it be the white-kasiṇa or even the light-kasiṇa—
among these three kasiṇas practiced by those who have performed merit,
it is here declared that the light-kasiṇa is the best.
Therefore, having produced either that [access concentration] or the other in due order,
the wise person, remaining on the level of access itself,
should increase it and establish it; they should not produce absorption.
If it arises, it is dependent upon the foundational jhāna.
The yogi must see the material form that has entered into the expansion of the jhāna;
for him who sees it, that form indeed exists.
For as long as the stage of preliminary work (parikamma) continues, the light remains;
but when that ceases, his light quickly vanishes.
When that has vanished, even the realm of forms (rūpagata) is no longer seen.
Therefore, having first entered the foundational jhāna and then emerged from it,
the bhikkhu must once again pervade [the mind] with light;
in this very sequence, the light will become powerful.
Thinking, "Let there be light here," he delimits however much space as there is.
Right there, he [perceives it].
But the light remains.
Even after sitting for a whole day, there is still the sight for one who looks;
the path traveled by a torch is the illustration here for a person.
The sequence of its arising is as follows: there,
having made that matter of the aforementioned kind the object,
when mental attention has arisen at the mind-door, those very [mental states] arise.
Taking form as their object, impulsion consciousnesses indeed arise.
These are either four or five types of sense-sphere consciousness;
the rest should be understood by the wise according to the method already explained below.
That mind which accomplishes the purpose is considered to belong to the fourth jhāna;
the knowledge associated with that mind is called the divine eye (dibbacakkhu).
[It is also the basis] for the knowledge of future existences (anāgataṃsañāṇa) and the knowledge of how beings pass according to their karma (yathākammūpaga).
There is no separate preliminary exercise (parikamma); they succeed through the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu).
Whether it be the knowledge of passing away and rebirth (cutūpapāta-ñāṇa) or the divine eye, these are one and the same in meaning, though there is a difference in terminology.
The knowledge of the divine eye.
That bhikkhu who here hears and applies this supreme bond within his mind;
Thus, by crossing over with this boat, one reaches the further shore of the great ocean of Abhidhamma.
Thus ends the section titled "The Description of Direct Knowledge" in the *Abhidhammāvatāra*.
The Sixteenth Chapter. 17.
The Seventeenth Chapter:
The Description of the Objects of Direct Knowledge (Abhiññā).
Knowledge of the future, knowledge of the passing away according to karma,
and the five beginning with the modes of psychic power— these are the seven direct knowledges (abhiññā).
Beyond these seven direct knowledges, however, [is further attainment].
I shall explain in brief the analysis of objects.
Regarding the four types of objects taught by the Great Seer in the triplet of objects,
listen to me as I describe the occurrence of the seven kinds of knowledge therein.
In this regard, how does the knowledge of the various kinds of psychic power (iddhividha-ñāṇa) proceed with respect to the sevenfold classification of objects,
beginning with the limited (paritta)? When one wishes to go by means of a body that is invisible—

With his mind, he determines what is the path and what is not the path;
for the yogin, it is thus: "This is the path," and "This is not the path.
Having discerned both the path and the non-path, this is the knowledge of stability.
"Knowledge of the path and the non-path was taught by Bhūriñāṇa.
They are skilled in the vision and knowledge of the path and the non-path;
they discern the essential from the non-essential, and they are established in the wholesome and the unwholesome."
"Knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path"—
this is what the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddha, those who speak with authority, declare.
Thus ends the section on the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What is the Path and What is Not the Path in the *Abhidhammāvatāra*.
The twentieth chapter:
[The Chapter on] Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way. The twenty-first chapter: The Exposition of Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way.
Insight that has reached its culmination by means of these eight knowledges is called the ninth knowledge: “Knowledge and Vision of the Way.
Here, the wise should understand that there are indeed eight knowledges.
Furthermore, knowledge that is extremely clear and free from secondary defilements—
namely, knowledge of arising and passing away, of dissolution, of fear, and likewise of danger,
as well as knowledge of the contemplation of disenchantment and knowledge of the desire for deliverance.
Reflective contemplation on formations, equanimity, and knowledge as the eighth—these are the eight knowledges; the ninth is that which conforms to the truths.
That which conforms to the truths is called "conformity" (anuloma).
By a bhikkhu practicing yoga who desires to achieve that [liberation],
application should indeed be made to these eight knowledges, beginning with the knowledge of arising and passing away.
For one who, according to the sequence, has applied the practice to those eight knowledges by way of impermanence and so forth,
and who dwells contemplating formations as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self":
Furthermore, by way of eight knowledges,
for the yogi who has reached the culmination of insight, there arises that which leads to emergence;
this alone is called "knowledge in conformity with the truths."
For that knowledge of equanimity towards formations, as the yogi cultivates it,
the path will now arise for him.
Equanimity towards formations [views] formations as impermanent or as suffering, or likewise.
Having reflected thus, it returns once more to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
Immediately after the life-continuum, however, by way of the method of entering into equanimity regarding formations,
it takes formations as its object by way of their impermanence and so forth.
In the case of forms, after the life-continuum has turned back, the adverting consciousness arises at the mind-door; immediately following that which has arisen,
the first impulsion-mind takes volitional formations as its object.
"That which arises is called the preliminary (parikamma) consciousness.
Immediately after that, another consciousness with a conditioned phenomenon as its object arises;
this is the second impulsion (javana), which is considered the access (upacāra)."
Immediately after that, there arises that [state] which has formations as its object;
this is the third impulsion-consciousness, known as "conformity" (anuloma).
Because it conforms to the preceding eight knowledges, it is called conformity.
By way of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhammā), both upward and in direct order;
for that very reason, it is called "knowledge in conformity with the truths" (saccānulomañāṇa).
Indeed, this knowledge in conformity with the truths was taught by the Great Sage.
“For it leads to emergence, and its end is the ultimate”—thus it is said.
That which is to be known in every aspect as the "end" is the *gotrabhū*.
Thus has it been praised by the Great Seer under various names.
Insight that is pure and leads to emergence—
One who is wise and desires to emerge from the great terror of the mire of suffering in *saṃsāra* should constantly apply themselves to that.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Exposition of Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way," in the *Abhidhammāvatāra*.
Twenty-second Chapter.
The Exposition of the Purification by Knowledge and Vision:
But beyond this, for the bhikkhu there arises the mind of change-of-lineage;
however, that is because it is the object to be adverted to by the path-consciousness.
It possesses neither the knowledge and vision of the way nor that very [knowledge and vision];
nor does it ever partake in the purification by knowledge and vision.
Between these two, it is simply beyond designation.
Because it has fallen into the stream of insight, it is called "insight" (vipassanā).
Or, because it proceeds having overcome the lineage of ordinary worldlings,
and since Nibbāna is called the "lineage" (gotra), it is therefore called "change-of-lineage" (gotrabhu).
Knowledge regarding the four paths is the purification of knowledge and vision;
therein, there is no other task for a bhikkhu to perform than the desire to accomplish that first path.
For whatever must be done by him, that has indeed already been done.
For by the yogi who has generated the sharp and keen insight culminating in conformity, all of that has indeed been accomplished.
At the conclusion of that knowledge in conformity [with the truths], however, there arises the signless,
the unconditioned, cessation, Nibbāna, the deathless state.
Making that its domain, it indeed takes Nibbāna as its object.
It is both the first adverting [of the mind] and the first application of attention.
Furthermore, it establishes its status as a condition for that [path] by means of six conditions,
such as the "immediately preceding" (anantara) and others.
For when that insight has reached its summit and attained the crest,
there arises for him the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) consciousness,
which does not revert and is directed toward the sublime object. This occurs through a single act of adverting and within a single cognitive process alone.
The state of having various objects and the conformity-change-of-lineage consciousness, having stood in the position of adverting, and that adverting itself,
cease as if having given their signal to the Path.
The path also gives it to him, not releasing its connection;
following that knowledge, it arises immediately thereafter.
For this path has never before been pierced at any time.
Arising as if shattering greed, hatred, and delusion—
this path not only effects the destruction of hatred,
but also closes the doors of its own means.
He completely dries up the great ocean of suffering— the cycle of saṃsāra whose beginning is unknown and which is exceedingly terrible and shoreless—
and as he is born, he abandons the eightfold wrong path.
Herein, it constantly pacifies all enmity and fear;
furthermore, it leads one toward the state of being a heart-son of the Buddha and brings forth manifold benefits for the practitioner.
Knowledge associated with the first path— consisting of the benefits for the giver and the many benefits for oneself— is "knowledge and vision.
This is the knowledge of the first path.
Immediately following that [registration consciousness], two or three resultant fruition-consciousnesses arise; beyond that, they do not arise.
Some, however, say there are one, two, three, or four.
But this should not be accepted, for they speak without knowing:
there is no repetition of a single [moment]; therefore, two are conformable (anuloma), and having obtained repetition through them, the third becomes change-of-lineage (gotrabhu).
But the fourth is the path-consciousness;
therefore, there are indeed three fruits,
and there are three conformities.
The fourth is the change-of-lineage consciousness;
the fifth is the path-consciousness, followed by two fruition-consciousnesses.
Thus, with seven consciousnesses at most, there is indeed a single adverting cognitive series.
To this extent, indeed, he is called a stream-enterer (sotāpanna);
at the conclusion of the fruit, there may be the transcending of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
Then, having cut off the life-continuum, [there arises consciousness] caused by the reviewing of the path.
It arises in the mind-door as the adverting consciousness.
When that has ceased, there arise seven impulsion moments known as the reviewing of the Path, occurring in successive order.
And this same method should be understood when examining the fruits and so forth as well;
there are nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge.
[They consist of] the path, the fruit, the defilements abandoned, and the remaining defilements.
And nibbāna— these five are the stages of reflection.
Having thus reflected upon his attainment of stream-entry,
the wise one applies himself to the second stage.
Furthermore, that which is comprised of the five aggregates, being included within the conditioned,
he thoroughly rubs with the knowledge that it is impermanent,
suffering, and non-self. Thereafter, he plunges into the path of insight for that duration.
For one who has practiced in this way, according to the method explained below,
then at the conclusion of equanimity regarding formations,
and likewise in the single-advertence series immediately following the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), [the path arises].
While bringing about the attenuation of ill-will and sensual lust,
this second path— the once-returning path— arises. This is the knowledge of the second path.
And regarding this knowledge as well, according to the method explained below,
the wise one should understand that there are either two or three fruition-consciousnesses here.
At this point, indeed, he is called a "Once-returner."
"Having come to this world but once more, he shall make an end of suffering.
In the manner explained below, there is fivefold reflection;
having thus reflected for the attainment of the state of a Once-returner (sakadāgāmi), [he reflects].
The wise and learned one begins the practice on the third stage in order to abandon ill will and sensual lust.
That which is comprised of the five aggregates is, moreover, subject to conditioned formations.
"He thoroughly rubs away [defilements] with the knowledge that 'it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
Thereafter, he plunges into the path of insight (vipassanā-vīthi) for that long.
For one who has thus practiced, however, according to the method explained below,"
Then, at the conclusion of equanimity toward formations (saṅkhārupekkhā),
and likewise within the cognitive process of a single adverting consciousness, immediately following the stage of change-of-lineage (gotrabhu),
one effects the total destruction of the roots of ill-will and sensual lust.
Then for him this third path, the non-returning path, arises.
This is the knowledge of the third path. And regarding this knowledge as well, by the method explained below:
The course of the resultant consciousnesses should be understood by the discerning one.
Up to this point, however, he is called a Non-Returner (anāgāmin);
because his nature is such that he does not return, he attains final nibbāna right there.
In the very manner described above, he performs the fivefold reflection.
Having thus reflected, that wise disciple,
a non-returner, undertakes the practice for the fourth stage.

And for the sake of abandoning attachment to the form of the body and so forth, the wise man likewise turns his attention toward conditioned phenomena by means of knowledge according to their impermanence and other characteristics,
and in that same way, he thoroughly investigates them.
Then, while he is thus practicing according to the method described below, the path of insight plunges forward for that duration. Then,
at the conclusion of equanimity regarding formations, it is exactly as before.
In the series of a single adverting consciousness, immediately after the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū),
this path of arahantship arises thereafter.
Furthermore, the knowledge of the fourth path is that which effects the destruction of the defilements such as lust for form.
Furthermore, the occurrence of the resultant consciousnesses in this knowledge should be understood by the discerning one according to the method explained below.
Up to this point, however, this—
The eighth is named the Arahant;
he is a noble person,
one whose great taints are destroyed.
The Sage, who has attained his own goal and whose fetters are destroyed,
[is supreme] in the world with its devas.
The one worthy of offerings is unsurpassed.
To this extent, all four purifications of knowledge and vision have been shown in brief for the benefit of the bhikkhus.
But by one who possesses faith, by means of right cultivation,
and by the cultivation of noble wisdom—
by that seeker of purity whose wealth is austerity— [these should be developed].
By the wise one aspiring for the destruction of existence.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Exposition of Purification by Knowledge and Vision," in the *Abhidhammāvatāra*.
Chapter Twenty-Three: The Discourse on the Abandoning of Defilements.
Indeed, among these [factors], whichever [defilements] are to be abandoned by whichever [means]—
Henceforth, I shall provide an exposition of these.

Furthermore, regarding these four types of path-knowledge, the abandonment of those phenomena that are to be abandoned by each respective knowledge should be understood as follows. For these [knowledges] respectively abandon the fetters, defilements, wrongnesses, worldly conditions, avarice, perversions, ties, courses, and taints.

These are the causes for the abandoning of what are known as the floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), misapprehensions (*parāmāsa*), clingings (*upādāna*), underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), stains (*mala*), unwholesome paths of action (*akusala-kamma-patha*), and unwholesome arisings of consciousness (*akusala-cittuppāda*).

In this context, "fetters" (*saṃyojana*) refers to the ten fetters. Namely: sensual lust, ill will, conceit, doubt, attachment to rules and observances, lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance.

These five are called the higher-fettering fetters (*uddhaṃbhāgiya-saṃyojana*). [The remaining five are] personality view, doubt, attachment to rules and observances, lust for form, and lust for the formless.
Sensual lust and aversion—these are called the five lower fetters (*adhobhāgiya-saṃyojana*).
Defilements (*kilesa*) are the ten defilements, namely: greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, doubt, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and lack of moral dread.

Wrongnesses (*micchatta*) are the ten wrongnesses, namely: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, wrong knowledge, and wrong liberation.
"Worldly conditions" (*lokadhammā*) refers to the eight worldly conditions: gain and loss, fame and insignificance, blame and praise, pleasure and pain.

However, here it should be understood that by the term "worldly conditions," there is an inclusion—by way of metaphorical designation of the cause—for the attachment based on gain and so forth, and for the aversion based on loss and so forth.

"Stinginesses" refers to the five kinds of stinginess: stinginess regarding dwellings, stinginess regarding families, stinginess regarding gains, stinginess regarding the Dhamma, and stinginess regarding praise.
These are forms of stinginess that function by way of an inability to endure others sharing in one's dwellings and so forth.

Perversions (*vipallāsa*) are these three perversions: the perversion of perception, the perversion of mind, and the perversion of view, which occur respectively as "permanent," "pleasant," "self," and "beautiful" toward objects that are actually impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul.
Fetters (*gantha*) are the four fetters: the bodily fetter of covetousness, ill will, adherence to rules and observances, and the bodily fetter of dogmatic insistence on "this alone is the truth.
Woes (*agati*) are desire, hatred, delusion, and fear. Taints (*āsava*) are the four taints: the taint of sensual lust, the taint of existence, the taint of wrong view, and the taint of ignorance.

“Floods” (*oghā*) and “yokes” (*yogā*) are also designations for those very same things. “Hindrances” (*nīvaraṇā*) refers to sensual desire and the rest. “Misapprehension” (*parāmāsa*) is a designation for wrong view.

“Clingings” (*upādānā*) are the four clingings, beginning with sensual clinging. “Latent tendencies” (*anusayā*) are the seven latent tendencies: the latent tendency of sensual lust, aversion, conceit, views, doubt, lust for existence, and ignorance. “Stains” (*malā*) are the three stains: greed, hatred, and delusion.
“Unwholesome courses of action” (*akusalakammapathā*) are the ten unwholesome courses of action, namely: killing living beings, taking what is not given... [and so forth].

Sexual misconduct, false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view—these are the ten. As for "unwholesome states of consciousness," these are the twelve: eight rooted in greed, two rooted in hatred, and two rooted in delusion. The personality-belief, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances—which lead to the states of misery and consist of sensual lust and aversion—are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the first path.
The remaining coarse forms of sensual lust and aversion are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the second path; the subtle forms are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the third path;
and the five [fetters] beginning with lust for the fine-material realm are indeed to be abandoned by the knowledge of the fourth path alone.

Among the defilements (*kilesa*), wrong view (*diṭṭhi*) and doubt (*vicikicchā*) are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the first path; hatred (*dosa*) is to be abandoned by the knowledge of the third path; greed (*lobha*), delusion (*moha*), conceit (*māna*), sloth (*thina*), restlessness (*uddhacca*), shamelessness (*ahirika*), and fearlessness of wrongdoing (*anottappa*) are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the fourth path.
Among the false states (*micchatta*), wrong view, false speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the first path;
wrong intention, malicious speech, and harsh speech are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the third path; and herein, it is volition (*cetanā*) itself [that constitutes these].

Wrong speech is to be understood as such; idle chatter, wrong effort, lack of mindfulness, lack of concentration, lack of liberation, and lack of knowledge of liberation are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the fourth path.

Among the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*), aversion is to be abandoned by the knowledge of the third path, while attachment is to be abandoned by the knowledge of the fourth path; some say that attachment to fame and praise is also to be abandoned by the knowledge of the fourth path.
The forms of stinginess (*macchariya*) are indeed to be abandoned by the knowledge of the first path alone.
Regarding the perversions (*vipallāsa*), however: the perversions of perception, consciousness, and view that take the impermanent to be permanent and the non-self to be self;
and the perversions of view that take suffering to be pleasure and the foul to be beautiful—these are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the first path.

The perversions of perception and consciousness that take the foul to be beautiful are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the third path. The perversion that takes suffering to be pleasure is to be abandoned by the knowledge of the fourth path.

Among the fetters (*gantha*), the bodily fetters of adherence to rites and rituals, the bodily fetter of dogmatic insistence on "this alone is the truth," and the bodily fetter of ill will are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the first path; the bodily fetter of covetousness is to be abandoned precisely by the knowledge of the fourth path.
The wrong courses (*agati*) are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the first path.

Among the taints (*āsava*), the taint of views is to be abandoned by the first knowledge, the taint of sensual desire by the third knowledge, and the other two by the fourth knowledge. The same principle applies to the floods (*ogha*) and the yokes (*yoga*).

Among the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), the hindrance of doubt (*vicikicchā-nīvaraṇa*) is to be abandoned by the first knowledge; sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), ill-will (*byāpāda*), and restlessness over wrongdoing (*kukkucca*)—these three—are to be abandoned by the third knowledge; sloth-and-torpor (*thinamiddha*) and agitation (*uddhacca*) are to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge.
Adherence (*parāmāsa*) is to be abandoned by the first knowledge.

Among the clingings (*upādāna*), because all mundane phenomena (*lokīyadhamma*) are included under the term "sensual pleasures" (*kāma*) by way of objects of sensual desire, [the clinging to] form and the formless...

Lust also falls under the clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*); therefore, that clinging to sense-pleasures is to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge, while the remaining [types of clinging] are to be abandoned by the first knowledge.

Among the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), the underlying tendencies of views and doubt are to be abandoned by the first knowledge; the underlying tendencies of sensual lust and aversion are to be abandoned by the third knowledge; and the underlying tendencies of conceit, lust for existence, and ignorance are to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge.
Among the stains (*mala*), the stain of hatred is to be abandoned by the third knowledge, while the others are to be abandoned precisely by the fourth knowledge.
Among the unwholesome courses of action, killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and wrong view are to be abandoned by the first knowledge;
malicious speech, harsh speech, and ill will are to be abandoned by the third knowledge;
and frivolous chatter and covetousness are indeed to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge.

Among the unwholesome types of consciousness, five—the four types of consciousness associated with wrong view and that associated with doubt—are to be abandoned by the first knowledge; two associated with aversion are to be abandoned by the third knowledge; and the remainder are to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge.

Whatever is to be abandoned by a particular [knowledge] is said to be abandoned by that [knowledge]. Therefore it was said: “These are, respectively, the abandoners of these states, beginning with the fetters.
And among these knowledges, by whichever...
Whatever phenomenon undergoes destruction,
that very thing has been shown by me,
indeed, thoroughly and completely in this manner.
In this discourse on the sequence for abandoning the defilements:
those tasks such as full understanding and the rest,
which were taught by the Teacher regarding the realization of the Truths— I shall explain them hereafter.
But for each of these, at a single moment of knowledge,
there may be both full understanding and abandoning.
Realization and development— these,
such as full understanding and the rest, are functions occurring in a single moment; however,
they should be understood by the wise according to their respective intrinsic natures.
Just as a lamp in this world, at this very moment,
performs four functions simultaneously—
neither before nor after— it reveals light and destroys darkness.
It consumes the oil and burns the wick simultaneously; even so,
that knowledge of the path, neither before nor after,
performs all four functions in a single moment.
By the very realization through full understanding, he realizes suffering;
by the very realization through abandonment, likewise the origin as well.
By the very method of cultivation, he realizes that path.
It is precisely through the act of taking [the cessation] as its object that one realizes cessation.

And this has been said: "The knowledge of one possessing the path is knowledge regarding suffering, it is knowledge regarding the origin of suffering, it is knowledge regarding the cessation of suffering, and it is knowledge regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. In this regard:
Just as a lamp consumes its wick, so does the knowledge of the path fully understand suffering (*dukkha*).

Just as it destroys darkness, so does it abandon the origin (*samudaya*). Just as it reveals light, so does it, by way of being a co-nascent and other conditions, develop the path consisting of right intention and the rest.
Just as it exhausts the oil, so does it [exhaust suffering] through the exhaustion of the defilements (*kilesa*).
It should be understood that one realizes cessation.
Just as the rising sun performs four functions here in a single moment, without first and last [being distinguished].
It illuminates forms and destroys even the darkness;
it reveals light and wards off the cold.
And just as a great ship [crosses] without first or last, so too—
But it performs four functions at the very moment of its action:
it abandons the near shore, it cuts the stream,
it carries the cargo, and it reaches the far shore.
Just as there is the abandoning of this river,
so too is the full understanding of suffering through the knowledge of the path.
Just as it cuts that stream, so does it abandon craving.
Just as that burden is carried by means of the co-nascent factors and so forth,
so too is the Path developed by way of being its condition;
and just as one reaches the further shore, so too does it have cessation as its object.
That supramundane development which has been demonstrated by the Supramundane One—
this I have clearly explained according to the method of summary.
For what man indeed in this world [could fully describe it]?
A wise person would not fail to cultivate that meditation which, through wisdom, brings about supramundane happiness.
Having understood this, he who indeed approaches the forest—
which is conducive to welfare, endowed with happiness, and beneficial—
shakes off the unsurpassed darkness of the mind.
And it attains the state that is free from grasping and trembling.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Exposition of Purification by Knowledge and Vision," in the *Abhidhammāvatāra*.
24. The Twenty-fourth Chapter:
Exposition of Conditions (Paccayaniddesa) By virtue of those phenomena which are conditions, these [others] are "with-conditions" (sappaccaya).
I shall now demonstrate to you the conditions for these phenomena (dhammas).

What are the conditions? It is said: they are twenty-fourfold, by way of root, object, predominance, proximity, contiguity, conascence, mutuality, support, decisive support, prenascence, postnascence, repetition, kamma, result, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, association, dissociation, presence, absence, disappearance, and non-disappearance.
In this context, the condition of cause (*hetupaccaya*) refers to these six states: greed, hatred, delusion, non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.

The condition of object (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) means that whatever mundane or supramundane state arises—whether it be a state of consciousness or a mental factor—by taking whatever [other] state as its object, those [targeted] states serve as the condition of object for those respective states.
Regarding "predominance condition" (*adhipatipaccaya*): here it is twofold, by way of co-nascent predominance (*sahajātādhipati*) and object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*).
Among these, co-nascent predominance is fourfold, according to desire (*chanda*), consciousness (*citta*), energy (*vīriya*), and investigation (*vīmaṃsā*).

Object-predominance, however, consists of everything remaining after setting aside grief, doubt, agitation, functional indeterminate states, unwholesome resultant states, and matter considered undesirable. Regarding "proximity condition" (*anantarapaccaya*): it refers to those [states] that have ceased immediately before.
Mental states and mental concomitants. Likewise, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-paccaya*) is also [these].

The conascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) consists of mental states and mental concomitants, as well as the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*). Likewise, the mutuality condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*) is also [these].

The support condition (*nissaya-paccaya*) consists of the material bases, the great primary elements, and mental states and mental concomitants. The decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) is...
It is threefold by way of object-predominance, proximity-predominance, and natural-predominance. Among these, object-predominance is identical to object-condition;

proximity-predominance is identical to proximity-condition; while natural-predominance consists of bodily pleasure, pain, weather, food, lodging, persons, as well as faith, virtue, learning, generosity, wisdom, lust, hatred, delusion, and so forth.

The prenascence condition (*purejāta-paccaya*) is twofold: by way of the physical basis (*vatthu*) and the object (*ārammaṇa*). Therein, "prenascence by way of the basis" refers to the material phenomena that constitute the bases;
"prenascence by way of the object" refers exclusively to present visible forms and so forth. The postnascence condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*) consists of consciousness and mental factors.
The repetition condition (*āsevana-paccaya*) consists of mundane wholesome, unwholesome, functional, and indeterminate states, excluding the two types of adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*).

The condition by way of kamma (*kamma-paccaya*) is twofold: by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and by way of different moments (*nānakkhaṇika*). Among these, those that are co-nascent are exclusively mundane and supramundane;
however, those of different moments consist of tainted wholesome and unwholesome volitions (*cetanā*), while untainted wholesome volition becomes a condition for its own result immediately after.
The condition by way of result (*vipāka-paccaya*) consists of resultant consciousness and mental factors. The condition by way of nutriment (*āhāra-paccaya*)...
It is fourfold by way of edible food, contact, volition, and consciousness.

Regarding the condition of the faculties (*indriya-paccaya*): there are twenty faculties, namely—the seven material faculties, the life-faculty, the faculties of pleasure, pain, joy, grief, and equanimity, and the faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*), the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*), and the faculty of one who has known (*aññātāvindriya*).

Among those, excluding the female faculty (*itthindriya*) and the male faculty (*purisindriya*), there are twenty faculties. The condition of jhāna (*jhānapaccaya*) is fivefold, by way of applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), rapture (*pīti*), happiness (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*).

The condition of the path (*maggapaccaya*) is ninefold, by way of wrong view (*diṭṭhi*), intention (*saṅkappa*), effort (*vāyāma*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samādhi*), wrong speech (*vācā*), wrong action (*kammanta*), wrong livelihood (*ājīva*), and wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*).

The condition of association (*sampayuttapaccaya*) consists only of consciousness and mental factors. The condition of dissociation (*vippayuttapaccaya*) consists of the pre-arisen bases (*vatthupurejātāni*) and the post-arisen [bases].

And [these are] mind and mental factors. The "presence condition" (*atthipaccaya*) consists of the life-faculty, edible food, objective fields, and prenascence conditions, as well as those phenomena mentioned under the dependence condition (*nissayapaccaya*).
The "absence condition" (*natthipaccaya*) is simply the proximity condition (*anantarapaccaya*); likewise for the "disappearance condition" (*vigatapaccaya*).
The "non-disappearance condition" (*avigatapaccaya*) is simply the presence condition. Thus, these are called the twenty-four conditions.

In this context, however, in how many ways does material form act as a condition for material form? It acts as a condition in seven ways: by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, nutriment, faculty, presence, and non-disappearance, as appropriate.

Material form acts as a condition for immaterial [form] in eleven ways: by way of object, predominance, co-nascence, mutuality, support, decisive support, prenascence, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance, as appropriate. There is no instance where material form is a condition for both material and immaterial [form].
Materiality is a condition for materiality in seven ways, and for the eleven [mental] factors in one way;

it is a condition for the mixed (name-and-form) in no way at all. Non-materiality is a condition for non-materiality as appropriate through the causes: root, object, predominance, proximity, contiguity, co-nascence, mutuality, support, and decisive support.

The immaterial (arūpa) is a condition for the material (rūpa) in twenty-one ways by way of: root, predominance, conascence, mutuality, dependence, postnascence, kamma, resultant, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, association, presence, absence, disappearance, and non-disappearance.

The immaterial is a condition for the material in fifteen ways as appropriate, by way of: root, predominance, conascence, mutuality, dependence, postnascence, kamma, resultant, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance.

The immaterial is a condition for the material and the immaterial in thirteen ways, as appropriate: by way of root, predominance, conascence, mutuality, dependence, kamma, result, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path, presence, and non-disappearance.
The mental is a condition for itself in twenty-one ways;
it is a condition for the material in three or five ways; but for both, it is in thirteen ways.
Materiality and mentality are a condition for materiality in four ways, according to circumstances: by way of conascence, support, presence, and non-disappearance.

Materiality and mentality are a condition for mentality in six ways, according to circumstances: by way of conascence, mutuality, support, faculty, presence, and non-disappearance. There is no instance where materiality and mentality are a condition for materiality.
Both [types of phenomena] serve as conditions for material phenomena in four ways;
for mental phenomena, they are sixfold; but for mixed phenomena, there is none at all.
Among these conditions, how many are material, how many are immaterial, and how many are mixed? Only the prenascence condition is exclusively a material phenomenon.

By way of the conditions of root, proximity, contiguity, posterior-nascence, repetition, kamma, result, jhāna, path, association, presence, and non-disappearance, there are twelve conditions that pertain exclusively to immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*).
However, it should be understood that the remaining eleven conditions are mixed, pertaining to both material and immaterial phenomena.
Furthermore, by way of time, [the conditions are] root, co-nascence, mutuality, dependence, prenascence, post-nascence, result, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, and path.
By way of association, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance, fifteen conditions are exclusively present.
The conditions of proximity, contiguity, repetition, absence, and disappearance are exclusively past. The kamma condition is either past or present.
However, the object, predominance, and strong-dependence conditions belong to all three times and are also timeless.
In this [conditionality], fifteen conditions are present; five are past,
and one alone is future.
One is shown as belonging to two times;
three belong to three times,
and there is also that which is independent of time.
It should be understood that all these twenty-four conditions are included within four conditions— namely, the object, decisive support, kamma, and presence conditions— as appropriate.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Conditions," in the *Abhidhammāvatāra*.
This is the *Abhidhammāvatāra*,
the excellent and supremely profound manual of the Abhidhamma;
it should be heard by a bhikkhu who desires subtle wisdom.
This [work] awakens the discernment of wise intellect,
destroys doubt and delusion,
and dispels the great darkness of evil thoughts.
He is considered by me to be one who produces the radiance of sharp intelligence;
for he is esteemed by Sumati both by name and by his character,
being honored through his solicitude and his sense of dignity.
Therefore, this meditation for the manifestation of welfare has been composed by me, always bringing satisfaction.
Herein, it is [established] both in meaning, in text, and in logical reasoning.
Whether it be improper or contradictory, if anything at all is seen, the wise person,
having examined the preceding and following context and having investigated it again and again,
should include it; it should not be rejected on account of a fault.
For although the modes of expression are threefold and the paths are twofold,
therefore, after careful investigation, it must be understood by one who possesses discernment:
[the teaching] unmixed with the tenets of other schools and free from confusion.
Since the meaning has been elucidated here, connected with sweet syllables and based on the oral tradition of the Mahāvihāravāsins,
therefore one who desires their own welfare should pay careful attention to this.
By whatever merit has been acquired by me through this work, performed with the desire for the endurance of the True Dhamma,
may all living beings attain happiness.
And may this [work] reach its fulfillment according to its purpose, without any obstacles.
Likewise, may all living beings attain success through their noble intentions.
In this place crowded with throngs of men and women, filled with various unadulterated families,
prosperous, endowed with every excellence, and possessing clear, white, and cool waters—
In the delightful city of Kāverīpaṭṭana, filled with various gems,
crowded with diverse market-stalls, adorned with many beautiful parks,
and graced by palaces shaped like the peaks of Mount Kelāsa.
Caused to be built by Kaṇhadāsa— beautifying and delightful—
with various kinds of lovely walls and gate-towers;
there, in the Eastern Palace, I always resided.
This [work], free from harshness and devoid of boastfulness, adorned with virtues such as moral discipline,
was well-composed by the wise and virtuous one when requested.
May the gods rain at the proper time, and may the clouds that bring the rain pour down their showers.
May the protectors of the earth guard the entire world according to the Dhamma.
As long as Himavat, the supreme mountain, stands in the world,
so long may the True Dhamma endure, for the sake of the Teacher, the King of Dhamma.
This work titled *Abhidhammāvatāra* (The Entrance to the Abhidhamma) was composed by the teacher Bhadanta Buddhadatta, a resident of Uragapura, who was perfected in virtue and conduct.
The *Abhidhammāvatāra* is completed.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Exposition of Name-and-Form:
The Introduction to the Treatise.
The Dhamma, perfectly and fully awakened to, and the Dhamma that illuminates it;
Having paid homage to the Saṅgha, the most excellent in the world and worthy of veneration,
I shall briefly explain the "Analysis of Name and Form" (Nāmarūpapariccheda),
based on the method of commentary of the Mahāvihāravāsins.
Chapter One: Analysis of the Threefold Designation.
Therein, it is held that [the ultimate reality] is threefold: consciousness, mental factors, and Nibbāna.
Name and form are twofold, distinguished as the primary elements and derived matter.
Therein, consciousness is fourfold according to the divisions of the sense-sphere plane and so forth;
the fifty-two factors associated with the mind are considered mental concomitants.
The elements of eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness;
the receiving consciousness; and likewise the two types of investigating consciousness—those accompanied by joy and those accompanied by equanimity.
Thus, the rootless consciousnesses are eightfold:
the wholesome and the results [of wholesome kamma]. Among these, excluding the investigating consciousness associated with joy, one should designate those same seven as unwholesome resultants.
The five-door adverting consciousness, the mind-door adverting consciousness,
and that which is called "laughing"— these three types of functional consciousness are said to be rootless. Thus, the eighteenfold mind is with roots.
By way of its fundamental divisions, unwholesome consciousness is considered to be threefold:
it is distinguished as being accompanied by joy, accompanied by equanimity,
and further divided into that which is associated with wrong view and that which is dissociated from it.
Furthermore, it is divided eightfold into "without volitional effort" and "with volitional effort";
therein they declare the unwholesome mind to have greed as its root.
[That which is] accompanied by displeasure and conjoined with aversion;
The root of hatred is twofold: that with volitional formation and that without volitional formation.
That accompanied by doubt and that associated with restlessness are likewise twofold.
The root of delusion is also twofold, being conjoined with equanimity.
Thus one should discern the twelve unwholesome states of consciousness;
thereafter, having set aside the rootless evil states, [one should consider] the beautiful states,
namely those accompanied by joy and likewise those accompanied by equanimity.
It is analyzed as twofold, being either associated with knowledge or dissociated from it;
furthermore, it is divided eightfold as being without effort or with effort;
these exist within the sense-sphere realms of wholesome, resultant, and functional states accompanied by roots.
In the sense-sphere, there are twenty-three resultant [consciousnesses], twenty meritorious and demeritorious, and eleven functional;
thus, in total, there are fifty-four.
Furthermore, that which is accompanied by applied thought, sustained thought, zest, happiness, and one-pointedness...
The first jhāna consists of the wholesome, the resultant, and likewise the functional.
The second is inferior by way of initial application (vitakka); the third, however, is inferior by way of sustained application (vicāra);
the fourth is inferior by way of zest (pīti), being endowed with equanimity and one-pointedness.
The fifth [dhyāna] is proclaimed as the form-sphere (rūpāvacara) in fifteen ways;
however, the fifth dhyāna alone is the single formless-sphere (arūpāvacara).
[This consists of] the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana), as well as the meritorious, ripening, and functional [types].
The base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness,
and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception— these would thus be twelvefold.
Then there is the path-consciousness of stream-entry, and likewise the fruit-consciousness.
The once-returner, the non-returner, and Arahantship— thus [the path] is eightfold.
By dividing each of these fivefold according to the application of the jhāna factors,
the unsurpassed consciousness in its full detail becomes fortyfold.
The fine-material-sphere consciousnesses, as well as the supramundane ones to be grasped, occur in the divisions of the first and subsequent jhānas;
the formless-sphere consciousness also occurs in the fifth.
Thus, there are twelve unwholesome states and twenty-one wholesome states.
There are thirty-six resultant states and twenty functional consciousnesses.
Thus, consciousness is of one hundred and twenty-one kinds, or alternatively, of eighty-nine types;
and likewise, the mental factors are divided according to their association with that consciousness.
Contact, feeling, perception, volition, and likewise one-pointedness;
life-faculty and attention are considered common to all [consciousnesses].
Discernment, investigation, resolution, energy, desire, and joy;
The miscellaneous factors are explained as six, being similar to the thirteen [mental concomitants].
The miscellaneous factors do not exist in consciousness; applied thought (vitakka) is absent from the second jhāna and above;
sustained thought (vicāra) is absent from the third jhāna and above; while resolution (adhimokkha) is absent in one who is possessed of doubt.
In the triad of investigating mind-elements, energy is likewise [the predominant factor];
in the fourth with pleasure, joy; and in the deluded state regarding the cause, desire.
Sixty-six, fifty-five, eleven, and sixteen;
One should illuminate those seventy and twenty states of consciousness:
delusion, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, and restlessness give rise to all evil;
envy, avarice, remorse, and hatred likewise arise from aversion.
Greed and greed itself, as well as views—both those associated with views and those dissociated from them;
conceit, and sloth-and-torpor: these are found among the five [factors] accompanied by volitional formations.
Doubt is present when there is uncertainty. These are the fourteen unwholesome [mental factors].
Among the twelve unwholesome states, these are established as being invariably absent:
faith, mindfulness, moral shame, moral dread, non-greed, non-hatred, and equanimity;
as well as tranquility, lightness, and malleability of body and mind.
Workability, proficiency, and buoyancy— these six pairs,
nineteen states in total, which are inseparable from one another,
occur in the fifty-nine beautiful types of consciousness.
Right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these are the abstinences.
In the supramundane path, all are always present together; in the beautiful sense-sphere realm, they are separate.
Compassion and appreciative joy exist separately in the fine-material realm, excluding the fifth [jhāna].
Sometimes in wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses, sometimes in functional consciousnesses with roots.
Wisdom is found in all types of three-rooted consciousnesses.
These twenty-five factors—faith and the rest—are the beautiful (sobhana) states.
Envy, avarice, remorse, abstinence, compassion, and so forth arise diversely at times;
likewise pride and sloth-torpor arise together.
Seven factors arise in all [consciousnesses], while six factors arise as appropriate.
The beautiful [states] are found only among the fourteen unwholesome states and only among the beautiful states themselves. Thus, having classified these fifty-two mental phenomena,
the wise person should discern them individually as they arise.
And those other than the beautiful factors are common [to all], except for the abstinences in the first jhāna;
reasoning and investigation are excluded from the second and so on;
joy is excluded from the third and so on; and compassion and the rest are excluded from the fifth.
Having abandoned [the lower fetters], one should not separate them,
but rather condense them into five groups. Thirty-five, thirty-four, thirty-three,
and then thirty-two and thirty respectively arise in the sublime realms.
Having taken all the abstinences and having abandoned compassion and the rest,
one should likewise count them as fivefold in the first jhāna, and so on for the second and subsequent ones,
excluding applied thought and the rest; thus, there are thirty-six [factors] in due order.
Thirty-five, thirty-four, two sets of thirty-three, and more.
In the wholesome and functional [consciousnesses] of the sense-sphere, excluding the beautiful, the others are common to both;
likewise, excluding the abstinences from the resultants, the abstinences, compassion, and so forth are common.
In [states] associated with knowledge, there are mental joys; in those dissociated from knowledge, they are excluded.
In states accompanied by equanimity, joy is absent; in dissociated states, both are absent.
Thus, one should count the pairs in each of the three types in four ways.
Some say that when equanimity is not present, there are compassion and the others.
In the wholesome [consciousness], there are thirty-eight, thirty-seven, two sets of thirty-six, and thirty-five;
in the functional, there are two sets of thirty-four and thirty-three.
In the resultant [consciousness], there would be thirty-three, thirty-two,
and thirty-one [factors] respectively, in the wholesome, resultant, and functional minds of the sense-sphere accompanied by roots.
Delusion and the others are common [to all], while greed and views are present in the first.
In the third [jhāna], nineteen arise with greed and conceit;
eighteen are devoid of joy in the fifth and likewise in the seventh;
in the ninth, twenty [arise] with hatred, worry, and stinginess.
Those mentioned in the first [jhāna] and so forth arise in the second and subsequent ones;
with sloth and torpor, there are twenty-one, twenty, and twenty-two transcendences respectively.
With the exclusion of desire and rapture, and for one who is doubtful, it occurs without certainty.
One should contemplate the foul things for fifteen moments while in doubt.
When one is settled and free from desire, there are twelve or eleven moments;
having abandoned rapture, there is resolution in the crossing over to bliss through energy.
Having abandoned the dyad, there is the mind-element; ten [factors] are present in equanimity and investigation;
seven are common to all; and five arise from the sense-consciousnesses.
Thus they are produced in the mind.
Fifty-two mental factors (cetasika-dhammas) are to be known according to their respective categories,
distinguished by the various types of consciousness.
The wise describe the deathless Nibbāna as having three aspects:
emptiness (suññatā), the signless (animitta), and likewise the desireless (appaṇihita).
It is that which, when taken as its object, causes the unsurpassed mind to proceed toward it.
The "liberation through emptiness, etc. is obtained from the perspective of its name and its object.
Furthermore, it is twofold by way of classification: the element of nibbāna with residue remaining and the other, the element of nibbāna without residue remaining.
This Nibbāna, which has emerged from the mouth [of the Buddha], has absolute peace as its characteristic;
it has the function of providing consolation and is grasped through its state of security.
It is called "Nibbāna" because it inclines [toward extinction]; others incline toward it.
There are fifty-three names, and in every way, fifty-four.
This method of connecting mind and mental factors—
this supreme mind— is thus elucidated.
Keeping this well in mind, the wise become upholders of the excellent teaching;
they have plunged into the wisdom of enlightenment set forth by the Buddha.
Having plunged into the entire Abhidhamma, which contains all phenomena, and having immersed myself in the collection of names without exception,
I have here compiled and diligently arranged everything.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Analysis of the Threefold Name," in the Exposition of Name-and-Form. 2.
The Second Chapter.
The Analysis of Characteristics, Functions, and Manifestations:
Intrinsic nature is called the characteristic; the successful performance of its function is its function;
its mode of being grasped is its manifestation; and the proximate cause is its footing.
They are comprised of self-apprehension and attainment in their actual meaning;
they are distinguished by their characteristics, functions, manifestations, conventional usage, and mental application.
Therefore, among the fifty-three entities, one should understand their classification as appropriate.
Hereafter, I shall explain [consciousness] by way of its characteristics and other aspects.
It is called *citta* because it "thinks" (*cinteti*) regarding existence, or because it is merely the act of thinking (*cintana*);
or else, because those associated with it think, and because it has that which is thought as its object.
"Phusati" (it touches) refers to contact (*phassa*) in the sense of becoming, or it is simply the act of touching;
or else, those associated with it touch their respective objects.
Thus, [the term] is used appropriately for the agent, the state of being, and the instrument.
Among the fifty-three categories, the etymological derivation of "sound" (sadda) is according to the method.
Mind (citta) has the characteristic of cognizing its object; it is grasped as having the function of reflection and the manifestation of thought.
It is understood through the method of "reflection" (cintā-kappa).
Contact has the characteristic of touching, its function is the convergence with an object,
and its essence is impact. In that regard:
"Conjunction" (sannipāta) is understood [as contact].
It has feeling as its objective essence and the characteristic of being felt;
it has the experience of the range [of objects] as its essence and is understood as "experiencing."
Perception is the grasping of an aspect; it has the characteristic of perceiving.
Its function is the production of a sign; it is understood as having the nature of discernment.
Volition is the mental effort; it has the characteristic of activity.
Its function is the accumulation of kamma; it is grasped as "provisioning.
One-pointedness is non-distraction; its characteristic is the absence of a separate nutriment;
its function is unification; it is grasped as "combining" the mind.
Vitality has the characteristic of maintaining those things born together with it;
its function is living, and it is grasped as the bond of life.
Mindfulness has the characteristic of attending; its function is mental attention.
The function of binding is understood as the application of the mind.
Vitakka has the characteristic of directing; it has the function of impelling the mind toward its object and is understood as the act of fixing [the mind] firmly.
Investigation has the characteristic of inquiry and the characteristic of repeated reflection;
its function is the application of the mind, and it is grasped as equanimity toward the object.
Resolution is the absence of wavering, having the characteristic of firm conviction.
It has the characteristic of being firm in conduct and is grasped as having the function of making one steadfast.
Energy, however, is effort; it has the characteristic of great exertion, the function of not shrinking from what is to be done, and is grasped as providing support.
Zeal is based upon an object and is characterized by the desire to act;
its function is the seeking of an object, and it is understood as "taking hold with the hand.
It is co-nascent, diffusive, and characterized by endearment.
Rapture (*pīti*) has the characteristic of swelling the essence [of the mind] and is understood as gladness (*pāmojja*).
Faith (*saddhā*) has the characteristic of trusting the mind and is characterized by conviction in what is real;
it has the function of leaping toward the beneficial and is understood as resolute confidence (*adhimutti*).
Non-forgetfulness regarding intrinsic natures, having the characteristic of retention, and having the function of not causing the loss of phenomena—this is understood as heedfulness (*appamāda*).
Moral shame (*hirī*) is disgust toward evil states; it has the characteristic of shrinking away from them.
Shame (*hirī*) has the characteristic of shrinking back from evil;
it is understood as having the function of shrinking away from evil. Fear of wrongdoing (*ottappa*) has the characteristic of agitation and dread;
it is understood as having the function of shrinking back from evil due to fear, and its essence is distrust.
Non-greed is non-attachment, characterized by the absence of possessiveness;
its function is to proceed with liberation, and it is understood as non-clinging.
Non-hatred is kindness of heart, characterized by the absence of malice.
Its function is gentle engagement, and it is understood as a state of mildness.
Non-delusion has the characteristic of penetrating;
its function is the illumination of the object, and it is understood as awakening.
Therein, equanimity is neutrality; its characteristic is balancing.
Its function is not to fall into partiality; it is grasped as even-flowing.
Tranquillity of body and mind has the characteristic of the absence of distress.
Its function is non-distraction, and it is grasped as coolness.
Lightness of body and mind has the characteristic of non-slowness;
its function is non-extension, and it is grasped as a state of being very light.
Pliability is the characteristic of both body and mind, defined by the absence of rigidity;
its function is the non-obstruction of activity, and it is understood as being "conducive.
Adaptability is the characteristic of both, defined by fitness for their respective functions.
Its function is the excellence of continuity, and it is understood as the state of being fit for yoga.
Likewise, the proficiency of the two [mind and body] has the characteristic of clarity;
its function is easy occurrence, and it is understood as the state of mastery.
Ujutā (straightness) has the characteristic of being non-crooked in body and mind;
it has the function of crushing crookedness and is understood as upright conduct.
Sammāvācā (right speech) is purity of speech, characterized by restraint in speech.
Wrong speech has the nature of death for the immortals and is grasped as the boundary of speech.
Right action is pure in performance and is characterized by right doing;
wrong action has the nature of death for the immortals and is grasped as the boundary of performance.
Right livelihood is characterized by purity and is marked by the avoidance of wrong livelihood;
wrong livelihood has the taste of death and is understood as improper conduct.
