Compassion toward distressed beings is characterized by the removal of their suffering.
Compassion has the characteristic of wishing for welfare; it is grasped as having the function of sympathy.
Appreciative joy has the characteristic of rejoicing in those who are well-established in happiness;
it is grasped as having the function of mental expansion and the manifestation of non-enmity.
Greed is the agitation of the mind, characterized by non-renunciation;
its function is the coveting of an object, and it is understood as "clinging.
Hatred is the corruption of the mind, characterized by malice.
Its function is the striking against an object, and it is grasped as ferocity.
Delusion is the confusion of the mind;
its characteristic is that of being bewildered.
Its function is the concealment of intrinsic nature, and it is understood as being blind. Moral shame (*hirī*) is disgust for evil;
its characteristic is the state of being modest. Its function is the avoidance of misconduct; its manifestation is the absence of impudence.
It is understood as having the characteristic of seizing upon impurity,
with the function of concealing evil. It is understood as "shamelessness" (pāgabbha), characterized by lack of agitation,
lack of moral dread, and lack of trepidation, with the function of leaping into evil.
View is a firm perversion; it has the characteristic of misapprehension.
Its function is the adherence to what is hollow; it is understood as a wrong grasp.
One who conceives "I am" possesses the characteristic of elation.
Its function is the grasping of a banner; it is understood as "I-making.
Envy regarding the success of others has the characteristic of an intolerant attitude;
its function is the shrinking of the mind; it is understood as "aversion."
Avarice regarding possessions has the characteristic of concealment;
it is understood as "miserliness" (veviccha), having the function of not enduring the state of a recluse.
Sloth (thīna) is the crushing of the mind; it has the characteristic of sinking down.
Its function is the breaking of energy; it is understood as "contractedness.
Torpor has the characteristic of deluding co-nascent states;
its function is the breaking of strength; it is understood as "sickness."
Restlessness is the distraction of the mind, characterized by lack of tranquility;
it has the function of preventing mental stability and is understood as a state of wavering.
Remorse is regret, characterized by subsequent sorrow.
Its function is self-reproach, and it is grasped as remorse.
Doubt is wavering; its characteristic is indecisiveness;
its function is to plunge into various possibilities, and it is grasped as being without a firm foundation.
Thus, the wise person should discern, by means of characteristics and so forth,
the characteristic of the mode of intrinsic nature among the fifty-three intrinsic natures.
Those skilled in the meaning of characteristics [should do so] regarding their own specific characteristics.
Even though the ultimate purpose is the characteristic itself,
they have described it by way of its characteristics and so forth,
solely for the sake of easily grasping those characteristics.
Having followed this very meaning, I have here stated it in many ways for the purpose of leading to the goal of the meanings of those [teachings].
May one here desire knowledge through the methods of the words and their underlying principles.
[This concludes] for those who desire the meaning, the method, and the purpose of the Buddha’s word.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled “The Analysis of Characteristics, Functions, and Manifestations,” in the *Nāmarūpapariccheda*.
3. The Third Chapter:
The Analysis of Classification and Compendium.
Thus, regarding those very things that possess the nature of classification, there is again their compendium.
Henceforth, I shall explain [the teaching] by way of its intrinsic natures and specific instances.
Having gathered together the concordant phenomena through his unique knowledges, the Visionary Teacher, the discernor of objects, demonstrated them.
In the sense of being an adherence to views, and because it is a distorted grasping of the true nature of things as they really are,
this supreme ignorance is called "clinging" (*parāmāsa*).
Because of its impurity as a defilement, it is like the scum that covers a wound.
Anointing the continuum, they are declared to flow.
Craving for sensual pleasure, craving for existence, views, and ignorance are the taints (āsava);
four by way of being taints, and three phenomena by way of their intrinsic nature.
These very things are called "slaughters," flowing out from the gates;
having spread abroad, they lead to ruin, carrying away living beings.
And these indeed are called "bonds" that bind living beings to existence.
Connected by clinging to the door-posts, bound as if by a mechanical device,
they seize the continuity of existence like a *māluvā* creeper seizing a great tree;
they grasp their firm support like a snake seizing a frog.
Craving for sense-pleasures and views are the fourfold types of clinging;
views are further divided into views, rules and observances, and the doctrine of self.
Those who bind body to body are difficult to release, being entangled in their pursuit.
The bodily knots are said to be craving, ill will, and views.
The adherence to rules and observances is thus distinguished as a view;
this insistence on "this alone is the truth" is fourfold in this way.
They obstruct renunciation and are hindrances to meditation;
they are like a membrane covering an egg, and they are called "envelopers.
Sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, and doubt—these are the five hindrances.
Ignorance, restlessness, and remorse are considered hindrances.
Having seized hold of what is deep, they plunge in and proceed;
they cause the continuity of the stream to flow like a river—thus it has been said.
Sensual lust, lust for existence, aversion, conceit, views, doubt, and ignorance—
these seven are considered the six underlying tendencies (anusaya). By means of the binding of doors,
objects, and fetters, they keep living beings within the circle of existence.
The fetters have been declared, like snares binding birds:
lust for sense-pleasures, form, and formlessness; aversion, delusion, and doubt;
views, rules and observances, conceit, and restlessness—these constitute the ten.
By including greed for the fine-material and immaterial realms and restlessness— excluding them from the Abhidhamma list—
and by adding stinginess for one who craves existence, they would become tenfold.
They defile the mental continuum and bring harm to living beings.
"They arise together with the defilements"—thus the defilements are explained.
Greed, hatred, and delusion;
views, conceit, and doubt.
With sloth, lack of moral shame, lack of moral dread,
and restlessness, there would be ten [factors].
Here, greed and wrong view are explained as not being included among the nine.
Ignorance is included in seven [factors], aversion in five;
doubt is included in four, pride and restlessness in three;
sloth is included in two, and remorse is included in one.
Shamelessness and lack of moral dread are twofold, as is envy mixed with them;
thus, in this way, they are said to be tenfold when included among the evil states.
They are also comprised under the categories of misapprehensions, taints, floods, bonds, acquisitions, and fetters.
From the perspective of the underlying tendencies to be suppressed,
from the perspective of fetters and defilements, there are fourteen in brief, but fifty-seven in detail;
one should apply these to the arising of consciousness according to the sequence of the phenomena.
Beyond that, one should explain the inclusion of those other than the unwholesome, distinguished by the categories of non-restraint and so forth:
mind, mental factors, matter, and Nibbāna.
Thus, having understood this supreme compendium of unwholesome phenomena, [one should proceed].
How are those called "mixed" to be understood according to their occurrence?
Greed, hatred, and delusion—
these three are exclusively unwholesome.
Non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion,
as well as the wholesome and the indeterminate,
are conditions for stability, like roots on the side of a tree.
The six root-conditions (hetu-dhammas) are explained as being the fundamental nature of phenomena:
initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), rapture (pīti), one-pointedness (ekaggatā),
and the feelings of joy (somanassa), grief (domanassa), and equanimity (upekkhā).
"Reflecting upon what has been struck, they are conditions in the sense of reflecting;
the Teacher called them 'states of jhāna' because of their fivefold substantial nature.
Right view, intention, effort, and the threefold abstinence..."
Right mindfulness and concentration, as well as wrong view and their arising, and right and wrong guidance—
these are conditions in the sense of leading out.
They are declared to be the twelve path-factors, though by way of intrinsic nature they are nine phenomena.
While manifesting personal existence, they successively take up nutriment consisting of nutritive essence,
the eightfold [material] qualities, feeling, rebirth-linking, and name-and-form.
This is physical food.
Contact, volition, and likewise consciousness—
these four are declared to be nutriments.
Of co-nascent phenomena, they are conditions in the sense of faculties;
likewise, they are followers in the sense of a self and a lord.
Faith, mindfulness, wisdom, energy, and one-pointedness as well—
Feeling, life, and mind, and the eight material faculties. How is it that life is one,
yet feeling is divided into pleasure and pain,
joy, grief, and equanimity?
In the path beginning with wisdom, there is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown";
in the middle, the faculty of final knowledge; and likewise at the end, the faculty of one who has already known.
These sixteen are established by their own nature through the analysis of the meaning of the faculties.
"They are called faculties"—thus it was said; one should discern them as twenty-two.
With a continuum firmly established, they are unshakable by opposing states;
by virtue of their powerful nature, they are declared to be the "powers."
Faith, mindfulness, moral shame, moral dread, energy, one-pointedness,
wisdom, non-greed, and non-hate— thus they are considered ninefold.
Faith is the eldest, in the sense of being the forerunner in the occurrence of both merit and demerit.
By way of the predominance of conditions, four predominances are stated—
namely, desire, consciousness, energy, and investigation— according to their respective natures as predominant factors for co-nascent states as appropriate.
Wisdom is comprised of five factors, while effort and one-pointedness are comprised of four;
the mind is comprised of four, and mindfulness is comprised of three.
Volition, feeling, and faith are considered to be comprised of two factors.
The remaining twenty-eight are spoken of as single-groupings;
thus, the sevenfold classification of the mixed grouping has been stated.
Likewise, [the factors] are classified by way of cause, jhāna-factor, path-factor, nutriment, and faculty.
By way of predominance, by the mixture of merit, demerit, and so forth,
and by their own intrinsic nature— thus, having summarized them as thirty-six, one should subsequently analyze them in detail according to their sixty-four divisions.
Regarding the classification of the arising of consciousness according to their possible occurrences:
The consciousnesses of adverting to the cold [object], receiving, and investigating—these eighteen are rootless;
those that are deluded have a single root.
The remaining wholesome consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge are two-rooted;
forty-seven other types of consciousness-arising are three-rooted.
Those in the midst of the fivefold sense-consciousness are said to possess two jhāna-factors.
The fourth and fifth jhānas are considered the third jhāna;
the second [set] consists of four jhānas, excluding pleasure in the sense-sphere;
while the first [set] consists of five jhānas, including pleasure in the sense-sphere.
The first supramundane jhāna is considered to possess eight path-factors;
the remaining supramundane jhānas are said to possess seven path-factors.
The first mundane jhāna, as well as those in the sense-sphere with three roots, are likewise [considered].
The types of consciousness-arising known as "possessing five path-factors" have been explained.
The remainder— namely, sublime jhāna associated with wrong view,
as well as those dissociated from knowledge— are considered to possess four path-factors.
Associated with aversion and restlessness, and dissociated from views;
the three path-factors and two path-factors are declared to be accompanied by doubt.
Paths are not without roots, nor is there mental stability in one accompanied by doubt.
The certainty [of nutriment] has been understood, yet it is not explicitly mentioned among worldly matters.
Among sensual pleasures, edible food is absent for those without consciousness;
in all instances of the arising of consciousness, the triad of nutriments is proclaimed.
The wise one should analyze the faculties in nine ways regarding the supramundane;
he should expound them in eight ways regarding the mundane states possessing three roots.
Furthermore, by means of knowledge, he should demonstrate the dissociated states in seven ways.
When there is doubt in five ways regarding the merit of the Sitavaṭṭhabhana offering,
one should direct the mind toward the remaining types of consciousness in four or three ways:
those with three roots have seven powers, while those with two roots have six powers.
Four powers are unwholesome; doubt is considered to have three powers;
two powers belong to the "to-be-eradicated-by-insight" (sita-voṭṭhabbana); the remainder is said to be powerless.
However, in the case of the impulsion (javana) and the predominance (adhipati) factors within a three-rooted (tihetuka) consciousness, whichever one [is present]...
In wholesome states with two roots, investigation is not found.
In worldly resultant states,
which are rooted in delusion and are rootless;
Because they do not arise simultaneously,
there is no dominant condition whatsoever for bodily consciousness. In the ripening of merit, however, the faculty of pleasure arises [as a dominant condition].
The faculty of pain (dukkhindriya) is also spoken of in that same context, within the ripening of evil karma.
There are sixteen types of mental joy (somanassa):
investigation (santīraṇa) and laughter (hasana), as well as those associated with the first through fourth jhānas. These constitute the sixteen types of joy.
Only two types of consciousness-arising have been explained as associated with displeasure (*domanassa*);
all others, however, are associated with equanimity (*upekkhā*).
Having thus analyzed the association with feeling (*vedanā*) in eight ways:
The arising of consciousness has been explained through the distinctions of causes, associations, and so forth.
One should now understand each of these— both individually and in combination— according to their specific separations and mixtures,
following the method as previously stated and according to what is possible.
Having thus applied [the analysis] to the mixed types of consciousness-arising,
one should then know those that are pure, comprised within the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya),
and as appropriate for the body, feelings, mind, and mental objects.
The foul, suffering, impermanence, and non-self are well-established.
Right mindfulness, through the distinction of its functions and its objective spheres,
is proclaimed as fourfold under the name of the foundations of mindfulness.
And for the abandoning of evil that has arisen and the non-arising of that which has not yet arisen;
or, for the production and growth of those [wholesome states] that have not yet arisen and have arisen—
exertion belongs to one who strives, distinguished by its function and its manifestation.
They are proclaimed as four by the name of "right exertion" (sammappadhāna).
Because they serve as the basis for supernormal power (iddhi), they are called "bases of power" (iddhipāda);
they are fourfold: zeal (chanda), consciousness (citta), energy (vīriya), and investigation (vīmaṃsā).
Faith, mindfulness, wisdom, energy, and likewise one-pointedness:
in the sense of faculties they are the faculties, and in the sense of powers they are the powers.
Mindfulness, the investigation of phenomena, as well as energy and joy;
Tranquility, unification, and desire are [factors] because they possess the nature of awakening.
Seven specific states are proclaimed as "factors of awakening" (bojjhaṅga);
in the sense of leading out, the eight factors beginning with right view are the "factors of the path" (maggaṅga).
Herein, effort is a fivefold aggregate, mindfulness and wisdom are impelled [by it];
concentration is called a fourfold aggregate.
Faith is said to be a twofold aggregate; the remaining factors are each single aggregates.
Thus, in this way, the sevenfold classification of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya) is summarized:
the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power,
the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the divisions of the path have been explained.
Concentration, mind, and equanimity; faith, tranquility, and joy;
right view and intention, effort, and the threefold abstinence;
right mindfulness and concentration—thus are the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyā) illuminated.
There are fourteen factors by way of their nature, and thirty-seven by way of their classification.
By means of these factors, one who awakens penetrates the Truths;
they are complete and unsurpassed, being free from both discursive thought and rapture.
They are obtained in the preliminary stage as well, according to what is appropriate for the mundane;
and at the time of the development of penetration, during the occurrence of the sixfold purification.
Thus, one should discern these three types of divisions as they are appropriate.

The "Gateway to Analysis and Synthesis" has been elucidated for the sake of the supreme method of analysis and synthesis within the Teaching that liberates through analysis and synthesis— a teaching praised by those wise in analysis and synthesis as the inclusion,
by way of commonality, of things distinguished by their intrinsic natures.
Thus, those whose minds are adorned with the manifestation of the Dhamma,
having become wise in the analysis of the specific nature of phenomena, partake in the taste of the Dhamma— the Dhamma of the teaching that is supreme among all things.
Thus ends the section on the Analysis of Classification and Compendium within the *Nāmarūpapariccheda*.
The Third Chapter. 4.
The Fourth Chapter:
The Analysis of Miscellaneous Topics.
From here on, [the exposition is given] according to function, the doors, objects, and bases;
according to plane and person, the occasions, and the producers as appropriate;
and according to inclusion and occurrence in rebirth-linking and the course of existence.
By way of the arising of consciousness alone, [the process] is summarized and concluded.
The great resultant states of the fine-material and immaterial realms, equanimity, the two types of investigation,
death, rebirth-linking, and the life-continuum— these are nineteen types of consciousness.
Adverting is a pair, as are seeing and hearing;
smelling and tasting, as well as touching and receiving.
Three are the investigating consciousnesses, and one is held to be determining.
In the five doors and the mind door,
one should specify fifty-five functions of impulsion (javana); these consist of wholesome,
unwholesome, and resultant [impulsions], excluding functional and adverting consciousness.
The cittas having that as their object are indeed eleven:
the eight great resultant cittas and the three investigating cittas.
They declare that there are five functions, including the two investigating [cittas] accompanied by equanimity.
The great resultants have four functions; the sublime states have three functions.

"Two functions" refers to the determining consciousness; "pleasant investigation" is what has been described. Furthermore, there is the triad consisting of the five sense-consciousnesses, the javanas, and the mind-element.
The sixty-eight wise ones declare that they have a single function;
thus, by way of the distinction of functions, the arising of consciousness is determined.
The elements of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body are, respectively:
The life-continuum has five doors, while the mind-door is said to have six.

The three beginning with the nose [olfactory, gustatory, and tactile] have their objects in the material realm; likewise, the five beginning with the eye [visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile] have their objects in both realms.
In the immaterial realm, neither exists; there, the mind takes that [immaterial state] as its object.
There are six process-consciousnesses for the six doors, and seven for the sense-sphere and fine-material realms.
For the three doors, there are six consciousnesses; for the mind-door and the immaterial realms, there are [the remaining].
Indeed, those beginning with rebirth-linking persist until the end as death.
Having interrupted the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) in its midst, a cognitive process (vīthi) arises for each [object].
When the eye-sensitivity and so forth are struck by a visible form as an object,
there arise the adverting consciousness and the others, following the two vibrations of the life-continuum.
In the transformation of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), when the object is fit for apprehension, a cognitive process (vīthi) arises in the mind-door accordingly as it occurs. [The stages are:
adverting, the fivefold sense-cognition, receiving, and investigating.
The determining consciousness with sense-desire as its object,
and the mind-consciousness having that as its object— thus there are seven process-thoughts and fourteen thought-arising moments in detail at the five doors, as appropriate.
By virtue of arising, presence, and dissolution, there are three moments of consciousness;
for material phenomena, there is a duration of forty-nine [moments].
In the dyads, there are two: "limited" and "limited," and "great" and "great."
The determining consciousness and the functional javanas follow in succession, taking that same object.
In the mind-door, however, when the object is clear, the adverting consciousness and the javanas take that same object; in detail, they number sixty-seven.
When there is a restriction regarding the objects of the thirty-seven impulsion-consciousnesses in the sense-sphere,
and when those objects are very prominent, that [consciousness] is said to have them as its object.
In the five doors, the mind-element occurs individually according to the sequence.
The pair of fivefold sense-cognitions has been explained individually.
However, in the mind-door, there is impulsion that is sublime or supramundane;
in the six doors, there is limited impulsion, which is easy to discern and to arouse.
The great resultant consciousnesses and the two types of equanimous investigating consciousness arise at the six doors, both within the cognitive process and occasionally as process-freed.
There are seventy process-consciousnesses, while the sublime resultants are [eight].
Both types, including those free from the nine paths,
are thus described as tenfold according to the distinction of doors. Having explained them in this way by way of the doors,
one should thereafter understand the arising of consciousnesses according to their appropriate objects.
Visible form, sound, odor, flavor, and tangible object are the five objective spheres (gocara);
the remainder—both the designation of form and the mental object (nāma)—are the sphere of mental phenomena (dhamma).
That which occurs at the five doors has, respectively, those five as its objects.
At the mind-door, there is an object that is past or even future. Furthermore,
that which consists of past designations and present occurrences, as well as what is grasped by the six doors—
namely, that which is reckoned as the six objects— mostly pertains to another existence.
For the mind-element and the courses of action involving signs, karma alone is the object;
likewise for rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death, as appropriate.
In the case of the five [sense] objects, the mind-element takes each one in its respective order.
The five pairs of consciousnesses have been explained individually.
The remaining [consciousnesses] ripen in the sense-sphere (kāma); laughing occurs in the limited (paritta) [realm];
and the stainless impulsive moments (javana) are meritorious deeds devoid of knowledge.
Wholesome kamma of the sense-sphere with three roots, mundane direct-knowledge,
and all [mental states] that arise taking all objects proceed without the highest path and fruit.
Functional direct-knowledge, the determining consciousness, and functional [consciousness] with three roots in the sense-sphere [proceed likewise].
All [mental states] proceed with an object; they become stainless in Nibbāna.
The second and fourth [jhānas] occur in the sublime immaterial attainments;
other sublime states occur in conventional discourse. This is the method regarding objects.
By means of the bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and heart,
seven elements are dependent upon these six bases in the sensual world.
And as for the five consciousness-elements, they possess the relationship of preceding and succeeding one another.
The mind-element and the remaining [elements], as well as the mind-consciousness-element.
Four elements exist in the realm of form, supported by three bases;
but in the formless realm, only one element proceeds without support.
It is explained that, depending on each of the five pasāda [senses] respectively and in due order, there arise the five pairs of consciousnesses (pañcaviññāṇayugalā).
The remaining [processes] have kāma as their object; first, there is the path and the adverting consciousness (āvajjana).
The pleasant [consciousness] belongs to the form realm and is based on a physical basis.
Forty-two types arise depending on a basis, and others arise without depending on one.
It is said that in the formless realm, the resultant types arise without depending on a basis.
Thus have the arising of consciousnesses been explained according to the classification of their bases;
beyond that, the wise person should discern them according to the classification of their planes:
in hell, in the world of ghosts, and likewise among animals and asuras.
They are reborn through the connection of the ripening of evil deeds among the gods who dwell on earth and among humans of low status;
they are born without roots of merit through the connection of the ripening of merit.
The gods of the Four Great Kings, the Tāvatiṃsa, the Yāma;
the Tusita, the Nimmānarati, and the Vasavatti.
Thus they are born among these six classes of devas and among human beings.
Through the link of great karmic fruition, people who have performed meritorious deeds in the realm of desire are born as the Retinue of Brahmā, as well as the Ministers of Brahmā,
and as Great Brahmās, by means of the link of the first jhāna.
The Limited and the Immeasurable-Light, and likewise the Radiant;
these are for the fruition of the second jhāna and for the transition to the third.
The Limited-Beautiful, the Immeasurable-Beautiful, and the Beautiful-Kin;
But in the fourth [station], those belonging to the plane of the third jhāna are born:
the Vehapphalas and the Asaññasattas. In the seven [stations] of the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa), they are born in the fifth [station], excluding the Asaññasattas and the mindless ones.
Aviha, Atappa, Sudassa, Sudassī, and Akaniṭṭha—
these five are proclaimed as the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa).
They correspond respectively to the results of the sphere of infinite space and so forth.
They arise in the planes of the base of infinite space and so forth.
Due to the power of death, rebirth-linking, and the life-continuum, there are sublime resultant states;
and in the sense-sphere, there are also resultant states with roots, because they have those [sublime states] as their object.

According to the method already stated, only one plane arises at a time among all instances of the arising of consciousness; however, those who are non-percipient are not considered [to arise] in this way.
Likewise, the mental consciousness dependent upon the elements of the nose, tongue, and body [arises in the same manner].
Thus, including the two types of aversion, there are eight [consciousnesses] among those desiring sense-pleasures.
Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, and the investigating mind-element arise in the realms of desire and form according to their occurrence, making ten in total.
The volitions of determining, desire, and merit—when dissociated from views—and that which is accompanied by restlessness: in all cases these are fourteen.
Doubt and those associated with views [are absent] in the Pure Abodes.
In the case of the pleasant [resultant], it excludes the sense-sphere javanas, the form-sphere, the formless-sphere, and the states of misery.
In the case of the sense-sphere and functional [states] that possess roots, as well as the three supramundane [paths and fruits], they exclude the formless-sphere.
The fourth formless-sphere javana excludes everything except the states of misery.
One should discern that, having abandoned the fine-material and immaterial jhānas,
as well as the states of loss, one is born respectively in the higher immaterial planes.
Furthermore, the four unsurpassed fruits, beginning with stream-entry, [are attained].
Excluding the Pure Abodes and the states of misery, they are born everywhere.
Excluding the Pure Abodes, the states of misery, and all formless realms,
the first path of the Unsurpassed arises in the remaining places.
Seventy-three [types of craving] are declared to exist among those in the states of misery seeking sense-pleasures;
fifty-five among those in the pure realms seeking form; sixty-nine among those in the realm of form;
forty-six arise among those in the formless realm, each according to their respective case.
Thus have the types of consciousness been explained according to the distinction of planes.

Among those with three roots, all [types] are included; however, among those with two roots and those without roots, one must exclude the limited types, as well as those that are results of knowledge, functional, or swift.
In worldlings there arise views and doubt;
in stream-enterers and those beyond, there arises their respective fruits.
For one free from lust, there is impulsion, the final, unsurpassed functional consciousness.
Repulsion is said to arise even in those who have not crossed over from the state of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).
Due to the speed [of its arising], it applies to the four beginning with the ordinary person. The remaining [factors] are subject to taints (*sāsrava*);
one should understand that for all five, they are subject to taints, faulty, and productive of karmic results.
Among worldlings there are sixty-three;
among the two beginning with stream-enterers, fifty-nine;
among individuals who are non-returners, fifty-seven arise; and thirty-five arise in those free from taints.
One's own path is found among those established on the paths; this is the method regarding individuals.
All rebirth-linkings [occur] following a death in the sense-sphere with three roots;
likewise, rebirth-linkings in the sense-sphere occur following a death with two roots or without roots.
From death in the fine-material sphere, there are rebirth-linkings with roots;
from death in the immaterial sphere, there are rebirth-linkings in the immaterial sphere, excluding the lower immaterial planes.
Likewise in the sense-sphere, there are rebirth-linkings with three roots.
Thus the wise one should apply the method of death and rebirth-linking.
Immediately after death there is rebirth-linking, and thereafter the life-continuum (bhavaṅga);
having then cut that off, there arises adverting (āvajjana).
When undesirable objects occur, the eye-consciousness and its concomitants are solely the result of demerit;
when desirable objects occur, they may be either the result of merit or demerit, according to the circumstances.
One should apply the process of the cognitive series (vīthicitta) in exactly the manner previously explained.
In the five sense-doors as appropriate, and in the mind-door,
the wise one proceeds with investigation toward that object;
it is pleasant when the object is desirable or neutral, and indifferent when the object is undesirable.
That object, accompanied by happiness, arises after the performance of equanimity;
there is no mental distress, but rather joy at all times.
Likewise, that object, accompanied by equanimity, arises after the performance of pleasure.
Elsewhere there is no fixed rule regarding the occurrence of that [feeling] as an object.
When the life-continuum is accompanied by joy, and the impulsion is accompanied by grief,
and that same object does not arise again, there would be equanimity-investigation.
Beyond the preliminary, access, conformity, and change-of-lineage [moments],
the fifth or the fourth impulsion becomes absorption.
It is endowed with the bliss of the four jhānas and follows immediately upon those associated with knowledge.
For those endowed with equanimity and knowledge, the fifth [jhāna] arises as the highest.
For worldlings and trainees, it arises from three-cause wholesome kamma of the sense-sphere;
for those free from lust, absorption arises from three-cause sense-sphere functional kamma.
Mind-door adverting, the fivefold sense-consciousness, receiving, investigating, rebirth-linking, death,
and all the conceptualization of the material and immaterial realms;
for one emerging from cessation, the two higher fruits follow.
The five direct knowledges as well as the paths are considered to last for a single moment of consciousness.
However, for the attainment of cessation, it occurs twice;
at the moment of entry, there is the impulsion of the fourth formless attainment and its object in every respect.
The fruit [of the path] occurs either twice or thrice immediately after the path;
the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and so forth, the determining consciousness (voṭṭhabba), and the impulsion (javana) and so forth, however, occur only once.
But the three-rooted sense-sphere impulsion, when not joined with absorption (appanā), [occurs only once].
It occurs at the mind-door three or four times.
But elsewhere in the six doors, the impulsion born of the sense-sphere element arises—
by way of possibility— for five, six, or seven moments.
In the case of the attainment-mind-moments and the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), no fixed rule has been stated;
however, at the conclusion of a cognitive process (vīthi-citta), there will be either the life-continuum or death (cuti).
Thus, by way of this immediate succession, the persistence of the arising of consciousness and death have been explained.
Having understood and grouped them, how can one calculate according to their possible occurrence?
One should illuminate ten types of consciousness through the five-door adverting;
through the remaining adverting, forty-five are spoken of.
From the fivefold sense-consciousness, there arise two resultant states of receiving that are evil;
from the highest [mental consciousness], one or two resultant states of receiving that are meritorious.
From the investigating consciousness with two roots, twelve resultants are born.
From a three-rooted desirable resultant [citta], twenty-one are said [to arise].
From a fine-material-sphere resultant, at most eighteen;
from a nine-station-arisen resultant, seven or six, respectively.
From the state with aversion (paṭigha), however, there are five; from the state with pleasure (sita), they say there are thirteen;
from the two-rooted wholesome and unwholesome, one should develop twenty-one;
from the two-rooted sense-sphere functional (kiriya), there are eighteen for those with equanimity (upekkhaka).
The wise analyze that from the state of one happy with pleasure there are seventeen [types of consciousness];
from the state of one happy with sensual pleasure and three roots, thirty-three;
and from the state of one happy with equanimity, fifty-three—thus it is declared.
From the wholesome action of the desire realm with three roots, twenty-four types of equanimity arise;
from that which is accompanied by pleasure, however, a wise person should illuminate twenty-five.
Ten, eleven, twelve, and thirteen [arise] from the fine-material realm and the immaterial realm respectively.
One should explain the fifteen formless attainments in their proper order.
It is said that from the fruit there are fourteen, while from the path there is its own fruit;
thus the confident one should reckon the inclusion of the subsequent.
From the fifteenth up to the twenty-first, following that;
from one [moment] arises the fivefold consciousness, and from the fifth, the receiving consciousness.
From the twenty-fifth onwards, there is the investigating consciousness accompanied by pleasure.
From thirty-three [factors], the two types of equanimity and investigation arise.
From forty [factors], there are those with a pleasant result that possess two roots;
likewise, from forty-one [factors], there are those with a pleasant result that possess two roots.
Likewise, forty-one [types of consciousness] in the sense sphere are associated with equanimity;
seventy are accompanied by happiness and possess three roots.
From seventy-two [factors] arise those accompanied by equanimity;
from fifty-nine, the material factors; and from both the resultant and non-resultant [factors], the immaterial ones.
From forty-eight [types of consciousness] by removing one, two, or three,
there are two fruits from the fourfold [set], and the final two fruits from the fivefold.
The sublime impulsions are triple, while the sense-sphere impulsions are twofold with respect to the path.
Thus has the preliminary compendium of the arising of consciousness been enumerated;
this classification of states should be understood as determined by what precedes and follows.
[The sections on] the ripening of form, great ripening, and the investigating mind-element;
It is said that nineteen [types of consciousness] produce only material form.
It is declared that all absorption and javana [consciousness],
whether sublime or supramundane, produce the material forms of the postures.
The registration consciousness, the sense-sphere javanas, and the direct knowledges (abhiññā), as appropriate,
may be the producers of the material phenomena of the postures and intimation. The fivefold sense-consciousness,
the formless-sphere consciousnesses, and the resultants produce nothing at all.
The rebirth-linking of all beings, as well as the death-moment of an Arahant—
thus the mind produces the triad of materiality and so forth even as it is arising itself;
this should be known as the "compendium of producers."
Thus, having condensed the method explained for each individual case among the divisions such as "duties" (kicca) and so forth,
one should analyze it according to the sequence stated.
For one whose stains of delusion have been dispelled regarding the Teaching—
Having grasped the well-scented method from scattered sources and having gathered the miscellaneous teachings,
the wise become those who have cast off all doubt regarding the guidance toward the welfare of others.
Having taken this raft, which is bound by many arguments,
the wise ones have freely crossed the ocean of the Conqueror’s word;
having carried away the essence of the subject matter, which is beneficial for all and capable, they have reached the further shore.
They thoroughly fill the heart, the treasury of jewels.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Analysis of Miscellaneous Matters," in the Investigation of Name-and-Form.
5. The Fifth Chapter:
The Analysis of Karma.
Now, as for the analysis of karmas—
Hereafter, I shall explain,
in brief and for the sake of non-delusion, the classification of the activity of the ripening of kamma.
Regarding "kamma as a condition by way of kamma": it is volition itself that is impelled there.
Furthermore, that volition is both of different moments and specifically meritorious or non-meritorious.
It gives [its fruit] by resolving upon the ripening, according to the appropriate associated states.
For volition exists in the sense of accumulating kamma;
indeed, phenomena that are subject to ripening arise within the continuum of latent defilements.
But for those whose latent tendencies have been abandoned, only mere functional activity proceeds.
The root-constituents of all [consciousness], as well as the two types of adverting,
and those [states] produced by kamma, proceed as results.
By way of the arising of consciousness, kamma is established in thirty-three modes.
The wise one should analyze [kamma] through the fourfold divisions of action— namely, as distinguished by the present life and so forth,

by the dark and so forth, by the productive and so forth, and by the harmful and so forth— and further by the sixfold divisions consisting of those pertaining to the present existence and so forth, and those consisting of sensual pleasures and so forth, respectively.
That evil which is mixed with pleasure and performed without difficulty is an action that brings happiness in the present but produces suffering in the future.
But if evil is performed with difficulty and mixed with suffering...
If merit is performed with difficulty, interspersed with suffering, it results in suffering in the present and produces suffering in the future. But if it is performed with ease,
it results in happiness in the present and produces happiness in the future.
That merit which is intermingled with happiness is performed without difficulty;
it brings happiness in the present and results in happiness in the future.
Likewise, that which is sweet yet mixed with poison, or bitter and poisonous, [is likewise avoided].
The Tathāgatas proclaim that karma is fourfold: as the simile of cow’s urine, honey, and medicine, respectively; distinguished by its undertaking and its ripening, and by pleasure and pain.
Karma such as the deeds of immediate retribution (ānantariya-kamma), which brings exclusively bitter results, is black with black ripening; it leads to the miserable destinies (duggati).
Karma such as that of the first jhāna, which brings exclusively happiness—
"Wholesome with wholesome result" refers to karma that leads to rebirth in the heavenly realms.
"Mixed karma" refers to that which leads to rebirth in mixed states of pleasure and pain.
"Black-and-white" is declared to be that which has black-and-white results.
They shake off both black and white [kamma], which brings about the ripening of both black and white;
this supramundane kamma in the world leads to the destruction of the kamma that determines rebirth.
Thus, within the process of the round of existence, there is the distinction between defilement and purification.
Kamma is said to be fourfold when classified according to the exhaustion of kamma:
namely, productive, supportive, obstructive, and destructive.
Thus, kamma is described as being fourfold by way of its functional differentiation.
One should produce the ripening that generates [the fruit], cut off that which oppresses, promote that which supports, and destroy that which harms. Thus it is said:
"He creates for himself an opportunity for the ripening [of karma]."
But that which is generative is the "maturing-giving" karma;
however, that which is oppressive is the "fructifying" karma.
Others call that which is injurious the "interrupting" karma.
Weighty, proximate, habitual, and that which has been performed—
these are the four kinds of kamma, distinguished by way of their ripening and sequence.
That which is sublime and that which is an immediate (ānantariya) deed is called "weighty" (garuka).
That which was done while one was near to death is called "intentional" (kata).
That which was habitually practiced is called "accustomed" (āciṇṇa) by way of its prevalence.
The remainder—both merit and demerit—is described as "kamma by way of having been performed" (kaṭattā-kamma).
To be experienced in the present life, likewise in the next birth,
or to be experienced subsequently— such is action according to its ripening. Furthermore, there is action that has passed its time,
depending on the timing of its fruition and the lapse of its opportunity.
Thus has the fourfold action been declared by the Kinsman of the Sun:
that which is to be experienced in the present life is the first [type], because it is the impulsion;
yet, due to a lack of repeated practice, it is incapable of producing a result in another existence.
However, that which is to be experienced at rebirth is said to culminate at the end of that very birth;
because the kamma is fully completed, it ripens in the immediately following existence.
But the remaining types of experience are, moreover, experienced in subsequent successive births.
Having obtained their fuel, they produce their result when conditions are present.
Those karmas are called "past" in every respect because their root of craving has been severed,
as well as because of the non-attainment of conditions.
Furthermore, it is described as fourfold according to the distinction of the planes beginning with the sense-sphere (*kāmabhūmi*);
within that, the karma of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacarika*) is twofold by way of merit and demerit.
Among these, demerit is blameworthy and yields undesirable results.
That [kamma] proceeds in two ways through the doors of action and contact.
The wise have spoken of the three doors of action— the door of body, the door of speech,
and the door of mind— and six doors of contact have been illustrated.
In the door of action and the mind-door, the five doors are included;
the door of contact and the mind-door constitute the triad of doors of action.
For likewise, having produced bodily intimation, volition is born.
Bodily action and verbal action— verbal action being that which proceeds through vocal expression—
and that which is accomplished by the two types of intimation (viññatti) are called "mental action.
Thus, this classification of actions is shown according to its various modes.
Action such as killing living beings arises from bodily preoccupation;
likewise, verbal action consists of false speech and so forth.
Covetousness and the like constitute mental action; thus, action is produced through the three doors.
The remaining [doors] are among the two doors; this is the analysis according to the ultimate sense.
The two types of intimation are said to occur at the door of contact and the mind-door;
they do not exist at the five doors. This is the determination in this matter.
Intolerance, ignorance, indolence, immorality, and forgetfulness— thus,
through the breach of restraint, they arise at the eight doors.
There are the three doors of action, and likewise the five other doors.
For the five types of non-restraint, eight doors have been explained.
Therein, that which has reached the level of a kamma-path and brings about rebirth as its fruit,
proceeds in ten ways through the divisions beginning with the destruction of living beings.
Killing living beings, harsh speech, and likewise malice—
thus this threefold action arises from the roots of hatred.
Sexual misconduct, covetousness, and likewise wrong view—
Thus, this threefold karma arises from roots of greed.
Theft, false speech, malicious speech, and slander—
this fourfold karma proceeds from two roots.
"Through desire, hatred, fear, and delusion, living beings commit evil;
therefore, by way of the divisions of desire and so forth, it becomes forty-fold.
Thus they explain demerit, which brings about the four states of misery."
Even when occurring elsewhere, it accomplishes the fruit of misfortune.
However, merit is threefold—blameless and yielding a desirable result:
giving, virtue, and meditation; these arise through the three doors.
Giving is said to arise from great respect, affection, compassion, faith, and gratitude;
it consists of bestowing wealth, livelihood, fearlessness, and the Dhamma.
Merit is performed by one who undertakes virtuous conduct, observances, and the formal precepts.
And for one who refrains from evil, there then arises that which consists of virtue.
That which is distinct from giving and virtue is called "cultivation" (bhāvanā),
because by means of it, they cultivate merit within their continuum, and thereby bring about welfare.
When merit is performed by means of bodily intimation after having prompted it,
then there is bodily action consisting of generosity, virtue, and mental development.
When merit is performed together with verbal intimation, [then there is verbal action].
Vocal action and mental action performed without intimation (viññatti) are said to belong specifically to their respective doors,
because one refrains from the evil associated with those specific doors,
whether the intimation is absent or present.
Generosity, virtue, and mental development; service, honoring, and rejoicing in merit;
the acquisition of merit, the giving of merit, and teaching the Dhamma;
hearing [the Dhamma], rectifying one's views—thus it stands in ten ways.
They proclaim meritorious deeds pertaining to sense pleasures, which bring about a happy destination regarding sense pleasures;
even when performed for other purposes, they bring about the fruit of excellence.
Through the various distinctions of the arising of consciousness, karma is established as twentyfold.
Thus do the discerning ones analyze the sense-sphere [kamma].
The form-sphere kamma, consisting of access and development,
proceeds in the mind-door, having taken as its object the kasiṇas and so forth.
Earth, water, and fire,
wind, blue, and yellow;
red, white, and space.
"Light" refers to those who are confident.
Those beginning their practice as yogis perceive the ten kasiṇas:
the bloated, the livid, the festering, and the devoured.
The rent, the scattered, the mangled and bloody, the worm-infested, and the skeletal—
thus the foulness (asubha) is established in ten ways.
[One should reflect] upon the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and upon one's own virtue and generosity.
The cultivation of recollection as taught for the purpose of honoring the deities,
mindfulness of death, mindfulness directed to the body,
and mindfulness of breathing— thus the ten kinds of recollection are enumerated.
Loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity—
these are called the four divine abodes and the immeasurables. Furthermore,
the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment is thus proclaimed.
The analysis of the four elements, the discernment of the four elements,
and the four sublime states— these, in brief,
are said to be the forty meditation subjects in the method of development for serenity.
Mindfulness of breathing and the kasiṇas there possess five jhānas;
the meditation on the parts [of the body] and the foul are said to possess the first jhāna.
Loving-kindness and the others possess four jhānas; equanimity is considered the fifth.
The remaining immaterial states are based on the immaterial [attainments] and access concentration;
they arise in relation to the kasiṇas, the foul objects,
and mindfulness of breathing.
The counterpart sign arises by taking that [object] as its basis,
and absorption occurs therein.
Among the remaining meditation subjects, no counterpart sign exists.
For it is thus that the immeasurables proceed within the conventional usage of beings:
the space revealed by the removal of the kasiṇa is the object of the first immaterial-sphere mind;
and the non-existence of the first immaterial-sphere is the sphere of the base of nothingness.
The formless attainments proceed by taking their respective objects in due order;
however, elsewhere—in all other cases—absorption does not occur.
First there is the preliminary stage, and after that, the preliminary concentration.
Access and absorption: thus meditation is fourfold.
They have explained three signs: the preliminary sign, the acquired sign, and thereafter the counterpart sign.
For the beginner yogi who is grasping the sign,
the preliminary sign is said to be the kasiṇa and so forth.
Now, for one who begins the meditation upon that sign:
The first preliminary work is also called "meditative development.
When that has been grasped by the mind and the mind-door has been clarified,
it is then said that the "acquired sign" has arisen.
Freed from the five doors and concentrated upon that [object],
this meditation is declared to be "preparatory concentration" (parikamma-samādhi).
It arises from the mode of learning (uggaha-ākāra) and is detached from the physical basis and the mental object.
The counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) is said to be born of meditation.
Having abandoned the objects such as visible forms and so forth,
and taking that [sign] as its object thereafter, the mind-door proceeds after the life-continuum has intervened.
Accompanied by the settling of the training precepts and liberated from the secondary defilements,
this is declared to be access concentration pertaining to the sense-sphere.
From access concentration, regarding the counterpart sign—
Absorption arises, brought about by the power of meditation.
Having made each preceding stage firm,
one thereafter attains mastery for the purpose of dispelling delusion regarding the gross factors and for the occurrence of the subtle factors.
For one who exerts oneself in absorption, there arises in due sequence that which is free from applied thought and so forth, yet endowed with sustained thought and so forth:
adverting, mastery, and likewise the attainment thereof.
Emergence, resolution, and reviewing— thus it is fivefold.
By transcending both applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*),
one attains the fourfold jhāna, and each [subsequent factor] separately the fivefold.
And for absorption as well as for each individual jhāna,
the development of the preliminary stages and so forth must be undertaken separately in every case.
That [development] is classified as inferior, middling, and superior.
The liberations (vimokkha), the masteries (vasībhūta), and the bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana);
the fourfold [classification] beginning with "limited" (paritta) and having "limited" as its range;
likewise, the practice that is painful (dukkhāpaṭipadā) and slow in direct knowledge (dandhābhiññā), and so forth.
It is fivefold according to the distinction of the jhānas— by way of predominance of zeal, consciousness, energy, and investigation— and fourfold according to the distinction of the objects,
as well as by way of being conducive to distinction, stability, penetration, and decline.
The merit of the development of concentration is said to reach absorption (appanā).
Thus, the wise analyze it as form-sphere karma that suppresses the defilements and leads to rebirth in the realm of form.
Kamma pertaining to the formless realm, which accomplishes the fourfold formlessness,
is said to be developed through the analysis of form-phenomena.
It consists of the fourfold purity of virtue, accompanied by the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga).
Having fulfilled that which is known as purification of virtue,
and thereafter having attained purification of mind together with access concentration,
as well as purification of view and the discernment of name-and-form;
The overcoming of doubt, the demonstration of the stability of conditions,
and the purification of the knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path;
thereafter, one who is concentrated in the purifications continues to practice insight.
Having accomplished the supreme knowledge and vision of the path,
the wise one thereafter attains purification through knowledge and vision,
which is designated as the fourfold path and bestows the fruits of recluseship.
Thus, by means of the sixfold purification, this supramundane action— which brings about the destruction of all suffering— should be developed in due order.
In this way, one should analyze the action by way of the six tetrads.
By whichever specific karma the continuum has been conditioned,
it revolves toward ripening through the state of rebirth-linking and so forth, as occurrences within the planes, existences, wombs, destinies, stations, and abodes.
How does volition of the mind generate both material and immaterial forms—forms known as "kamma" and those born of kamma—as appropriate?
Its plane is twofold: it stands as both supramundane and mundane.
They are classified as limited, exalted, and immeasurable.
There are eleven types of existence in the sense-sphere, sixteen in the fine-material sphere, and four in the immaterial sphere;
thus, the compendium of existence is threefold.
There is one state that is non-percipient, and there is the state that is neither percipient nor non-percipient;
all remaining states are percipient.
Thus, existence (bhava) is also threefold.
The formless realms possess four aggregates; those possessing one aggregate are the perceptions of consciousness;
the remainder is called existence with five aggregates.
In hell and among the gods, there are various types of spontaneous births (opapātika);
those born from eggs, those born from a womb, those born from moisture, and those who are spontaneously born.
[These exist] in the world of hungry ghosts, among animals, among the terrestrial deities, and among humans.
And asuras— thus are the fourfold classes of birth comprised.
The destinies are hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and all gods—
so says the one with five stainless eyes.
Among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, the Vepacitti asuras have gone;
those asuras named Kālakañcā have gone entirely among the petas.
This is due to the diversity of their mental intentions and the diversity of their bodies.
"Perceiving diversity of body" refers to those deceased in the realms of sensual pleasure and the higher happy destinies,
as well as the planes of the first jhāna. "Perceiving unity of body and diversity of perception" is declared to refer to the four planes of the woeful states.
Those of the second plane perceive diversity in a single body;
those of the higher form realms perceive unity in a single body.
There are seven stations of consciousness, including the three lower formless realms.
In this [realm], they do not grasp [the aggregates] because consciousness is always absent.
And the fourth formless plane [is excluded] because of the loss of sharp consciousness.
Having taken both of these together, the abodes of beings are declared to be nine.
The realms of desire are threefold: gods, humans, and the states of misery;
the planes are fourfold, distinguished by the levels of the first jhāna and so forth.
The formless realms are fourfold, distinguished by the first formless attainment and so forth.
The unsurpassed [states] are considered fourfold by way of the distinctions of stream-enterer and so forth.
When further divided individually according to the distinctions of hell and so on,
the birth-grounds of sentient beings become thirty-one in number.
Thus, among the various distinctions of the planes and so forth, sentient beings subject to taints are born;
and how do their karmas ripen according to their occurrence?
How is it that beings, having passed away from the states of loss, are born within the realm of sense-desire?
Those who have passed away from the remaining realms of sensual existence are born in all places.
Those who have passed away from the Pure Abodes are reborn in the Pure Abodes.
Those who have passed away from the non-percipient realm are reborn in the happy destinies of the sensual world.
Beings who have passed away with a formless nature (ārūpa) are born in the realms excluding the woeful states (apāya);
those from the higher formless realms are born in the sense-sphere happy destinies (kāmasugati), and there too.
Only worldlings (puthujjana) are born in the non-percipient realm (asañña) and the woeful planes.
Persons who are non-returners (anāgāmin) are born in the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa).
Established in the Vehapphala, Akaniṭṭha, and the Peak of Existence (bhavagga),
all these noble persons (ariyapuggala) are not born anywhere else again.
Those noble ones who have gone to the Brahma-world do not return from below;
having utterly cut off the root of suffering, they attain final Nibbāna, free from taints.
This is stated according to the fixed rule for those who are being born and those who have already been born.
Kamma that has passed into the course of existence produces both form and formless states during the process of rebirth and the subsequent life-continuum in the fourfold plane;
in the case of the non-percipient beings, it produces form alone; and in the fivefold plane, it produces both form and formless states.
The immaterial and supramundane kamma ripens as fruition alone; likewise,
the materiality produced by past kamma (kaṭattā-rūpa) and its fruitions, as well as that determined by the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere,
[arise] according to time, basis, effort, and destiny, as appropriate.
Prosperity and adversity ripen depending upon karma.

Having given [gifts] during one's worldly existence, those who have established connections with the lower realms and are of inferior character [experience results] in all twelve unwholesome volitions within the fivefold realm of existence.
The seven unwholesome resultants ripen accordingly;
but the sense-sphere wholesome karmas ripen in a fortunate rebirth within the sense realm.
Resultants accompanied by roots [ripen] during both the process of rebirth-linking and the course of existence.
In the five-aggregate realm, they arise according to their respective conditions, even without a cause.
Having given the most excellent three-rooted merit, one obtains a three-rooted rebirth-linking;
thereafter, sixteen results ripen during the course of existence.
The minimum three-rooted [kamma] gives a three-rooted rebirth-linking during the course of existence, while that which is two-rooted gives a two-rooted one;
however, during the course of existence, it excludes the three-rooted.
The minimum two-rooted merit gives a rootless rebirth-linking.
Having given results that are causeless and matured, it itself matures during the course of existence.
It does not mature results that are effortless or those with effort;
some say it does not mature results that have effort or are effortless.
Having developed the limited first jhāna, the middling, and the sublime,
one is reborn as a member of the Brahmā’s retinue and so forth in all three realms.
Likewise, having developed the second and third jhānas in their proper order;
Having developed the first three jhānas, they are born among the Parittābha and other deities of the three [lower] realms.
Likewise, having developed the fourth jhāna in its three modes while concentrated,
yogins are born among the three [realms] beginning with the Parittasubha.
But having developed the fifth [jhāna], they go to the Vehapphala realm;
having developed the fading away of perception, they are reborn among the non-percipient beings.
Non-returning persons are born in the Pure Abodes.
But having developed the formless attainments, one produces, in due order within the formless realms,
great merit established according to its respective plane;
it generates a corresponding fruit in both rebirth-linking and the course of existence.
Supramundane merits, however,
produce a corresponding fruit both immediately upon arising and at the moment of attainment.
Because its nature is fully matured, the sublime immediate [kamma] [produces its result].
Kamma that has passed away due to immediate succession, or that has passed away due to time, does not ripen. Furthermore,
kamma that is subtle by nature, subtle in its manifestation, or sublime,
does not ripen within the continuum when it is corrupted by opposing factors.
When a similar practice has been acquired and is present with great power,
yet one does not obtain a cause such as that, direct knowledge does not ripen.
For those who have passed beyond their own plane, the unsurpassed [knowledge] does not ripen.
It is explained that [the fruit] has action as its proximate cause and the continuity [of the stream] as its basis.
Thus, thirty-three types of actions have been stated, along with thirty-six results;
the remaining [states] are mental occurrences that are merely functional (kriyā), because they proceed as mere activity.
Thus, by way of the arising of consciousness, there are eighty-nine types;
fifty-three are considered to be by nature consciousness and mental factors.
Thus, consciousness, mental factors, and Nibbāna—these are the supreme among men.
The Visionary One, the best among speakers, proclaimed the name in three ways. Thus,
those wise in the ripening of karma, within the teaching on measured karmic results—
having reached the further shore of beneficial karmic results— spoke of the fourfold ripening of karma.

Wherein, regarding the determination of ultimate reality, people have fallen into confusion concerning the investigation of what is beneficial and what is harmful— due to a common misconception based on abundance—
the Buddha, the Sugata, having gone to the abode of the gods, proclaimed this at the seat of enlightenment.
Thus, the method for determining the ripening of kamma has been briefly illustrated.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Analysis of Kamma," in the Exposition of Mind and Matter.
Chapter Six: Analysis of Matter (Rūpavibhāga).
Thus ends the compendium of meanings as delimited by the five chapters.
Having clearly explained mental phenomena (nāmadhamma) according to their intrinsic nature without exception,
I shall hereafter describe material phenomena (rūpadhamma),
which are shown to be of two kinds through the classification of the primary elements (bhūta) and derived matter (upādāya).
How is it that [the term "rūpa"] generates a classification by way of its definition through enumeration and so forth, as well as from the arising of aggregates, according to their respective order?
It is called "rūpa" because it is "disfigured" (ruppati) when conditions for transformation exist.
Visible form, as well as that which is further included within the category of form;
then the primary elements—earth, water, fire, and likewise wind—and derived form: thus it is spoken of here.
Dependent upon the primary elements (bhūta-rūpa), it proceeds and not otherwise;
thus is "derived matter" (upādāya-rūpa) described, while the remaining matter has been explained.
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body are fivefold.
Sensitive matter has been explained; the other, however, is non-sensitive.
Matter is fivefold: visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible object.
Matter is the domain of the sensitive faculties, while the sensitive faculty has the latter as its range.
Femininity and masculinity are declared to be the materiality of sex;
the life-faculty is materiality that is clung-to and causes the continuity of existence.
The heart-base, however, is the materiality which is the support for the two elements.
The wise have called edible food "matter" (rūpa).
Because it possesses the intrinsic nature of material phenomena, it is designated as "matter.
Thus, in eighteen ways, the matter of form has been explained.
Because its intrinsic nature is unproduced, matter characterized by the appearance of form—
matter termed "unproduced"— is explained in ten ways.
Space is declared to be matter consisting of the delimitation of matter.
The intimation of body and speech—these two are the material qualities of intimation.
Lightness, malleability, wieldiness, together with intimation, are called the material qualities of change;
thus the discerning declare them to be fivefold.
Accumulation, continuity, aging, and impermanence—
thus the fourfold characteristic-form has been explained in the Section on Matter. In this way,
the wise one [should understand] even these twenty-eight kinds.
One should analyze visible forms according to their characteristics and so forth in due order:
The earth element is solidity; its characteristic is hardness.
Its function is to serve as the basis for a group [of material qualities], and it is grasped as "receiving."
The water element is cohesion; it has the characteristic of trickling.
Its function is to bind together aggregates; it is apprehended by way of its property of holding things together.
The fire element is heat; it has the characteristic of burning.
The digestive taste is understood as the production of softness.
The air element is the state of blowing; it has the characteristic of distension and is understood through its function of impelling by way of the quality of fanning.
Though inseparable in all respects, they possess unmixed characteristics;
they are specifically defined by the predominance of their respective constituent factors.
Mutually supporting one another, they serve as the basis for the remaining types of material form.
Thus, among the four groups [of the eye], the great primary elements (mahābhūta) are predominant.
Within the eye as a composite whole— composed of seven layers of membranes and situated in the center of the black pupil—
it is called "translucent matter" (pasāda).
That clarity of the eye by which one perceives forms—
this is limited and subtle, comparable to the head of a louse.
The ear, resonating within the ear-canal...
Likewise, that which is covered with fine hair and has the shape of a finger-ring is called the "clear nose" (pasāda).
The anus is situated at the seat of the anus; the nose is located within the nostrils;
the tongue is in the middle of the tongue, which resembles the shape of a blue lotus.
Thus, these four [organs] are each established in their respective locations.
The sensitivity of the body within the body is fivefold as "clung-to.
Resembling the moisture on a layer of cotton, it depends upon the primary elements;
these sensitivities protect life and are surrounded by visible forms and the other sense objects.
The two daughters of the prince, dwelling within the sheath,
are each like a gateway for the fivefold cognitive process; or rather, they are,
respectively, the primary elements capable of receiving the impact of visible forms and so forth.
Or rather, for those [mental states] whose karma consists precisely in the desire to see and so forth:
the fivefold pair of consciousnesses— characterized by clarity and having the function of impinging upon visible forms and the rest— is apprehended by way of being the doors.
Visible form is the appearance of the primary elements, sound is likewise their resonance;
odor is their being smelled therein, and taste is their state of being tasted.
Thus, these four objects of experience are dependent upon the primary elements.
The tangible consists of the three primary elements (bhūta), excluding the water element.
Sound therein is indeterminate; other than that, there are those that coexist, distinguished by their respective individual natures and characterized by their respective sense doors.
Only five are considered the objects of the cognitive process of the fivefold sense-consciousness;
they are characterized respectively by the striking against the eye and so forth.
Likewise, their function consists in being the objective support for the pairs of the fivefold sense-consciousness.
The pair of fivefold consciousnesses is included by way of being their objective field.
The female faculty, moreover, is described as "femaleness" and "the state of being female";
likewise, the state of being male is designated by the name "male faculty."
Furthermore, that dyad is found everywhere within the non-clung-to body:
both as distinct from other groups [of material phenomena] and as occurring within a different continuity.
It causes the gender-characteristics—the marks of femininity and masculinity—to function.
"Female" and "male" likewise have the function of making known.
They are understood respectively as the causes for the female and male genders,
as well as for their physical marks, gestures, and modes of conduct.
Beings die by the destruction of that through which their life-breath functions;
it is that by which the distinction between living and dead bodies is characterized.
Thus, this has the characteristic of maintaining those born of karma.
Life is the essence of living, and it is grasped as being bound to vitality.
Likewise, for the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element,
the heart-base is recognized as the supporting characteristic of material form.
The flavor of concentration is grasped by means of non-distraction;
it is that at which living beings become distracted at the time of anger.
Following the course of which, the body is exhausted by the agitation of the mind.
When that [consciousness] has ceased, the stream of consciousness also ceases.
That which it depends upon for its establishment as rebirth-linking in another existence—
this is born of kamma in the five-aggregate plane.
In the middle of the heart-cavity, within half a *pasata* of blood,
it functions by taking up the primary elements (*bhūta-rūpa*), just like the eye and other faculties.
Edible food has the characteristic of bringing in material form (*rūpa*).
Its function is to sustain the body, and it is grasped as a support.
That by which living beings in the sensual world subsist through the power of the moisture of food—
that very thing is thus called "sustenance."
The space element has the characteristic of being the limit of material phenomena;
its function is delimitation, and it is apprehended as the boundary of matter.
In the grasping of material phenomena delimited by their own specific characteristics—
Out of compassion for yogis, the One Supreme in Mercy taught [this] according to the nature of the limited aggregates (kalāpa) as they appropriately are; indeed,
this "form" is spoken of only with respect to those that have limits.
In the occurrence of the vocal sounds of going and so forth, there is, respectively,
the modification and the capacity of the air and earth elements for the production of action and speech, which are co-nascent and grasped.
This specific modification of consciousness, which arises due to the cause of vibrating contact and follows the mind,
is declared to be "intimation" (viññatti),
because it makes known what has been thought by means of body and speech.
Some say that for beings who are subject to the earth and wind elements,
it was spoken by the Tathāgata for the sake of the comfort of maintaining the body—
that body by whose power [it exists].
He appears as if still possessed of effort;
though fallen away from cessation,
he lies as if devoid of consciousness.
In the world, conceptual proliferations (papañca) proceed in many ways, by which they are fashioned;
by which fools are deceived, they imagine themselves as a body.
This [craving] is characterized by its nature as the gateway for bodily and verbal action.
It has the characteristic of being a modification in form caused by the impulse of bodily or vocal activity.
Its function is to manifest the intention of body or speech.
It is apprehended as the state of being the cause for the impulse that sets the body in motion.
Lightness (lahutā) of material phenomena has the characteristic of non-slowness;
it has the function of non-extension and is understood as the mode of being light like an arrow.
Softness (mudutā) of material phenomena also has the characteristic of the absence of hardness.
Its function is the non-obstruction of what is to be done, and it is understood as being in conformity.
It is the adaptability of material phenomena, its characteristic is the fitness for action,
its function is the excellence of occurrence, and it is understood as the state of being ready.
When the material form proceeds, having obtained suitable mother’s milk as nutriment and a mind free from affliction,
it becomes light, soft, and wieldy. Thus, for the material form so proceeding,
there is a differentiation according to its mode of proceeding.
These three qualities—lightness and so forth—then exist together as a concomitant state.
They are conducive to the penetration of what is suitable and assist in the practice;
thus was the perfection of form, with its specific modes, described by the Great Sage.
The accumulation of matter is defined by the characteristic of the building up of matter;
its function is to cause matter to emerge, and it is understood as fulfillment.
The continuity of matter is declared to have the characteristic of occurrence.
Its function is continuous connection; it is grasped as non-interruption.
Matter arises again and again by way of accumulated form;
to the yogi who observes its mode of accumulation, birth is thus grasped.
When one observes that "it arises" in the manner of continuous succession,
then the aspect of continuity presents itself in the mind. Thus,
by way of its distinct manifestations, the nature of birth is divided into two kinds.
Whether arising through the state of having attained its object, or else as something solitary,
it is accumulated by what precedes it in a space devoid of visible form;
yet, proceeding from non-existence to existence, this is called "continuity" (santati).
Though distinguished by such varieties of form,
the one who possesses the excellence of all modes divided birth-form into two types—
he who illuminates birth-form and decay. Decay is the wearing away by time, characterized by the ripening of forms.
The state of being new is its function, and it is grasped as "antiquity.
Impermanence has the attainment of the final moment as its characteristic and the act of taking away as its function;
it is grasped by way of its state of exhaustion.
Thus, characteristic-form (lakkhaṇa-rūpa) is threefold and distinct according to time;
among material phenomena possessing intrinsic nature, it is characterized by its respective time.
That by which a form is characterized as having a distinct appearance moment by moment—
"For the sake of the method of insight (vipassanā-naya), the Tathāgata has thus spoken of it.
In this way, with its delimitations, its modifications, and its specific characteristics, [the Buddha]—
out of compassion and being equanimous (tādī)— taught that which is not difficult to penetrate.
It is said that material phenomena exist by way of their own intrinsic nature;
how then do they diversify in many ways through distinctions such as internal and so forth?
It is merely imagined that, acting as gateways, they cause the mind to proceed.
Therefore, internal material form consists of the sensitive faculties, while external material form consists of the others:
color, odor, flavor, and nutritive essence, as well as what is called derived materiality from the primary elements.
These are termed inseparable materiality, whereas the other is separable materiality.
Because they serve as the respective supports for the seven consciousness-elements,
the sensitive organs and the heart are taught as the "bases" (vatthu) by way of their being bases.
