Furthermore, the five types of consciousness, the appropriated [materiality], the sex characteristics, and so forth, are included by way of their occurrence.
The sensitive organs (pasāda), life, and the [mental] states are faculties, but not the other faculties.
Because they are the mode of occurrence for the fivefold consciousness and kamma,
the sensitive organ and intimation are declared to be the supreme doors, being the door itself.
But as for the sensitive faculties and their objects, they strike against one another;
therefore, material form is called "with resistance" (sappaṭigha), while the rest is "without resistance" (appaṭigha).
They are manifest through their status as doors and objects, and by their very intrinsic nature.
Those [two] are gross; therefore, the remainder is said to be subtle.
Because of their gross nature, there is ease in discerning them;
thus they are "near-form," while the other is "distant-form."
Because it has been taken up by karma accompanied by craving and views, the category of karma is "clung-to" (upādinna); the other is "not clung-to" (anupādinnaka).
Because it is seen by the eye, it is named "with visibility" (sanidassana).
They declared that from those [factors], visible matter alone is "with visibility.
Likewise, there is matter with visibility and matter with resistance;
however, the other is considered invisible and grossly resistant.
Non-indicative matter and the rest as non-reacting;
thus do the wise analyze matter into these three types.
The pair beginning with the eye consists of matter that grasps its object without reaching it.
The triad beginning with the nose is that which grasps what has been acquired; it does not grasp the matter that is yet to be acquired.
Visible form is "seen," sound is "heard," and the triad beginning with odor is "sensed";
because they are to be known by consciousness alone, there may be another [category] called "cognized."
In this context, the heart is only a basis; the two types of intimation are doors;
the sense-faculties are both bases and doors; while all other matter is devoid of both.
Having thus analyzed matter, the wise person [should further analyze] that very same [matter].
One should distinguish, as appropriate, wholesome and unwholesome karma according to its originators. Thus, it is established in twenty-five ways:
past, occasional, and likewise pertaining to the fine-material sphere.
From the moment of rebirth-linking, it produces at every moment, as appropriate,
material forms born of kamma within the realms of sense-desire and form;
excluding those that are arising, the fivefold sense-consciousnesses, and the resultants and the immaterial.
Starting from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), it brings about the arising of the mind.
At the moment of its persistence, the fire element is designated as "cold," "heat," or "season."
In the same way, food that has been swallowed is established in the body within the sense-sphere.
However, while four [nutriments] are internal, the external one is not found [within].
In all cases of sensual existence and fine-material existence, nutriment is not mentioned [as a cause for rebirth].
During the course of existence there are four [nutriments], but for rebirth it is karma alone.
For one who is living, all [four] exist, but for one who is dead, they may or may not exist.
Thus, the wise have declared that kamma, consciousness, nutriment,
and so forth are conditions for material phenomena by way of their productivity.
The heart-base, the faculties, and the material qualities born of kamma, as well as those born of consciousness—
The two types of intimation are considered sound produced by mind and heat.
Lightness and the other [characteristics] arise from mind, heat, and kamma;
one should explain that the remaining ones are born of kamma, mind, heat, and nutriment.
It has been declared that because the natures of "being born" and so forth are merely [conceptual],
these characteristics do not arise at all. If "born" and the others were indeed their [the characteristics'] own nature, then they would necessarily [arise].
And regarding their characteristics, there will be no fixed limit.
They arise respectively from eighteen, fifteen, thirteen, and twelve [factors]:
namely, from kamma, consciousness, season, and nutriment.
The wise, having grouped those kalāpas as appropriate—
nine, six, four, and two— cultivated twenty-one.
Life and the inseparable material qualities [are included] because they coexist.
Having grouped together the tenfold eye-base, it was spoken taking the eye as the starting point.
Likewise, one should explain the ear, the nose, the tongue, and the body in their respective order;
and taking the female state and the male state as the bases, one should illuminate them.
With the inseparable material quality (avinibbhoga-rūpa), there would be the life-nonad (jīvita-navaka).
Thus, the groups born of kamma are established as ninefold.
And the inseparable material quality is declared to be the pure octad (suddha-aṭṭhaka).
Together with bodily intimation, it is called the "ninefold.
Likewise, with vocal intimation and sound, the "tenfold" is spoken of;
and with the three qualities beginning with lightness (lahutā), the "elevenfold" is formed.
A group of twelve is recognized by means of bodily intimation-lightness and so forth;
likewise, a group of thirteen by means of vocal intimation-lightness and so forth.
Having taken into account the distinctions in their modes and characterized by their respective times;
Thus, six groups originating from consciousness have been described.
The first is the pure octad; with sound, it is considered a nonad;
and when joined with lightness and so forth, it is an ekādasaka (elevenfold group).
By means of sound, lightness, and so forth, there would likewise be a group of twelve;
thus, the groups produced by temperature are declared to be fourfold:
the pure octad, and the elevenfold group beginning with lightness.
Arising from the nutriment of the groups (kalāpa), they are analyzed as being of two kinds.
Because it has the characteristic of delimiting the groups,
space and the [other] characteristics are called "non-members of the group" by the wise.
Thus, twenty-one groups (kalāpa) are produced from these four [factors];
all of them are found internally, having arisen from external temperature.
The "octad" and the "sound-nonad"—thus have they been explained in two ways.
The wise have said that these same [mental phenomena] may exist even in a dead body.
All of them are found in relation to sense objects, according to their respective natures;
however, in the case of those with complete sense bases, all four [mental aggregates] arise during the course of existence.
All ten [material groups] are born of kamma at birth;
however, the decads of eye, ear, nose, and sex may not be present.
There are also the decads of the physical bases (vatthu) and the body, as well as the decads of individual essence (sabhāva).
For beings born from a womb, the remaining types of birth arise from that [consciousness];
thus does kamma produce form,
and mental [kamma] produces what follows the rebirth-linking.
The fire element reaches its stability,
and likewise, it is consumed by food. Thus,
the continuity of form for those in the realm of desire is produced from these four [elements].
The connection between the flame and the wick continues for as long as life lasts;
it is severed either by the exhaustion of the lifespan, or by the exhaustion of karma,
or by another "cutting-off" karma acting upon those who are dying.
The lifespan of material phenomena is said to be seventeen thought-moments;
after the seventeenth thought, it ceases following the death-consciousness.
From the time of its arising until that duration, the kamma-born matter does not exist beyond that.
Then the [matter] derived from kamma ceases, and after that,
the mind-born and nutriment-born [cease]. Thus, for deceased beings, in another existence,
matter proceeds in the same way, beginning with rebirth-linking.
Furthermore, the material phenomena born of the tenfold sets of nose,
tongue, body, and sex, as well as those born of nutriment, do not exist in the fine-material realm (rūpabhava),
whether in the moment of rebirth-linking or during the course of existence. Regarding this, some maintain that odors and tastes are not found there either.
And the [temporal] units (kalāpas) must be enumerated;
herein, these [units], with the exception of matter, cease at the very moment the consciousness stands.
They also deny the arising of matter at the moment of the destruction of consciousness.
Even among non-percipient beings, the eye, ear, their bases, sounds, and mind-born matter do not exist;
furthermore, in the formless realm, material phenomena are not found in any way whatsoever.
Thus, for the sake of clear exposition here, by Vimala—
Having approached the well-spoken Dhamma, which is the abode of the wise,
that form characterized by its division into the formed and the formless has also been stated by me according to the method of the Abhidhamma.
When one constantly analyzes this well-classified classification of matter within the mind,
wisdom flourishes regarding the phenomena proclaimed by the Victor that abound in matter.
Thus ends the section on the classification of matter in the *Nāmarūpapariccheda*.
The Sixth Chapter. 7.
The Seventh Chapter:
The Analysis of All Compendia.
For fifty-four states have been spoken of by name and designation;
eighteen kinds are stated in every way as material phenomena (rūpadhamma).
Seventy-two [states] are proclaimed according to their intrinsic nature (sabhāva) as those to be directly known (abhiññeyya).
The ultimate realities, which are the true and actual state, are the entities possessing their own specific characteristics.
Now I shall explain the all-comprehensive method for these,
the unsurpassed core treasure in the hands of the Abhidhamma bhikkhus.
The dyads and triads, from the perspective of aggregates,
bases, elements, truths, dependent origination, conditions, and designations;
and Nibbāna itself as a condition that is unconditioned and without a cause.
The unconditioned is non-arising, eternal, and characterized by immovability.
Conditions are indeed formations (*saṅkhāra*), and everything else is conditioned (*saṅkhata*);
they are subject to the nature of arising and passing away, as well as being established through conditions.
Nibbāna and material phenomena are entirely dissociated;
they are merely objects, for they do not take anything as an object.
They arise and cease together, and they share the same object and basis.
Conjoined and associated, co-nascent as appropriate,
mutually supported, and always occurring together;
possessing objects and having objects— such are considered the mind and mental factors.
Regarding the "stages of insight," therein they are considered to belong to the three planes;
they are mundane, included within the world, subject to the phenomena of the cycle of existence, surpassed by others,
the phenomena of self-identity, accompanied by fear, and named after this shore.
They are described as fetters, as impurities, likewise as hindrances,
as defilements, as misapprehensions, as objects of clinging,
as with-outflows, as floods, as yokes, and as bonds.
Others are unincluded, turned away from the cycle, and not to be seen [as objects];
they are supramundane and unsurpassed, and are not subject to fetters and so forth.
Those born of kamma and grasped are called "with taints" (sāsavā).
Those called "not-clung-to" (anupādinnaka) are the remainder from that [list].
Phenomena (dhammā) with counterparts are considered wholesome and unwholesome;
one should explain other phenomena as being without counterparts.
The states accompanied by conflict (*saraṇa*) are to be abandoned, as are the twelve unwholesome states;
others than these are called "without conflict" (*araṇa*), and they are not to be abandoned by anyone.
Material phenomena are the form-possessing (*rūpin*) dhammas, while mental phenomena are the formless (*arūpin*) dhammas.
One should discern the twofold classification according to these and other distinctions:
the "dull" states (*bālā dhammā*) are those that cause remorse, are dark, and yield bitter fruit;
they are not to be cultivated and are blameworthy—these are considered the twelve unwholesome [states].
The wise, those conducive to heat, the bright, and those that bestow happiness;
those to be cultivated, the blameless, and the wholesome—these are twenty-one.
Action, result, form, and Nibbāna: thus they are fourfold.
States that have been spoken of as "undeclared" (avyākata) are so called by their very nature.
States that are inferior and limited are those belonging to the plane of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).
Those belonging to the planes of the fine-material and immaterial realms are called intermediate and sublime (mahaggata), respectively.
The immeasurable and sublime states are considered supramundane;
likewise, there are the twelve unwholesome states, which are both defiled and defiling.
Furthermore, there are other states belonging to the three planes that are undefiled yet defiling.
Unafflicted and non-afflicting, they may be the nine supramundane states.
These are called "resultants"; resultants belong to the four planes.
Those termed "states that are results" are considered to be wholesome and unwholesome.
Nibbāna is neither an action nor a form; it is not a ripening, nor does it ripen.
The phenomena leading to accumulation are only the meritorious and demeritorious states associated with the taints (āsava).
However, those leading to non-accumulation are the wholesome and unsurpassed states.
Nibbāna is both action and form, while the results are devoid of both.
The first is the unsurpassed path; the others are vision and cultivation.
All others besides these are exempt from the two; yet all are, in the ultimate sense, [conditioned].
The seven supramundane states previously mentioned are called "those in training" (sekkha);
the fruit of arhatship alone is declared to be "beyond training" (asekkha).
Furthermore, mundane [states] and Nibbāna are excluded from both categories.
One should discern that it is threefold by way of such categories as these:
past matter, future matter, and another, which is present;
internal or external, as well as subtle or gross.
Whatever form is inferior or superior, far or near— all that form,
taken together, is called the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha).
Likewise, the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) consists of whatever feeling there may be.
"The aggregate of perception" refers to perception spoken of as a collection.
These two aggregates were taught in order to demonstrate, by way of analysis, the gratification found within the phenomena of the round of existence and the indulgence in that gratification.

Some maintain that feeling and perception are established as distinct categories with the intention of demonstrating the root of dispute, the cause of the cycle of existence, and the cause of craving.
However, regarding those phenomena associated with consciousness, it is by way of volition [that they are distinguished].
The mental factors (cetasika) are considered the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha).
Likewise, all varieties of consciousness (citta) are recognized as the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha).
Because it is devoid of differentiation, Nibbāna is excluded from the inclusion within the aggregates.
By way of being an object, and by way of assisting through grasping,
the five aggregates of clinging— excluding those that transcend the world— are so called.
Just as coarse [food] is for the benefit of the practitioner who consumes it, [so too are these aggregates].
The phenomena of the three planes are taught for the sake of becoming a single plane.
The vessel, the food, the condiment, the eater, and likewise the one who causes eating—
these five correspond respectively.
The sickroom, the illness, the indulgence in what is unwholesome,
the origin, and the sick person— thus do the wise understand.
The prison, the cause, the offense, and the offender therein.
Furthermore, they are compared to a thief because of their offenses;
they are described as a "burden" in the sense of constant oppression;
and by way of the suffering of the defilements, they are incessant devourers.
They bring about misfortune and are like enemies with swords perpetually raised;
because they are subject to the Lord of Death, Māra, they are called "slayers.
Form is incapable of withstanding crushing, as fragile as a lump of foam.
Feelings are like bubbles because they are charming for only a moment;
perception is like a mirage because it causes perversion;
and mental formations are pithless, resembling the trunk of a plantain tree.
Thinking in various ways, deluded by various defilements, consciousness arises as "I am"; it is said to be like an illusion.
Thus, these five aggregates of clinging are merely aggregates.
One should understand that they are taught by the name "the five aggregates.
The internal and external causes for the arising of consciousness are declared as the two bases,
distinguished by way of door and object.
Therein, the internal sense-base consists of the eye and so forth—the sixfold base of doors;
likewise, the external sense-base consists of the objective fields such as visible forms.
Thus is the compendium of doors and objects for those processes occurring in the cognitive series.
In the Āgama and the Abhidhamma, however, in every respect as appropriate:
likewise, the immediately preceding past [consciousness] is the mind-base for that which is presently arising;
and all mind whatsoever is the mind-base for all [subsequent consciousness].
Likewise, consciousness is considered a sense-sphere (āyatana) in the sense of being the precursor for those that arise simultaneously and are formless, and by way of being the door.
Thus, the mind-sphere (manāyatana) and likewise the sensitive matter-spheres (pasādāyatana) are established.
Thus one should analyze the phenomena associated with the five types of consciousness in six ways:
the objects of the five sensitive faculties, which are considered the five bases;
the remaining form; Nibbāna; and all mental factors.
Fifty-nine of the [sixty-two] phenomena are included within the sphere of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*);
thus the Buddhas declare the external sense-spheres in six ways.
They should be viewed as like an empty village, being devoid of a core and lacking substance.
Just as one might kill an external village-destroying thief, so too,
for those who are deluded regarding the occurrence of names,
the Great Seer has here stated that the cause for the arising of those names is the twelve sense-bases (dvādasāyatana).
They bear their own specific characteristics merely by their existence;
they are divided according to the method of the doors, the objects, and that which arises from them.
Herein, it is said that the mind-base consists of the seven consciousness-elements.
The eleven as previously described, together with the [six] sense-spheres,

constitute these eighteen elements. The mind-element, beginning from the end [of the sensory process], stands by way of the metaphor of a "door" during the entry and exit of the mind-consciousness element.
The sixfold [set] is like the sounds of a drum, a cymbal, and a kettle-drum, respectively;
and the threefold [set] would be like fire produced by wood, a fire-drill, and so forth.
Suffering, its origin, and likewise its cessation;
And the Path is fourfold: the Truth, and the Exertion for the Truth.
The burden, the taking up of the burden, the laying down of the burden, and likewise the means for laying down the burden—this is the simile, respectively.
Disease, the cause of disease, the allaying of disease, and likewise the medicine for disease—
these are illustrated by means of similes.
Furthermore, the spreading tree, the root of the tree, and the cutting down of the tree [are used as examples].
The "axe for cutting down trees" is likewise compared in four ways:
the near shore is known as this side, the far shore is likewise the other side;
and the wise compare that which is the means for crossing over it.
Having personally realized the direct evidence through appropriate analogies in their proper order,
he proclaimed the truth for the sake of liberation, according to the principle of the carpenter.
For indeed, suffering is not a non-affliction, nor is there anything other than suffering that causes affliction.
By way of the principle of oppressiveness, the truth of suffering has been declared.
Without that [craving], suffering does not arise from anything else, nor does it cease when that [craving] is gone.
By way of the principle of being the cause of suffering, the Buddha spoke of "clinging" (visattikā) as a truth.
There is no peace other than Nibbāna, nor is there anything peaceful that is not it;
by virtue of its state of peace, Nibbāna is the supreme truth.
There is no deliverance other than the Path, nor is that [Path] itself undeliverable.
Therefore, because it possesses the quality of leading out, the path is recognized as a "truth.
Thus, the state of being real and non-perverted is designated as the meaning of "truth" (sacca) for all four [noble truths], without distinction among suffering and the others.
The meaning of oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of burning, and the meaning of change—
thus the fourfold nature of suffering is explained. Furthermore,
it is explained from the standpoint of accumulation, its source, conjunction, and as an impediment.
The four meanings of the origin of suffering have been proclaimed;
likewise, the four meanings of the escape from it—seclusion and the unconditioned—have been set forth.
Thus, the four meanings of the cessation of suffering have indeed been expounded.
From the perspective of leading out, from the perspective of cause,
and from the perspective of vision as the dominant factor—
thus the Path also has exactly four [aspects].
Conceptualization stands in sixteen ways.

Here, the wise establish the meaning of truth as that which is real in its ultimate sense, from the standpoint of the realization of what is true, and also as the meaning of suchness from the standpoint of truth.
The Noble Ones alone penetrate this fourfold [truth] which has been called the Noble Truth;
therefore, how could the Protector have failed to teach it?
Birth, aging, death, sorrow, and lamentation;
Suffering and mental grief, as well as further despair;
union with the unpleasant and separation from the pleasant;
and not obtaining what one desires—this too is considered suffering.
Reborn in the realms of misery, passing away from the world of the gods,
and growing old among humans, they are oppressed by various calamities.
Mourning and lamenting, they experience painful sensations.
Tormented by mental distress, afflicted by the taints of despair,
they are joined with things undesirable, unwelcome, and disagreeable— namely,
with conditioned phenomena that bring about manifold misfortunes for living beings.
Separated from what is desired, beloved, and pleasing—
from conditioned phenomena and from beings who bestow various forms of prosperity—
those who desire the removal of suffering and long for the arrival of happiness [should practice].
Among those whose nature is unattainable, their minds are afflicted by thirst;
fallen into hardship, wretched, writhing with tearful faces,
they are slaves to craving and ruined within the perilous straits of the cycle of existence.
How could they experience that bitter and intense sensation— the outflow of the three realms,
the fruit of *saṃsāra*— without birth and the other [stages]? Therefore,
through the distinctions of birth and so forth, it brings affliction and inspires fear.
Suffering and the basis of suffering have been elaborated in many ways.
In brief, all these are simply the five aggregates of clinging;
they are determined as suffering by virtue of their being the foundation for suffering.
Therefore, the Sage, skilled in teaching, declared that all phenomena belonging to the three planes, when devoid of craving, constitute the truth of suffering.
Through the attainment of the splendor of dispassion, [he saw] that which was moistened by the moisture of craving.
Like a poisonous tree that produces various fruits of harm from the moment it is born,
the continuum— dragged down by the persistence of delight and lust—
revolves through the process of the production of renewed existence.
And there it is established, indulging in self-attachment;
bound by the lure of its own range of experience, intoxicated by passion and deluded.
It is defiled by a mass of afflictions and struck down by calamity and misfortune.
Pierced by the arrow of suffering, one is tormented without interval.
Indeed, when [the continuity] is entirely severed by the power of dispassion,
by what bond could the continuum be made to go to another existence?
When another existence has not been reached and the continuum has ceased to evolve,
upon what basis do phenomena such as birth and other forms of suffering proceed?
Therefore, it is craving, the adversary of liberation, that brings about suffering.
"The origin of suffering," so the Leader has called it a truth.
That which is liberated from all suffering and released from all defilements is called the truth of the cessation of suffering, the deathless.
Fully understanding suffering and abandoning the origin of suffering,
he set out upon the path of cultivation directed toward the state of Nibbāna—
the Noble Eightfold Path leading to liberation from all suffering.
"Leading to the cessation of suffering"— this is why it is called a Truth.
All other supramundane states, whether associated with the factors of the Path or being fruition-states, are considered to be entirely outside the [noble] Four Truths.
Thus the Guide, for the benefit of those practicing the path, has clearly explained suffering together with its cause, and the extinction of that suffering along with the means thereto.
Having taught the Dhamma accompanied by these three wonders, the Unsurpassed One—
One should analyze and discern the Four Noble Truths by way of their presence and absence,
characterized by the mode of conditionality:
the three periods of time, the twelve links, and the inclusion of the twenty modes.
It has three connections, four compendiums, three rounds, and the three characteristics;
it belongs to the three planes, has two roots, and is adorned with the fourfold method.
It is individually profound in four ways and established in successive order.
Consisting of a mass of ignorance, a circle that severs bonds,
the outflow of sorrow, dejection, and distress— a mere heap of suffering—
this is called the Wheel of Existence known as Dependent Origination.

When true knowledge has been penetrated and ignorance regarding dissolution has been entirely destroyed, how is it that the destruction of causes occurs through the successive stages of turning away (*vivaṭṭa*)?
"When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises."
"When that which is non-existent is not present, it breaks apart through its own dissolution.
Having placed this matter foremost, the stability of conditions has been shown in the method of specific conditionality within dependent origination."
For thus, O Great Sage, you have declared the conditionality of birth for those things subject to aging and death,
even though there is a difference in their measure, they being identical in substance.
Such is not the nature of conditionality when it comes to the status of a direct (āhañca) condition.
In this context, the meaning of conditionality has been elucidated as pertaining solely to one dhamma [in relation to another].
This was stated by the Teacher in the *Paṭṭhānanayasaṅgaha*;
it has been explained at length here for the purpose of demonstrating the method of what is obtainable.
Therefore, having disregarded this [distinction], the wise one, having firmly established the rule,
should discern the meaning of conditionality merely by the fact that [the effect] exists when [the cause] exists. Therein,
ignorance and volitional formations are spoken of as belonging to the past time-period.
Consciousness and name-and-form, that which is called the six sense bases,
contact, feeling, craving, clinging, and becoming:
these constitute the present period of existence and the future period of existence.
Birth, aging, and death are twofold and also universal;
it should be shown that the determination of the three times constitutes the "three periods.
Therein, ignorance is said to be non-knowing regarding the four truths.
Regarding the past and the future, as well as the stability of conditions:
twelve volitions are described as unwholesome formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra),
and likewise, wholesome formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) are spoken of in the realms of sense-desire and form.
The "imperturbable formations" refer to the fourfold immaterial states;
these very volitions, having reached the doors of body, speech, and mind,
are called "formations of body, speech, and mind" by the Great Sage.
Regarding the analysis of "volitional formations" (saṅkhāra), there are twenty-nine types of volition.
Likewise, at the moment of rebirth-linking, consciousness—consisting of the resultant mind—is of nineteen kinds;
during the course of existence, it is of thirty-two kinds.
Feeling, perception, and mental formations are analyzed as being threefold;
name-and-form, however, is twofold, through the division into primary elements and derived matter.
That which is reckoned as the six sense bases is considered to be the internal [bases], beginning with the eye.
Contact is explained as sixfold, divided into eye-contact and the rest.
Feeling is threefold: pleasant, painful, and neutral.
Craving is considered to be threefold: for sense-pleasures, for existence, and for non-existence.
The clingings are fourfold, distinguished by sense-desire clinging and the rest;
existence is considered twofold, by way of the distinction between kamma-existence and rebirth-existence;
birth is the manifestation of the individual existence, while aging—
The state of being old is death; this is declared to be the conclusion.
Thus has dependent origination been analyzed by the Great Sage according to its twelvefold division:
it consists solely of conditions.

"Because they exist dependently as effects, remaining within themselves with mutual expectancy, and by coming together without rejecting one another, they cause [the result] to arise; thus they are called 'conditions' (paccaya).
However, when ignorance (avijjā) and volitional formations (saṅkhāra) are grasped, those [other conditions] are already included therein."
Craving, clinging, and becoming—these are the five causes here.
Furthermore, when craving, clinging, and becoming are included, ignorance and formations are likewise included; thus, there are exactly five causes here as well.
The fivefold fruit is shown by way of consciousness and the rest;
that very same [fivefold fruit] is again grasped by way of birth, aging, and death.
In the past there were five causes; now there is the fivefold fruit.
Now, the wise, having classified the twelve factors according to their divisions— namely, five causes and five future fruits—
proclaim them in twenty modes through the distinctions of meaning and application.
Cause and fruit, fruit and cause, and again cause and fruit—
those who are discerning call this the "three connections" and the "four groups. Ignorance, craving,
and grasping are declared to be the cycle of defilements (*kleśa-varta*).
Formations are one part of existence; beyond that is the cycle of karma.
Thus, what is called the cycle of result is not separated from the cycle of liberation;
having become integrated with these three cycles, this wheel of existence proceeds.
Impermanence in the sense of destruction, suffering in the sense of terror, and non-self in the sense of corelessness—
thus the cycle of existence possesses these three characteristics.
This succession of conditions has been described as belonging to saṃsāra itself.
Regarding "dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), it is considered to pertain to the three planes of existence.
Bound by the eggshell of ignorance (*avijjā*), devoid of the distinctions of true knowledge (*vijjā*) and so forth,
they fail to attain the essence of liberation and remain parched with the thirst for existence (*bhavataṇhā*).
Through the state of volitional formation, the continuity is bound;
thus formed, it turns toward the state of fruition.
Again, from fruition come kamma-formations, and from kamma, further fruitions.
Thus, in this manner, this saṃsāra proceeds.
Therefore, ignorance, existence, and craving are considered the supports of the round;
since they are both associated with and latent within [the mind], the round has two roots.
Furthermore, due to the distinction between conditions, the conditioned, and the continuity [of the stream],
those things that have become diverse are not entirely [separate], like seeds, trees, and so forth. Nevertheless,
because of the distinction between their bases and characteristics, those phenomena...
Just as with the tips of the wicks of a lamp, there is no absolute identity [between cause and effect].
Arising from causes and conditions, it is devoid of effort and exertion;
therefore, it is considered to be without activity in either the condition or that which is conditioned.
Furthermore, when ignorance and the rest arise, the volitional formations and so forth arise accordingly;
thus, by the very nature of things, they remain as such.
In this way, there is identity and diversity, and likewise another [aspect]: non-agency.
And herein, the nature of things (dhammatā) is thus; the methods are said to be fourfold:
the arising of conditions for the fruits, the meaning of conditions in the case of causes, the penetration of intrinsic nature, and the variety of the teaching.
The fourfold profundity is proclaimed according to sequence because of the extreme profundity of the penetration of the meaning and the teaching,
and because the succession beginning with ignorance is the primary cause.
In due order, the conditions for formations and the rest are thus established.
For it is only from birth that aging and death arise; how could there be aging or death for those who have not been born?
Birth, which is designated as "arising" (sāvopapatti), is said to proceed from kamma-existence (kammabhava);
like a sprout from a seed, it is found in various places.
It is established upon clinging (upādāna) through association (sampayoga) and underlying tendencies (anusaya).
They accumulate kamma, drawing forth their future rebirth;
thirsting with the moisture of craving for things that breed clinging,
they strengthen their grasping, delighting in forms that are dear.
For one who contemplates gratification in phenomena that are to be felt,
craving arises with feeling as its condition and increases.
Furthermore, for those who experience a range of objects— whether desirable, undesirable, or neutral— craving likewise arises and grows.
They indeed experience what is called feeling, for they never fail to touch it.
This [feeling] touches an object when the six sense bases have arisen;
in the absence of the doors [of the senses], how could its arising occur?
This sixfold sense base, dependent upon name-and-form,
proceeds according to its respective function as the door for the six types of contact.
It is established by consciousness through its role as the precursor and the foundation.
Name-and-form, having been produced by volitional formations,
becomes established in another existence through the process of rebirth-linking and the course of existence.
If consciousness were absent as its producer, how could its arising occur?
In a mental continuum that is underlain by ignorance,
opposed to penetration, and following the cycle of existence,
volition— by its very nature— arises as a phenomenon that ripens and brings about rebirth-linking.
"With ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be"—thus it is considered from that point.
When the Truths have been penetrated, the entire succession of conditions is brought to an end;
consequently, the cycle of existence turns back.
Because it stands in opposition to ignorance and because it constitutes the compounding of that very process of worldly existence, ignorance is considered the "summit.
For one whose mind is oppressed by the compounding of aging and death—
For those overcome by the suffocation of the defilements, that ignorance increases further.
Thus, this circle of specific conditionality— unbound and uninterrupted—
is turned in succession like the rim of a wheel.
He showed the outflow as an illustration of that twelvefold round of existence belonging to the three planes— that mass of suffering—
consisting of sorrow, lamentation, and likewise bodily pain.
Grief and despair, the occurrence of various calamities— thus,
this conditioned world is impermanent, crowded with great misfortunes,
and beset by many defilements; in brief, it is suffering.
Thus, this collection, analyzed as the five aggregates of clinging,
is like a mechanical doll with its hands released,
a chariot of personal existence wandering incessantly through the various realms of rebirth, stations, and abodes.
Because it moves by means of a wheel, this is considered the wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*).
Having burst open the eggshell of ignorance through the activity of penetration,
the conditions and the things arisen from conditions stand forth clearly according to their own nature.
Perceiving them as impermanent, suffering, and subject to destruction,
as bringing fear and fraught with danger, one stands firm in turning away from them.
Then craving, along with its underlying tendencies, ceases regarding future existence.
Due to the absence of delight in continuity, one does not leap into the junction.
Because of the state of non-growth, the cycle of existence is opposed there;
because of the state of volitional formation, volitions do not proceed.
Neither at rebirth-linking nor during the course of existence do they produce [results] in another becoming;
thus, through the cessation of ignorance, volitional action (kamma-cetanā) has ceased.
Because of the cessation of formations through the cessation of their causal conditions, [the cycle is halted].
Because there is no longer a producer, consciousness is said to have ceased.
And through the cessation of consciousness and the rest, name-and-form and so forth likewise cease;
thus, the cessation of this entire mass of suffering is proclaimed.
Thus, by its power, the turning and the unturning of the cycle have been analyzed in two ways;
this dependent origination has been taught by the Great Sage.
All phenomena are conditions for all conditioned phenomena.
And the Janakas are the supports, distributed as appropriate.
Having reached twenty-four types by way of the sense of condition—namely:
root, object, predominance, proximity, and contiguity.
Co-nascent, mutual, and support conditions; decisive support;
pre-nascent, post-nascent, repetition, and kamma;
as well as fruition, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, path-factor, and association.
Dissociation, presence, and absence; and the departed and the undeparted. Five are said to be past karma, while the present is also mentioned;
in every way, three are stated [as past], and the others are present.
The name of name is fivefold; the name-and-form of name-and-form is fivefold;
again, the form of form is singlefold, and the name of form is also singlefold.
The two—conceptualization and name-and-form—are twofold for name.
And "of two [types] in nine ways"— how are there six kinds of conditions?
Only mental phenomena (nāmadhamma), arising immediately after those that have just ceased,
are the generators and supporters of [subsequent] mental phenomena.
Because they proceed without interval, each immediately following its predecessor,
they are declared to be a condition by way of the proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya).
By virtue of their state of immediate succession, those very same factors serve as conditions for one another.
Those very same [conditions] which, by the name "immediately preceding," were declared to be conditions for the existence of phenomena,
are called by the Tathāgata "absence conditions" (natthi-paccaya) because they assist in the non-existence of those phenomena.
By virtue of providing space, those phenomena which are helpful to the swift are called both "the swift" and "the conditions for the swift.
Through their proficiency, they assist the swift.
Regarding the condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*): it is considered that which has ceased immediately prior.
It is a condition for associated and co-nascent states by way of association. The condition of association (*sampayuttapaccaya*) is said to be the conditioning of mental states by mental states.
Thus, one [condition] while occurring, and five past ones as appropriate;
for immaterial states, the immaterial conditions are considered to be sixfold.
[These apply] to those born of consciousness during the course of existence, and to those born of kamma at the moment of rebirth-linking.
The six factors that have become causes— by way of their nature as causes— are supportive in the sense of being roots for the co-nascent material and immaterial phenomena;
thus they are declared to be a "condition" by virtue of being a causal condition (*hetu-paccaya*).
Likewise, in the sense of contemplation, those very factors that assist [the mind] are analyzed as "jhāna-dhammas" by the name of jhāna-condition. Similarly,
in the sense of leading out, they are declared to be "paccayas" (conditions).
By the name of "path-condition," the path-factors were taught by the Great Sage.
And of those very same phenomena, volition is the "conascent" condition,
existing as such through the absence of karmic activity.
Volition that is asynchronous with the resultant material phenomena produced by past kamma is considered a productive condition by way of its formative nature. Thus,
volition is twofold according to its divisions, in the sense of its pervasive influence.
By the name of kamma-condition, it is declared as a condition for co-nascent material phenomena that are not themselves material;
they are proclaimed as results by virtue of their existing state.
The conditions for name-phenomena alone, which consist of both name and form, have been stated as fivefold: four from the "one-pointed" (ekotīta) and one as "presently occurring" (vattamāna).
Among these, the postnascent (pacchājāta) condition is an assistant to this material body.
The postnascence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya) is of one kind for name and form:
during the course of existence, it consists of the six bases for the seven consciousness-elements,
and for the five-door cognitive process, the five objects respectively.
By way of distinction of what has arisen previously, those things that assist names are the "pre-arisen condition" (purejāta-paccaya). Thus, matter is a condition for name in one way.
Mental states and mental factors arise by taking whatever [object] as their basis.
All this is called the object-condition (ālambana-paccaya).
Whatever named phenomena (nāma-dhammā) proceed by taking an object as their support—
that very thing is declared to be the object-proximity-support (ālambanūpanissaya).
Those phenomena which are recognized as conditions by way of the proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya) are themselves declared to be the "proximate, material, and supporting" [conditions].
Phenomena such as lust and faith, when perfumed within the internal [mind], [function as such].
The seven conditioned phenomena that are cultivated externally— namely, the states of lust,
faith, and so forth— are the decisive kamma for their respective results;
thus did the Tathāgata establish them as natural decisive supports (pakatūpanissaya).
Thus, by way of strength, support, and assistance, this condition is considered threefold under the name of decisive support (upanissaya). It consists of both the material and the immaterial,
and likewise pertains to the three times as well as to that which is timeless.
The condition for mental states (nāma) is considered to be twofold: that which consists of designations (paññatti) and that which consists of names (nāma).
For mental states, there are objects (ālambana) and predominance (adhipati) conditions, as well as those with a weighty object (garu-gocara);
and for co-nascent states, there are co-nascent predominance (sahajā-adhipati) factors, each according to its appropriate role.
The condition by way of predominance for name-and-form is thus explained as twofold:
that which is co-nascent with name-and-form, and that which consists of the great elements for material things.
At the moment of rebirth-linking, the physical basis (vatthu) is in every way a support for mental phenomena (nāmānaṃ).
Because they assist other phenomena through their specific co-nascent qualities,
these are analyzed as threefold under the heading of the co-nascent condition (sahajāta-paccaya).
The four formless aggregates, the four great elements,
the links [of dependent origination], and the names of the bases are always co-nascent.
They exist as mutual supports and proceed in such a manner toward one another.
The condition of mutuality (aññamaññapaccaya) is considered to be threefold when analyzed:
[it applies] respectively to the seven consciousness-elements, to the primary and derived material phenomena, and to co-nascent mental and material phenomena.
The four aggregates that have become the physical basis (vatthu) assist by way of being a support;
this is known as the support-condition (nissaya-paccaya), which is considered to be threefold.
Edible food (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra) is the condition for the material body.
But the immaterial nutriments are conditions, in the sense of maintaining, for their respective co-nascent name-and-form. Thus, in the sense of maintenance,
the nutriment-condition has been explained as being of two kinds.
The mental states consisting of the faculties of confidence and the life-faculty,
and the material phenomena, are conditions for the fivefold consciousnesses and for the appropriated material phenomena respectively, by way of being co-nascent and by way of mutual dependence.
The faculty-condition alone is declared to be threefold:
the six bases for the seven consciousness-elements as appropriate,
and likewise the mind and mental factors that are postnascent to the body.
Non-material [phenomena] are considered to be of three kinds as conditions for co-nascent material phenomena:
namely, the dissociation condition, which assists through dissociation.
It is entirely of three types: co-nascent, pre-nascent, and post-nascent.
Edible food and material life-force—
these are the conditions reckoned as "presence" (atthi-paccaya). This condition is considered fivefold,
according to its respective function, by virtue of its existing nature.
Those very same [mental and physical phenomena], having not yet ceased and acting as present supports,
were defined by the Sugata as the "non-disappearance condition.
Thus, these eight present mental and physical phenomena are conditions.
"And the predominance in all cases"— thus, in nine ways,

the inclusion of the principles of the *Paṭṭhāna* regarding name-and-form has been briefly stated and then explained by the Great Sage, well-classified according to the wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth.
The wise proclaim twenty-four conditions established in three ways by way of designation, name, and form.
Designation is twofold: as that which is designated and as that which designates.
How can those things designated by the Tathāgata be said to be dissociated from name-and-form?
[They are so designated] by way of the various modes of transformation of the primary elements,
such as the earth, mountains, stones, grass, trees, creepers, and so forth.
Concerning the mode of the requisites, there are those distinguished by their specific arrangement,
such as vehicles, paths, forests, groves, heaps, essences, cloths, and so forth.
The mode of the agent and the experiencer is characterized by intimation and the faculties.
By clinging to the five aggregates, there arise [the notions of] mortals, asuras, gods, and so forth.
Through the revolution of the moon and other such phenomena, there arises the conventional designation of directions, time, and so on.
Through lineage, descent, family, and so forth, there arise [the notions of] birth, clan, and lineage.
The *kaṭhina* and so forth are designated through various distinctions such as specific actions;
likewise, wells, space, caves, and so on are not touched by those respective collections [of parts].
When one reflects upon various signs, these [concepts] become well-established.

Designations such as the "kasiṇas" and so forth have as their objective domain that which consists of mental development (bhāvanāmaya). Because they lack prior existence, [terms such as] "the removal of the kasiṇa" and so on,
as well as "cessation" and "attainment," are characterized by the absence of any specific entity.
Thus, depending on this or that [basis], it is designated in such and such a way;
it is proclaimed as a conceptualization (*saṅkhā*), a designation (*samaññā*), a description (*paññatti*), and conventional usage (*vohāra*).
Even in the absence of an existing entity, it exists by way of its object and its mode.

Produced by the process of conceptualization, appearing like a shadow of the actual object, and because it makes something known, it is called "conceptualization" (paññatti); this is what is meant by "name" (nāma).
Furthermore, it is "dependent conceptualization" (upādāya-paññatti) and "relative conceptualization" (upanidhāya-paññatti).
Conceptualization is so called because it makes things known, as proclaimed by the wise.
It is twofold: that which does not exist and that which exists.
In terms of worldly convention, something may be conceptually designated as existing in the ultimate sense.
When they designate something that does not exist by means of this [designation],
it is then called a "designation of the non-existent.
But when they designate something that does exist, it is then called a "designation of the existent."
Thus, it is called "conceptualization" (paññatti) because it makes known both the dhamma as a concept through its specific conventional meaning,
and the dhamma as an entity through its specific characteristic such as form and so forth;
this is what is spoken of as "name."
That which is designated by such names as "name" (nāma) and "name-action" (nāmakamma) is distinguished by categories such as non-existent and existent;
[for example,] the word "woman" and "one possessing the six super-knowledges," while the speaker is the prince.

[The types of nouns are: those based on action, those based on cause, those based on purpose, those based on conventional usage, those that have become established by common usage, those based on relationship, those based on accumulation, those based on state, and likewise those dependent on shape.
For example: "Devadatta," "the wise one," "feeling," and "the moon."
"A khattiya," "a lion among men," "the brother," "the young one," "red," "an earring," "a cloth"—
through such distinctions as these, the categories [of nouns] are characterized by conventional usage and the forms of expression regarding their meanings and essential natures.
In the evening, it arises at the moment of a sign consisting of clothing according to one's wish;
it follows the mode of the object to be known through the specific purpose of conventional usage,
by means of the sound of speech, following the cognitive process of auditory consciousness.
They are the objects of the mind-door that arises immediately after the [sensory] process has occurred;
they are understood by means of their subsequent conformity,
and they are recognized as having both conventional and natural characteristics, sharing in the nature of prior conventions.
That which appears according to the specific mode of its object—
such as the sound of speech consisting of feeling and so forth—
is to be understood as a designation (paññatti) fashioned by worldly convention, following the nature of the mind.
Some maintain that sound alone is accompanied by vocal intimation.
Thus, two types of designations (paññatti) have been stated as "designated phenomena" (paññattidhamma);
likewise, there are phenomena called "terms" (adhivacana), which are also referred to as "expressions" (nirutti).
The wise declare that conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is that which establishes worldly discourse by way of being non-deceptive.
The Teacher, whose supreme qualities are unsurpassed, [taught] that which is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya): namely, "name" and "form."
Skilled in the phenomena of intrinsic nature, he distinguished them into two types, having become disillusioned with other doctrines;
he explained another category as being knowable through conventional usage and specific purpose, according to its designation.
Thus, this entire work, which I have undertaken in due order, has been thoroughly brought to completion.
The Dhamma which the King of Dhamma, having attained unexcelled perfect enlightenment through the path at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree,
performed a supreme and peerless miracle in an instant; having manifested it there,
he reached the assembly of the noble city with the rays of his radiant and charming voice.
Therein, the essence of the meaning has been spoken concisely; may it endure for a very long time, conforming to the recitation.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Analysis of All Compendia," in the *Nāmarūpapariccheda*.
Thus is completed, in every respect, the analysis of the ultimate meaning of the Abhidhamma in the "Discrimination of Mind and Matter.
Chapter Eight.
The Analysis of the Totalities and the Foul:
Hereafter I shall explain the supreme method of meditation for one who desires to practice after having discerned name-and-form.
Therein, cultivation is twofold: serenity and insight.
Therein, serenity is twofold: limited and exalted.
That which has reached access is called "limited."
The mundane serenity that has reached the access of the sublime is considered [worldly].
There are the ten kasiṇas, the ten foulness subjects, the ten recollections,
as well as the immeasurables, the perceptions, and the meditation on the parts of the body.
The wise have declared that there are forty subjects of meditation therein,
by practicing which one develops the two kinds of serenity.
Having attained the perfection of means through the purification of application, [one proceeds].
Having purified one’s underlying intention, it is said that [the training] must be developed.
How does one practice conduct while avoiding prohibited conduct?
Having undertaken the Pātimokkha, one should fulfill it through faith.
Having cleansed the influx of impurity at the six doors through reflection,
the wise one should guard the six faculties with the protection of mindfulness.
Free from attachment to a wicked livelihood and escaped from deceitful conduct—
One should purify one’s livelihood, being resolute for the sake of purity of heart.
Having undertaken this goal and reflecting thoroughly and wisely,
the wise person should use the requisites with clear comprehension.
Having undertaken the fourfold restraint— namely, the Pātimokkha, virtue as the restraint of the sense faculties,
purity of livelihood, and likewise that which depends on the requisites—
one should thereafter resolve upon them.
As an accompaniment to that very [practice], there are the ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas) as appropriate:
the practice of wearing rag-robes, the practice of possessing only three robes, the practice of possessing only two robes;
the practice of eating only almsfood, and the supreme practice of begging from house to house in regular order.
The practice of not eating after the proper time, the practice of eating only from the alms-bowl,
and the practice of eating at a single sitting— thus, three are established regarding food.
The forest-dweller’s practice, the practice of living in whatever dwelling is provided—
The threefold practice of dwelling at the foot of a tree; the practices of dwelling in the open air and in a charnel ground;
and likewise the practice of sitting meditation.
Regarding the thirteen ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) beginning with the [restriction on] lodgings,
and also regarding the freedom from greed even toward what is permissible, one should practice the proper conduct for the sake of a life of effacement.
Having fulfilled the fourfold pure virtue (catupārisuddhisīla),
surrounded by the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), and thus purified through the purity of application,
the Great Sage has proclaimed these [precepts] by means of the three conditions.
Then, having fulfilled his aspiration and being confident in meditation, how should one who delights in seclusion apply the means? [Namely:
dwelling, family, and gain—
The group, the legal act as the fifth;
the journey, the relative, the illness, the tie,
and psychic power— these are the ten.
Having cut away the obstacles as appropriate, the wise yogi,
free from attachment and free from striving, [dwells at peace].
Delighting in the stilling of conceptual proliferation, one should rely on a teacher who is beloved, venerable, and inspiring; who speaks appropriately and patiently endures being spoken to;
who is capable of delivering exceedingly profound discourse and provides guidance regarding the proper course of action.
Having approached a learned and virtuous teacher, the wise person—
patient, receptive, upright, and noble— should,
having won him over, receive from him that giver of the meditation subject.
Having examined his own meditation subject to see which temperament it suits,
the wise know that there are three temperaments: lust, hatred, and delusion.
They cultivated these sixfold factors through faith, understanding, and reflection:
the meditation on the foul aspects of the body,
which are suitable for one who is overflowing with lust.
The immeasurables are for those in whom hatred predominates, and the fourfold [meditations] on blue and so forth are for those in whom delusion predominates.
Mindfulness of breathing is taught for those in whom delusion predominates;
the recollections of the Buddha and so forth are said to be for one of faithful temperament.
The perception of the nearness of death and the defining of the object are for the wise;
the rest, however, are for all. Even among those, the wise favor the kasiṇa.
For one whose temperament is characterized by applied thought, the limited object is suitable for one who wanders in delusion.
Having first taken up what is "great" as being suitable,
thereafter one should consider a great dwelling— whether new or old,
near a road or a tavern, strewn with leaves, flowers, and fruits, and much sought after with great honor.
A place dependent on a village boundary, a city boundary, or a field boundary;
one with dissimilar neighbors, unfavorable, a port, or where friends are hard to find—
these places that do not lead to success a wise person should avoid.
One should, without sloth, frequent a dwelling suitable for meditation—
one that is neither too far nor too near, quiet and undisturbed,
well-suited for coming and going, and free from gadflies and dangers.
Arising from conditions that require no effort, suitable for a community of modest monks,
abundant with secluded places, and frequented by those of great learning;
free from fear, devoid of anxiety, lacking in fault, and possessing great virtue.
Frequenting the monastery there with a mind free from attachment,
one should then sever, as is appropriate,
even the minor impediments such as the clipping of hair and nails and the dying of robes.
Avoiding an unsuitable dwelling, range, speech, person, and likewise food,
as well as his own posture, and cultivating the seven suitable things— thus does one who exerts himself proceed.
Endowed with the means of cultivation, secluded and gone to a solitary place,
having seen the danger in sensual pleasures and seeing renunciation as security,
how should one who is weary of obsession purify their underlying intention?
Sensual pleasures have little flavor but great suffering; their fruit is bitter.
They are difficult to withdraw from and difficult to guard, established in many dangers and calamities.
Like bones being gnawed, they lead only to ruin when broken apart.
They are seized and held fast like a piece of meat by birds;
like a grass torch in a headwind, they burn their possessors,
resembling pits of glowing embers that scorch every limb.
Like food already consumed while lying on one's back, it cannot satisfy anyone;
yet like borrowed ornaments, they do not belong to anyone permanently.
Like fruit-bearing trees that are being shaken, those who destroy the progress of others [reap the consequences].
Like swords and spears, they constantly strike down living beings;
like spears and spikes, the arrows of craving pierce them deeply.
Filled with terrible and harmful poisons, they are like the heads of black snakes.
Defiled by all taints, the basis for all corruptions,
vulgar, fickle, low, and cherished by worldlings—
these are common to many and desired by one's enemies.
Bringing about great calamities, involving much exertion, and fraught with fear;
undertaken with great effort, yet quickly crumbling away;
they enter like arrows of sorrow and vanish day after day.
They are not able to provide protection for anyone, nor are they able to offer consolation;
the servants of Māra are like deceitful gamblers, untrustworthy,
fashioned with sweet appearances only to bring harm to living beings.
Captivating things enter the continuum like a female demon;
those by whom the foolish are possessed give rise to calamities.
Overcome by perversions and falling into affliction, they suffer.
Fashioned from intentions of the mind, attended by delight and passion,
like the edge of a sword smeared with honey, they are pursued through harmful intent.
Appearing beautiful and charming, they are perceived as pleasant forms.
With faces of friendship, yet harboring enmity, they deceive the great masses.
By whomsoever these fools are deceived, their every prosperity is destroyed;
strayed from the path of safety, they bring about their own destruction.
Assuming various hideous forms,
these seductive beings crush the minds of the untrained fools,
just as deer in the forest, pierced by the arrow of passion, are struck down by that very shaft.
Chasing after this and that, they writhe incessantly.
Growing through the notion of "mine," like a terrible venomous snake,
the ignorant take delight in the phenomena of possessions when they are let loose.
These lead to misfortune and ruin, for living beings fall under their power;
they appear in various forms and shapes, like a city of goblins.
Fools, bringing them harm, do not perceive them as a snare.
Right there they turn back, like those who, being infatuated, are slain.
This great flood carries swiftly; the cycle of defilements is a source of great terror.
It is a thorny thicket and a mire difficult to cross over.
This is a place that deludes the mind, a link to negligence;
it is a snare, lax, and a bond difficult to release.
It is spread wide in the world like a net.
The snare of Māra is cast out;
it is a cage and a prison,
bringing misfortune to living beings.
Where they are bound by passion and lie hidden away,
like monkeys tied with glue, they groan in distress.
Like food covered over with a baited hook, it is as if poisoned.
Like bait set out for the destruction of deer,
so are those ordinary people who, like fish greedy for a hook, swallow it;
having fallen into the terrible jaws of death, they lament as their portion is the states of misery.
This place is a field of evil, where wrong greed is cultivated;
it is where the sprouts of misconduct grow and where the fruits of the lower realms are filled.
And those who are obsessed with this are consumed by the burning heat of greedy infatuation.
Blazing with the fever of anger, fumigated by envy and stinginess,
armed with the weapons of aggression and brandishing their desires,
they stand ready for the world’s ruin, bound by craving and possessing great defilements.
There is no blame in them, and nothing remains to be done;
yet, because they have forgotten the truth, goodness finds no footing among them.
Delighting in harming others, they are turned away from the nature of compassion.
Lacking trust toward all beings, suspicious in every situation,
abounding in fear and terror, pursuing every kind of harm,
they bring about the four states of misery, placing evil deeds before them.
Plunged into great peril and beset by obstacles,
fools who are attached to sensual pleasures and to existence are struck down by the nature of suffering.
Therefore, those deluded by the delight of play remain free from fear of death.
Eating like those who consume *kiṃpākka* fruit, they oppose what is delightful;
like village piglets drenched in filth,
they are lured in this world by the work of the yak-tail chaser, overwhelmed by the impurity of sensual desires.
Being incessantly devoured by defilements as if by worms,
they become infatuated and surround it, unaware of its decline.
Then, incinerated by old age, youthfulness is utterly lost.
Sensual pleasures wane and life itself is cut short.
Beyond heedfulness lies the great flood of evil defilements;
from that flows the river of craving, which fills the ocean of the states of misery.
Having abandoned this world and ruined their prospects for the next world,
like crows feeding on the filth of the Ganges, they lie down devoted to sorrow.
Thus, bound by sensual desires, beings neglect both their own welfare and the welfare of others.
Having been shattered, they perish both here and in the world beyond.
Thus sensual pleasures are fraught with danger, as terrible as the silk-cotton tree;
therein fools sink down, but for those who understand, there is no attachment.
Thus the One with Vision has proclaimed the unsurpassed Threefold Training as the state for those terrified by sensual desires, for the sake of liberation— namely, renunciation.
This practice is the supreme means for the destruction of all taints.
Not relying on the two extremes, the Middle Way has been proclaimed.
It is the eradicator of all suffering, the supreme and ultimate purity;
it is the perfection of true knowledge and conduct, which accomplishes every form of excellence.
This place is a field of merit, a site for the practice of ascetic deeds;
it is where the sprouts of faith and virtue grow, fulfilling the fruit of prosperity.
It is the unsurpassed gateway for liberation from the prison of the defilements.
A raft for crossing the great flood, leading safely to the further shore;
an unsurpassed path of security that destroys evil and thieves;
free from thorns and dense thickets, straight, and proclaimed by the virtuous.
For the sake of liberation from the great bond,
this wonderful cry was uttered by the Victor:
"The relinquishing of impediments."
An open space, free from plastering;
a crossing over the mire of attachment; the unraveling of the knots;
the liberation from the slavery of craving—this state of independence brings happiness.
The severance from all bonds, the cessation of all sorrow,
the dismantling of all bases for attachment, the departure from all suffering—
this is the unsurpassed state attained, which utterly cuts through the snares of Māra.
It destroys the darkness of delusion and shines with the light of true knowledge.
This state is free from ill will, fearless, and secure;
it is the refuge for those who practice asceticism and the confounder of Māra’s eye.
This is like cool sandalwood, removing all torment;
it is the stainless water of the Dhamma, cleansing the impurities of defilement.
It is a bridge across the cycle of existence, well-constructed, and adorned with the factors conducive to enlightenment.
It is the extractor of the thorn of sorrow, a machine well-constructed;
it dispels the mental ailment, a medicine for the happiness of enjoyment;
it is the vomiting forth of worldly baits and the purging of the defilements of the mind.
They call the food of the Dhamma the cause of ultimate satisfaction;
the drink that removes thirst is the exquisite nectar of liberation.
The garland of virtues is fragrant with the sweet scent of praise and renown.
The covering that conceals evil deeds, variegated with moral shame and dread of blame,
the utterly pure garland of the jewels of the True Dhamma—
the ornament of the Noble Ones, which follows one and bestows glory.
This is the supreme pacifier of all ill omens that arise from anxiety;
this is the most excellent protective chant for warding off misfortune.
It is the auspicious blessing taught by the Victor for the destruction of obstacles.
For liberation from wrong grasp, this is the blessing spoken by the Fully Awakened One:
it is irreversible, directly visible, unique, and not to be borne by another;
it is the nectar-like medicine, the ultimate means for achieving freedom from aging and death.
Having established themselves in this, they attain the threefold supreme enlightenment,
which is filled with the perfection of all attainments and virtues.
Endowed with the excellence of every aspect, this is what is considered true renunciation.
With virtue as its deep moat, the ascetic practices as its raised arches,
the pathways of concentration as its broad thoroughfares, and mindfulness as its ramparts and gate-towers;
it is in full bloom with the excellence of faith and is beautified by the palace of wisdom.
The delightful banner of right livelihood, shielded by moral shame and dread of blame;
The enjoyment of the deathless liberation, frequented by those people who are to be trained;
The invincible city bestowed by the Sugata, which cannot be breached by enemies of evil.
The great seers have practiced the way that is free from harm and free from calamity.
Having attained supreme consolation, their wishes fulfilled,
they have transcended all attachments and gone forth, fearless from any quarter.
Having fully understood the goal rightly, those who have abandoned the realm of death and crossed over the flood of all suffering—
the wise— go to the further shore.
Thus, [this Dhamma], endowed with every factor and frequented by hosts of great seers, is proclaimed.
Renunciation is that which has departed from sensual desires, the supreme path of the True Dhamma.
Those who have come to ruin, being infatuated, fail in this;
they call such evil conduct "obsession."
This is a mental hindrance that obstructs the eye of wisdom;
it causes the destruction of virtue and is associated with the distraction of the mind.
It is the foundation for infamy and the destroyer of the splendor of one's qualities.
It burns away all prosperity, brings about the four states of misery,
is possessed of the stain of all taints, and is a heap of all secondary defilements;
it is like an evil yakṣa and a gathering of venomous snakes of hatred.
One who has strayed onto the path of negligence, who has fallen into the company of a host of enemies,
who gives rise to great fear, who is a mass of great calamity, who has ascended to the suffering of the lower realms,
and who stands upon a state that brings harm— [such a person is lost].
Terrible, causing all manner of harm, and bringing about all suffering—
shame on those of evil nature who destroy every excellence!
Though they have obtained the perfection of opportunity so difficult to find, it has been squandered by them.
For their active practice destroys the Buddha’s teaching— which is so difficult to find—
just as a thunderbolt destroys a mountain of jewels.
They are thieves of the wealth of the True Dharma and obstacles to renunciation.
Those who destroy the practice cause living beings to be bound by fetters.
These are the slayers of those who trust them, the murderers of those who have placed their confidence in them;
by these fools are people struck down so that they lie fallen, even though they relied upon the Conqueror’s dispensation.
The foolish dwell on the edge, free from fear and shrouded by delusion,
with the terrible, venomous snake within their own minds, as if in the hollow of their laps.
For their own destruction, they remain unafraid of that which has escaped from the cage of the afflictions.
Those who walk the path of ruin do not perceive while they are thinking;
like those eating halāhala poison or embracing a wicked person,
those who revel in evil states will inevitably be destroyed.
People overwhelmed by evil thoughts, agitated by discursive thinking,
fall away from both worlds, destroying their twofold welfare.
They are devoid of freedom from anger and malice, and are defiled by envy and avarice.
Deceitful, hypocritical, and contentious, lacking deference and respect;
abounding in pride and arrogance, vainly talkative and fierce;
restless and negligent, stubborn and grasping at their own views.
Those whose minds are made barren by mental obstructions and are entangled in fetters,
like a great flood destroying crops, destroy the quality of their asceticism.
Distracted by the gratification of sense objects, they are scattered and their faculties are uncontrolled.
Mindless and indolent, they live a life in vain.
Gluttonous, seeking luxury, lacking wisdom, and clinging to physical comfort,
they are bound by the fetters and hindrances, brought under the sway of desire and greed.
With mental continuums seized by defilements, delighting in frivolous talk,
devoid of discipline and tranquility, and wandering in the sphere of improper conduct;
difficult to support and difficult to satisfy, they are addicted to the comforts of delicacy.
Dissatisfied and full of great desire, marked by greed and improper conduct,
like dogs repelled by a foul odor yet infatuated with the smell of raw meat,
they run hither and thither and find no firm footing in the Teaching.
Shameless and devoid of fear of wrongdoing, they are infatuated with worldly conditions;
having evil desires, they are disguised by hypocrisy and enticed by wrong livelihood.
Crooked, impudent, and deceitful, they are inwardly rotten and lustful.
Those of suspicious conduct, who are like dregs, lax, and dull-witted;
whose minds are fickle with vanity, and who are attached to their putrid bodies;
sinking down and fallen into despair, they do not flourish in the Teaching.
Associated with evil persons, having arrived at evil views,
lacking faith, cut off from the Dhamma, wicked, difficult to speak to, and harsh;
they smear the state of recluseship and defile the teaching of the Conqueror.
Transgressing the teaching of the Victor, fools are destined for miserable rebirths.
Greedy for sensual pleasures, of evil conduct, immoral, and shrouded by delusion,
they are being devoured, turned to mud, as thorns in the teaching of the Victor.
Not knowing what is beneficial or harmful, they are subject to attraction and aversion;
their mental continuums are afflicted, deceived by the perversions.
With their worldly tasks ruined and disordered, these evildoers are utterly defeated.
They suffer for a long duration, consigned to the states of deprivation.
Thus, this evil path is a track of dust that utterly cuts off one's welfare;
having understood it as the manifestation of wicked qualities, the wise man [turns away from it].
Confidently, one should restrain the spreading defilement of obsession by means of reflection,
just as one would neutralize a potent poison with a mantra.
One should quickly extinguish the fire of evil that has arisen, like a person whose clothes are ablaze.
By the sprinkling of the water of meditation, one should extinguish it without interval.
With diligence, the wise person— like a dam holding back a great river—
should block the flood of evil moment by moment.
Like a perilous wilderness, like a terrible venomous snake,
like a deep precipice, and like a heap of filth— the wise man,
having abandoned obsession, is intent upon renunciation.
Having virtuous friends, seeing danger in faults, and being well-restrained;
free from the poison of sensual lust, having no attachment to wealth or possessions;
liberated from desire and greed, without the sense of "mine," and without possessiveness.
Tranquil, sociable, and gentle, showing loving-kindness and intent on compassion;
with a mind free from malice, steadfast, peaceful in heart, and devoted to forbearance—
one who seeks the welfare of all living beings.
Freed from envy and avarice,
he delights in the pacification of anger, resentment, ill will, and hostility.
The yogi with an undepressed mind, constantly diligent in effort,
with well-composed intentions, serene and untroubled—
confident and being liberated through practice, he is possessed of wisdom.
Rejoicing and holding me dear, [he honors] the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Thus, freed from the hindrances and bearing the radiance of the light of knowledge,
he worships the Perfectly Enlightened One through the practice of the True Dhamma.
Endowed with the virtues of moral shame and dread of blame,
possessing excellent conduct and sphere of activity,
and free from hypocrisy and flattery.
He is respectful and reverent;
he is upright in conduct and character, free from deceit and hypocrisy;
he is detached from stubbornness and agitation, and is gentle and pleasant in his behavior.
Averse to pride and arrogance, respectful and reverent toward the true Dhamma;
crushing the negligence of others, always full of spiritual urgency;
with a mind and intention purified, free from the stain of evil desires.
Having transcended wrong view and being established in the true Dhamma,
he cuts through the deserts of the mind and unravels its fetters;
he gladdens the heart through liberation from defilement.
Living in seclusion, unattached, peaceful, and delighting in fewness of desires;
adorned with the lineage of the Noble Ones, well-rested, easy to support, and happy;
living a life of effacement, possessing the ascetic virtues, and devoted to the destruction of evil—such a one is truly a bhikkhu.
The Sage, whose conduct inspires confidence and who abounds in faith,
is unagitated and not fickle;
he is tamed, guarded, and has his faculties restrained.
One who values mental concentration,
being clearly comprehending and endowed with mindfulness,
having conceived an aspiration for the true Dhamma, and having generated a constant desire for it;
One who acts with persistence, possesses a good character,
and is devoted to practice, having removed the blackness from the mind,
thoroughly receives the supreme essence of meditation, just as a well-washed cloth takes up dye.
Thus having accomplished his form, with purified intentions,
moving without danger, he has reached safety, free from defilement.
Released from the grasp of evil, like the moon freed from Rāhu.
Surrounded by a halo of virtues, he brings splendor to the Conqueror’s teaching. Thus,
the wise one [praises] non-greed and non-hatred, as well as the absence of delusion,
furthermore renunciation, seclusion, and likewise deliverance.
Exerting himself and purifying his underlying disposition without remainder,
the wise one practices so as to attain the supreme happiness of meditation.
