Thereafter, with refined resolve and freed from all impediments, he proceeds.
Freed from obstacles, devoid of the dwelling-place of hindrances,
with a mental continuum inclined toward meditation, possessed of a pliant mind and self-confident—
how should such a one develop serenity (samatha) by undertaking the kasiṇas and other objects?
First, having made a well-rounded disk of dawn-colored clay measuring one span and four finger-breadths for the earth-kasiṇa,
and having placed it at a distance of a yoke’s length, one should sit comfortably in that spot.
Having formed the mental application with the conventional designation "earth," one should develop it.
They say that even on unplowed ground such as a threshing floor,
the sign arises without difficulty for one who possesses prior practice, provided it is within a circular area.
One should take up the water-kasiṇa disk in water contained in a vessel or the like;
the fire-kasiṇa in a flame; the air-kasiṇa disk in a hole in a wall or the like, or in a fan or similar implement.
The counterpart practice arises only in a place that has been touched [by the mind].
Whether it be a cloth, a flower, or a colored mineral used for the blue and other kasiṇas,
or the circle of space appearing in a hole in a wall and so forth— [these are the bases for the sign].
Just as one might take up the light that has entered through a crack and become established—
whether the light of the sun or other varieties— upon the ground or against a wall;
so too, for the yogi, there are ten ways [of establishing the mind] within the kasiṇas, wherever they may be.
For one performing the preliminary work, what is called the "learning sign" arises.
When that has become well-established in the mind, while still seeing it with the eye,
one should apply the meditation upon the sign of learning.
Warding off distraction and clearing away obstacles,
one should direct the mind toward the sign alone.
As he practices in this way, his mind becomes concentrated.
The defilements settle down and the counterpart image arises.
Therein, one should apply oneself to the development of meditation upon the sign consisting of the conceptual designation, and likewise upon the counterpart image.
Devoted to that, mindful, skilled in discerning the signs,
he balances the faculties while observing what is suitable.
Having restrained the agitated mind and uplifted the sluggish mind;
Encouraging the one who has been exhorted, and looking with equanimity upon the one who is concentrated—
just as the activity of bees and others is rightly described in relation to a lotus petal, a thread, a boat, and a tube.
The wise one, carefully observing the mode of the mind's activity,
should exert himself with self-exertion in such a balanced manner.
Having observed the mode of its even progression continuously, he should proceed.
For one who practices in this manner, what is called absorption (appanā) arises. However,
one should further expand the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta), whether it be the kasiṇa itself,
or at some point on the level of access (upacāra-bhūmi), or within absorption.
Expanding by means of the mind alone— just one finger-breadth, two finger-breadths, and so on— in due order, skillfully as far as desired;
having thus attained the first jhāna and made it proficient, then...
Having thus attained mastery, the wise one emerges from that [first jhāna] and proceeds accordingly to abandon the gross factors, beginning with applied thought (*vitakka*).
By practicing in this very manner, he attains the second and subsequent jhānas.
Having thus developed the ten kasiṇas in this way, the yogi,
having produced the fourfold and fivefold jhānas, becomes free from distraction.
With defilements thoroughly washed away, his mind is peaceful and concentrated.
They experience the flavor of seclusion at their own pleasure.
But how can one who is developing the meditation on the foul grasp the sign of the foul—
consisting of the bloated and other such stages— anywhere at all?
That which has passed beyond one day and so forth, called the "swollen" (uddhumātaka);
the "skinless," the loathsome, the "bluish-form" (nīlākāra), and the "livid" (vinīlaka).

one trains as a mental cognizer who experiences the mind while performing these.
Gladdening that very mind through concentration accompanied by rapture,
one is said to "train while gladdening the mind. Then,
steadying that very mind through both absorption and access [concentration],...
The yogi is described as "training by concentrating the mind";
likewise, he is said to be "training by liberating the mind" while releasing it through suppression and eradication of opposing states.
Mindfulness of breathing is a meditation subject according to its appropriate divisions;
that which is called "contemplation of mind" occurs here in four ways.
For it is specifically through its following after impermanence by means of insight [that it is so designated].
Contemplating, the wise one trains in the contemplation of impermanence.
Then, contemplating dispassion, having become disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate;
likewise, contemplating cessation, he brings to cessation the phenomena of the stages.
But through leaping forward, relinquishing, and renouncing,
one is said to "train as one who contemplates renunciation.
By means of the very gateway of mindfulness of breathing, there is insight into the phenomena of the stages.
Thus, the contemplation of mental phenomena (dhammānupassanā) is said to be fourfold.
In this way, through sixteen aspects established upon the three trainings,
one fulfills the fourfold development of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna).
Having grasped mindfulness and exerting himself in insight through the thirty-two aspects,
one is called "one who acts with mindfulness. And thus,
having developed serenity by means of counting and the other methods, thereafter—
Having made "insight" (vipassanā) his designation, and having again performed the observation [of the three characteristics],
he reaches the path called turning away (vivaṭṭana); established in the fruit of complete purity,
he attains the mindfulness-observation known as reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa).
Thus, mindfulness of breathing is fulfilled in its entirety;
it is said to be "developed" when accompanied by its aspects and its classifications.
This incomparable concentration on breathing is the supreme legacy of the Buddhas.
Having developed mindfulness, clear comprehension, and vastness— which remove the dust of evil defilements, provide a gateway to happiness,
extinguish the fire of suffering, and destroy distraction— they shall attain the supreme, unsurpassed,
and deathless state that pervades the three types of enlightenment.
To the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha, who are honored by many; to pure virtue and noble generosity;
to the deities established in the Dhamma—may they bring peace to death, to the body, and to the life-force.
With mindfulness concentrated for the sake of fearlessness in wisdom, may there be the arising of the path to enlightenment.
This guide to the True Dharma, endowed with the qualities of peace, should be practiced with diligence.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Analysis of the Ten Recollections," in the *Nāmarūpapariccheda*.
10. The Tenth Chapter:
The Analysis of the Remaining Meditation Subjects Having seen the danger in ill-will and so forth, and the state of security in patience;
But how can one develop the immeasurables while removing aversion?
Anger is a tormentor of the mind and a disturber of serenity.
It makes one ugly and hideous,
it destroys the complexion of the face;
it gives rise to impurity of virtue and brings about distraction of mind.
The destroyer of the lamp of wisdom, the obstructer of practice,
the path leading to the states of misery, the binder with the thorns of evil, the cutter-off of the path of Dhamma, and the closer of the door to the path.
This ill omen has arisen, destroying fame, beauty, and conditioned existence;
it shatters the root of virtue, brings about the convergence of suffering,
and creates ruin and calamity— the destroyer of all prosperity in this world.
The arising of a comet, the destroyer of the entire world;
the emergence of an ill omen for all wholesome qualities;
the eradication of beneficial undertakings; and the convergence of obstacles.
Repulsive in every aspect, a cause for universal loathing;
arisen as a gateway to misfortune, it is desired by one's enemies.
Terrible, it creates adversaries and brings about every kind of harm.
Fear born from within— people do not perceive it.
It is like licking the edge of a razor, or swallowing fire,
or eating a bitter gourd, or grasping a flaming weapon.
Fools, merely to satisfy their own malice and for their own destruction,
caress one who is entirely full of ill will, just as they would a fierce,
venomous snake. Through the heat of hatred, he is like a tree with fire that has climbed into its hollow.
Though being burned by their own fires, the afflicted ones writhed in agony;
yet the dull-witted do not realize they are being consumed by the wind of mental intentions,
blazing again and again like the interior of a furnace.
They have ascended the path of fear, opposing the path of security;
they are corrupted, covered in evil deeds, and opposed to the two goals.
They are without a protector, pierced by arrows, distracted, and full of lamentation.
Like blind deer in the forest, they wander about with their sight destroyed.
Fools who fail to prepare for the future, driven by the power of anger,
quickly abandon prosperity and fall away from fame and wealth.
Those who have undertaken their endeavors poorly, being deluded by the agitation of anger,
do not find the savor of the nectar of the Dhamma,
for they lack true knowledge. Indeed, this [life] is full of many dangers, like a disease that has arisen.
The wicked look on with indifference as if at a fire born upon their own laps.
Constantly prodding others with sufferings, defiled by the habit of the afflictions (kleśa),

Having reflected thus, one should wisely regard aversion as a wild beast rushing at one, or as a demon entering one,

Established by the Great Sage for the sake of well-being and security,
she who is named Khamā is the mother of those possessed of noble qualities; endowed with great psychic power,
she treats all beings with impartiality and brings about every form of excellence.
The sprinkling of water on the fire of anger,
the seat for removing the pain of grief and despair,
the extractor of the thorn of malice—
The release from resentment,
the arising of praise and fame, and the cultivation of the roots of virtue— these three,
when their doors are opened, lead to the perfection of two goals.
The complete exhaustion of the months of affliction,
the thorough pacification [of the mind], the sandalwood that brings joy to the heart,
the uprooting of all suffering, and the supreme manifestation of bliss.
The severance of misfortune and its arising, the removal of fear and terror,
the support for serenity of mind, and the bringer of the fruit of inspiration—
this sublime provision for enlightenment is practiced by humans and non-humans alike.
It is the crossing over the wilderness of evil, the blocking of the four states of misery,
and the closing of the gates for rebirth in the world of the gods.
It consists of wisdom, virtue, and concentration, and it is the purifier of practice.
Loving-kindness and gentleness are rare and much desired.
They are declared to be the virtue of forbearance, the very method for protecting oneself by restraining agitation, distraction, and restlessness caused by the defilements.
It is the liberation from cruelty, delight in harming, and aggression;
it is the destroyer of enmity and evil, the cause of benefit for the world,
the maker of the lamp of Dhamma, and the purifier of the stains of bondage.
Dispelling the darkness of delusion, establishing the attainment of prosperity,
and having accomplished both his own welfare and the welfare of others,
one who is devoted to forgiveness achieves all success, both in this world and in the next.
Endowed with the virtue of patience, compassionate toward living beings,
his actions unagitated, gentle, amiable, and pure; humble,
restrained in conduct, fortunate, and pleasant to behold.
Having attained the power of reflection, steadfast and sharp in intelligence,
unshakable and enduring all misfortunes and dangers;
Moving through the battle with Bhīma,
he shines like a noble elephant.
Thus, for one who reflects upon forbearance, there is auspiciousness on all sides.
Having arisen, patience calms the agitation of ill will,
just as divine medicine dispels disease, or as rain extinguishes a fire.
Forbearance quickly causes one’s own anger to vanish.
Endowed with manifold virtues and the dispeller of manifold faults,
one should first, with a mind serene and steadfast, resolve upon the quality of patience and cultivate the supreme meditation on loving-kindness.
Making oneself the standard of comparison, for the sake of increasing the welfare of beings:
may all beings— whether creatures, living things, spirits, or persons— be free from affliction,
free from enmity, free from distress, and possessed of happiness.
May those of great renown increase their wealth through the attainment of true knowledge;
may they possess the strength of a retinue and be free from fear and calamity.
May they be amiable, pleasant in conversation, and free from mutual conflict.
May all be well-fed and content; may no evil come upon them.
Abounding in faith and gladness, with great celebration of giving and virtue, their continuums adorned with noble qualities, may they preserve a life free from affliction.
Placing right view at the forefront, may they accomplish through the practice of the true Dhamma the means to welfare—
the ultimate instrument for achieving happiness.
Thus, with a mind intent on the benefit of beings in manifold ways...
Even as a mother would feel for her beloved son, may [I] extend [this feeling] continuously.
Avoiding attachment and destroying ill will,
with a completely pure mind, may I desire only the welfare [of others].
Cultivating loving-kindness toward friends, neutrals, and enemies respectively,
one effects the breaking down of boundaries and radiates it equally upon oneself.
As one thus practices that very concentration which is intent upon the welfare [of others],...
Taking the sevenfold designation as his object, the mind becomes concentrated.
Thereafter, free from distress, one-pointed, and with his desires stilled,
he enters the threefold or fourfold jhāna through the liberation of the mind by loving-kindness.
In beings distinguished by the divisions of earth, gods, and so forth, [compassion] applies specifically (odhiso);
in all beings without distinction (anodhiso), it applies according to possibility.
Thus, even toward a single being, because of the necessity of delimitation, [it is established].
It proceeds toward many beings and toward all. One whose mental continuum has been thus cultivated through the liberation of mind that is loving-kindness,
[attains the destruction of the taints].
Thereafter, one should begin the practice of the cultivation of compassion (karuṇābhāvanāyoga),
having properly directed the mind toward the state of suffering of sentient beings.
Thinking, "Alas! May all beings be liberated from suffering," how is it that this young man,
trembling with fear and terror, pierced by calamity and misfortune, writhes in distress?
Thus these people, practicing for the sake of separation, are antagonistic;
possessed by ill will and overwhelmed by mental suffering, they are tormented.
Furthermore, others lament, fallen into misfortune and ruin.
Those whose intentions are based on base means partake in sorrow and despair. Furthermore,
others who have come to ruin, brought under the sway of sensual desires and afflictions,
and fallen into the darkness of delusion— such beings go to an evil destination.
There, experiencing their own bitter and terrible fruit, pierced by the pangs of suffering,
they wail with arms outstretched in the caves.
This is due to their long-standing devotion to the prosperity of the world of the gods.
The deva-bodies pass away, turning back against their will.
Having blazed for a long time like the sun within the sky,
even the Brahmas fall down, though they have the Brahma-world as their ultimate destination.
Thus, this house of suffering called the five aggregates,
scattered among various destinies, afflicts the multitude of living beings.
Helpless and fallen into misfortune, they are agitated by the fear of decline.
He turns around like a bird tossed by a whirlwind.
Having seen, heard, or even merely inferred this,
desiring the removal of suffering and aspiring for the removal of suffering—
Among those who are happy, the wise person,
recollecting the nature of suffering, should practice the absorption of the cultivation of compassion,
filled with pity: "Oh, may beings be liberated in every way from states of suffering!"
“May weariness, sorrows, and lamentations be stilled;
may evil states be exhausted, and likewise may our defilements be pacified;
and may the fetters of sentient beings be utterly severed.”
“May ill will depart, and may calamities turn back;
may misfortunes perish, and may failures vanish.
May affliction and distress, and fear and terror, be extinguished.”
"May those who have been released go back; may living beings see safety.
Thus, feeling compassion for all beings in every way, he feels compassion while aspiring for the uprooting of all suffering.
Preventing the arising of sorrow and removing harm from afar,
the meditator brings the absorption of loving-kindness to its culmination;
immediately after compassion, the yogi should then develop sympathetic joy.
Having properly reflected upon the manner in which beings experience happiness, [he asked]:
"How is it that for a long time the Brahmās— possessing great splendor and great psychic power,
feeding on rapture, abiding in beauty, and free from disease— rejoice?"
The devas possess great wealth,
high authority, and renown;
they are surrounded by throngs of celestial nymphs.
They sport in the Nandana grove.
Having attained the glory of royal consecration, adorned with parasols and fly-whisks,
they enjoy royal pleasures, happy, having resolved upon sovereignty.
With the enjoyments thus provided, as well as other living beings who have achieved their desires,
they rejoice with happiness and joy. Even those beings belonging to the four states of misery,
through the exhaustion of their evil karma, [attain this state].
Having passed away from there, they rejoice, established in a state of happiness.
Having attained the supramundane state— the uprooting of all attachments—
they, with their distress stilled, experience a joy that is not small.
Having seen or heard this, and having reflected upon it again and again, one who endures the conditions of beings rejoices in the aspect of happiness:
"Oh, how good! Oh, how excellent!"
Truly, living beings rejoice!
Oh, what a great gain for sentient beings—
that their desired prosperity has been attained!
“With serene facial complexions and fulfilled aspirations,
abounding in rapture and gladness, may they live long and in good health.
Having transcended the path of fear, released from the mass of suffering;”
Having attained the path of peace, blooming with the perfection of rapture—
united, well-satisfied, and longing for reconnection— they,
adorned with noble qualities, experience supreme attainment.
Thus, rightly desiring the perfection of attaining happiness,
rejoicing in beings and pervading them equally with sympathetic joy,
one abandons attachment to aversion and is freed from the delight in lordship.
Through loving-kindness, one attains access concentration and the absorption of sympathetic joy.
Having cultivated sympathetic joy, however, one should cultivate supreme equanimity,
abandoning both aversion and attachment, and becoming even-minded.
Seeing that gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise are the inherent nature of the world,
one should remain equanimous.
Only pleasure and pain.
How does this world revolve through the ownership of one's own karma?
One who is ruined by worldly conditions is deprived of self-mastery.
What indeed is there here that is capable of causing [beings] to proceed according to their own desire?
Or by whose will are they happy or miserable?
For the happiness and suffering of living beings arise solely from their respective conditions.
It is not possible for anyone else to turn them back again.
By adhering to the wrong path, the conceited fail;
but by placing the right path before them, they succeed once more as they truly are.
Therein, by way of their bodies, these beings revolve otherwise;
they perform whatever work they please, each exercising his own independent power.
This worldly wandering seems to me a pursuit devoid of purpose, a mere infliction of suffering.
This is peaceful, this is sublime: namely, that equanimity toward those [objects].
Who am I, and who are these people?
Why do I, not understanding the proper place, become distressed within myself while looking around at others?
Whether they be happy or not, whether they be freed from suffering or not,
whether they be prosperous or poor— what concern of mine is it here?
Let living beings fare according to their own desires, protecting themselves as they wish.
There, for me, there is no hindrance, nor proliferation, nor ill-will. Thus,
observing with equanimity toward all formations— even while desiring the welfare of living beings—
he pervades them evenly and methodically with impartial equanimity.
Having emerged from equanimity toward the unknown and having dispelled attachment,
he reaches the absorption of the fifth jhāna, which is like loving-kindness.
Thus did the Best of Speakers proclaim these four immeasurables.
The Great Sage, the great steed among Great Beings, desiring the welfare [of others],
taught that for a beginner yogi, loving-kindness should never be developed toward deceased beings who possess a different gender from one's own.
The aspect of the attainment to be reached, the aspect of suffering in living beings,
the aspect of rejoicing, and likewise the aspect of being dependent on others;
[these are applied] to oneself, to a friend in distress, and to a neutral person, respectively.
Having first begun the practice of meditation, thereafter,
by breaking down the boundaries among oneself, friends, neutral persons,
and enemies— these four— one should maintain an even mind toward all.
Whether distinguished by way of their divisions such as the stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth,
or undistinguished, these [perfections] are said to be "to be cultivated.
With mental continuums that are unagitated, they become compassionate toward living beings through those [cultivations].
They are considered "sublime abodes" (brahmavihāra) because they dwell as the highest states.
They are designated as "immeasurables" (appamaññā) because their objects are immeasurable, because they are practiced correctly,
and because they are immeasurable with respect to sentient beings.
Thinking, "Beings who have not attained prosperity are suffering,
while those who have attained it are their own masters of karma," he then [directs his mind] toward them in due order:
"May they succeed through prosperities..."
May living beings be freed from suffering;
oh, may beings attain happiness;
may beings be well in every way.
Desiring his increase, as well as the removal of suffering,
he rejoices when [the son] prospers and looks on with equanimity when he is gratified.
Just as a mother toward her young child, so does he act toward one who is ill or established in youth.
And when intent upon its duty, it proceeds in four ways.
Thus, the right application of the mind toward beings is fourfold;
in every respect, it is indeed fourfold, as stated by the Great Seer.
But one who develops this [mindfulness], with a serene face and mind,
sleeps happily even when asleep and sees no evil whatsoever.
Waking up without fear, they rejoice as if already awake.
And one quickly attains composure of mind;
dangers are abandoned, and calamities vanish;
even deities protect one who is undeluded and unperturbed.
Just as people at the proper time behold a blooming lotus or the stainless moon,
so do they look upon him with eyes of affection because of his gentle and amiable qualities.
Unshakable and unagitated, the wise man remains steadfast in all circumstances.
The Great Sages describe the commencement of activity that proceeds equally as embracing the entire world;
yet when it occurs in a single individual for a mere moment,
they describe it as immeasurable once it has fully blossomed.
Just as the cultivation that has reached absorption toward all beings—
these four, having become equalized and mastered without interval,
and flowing with a stream of merit, fill the wise one.
Like the immeasurable great ocean garlanded with waves,
it has been declared that all merits consisting of acquisitions are not worth even a sixteenth part of the merits made up of the immeasurables.
Not in vain is the renunciation of one who has reverence for these [precepts];
abounding in subtle energy, he trains well in the three trainings.
He partakes especially of the alms-food of the kingdom not fruitlessly.
Even that gift of faith becomes of great fruit when it is firmly established.
The wholesome qualities beginning with faith increase unimpaired,
and the greatness of his conduct in perfect enlightenment becomes manifest.
For the penetration of what is difficult to penetrate,
the supreme foundational jhāna is the straight and direct path for rebirth in the Brahma-world.
These states partake of the residual impression and serve as the equipment for enlightenment.
They lead to heaven, they bring happiness, and they are the unsurpassed protection of the world.
Having immeasurable benefits and arising from immeasurable virtues, these are therefore called the "immeasurables" (appamaññā); a wise person should not be negligent regarding them.
But cultivating the supreme perception of repulsiveness regarding nutriment—
comprising solid food and the like,
such as what is eaten, chewed, drunk, and tasted— he goes into solitude.
One should contemplate it as repulsive: "How is it that,
having left this delightful and undisturbed penance grove,
one must go for the sake of food to a village crowded with villagers?"
There, in that place defiled by impurities, a mixture of the refuse of the wicked,
one remains standing, eating food from house to house—
food that is soiled with spittle and mucus, having been turned over by the tip of the tongue.
Mixed with powdered tooth-sticks, it defiles its color and fragrance.
Enveloped by bile and phlegm, mixed with pus and blood, as it enters,
it is repulsive, loathsome, and more wretched than a corpse.
In the belly, strewn with corpses and permeated by foul odors,
it is like the vomit of a dog in a dog’s trough,
or like a hot pit of sand teeming with various kinds of worms.
Therein, covered by a membrane like a bubble,
it cooks while steaming; and as it cooks, permeated by its own inherent nature,
it increases the mass of various putridities, such as hair, body hair, and so forth.
Furthermore, it is subject to decomposition and brings about manifold calamities;
it is the source of hundreds of great diseases such as leprosy, sores, and skin eruptions.
It has become putrid, is ripe with decay, and is accumulated through many openings.
Like a mass of pus that has turned foul, it constantly oozes.
Because the body has become putrid, it perpetually emits a stench;
even though it is washed continually, it never attains a state of purity.
This food is loathsome,
a nourishment for the impurity of the body;
its outflow is filth and excrement.
It brings about the fruit of secondary defilements;
it is the origin of sensual lust, the bond for the birth of disease,
the basis for intoxication and negligence, and the great highway for evil deeds.
This path leads to what is harmful, giving rise to fear and terror;
it is a gateway for the arrival of calamity, a mouth that brings one to the states of misery.
Therein, those who are intoxicated by gluttony wander about, utterly self-indulgent.
The foolish, performing defiled deeds, become partakers of suffering. In this regard,
for the sake of the fading away of the mind, what [is there] in that which resembles a ripe fruit—
appearing sweet and pleasant to the taste, yet accumulated with terrible danger?
For one who thus cultivates the perception of repulsiveness and makes it manifest,
the mind, having reached the stage of access concentration, becomes concentrated.
This [state] is the "tranquilized-nutriment" (passambhitāhāra).
He is discerning and possessed of vision;
he has emerged from intoxication and negligence, and is free from attachment to the tasting of flavors.
He partakes of food as if he were anointing his eyes with medicinal ointment,
or as if he were eating the flesh of his own son;
thus does one born into the lineage of the Noble Ones consume his meal.
Exalted by qualities such as fewness of desires,
the wise person, having torn apart the net of sensual pleasures, attains safety.
Furthermore, while developing the analysis of the four elements in five ways,
one should comprehend all four elements according to their intrinsic nature:
in brief and in detail, as requisites and by way of their specific characteristics.
How should one divide [the elements] fourfold, both internally and externally?
Whatever hardness there is, such as hair of the head, hair of the body, and so forth, is called the internal earth element; that which is beyond this is the external.
Whatever is called "become fat," it is water that causes maturation;
one might take it to be fire or wind.
One should meditate on the distending [element] in its entirety.
Even in detail, one should contemplate the twenty components beginning with head-hairs and body-hairs,
as well as the twelve beginning with the earth element and bile.
By that heat by which this body is warmed, grows old,
is thoroughly consumed, and by which food and other things eaten are digested—
this is the fourfold constituent of the body's own origin.
One might grasp at it as the fire element, and another as the wind element:
the winds moving upward and downward, those in the belly and the bowels, those circulating through every limb, and likewise the sixfold inhalation and exhalation.
Taking up each respective characteristic and determining its specific mark,
one should everywhere enumerate the fourfold inclusion of elements.
Thus, this fourfold division—
This body is merely the elements; it is insentient, devoid of a being,
substanceless, and food for others.
Empty, void, and hollow; secluded and renounced;
neither self nor anything belonging to a self.
There is not even the slightest bit of self here.
It is merely this body, impelled by volition, that moves about;
shaken by it like a machine, it appears as if it possessed intention.
When life, heat, and consciousness leave this body,
it then lies cast away like a useless log.
Those who are shrouded by delusion proliferate manifold conceptualizations in a distorted manner.
Wherein ordinary people, overcome by wrong perversions,
do not transcend the desert of the cycle of existence— a place crowded with the four states of misery and a means leading only to manifold calamities— those who are evil-doers.
When he thus sees [them] in four ways by way of the analysis of the elements,
for him there is that which is called the "accessory" [meditation].
Tranquillity arises in the mind.
Having thus performed the analysis of the elements,
one should accordingly [analyze] all derivative material phenomena and mental phenomena in every way.
Having grasped the stages as they have become, and seeing the stability of conditions—
both internally and externally— he contemplates their arising and passing away.
Having understood them as they truly are through direct knowledge, he becomes disenchanted and is dispassionate.
Having become dispassionate and liberated, one is called "one who has gone beyond.
Furthermore, while developing the formless attainments as a pure meditation subject,
having reached the fourfold and fivefold jhānas within the kasiṇa-maṇḍala.
Having mastered mastery over the fifth jhāna, emerging from it,
he frequently reflects upon the faults of material form, such as the taking up of sticks and so forth.
Becoming disenchanted with that form and with its mode and objective field, he...
Desiring the transcendence of even those phenomena that serve as objects,
the steadfast and mindful one, having spread out whatever object there may be— apart from the space-kasiṇa— then removes that very kasiṇa.
He does not attend to it, nor does he blame it, nor does he look at it;
completely freed from the application of thought regarding the kasiṇa in every way,
his mind turns toward the space known as that very [kasiṇa].
He practices thoroughly, reflecting with systematic wisdom.
His mind proceeds toward the contemplation of space— the realm free from the kasiṇa—
accomplished through mindfulness and established by means of skillful methods.
Having thus made it disappear, one should thereafter pervade the entire kasiṇa,
which is immediately adjacent and has space as its range.
By developing it there according to the method already stated, up to the stage of access (upacāra);
He attains the first formless state, whose domain is the infinity of space.
Then, having mastered that and emerged from it, he reflects:
"This is the adversary to the neighboring fine-material-sphere jhāna."
Having exhausted attachment to that sphere of space,

he proceeds from there to enter the peaceful stream of consciousness of the second formless attainment, pervading it as infinite. From there, he proceeds to the first formless consciousness, pervading it as infinite.
He attains the second formless state, whose range is the infinity of consciousness.
Then, through the non-existence of the consciousness of the first formless state,
he attains the third formless state, the sphere of nothingness.
Then, seeing the third formless attainment as "peaceful," one enters the fourth formless attainment within the domain of the third formless attainment.
It is like one person clinging to a pavilion built over excrement, while another, depending on that first person, clings to it as well.
One stands outside, independent; another stands supported by this or that.
These four persons, standing respectively, should be understood by the discerning one as being equal in their commonality.
Through the distinctions of their objects, the development of the formless attainments is fourfold;
yet even so, they do not speak of a distinction in their factors.
Nevertheless, they become increasingly more refined, each higher than the last, according to their sequence.
Just as the celestial attainments of the Four Great Kings and others [are gained],
so too, having developed the fourfold immovable attainment,
one whose intention is well-concentrated possesses an unshakable mind.
Seeing things as they truly are and having realized the supreme fruit,
one who is liberated in both ways is called an Arahant.
Having understood the forty-fold method of meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), therefrom...
The higher knowledges (abhiññā) are to be understood within the method of development for serenity (samatha):
the various supernormal powers (iddhividhā), the divine ear (dibbasota), the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariya-jānanā),
the recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussati), and likewise the divine eye (dibbacakkhu).
Released from mental concentration, the five direct knowledges are manifested;
they consist of form-sphere phenomena belonging to the plane of the fifth jhāna.
The resolve for multiplicity and so forth, as well as the transformations such as becoming a youth and so on—
Thus, there are three kinds of supernormal powers: the creation of mind-made forms,
as well as divine and human sounds,
whether far or near.
That by which they hear is called the divine ear-element (dibbā sotadhātu).
Knowledge of the minds of others (cetopariyañāṇa) is [the knowledge] of the mind of another person.
It is described as that which distinguishes between those with lust and those free from lust, and so forth.
The knowledge regarding the recollection of previously lived aggregates is described by the name "knowledge of the recollection of past lives" (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa). Such is it.
As beings pass away and are reborn— whether in the realm of form or the formless realm—
as well as human forms, whether gross or subtle,
near or far, manifest or concealed— it is by means of this that yogis see them all.

they are seen vanishing, wasting away, and disappearing;
formations are being destroyed, falling, and perishing.
That is declared to be the knowledge of dissolution, by which knowledge one who sees [the three characteristics] pursues impermanence in all three ways of insight.
For impermanence is indeed manifest in the dissolution of arising and passing away.
Then, through the penetration of fear, danger, and disenchantment, the three characteristics— suffering, non-self, and impermanence—
become manifest to the yogi who contemplates the three characteristics while focused on dissolution. Thus, for the practitioner,
all conditioned phenomena appear as being fraught with peril.
Like those pursued by wild beasts, like those sinking in the great ocean,
like those seized by non-human spirits, or like those surrounded by enemies;
like those licked by black serpents, or those attacked by fierce elephants.
Like those who have fallen from a precipice, like those falling into a blazing fire,
like great thieves who have reached their destined death, like those whose heads are being severed,
like those being impaled on a stake, or like those cast down from a mountain.
Caught in the straits of birth, oppressed by old age and disease,
struck down by the thunderbolt of death, they are partakers of great calamity.
Constantly assailed by death, they are overwhelmed by the burden of suffering.
Flowing from the seat of fear, destined for lamentation,
beings here are intoxicated by their infatuation with craving and views;
though bound by fear as if they were bound, they imagine themselves free from fear as if they were released.
Thus, for one who observes the arising of fear within conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*),
the great seers who have transcended fear call it "knowledge of fear.
Furthermore, conditioned phenomena are seen everywhere as being accompanied by fear.
It brings harm, is unwholesome, and constantly possesses danger without interval.
It is like a pit of putrid excrement, like fire covered by ashes,
like water infested with demons, and like food mixed with poison.
A forest infested with wild beasts, a path beset by the great terror of robbers,
a great ship breaking apart, or like a thunderbolt striking down fruit-bearing trees;
[or] those clad in armor and standing on a battlefield crowded with weapons.
A great army has gathered, terrible and directed toward misfortune;
it carries a chariot mounted with wheels, drawn by mares,
with the great onset of the world’s end, as if the eon itself were passing between one's fingers.
Likewise, the worlds are possessed of that [suffering],
crowded with great calamities,
and are being consumed by the eleven fires.
Devoted to frantic struggling,
the abodes of beings— the wombs of existence, the destinies, and the stations—
have become like a great forest on fire, resembling glowing embers.
The great elements are venomous snakes; the five aggregates are murderers;
the eyes and other faculties are empty villages; and the sense objects are the village-destroyers.
Thus, this entire circle of the ocean of existence is strewn with such perils.
No shelter, no protection, no support, and no refuge exists.
Here, fools who have mounted [the chariot] are like fish with crooked hands;
they are as if launched from a great cart and stand in the midst of great terror.
Being born and passing away, oppressed by various misfortunes,
fallen into the whirlpool of calamity, with their resolve bound for death;
shrouded in the darkness of delusion, they are overwhelmed by the four floods.
Pierced by the dart of suffering, they are tormented and distressed.
Thus, like a poisonous flower, it brings various kinds of misfortune;
it is a confinement followed by suffering, arisen like a disease.
Like an enraged venomous snake, a source of terrible fear;
like a brandished sword, a state that accumulates suffering;
like water that is boiling, seething, and parched.
Knowledge that perceives arising and occurrence, as well as the sign and accumulation,
and rebirth-linking, is considered knowledge of danger; by means of it,
one penetrates the lack of growth in things belonging to the three planes.
When contemplating conditioned phenomena that end in fear and terror,
and which are the basis for many dangers, one becomes disenchanted and free from attachment.
Like one who desires life avoiding poison, or like a coward avoiding enemies.
Like a Naga king toward a Supaṇṇa, or like a man of great wealth toward a thief,

one who discerns [the truth] while being oppressed by the constriction of the underlying tendencies to suffering inspires a sense of spiritual urgency in those who are joyless and agitated by the fear of obstacles.
Like one who is pure regarding urine and excrement, like one who is satisfied after vomiting,
like one well-anointed regarding a foul odor, or like one well-bathed regarding a courtyard;
[so it is] with that which is defiled by lust and hatred and putrid with the four taints.
Even while loathing conditioned phenomena— which have the trivial worldly pleasures of the inferior realms as their essence and are defiled by the poison of affliction—
the wise person does not take delight in them.
This relinquishing of delight by him is what they call the knowledge of disenchantment.
Having seen the danger and peril in conditioned phenomena,
the wise person becomes disenchanted with them and desires to be liberated from them—
like fish caught in a net or birds trapped in a cage.
Like a bird bound in a cage, like a serpent confined in a basket,
like a great elephant stuck in the mud, like the moon that has entered the mouth of Rāhu,
or like a deer caught in a snare— such is one in the prison of *saṃsāra*.
Enveloped by ignorance, spread over with the five aggregates,
concealed by the net of views, and encircled by perversions;
bound by the five hindrances, and raised upon the pillar of conceit.
Deep as the fall of a thunderbolt, causing ruin and downfall;
arising from old age and disease, appearing like a comet;
a conflagration of anger and resentment, smoldering with grief and despair.
In this place besieged by madness and negligence, dragged away by the craving for existence,
terrified by separation, and agitated by the constant fear of the states of woe;
constantly struck by the six objects of sense and battered at the doors of contact;
With volition as the cause and feeling as the effect,
amidst the clamor of meaningless chatter and the agitation of the demons of the defilements,
one who is bound seeks liberation at the commencement and conclusion of death.
Like impure matter touched by fire, like a corpse seized by one wishing to devour it, or like a weapon being brandished;
for one who desires to abandon conditioned phenomena that are beset by great calamity.

It is said that "the knowledge of the desire for liberation has arisen" regarding those things that are difficult to abandon, which act as fetters, and which are the meeting place of the knots and underlying tendencies—
the grasping of craving and clinging, bound up with delight and lust.
One who constantly releases conditioned phenomena— hardened by the intoxication of views and pride,
bound tightly by the snare of greed, in the great wilderness of the fetters that have proliferated for a long time—
must do so as if having struck a serpent with a stick.
Without over-reflecting on the characteristics, but rather with subtle and systematic attention,
one who grasps with equanimity investigates,
in particular, the fruit of the *vagguli* tree for the sake of liberation free from longing.
Like cotton that has been beaten, beating it again and again;
like grinding a fragrance, grinding it thoroughly and well.
Mindful and well-concentrated, [he contemplates]: "Impermanent, suffering, and non-self."
Piercing through and penetrating, he contemplates the characteristics.
As he thus contemplates, the wise call that subtle knowledge "contemplation by way of reflection" as it investigates.
Thus, seeing correctly and having realized the three characteristics through their true nature as it really is, he contemplates right there:
"Impermanent indeed are conditioned phenomena, though formerly they were grasped as permanent."
What is suffering has been seen as happiness; what is non-self has been seen as self.
Furthermore, that which is conditioned is in every way impermanent, suffering, and non-self;
it is a state that cannot be obtained [as one wishes], and likewise, it is subject to being done against one's will.

Merely consisting of elements, dependent on others, devoid of what belongs to a self, brought under the sway of the realm of death, and having as their range of experience that which is struck down by acquisitions—
such is the conventional expression "I" or "mine," whether referring to another or belonging to another.
Neither a self nor anything belonging to a self exists anywhere in terms of substance.
Just as the word "chariot" arises when the collection of parts is present,
so too, when the aggregates exist, there is the conventional designation "a being."
Therein, foolish people of dull wit imagine a self, whether internally or externally;
yet for one who sees, there is nothing whatsoever.
Whether happy or suffering, a so-called "person" does not exist anywhere at all.
In every respect, there is no self as a substantial entity; conditioned phenomena possess that very nature. Arising, decaying, and passing away, these conditioned things are themselves suffering;
yet they do not belong to anyone for the sake of suffering.
For it is suffering alone that arises, suffering that persists and passes away;
nothing other than suffering arises, and nothing other than suffering ceases.
Herein, there is nothing to be grasped; let this conceptual proliferation be abandoned.
"The impulses have ceased; their arising was purposeless.
Let formations be impermanent, or suffering—what does that matter to me here?
Or let them be non-self. Thus the knowledge of equanimity towards formations proceeds.
Having thus seen things as they truly are, up until their dissolution and beyond that,
insight— having conceived the embryo of meditative development and reached full maturity—
is certain to reach the conclusion of dissolution when fear, danger, and disenchantment arise.
Having become disenchanted and becoming dispassionate, he contemplates with equanimity.
Therein, it is like discarded urine and excrement, or like a lump of spittle;
like a neglected son born of another, or like a neglected wife.
For one who contemplates with equanimity both the process of occurrence and the sign—
whether regarding all conditioned phenomena or the destinies, wombs, and states of existence—
it is like water on a lotus leaf, or a mustard seed on the point of a needle.
Like a chicken’s footprint in a field, or like parched grain in a fire, the mind does not spread out;
it does not cling, nor is it bound.
Its attachments dissolve away, and it turns back from the cycle of existence.
Just as one oppressed by heat longs for coolness,
as one with an empty stomach craves food, and as one who is thirsty desires water, so too [does the seeker long for the Dhamma].
Like one who is ill seeking a great physician;
like one who is afraid seeking a land of safety; like one in distress seeking a great treasure;
like one lost seeking the direct path; and like one in the middle of the ocean seeking an island.
One yearns for Nibbāna— the state that is free from aging and death,
unconditioned, taintless, and the exhaustion of all suffering.
And this insight (vipassanā), having reached the peak, leads to emergence.
Like a bird seeing the shore, she proceeds in accordance with the natural order.
But seeing that the sign of non-arising is peaceful,
like a bird abandoning a fruitless tree, she emerges from the conditioned.
"Access concentration" refers to the development belonging to the sense-sphere;
this is the mundane path, the preliminary insight.
Thus, when development has been cultivated, it reaches full maturity in due course.
Relinquishing conditioned phenomena and leaping into the unconditioned,
one generates the unsurpassed Path through the excellence of its cultivation— just as fire,
smoke, and radiant light arise from the friction of rubbing wood together.
Just as the sun rises preceded by the dawn,
so too does the factor of the path proceed preceded by insight (vipassanā).
And proceeding in that manner, it has the state of Nibbāna as its domain.
By way of the threefold liberation, according to what is appropriate and without exception,
it arises for a single moment of consciousness and vanishes—
having struck down the defiled continuum— just as a thunderbolt strikes a mountain.
In the very manner previously described, one should set forth upon the method of absorption (appanā);
according to the distinctions of the foundational jhānas (pādakajjhāna), there will be a fixed determination of the jhāna factors (jhānaṅga).
The spheres of activity (gocara) are designated as preliminary (parikamma), access (upacāra), and conformity (anuloma).
Whatever characteristic or mode [of the formations] arises for one who is practicing insight,
the change-of-lineage (gotrabhu) moment is born after that, having taken Nibbāna as its object.
Therefore, because it has emerged from the external aggregates, it is called "emergence" (vuṭṭhāna).
Then the path proceeds as it is being liberated from the defilements;
therefore, there is emergence from both—the aggregates and the defilements.
There are two or three fruits, and after that [the path].
Having severed that [defilement], there occurs a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and then reflective knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā) arises.
The wise person reflects upon the Path, the Fruit, and Nibbāna;
as for the inferior defilements and the remaining ones, he may or may not reflect upon them.
Having developed [the path] and established himself in the first fruit,
such as stream-entry, he then further grasps name-and-form as before.
And practicing insight by stages, once again as appropriate, he proceeds.
In due order, there are the once-returners and so forth.
Thus, in this exposition of the analysis of ripening,
and in this meditation cultivated by those who have awakened following the Buddha;
One who goes to the further shore of the ocean of existence relinquishes [the fetters];
the Great Sage’s path leads to the further shore of the ocean of qualities.
Thus, this tenfold classification of meditation—
Having gradually developed that which brings supreme benefit,
the wise ones eventually attain the ageless and deathless state and relinquish all defilement forever.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Analysis of the Ten Stages," within the Section on the Delimitation of Name-and-Form. Chapter Thirteen.
The Analysis of the Outflow Result:
What has been called "the outflow of insight" will hereafter be explained in due order,
beginning with the penetration of the Truths.
Full understanding, abandoning, realization, and development:
thus they say there are four kinds of tasks regarding the truths of suffering and the rest.
All of these will be performed at the time of the Path, and thereafter.
Because their function has been pacified, how is it that the fruit is already accomplished?

Like a palmyra tree whose roots for further fruit have been severed, the aggregates— whose underlying tendencies (anusaya) are cut at the root— are no longer capable of being a basis for the occurrence of the perversions (vipallāsa).
Because they are the absolute opposites of the four paths, when those paths proceed,
the defilements do not arise again, just as a sprout does not grow from a burnt seed.
By way of their specific function of leading out, they serve as mutual conditions for one another.
One develops path after path, or again, as it arises.
"Development" is said to occur within the continuity of the path's occurrence;
by that which is currently present, the task is brought to completion without remainder.
Thus, by way of their function, one penetrates all three truths simultaneously with the Path while realizing Nibbāna.
And herein, penetration is so called because of the manifestation of their respective functions.
And this path accomplishes that very thing, leading forth with peace as its domain.
Having completely relinquished all conditioned formations, it aims at the extinction of the path;
it is described as the accomplishment of the task, leading out through the truths.
For the path alone leads out; the rest are its auxiliaries:
the states of jhāna are those that bring one near, and the factors conducive to enlightenment are those that awaken.
Therefore, they specifically explain the emergence from that very [path].
Having formed a conviction regarding the aggregates, the defilements,
and the threefold liberation— wherever and however it may be—
and having thereafter comprehended the phenomena of each stage and practiced insight, [one proceeds].
If there is emergence from anything whatsoever by way of impermanence,
one becomes abundant in resolve through the excellence of the faculty of faith. Thus,
the seven types of persons who are leading out by means of the signless liberation—
The faith-follower is in the first stage, the one liberated by faith is in the middle, and the one liberated by wisdom is at the end; thus do the Tathāgatas describe him.
Having seen conditioned phenomena as suffering, that person emerges [from them].
Having become abundant in tranquility through the attainment of the faculty of concentration, one may likewise be delivered by means of the wishless; thus there would be three ways of deliverance.
Having emerged from [the contemplation of] non-self, through the application of abundance in knowledge (veda),...
Leading toward emptiness through the excellence of the faculty of wisdom,
one is a "Dhamma-follower" in the first [moment], and thereafter one "attains vision";
finally, one is "liberated by wisdom"— thus do the wise explain it.
Having realized Nibbāna through the distinction of the body of jhāna based on the immovable (āneñja) and the body of form, six are "body-witnesses" (kāyasakkhin) in the middle;
and [others] through the formless (arūpa) by means of the Path and through the immovable (āneñja) by means of form.
Liberated, one becomes an Arahant liberated in both ways.
Having become the gateway to the three liberations,
insight (vipassanā) brings about emergence and accomplishes the classification of the seven types of persons.
Faith resolves with respect to the true nature of the basis,
while wisdom penetrates everywhere among all knowable phenomena.
Therefore, both faith and wisdom have the characteristic of determining the basis.
This insight characterized by the three marks is established upon a foundation.
Therefore, the meditator whose vehicle is faith, having seen the gross characteristic,
subsequently resolves upon the subtle as "not-self."
For one who is thus resolved, either faith alone,
or faith accompanied by a predominance of the faculty of concentration, becomes the "hourglass" for emergence.
For one whose insight is dominated by wisdom, there is delusion regarding the coarse characteristics.
Having reached the true nature of phenomena (dhamma-sabhāva), one penetrates the subtle.
Therefore, for one whose burden is faith, the two types of emergence occur first;
at the end, wisdom reaches full perfection in one who follows after faith.
Some teachers, however, maintain that for one whose burden is wisdom, the rest [of the factors] are subordinate;
they have explained what is called the "convergence of the burdens" in relation to the stages of emergence.
And [the stage of] "one who has seven births at most,"...
The "one who goes from family to family" and likewise the other,
the "one-seeded"— thus the stream-enterer is said to be of three kinds.
Having come to this world only once more, the person is further declared as the "Once-returner" (Sakadāgāmin).
Likewise, there is the one who attains Parinibbāna in the interval (Antarāparinibbāyī), and another who attains it upon reaching [the next life] (Upahaccaparinibbāyī).
The one without exertion, the one with exertion, and the one who goes upstream—thus there are five.
The non-returner is the third, and the fourth is the arahant.
In this way, there are four who stand at the fruit, and those beyond them are those standing on the path.
By way of the sequence of development and according to penetration,
there are four pairs and eight types of noble persons.
Views and doubts are abandoned in every way by the first path.
Even that which leads to the states of misery, as well as other evil things, is abandoned.
Likewise, by the path of the once-returner, the gross [defilements] are destroyed;
and by the path of the non-returner, the faults of sensual desire are entirely eliminated.
By means of Arahantship, all defilements are exhausted in every way;
the wise person should understand that the abandonment of defilements occurs according to the appropriate application.
There are four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā): regarding meaning, phenomena, language, and [insight].
The wise speak on inspired eloquence and knowledge that has reached its culmination;
cause and fruit, Nibbāna, the meaning of what was spoken, and likewise another,
namely non-action as a result— these five are spoken of by way of their meanings.
The cause, the noble path, and another thing that has been spoken of—namely, the wholesome and the unwholesome:
thus five categories of phenomena have been elucidated.
Within those very [categories], there is a tenfold division according to the meaning and the phenomena as appropriate.
Whatever expression exists by way of intrinsic nature is agreed upon as "nirutti" (etymological derivation).
That knowledge which occurs here and there, distinguished by various factors such as its respective object and function, is called "paṭibhāna" (perspicuity).
Previous application, great learning,
knowledge of the local dialect, the traditional scriptures,
thorough inquiry, and realization—
Support consists in the attainment of friends.

Having obtained such proximate support, the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) may arise either on the level of one beyond training (asekkha-bhūmi) or indeed on the level of one still in training (sekha-bhūmi).
The wise proclaim that the arising of the name [of the fruit] is threefold: from the tradition of the Sārassata, from the source, and also from the object.
From that, the attainment of the fruits, beginning with the fruit of stream-entry, is likewise threefold.
The void, the signless, and likewise the desireless— these attain their own fruit for one who,
desiring to enter them, is practicing insight into formations in the manner already described.
But one who attains the attainment of cessation is an obtainer of both the fine-material and immaterial realms;
whether it be a non-returner or an arahant,
they enter the attainment of cessation in due order, first the fine-material and then the immaterial.
Having emerged and practicing insight into the conditioned phenomena right there,
he sets in motion the union of serenity and insight;
reaching as far as the base of nothingness, and beyond that.
Having made his resolution and applied his attention as is appropriate,
the wise one enters the path and the formless attainments.
Thereafter, beyond two moments of consciousness, he touches cessation.
The non-existence of that very mind is thus called "cessation.
The emergence from it is shown to be the simultaneous arising of the resultant consciousness;
then, having cut off the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), the wise one performs the reviewing.
The wise yogi, aspiring to his own welfare, should cultivate the supreme development of wisdom, which is the repository of many virtues.
Thus, having perfectly accomplished virtue and mind—
Establishing themselves in the purification of wisdom,
having attained enlightenment and being free from sorrow,
they protect supreme security for a long time.
Having attained their goal, supremely confident,
those great seers whose stains of defilement have been washed away,
because they shine with qualities of ultimate purity—
May they become the most supreme recipients of offerings for the world.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Analysis of the Resultant Flow," in the Exposition of Name-and-Form.
The detailed analysis of insight (*vipassanā*) is thus completed in every respect.
This is the concluding discourse:
To this extent has that which was promised at the beginning—"I shall speak"—been fulfilled.
The *Nāmarūpapariccheda* has been completed by me.
Thirteen chapters have been analyzed, with seven being the primary ones;
these are the recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*) revealed in the *Nāmarūpapariccheda*.
The ultimate meanings of the Abhidhamma, serenity, and insight are analyzed separately;
thus, in this context, they are considered to be threefold in their classification.
This [treatise], consisting of the sciences and liberations, is manifest in the hearts of those who discern.
Presiding over Vallabhaṭṭa, may the wise one— who, like the sun’s rays, dispels whatever has entered the mind of those seeking the teaching here—
long display his light within this treasury of the jewel of the True Dhamma.
For a monk who aspires here in the teaching of the Sugata to wisdom regarding the ultimate meanings and proficiency in practice,
[this work on] the delimitation of name-and-form is unconfused and untroubled.
By me, who desired the welfare of the world, this well-constructed Kubbata was built.
It is a residence resembling Mount Meru, adorned with a Great Cetiya,
and it has ascended to the status of a Great Monastery with the great festival of the Great Enlightenment.
O you whose wealth is asceticism, free from blemish, you are fully capable of adorning for a long time this island of Laṅkā,
which is itself free from stain, as its ornament.
[The Analysis of Name-and-Form]
Just as it was completed without obstacle,
so too in this world,
those with pure intentions have reached their goal.
Thus ends the treatise on the Analysis of Mind and Matter composed by the teacher Anuruddha.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Paramatthavinicchaya:
Introduction to the Work.
Having paid homage to the Three Supreme Jewels, who are worthy of homage;
I shall explain, in brief, the determination of ultimate reality.
First Chapter: 1.
Analysis of Consciousness (Cittavibhāga)
1. Discourse on the Compendium of Similar Forms Mind, mental factors, matter, and Nibbāna— thus the Peerless One,
the Proclaimer of the Four Truths, taught the Dhamma in four ways.
One should analyze therein the mind as being of eighty-nine kinds,
or ninety-one kinds, or even one hundred and twenty-one.
As for the mental factors (cetasika), they are considered to be fifty-two in number according to their specific forms.
Mental states are divided according to the arising of consciousness and by way of their association.
Materiality is twenty-eightfold, distinguished as primary elements and derived matter;
furthermore, materiality is twofold, consisting of eighteen types.
But they illuminate Nibbāna, the unconditioned and unsurpassed;
it is called a "description" (paññatti) in two ways according to its name and its essence.
Now, I shall explain their distinction in due order.
How are the ultimate realities fourfold and the designations twofold?
By way of the classification into wholesome and so forth, therein the mind is fourfold;
likewise, by way of the classification of planes, how is it [fourfold] starting from the sense-sphere plane?
It is divided as accompanied by joy, likewise associated with equanimity,
and further distinguished as associated with knowledge and dissociated from it. Again,
it is divided eightfold as being without effort and with effort.
Wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere brings about a happy rebirth in the sense world.
Wholesome first jhāna, endowed with initial application, sustained application, zest, happiness,
and one-pointedness of mind, is declared to have five factors.
The second jhāna is devoid of applied thought and possesses four factors;
the third jhāna is devoid of sustained thought and possesses three factors;
and the fourth jhāna is devoid of rapture and is endowed with equanimity and one-pointedness of mind.
And they explain the fifth [jhāna], both of which consist of two factors.
Thus, by way of the division of jhāna factors, the mind becomes fivefold:
wholesome consciousness of the fine-material sphere, which occurs on the fine-material plane.
The base of infinite space is the first wholesome [attainment];
the base of infinite consciousness is the second, and likewise the third.
The base of nothingness, however, is the fourth mental state.
And the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception: thus it is fourfold.
This is called wholesome immaterial (āruppa) kamma, endowed with equanimity and one-pointedness;
all of this possesses two factors and brings about existence in the immaterial realm.
The path-consciousness of stream-entry, likewise the first unsurpassed [path],
the once-returning, the non-returning, and arhatship— in every respect,
there are fourfold divisions by way of the paths and fivefold divisions by way of the jhānas.
Wholesome [states] included within the twenty [factors] are mixed with two [others].
Thus, by way of the classification of planes, the wholesome is fourfold:
[namely,] twenty-one, twenty-two, or thirty-sevenfold.
It is divided as accompanied by joy (*somanassa*) and likewise associated with equanimity (*upekkhā*);
it is further distinguished as associated with views (*diṭṭhigata*) and dissociated from them.
It is again divided eightfold as being without effort (*asaṅkhāra*) and with effort (*sasaṅkhāra*).
They explain [the first type] as having greed as its root, with greed and delusion as its two causes.
However, that which is accompanied by mental grief and conjoined with aversion is divided into two kinds: that without volitional effort and that with volitional effort.
They explain that which has hatred as its root, having both hatred and delusion as its causes;
that which is accompanied by doubt, and likewise that which is associated with restlessness.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of delusion, conjoined with the feeling of equanimity.
They proclaim that these have delusion as their root and are caused solely by delusion.
These are known as the twelve unwholesome [mental factors], which bring about the four states of misery;
they yield the fruit of misfortune even within a happy realm of rebirth.
Those termed eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness are the five pairs of consciousness;
then there is the pair of receiving consciousness.
Likewise, there are two types of investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity.
By way of merit and demerit alone, resultant states are established as twofold.
Among them, twelve mental states are said to be accompanied by equanimity;
the pair of body-consciousnesses are associated with pleasure and pain, respectively.
That investigating consciousness accompanied by joy is said to be exclusively the ripening of merit;
there exists no ripening of demerit therein.
Furthermore, it is twofold by way of the five doors and the mind door.
Associated with the feeling of equanimity, it is called functional adverting.
Associated with joy, it is the mind that produces a smile.
Thus, there are three types of rootless functional javanas.
There are eight types of resultant wholesome consciousness and seven types of resultant unwholesome consciousness;
together with the three types of functional consciousness, there are eighteen rootless consciousnesses.
When combined with their corresponding wholesome states, the great unwholesome and great functional consciousnesses [make up the remainder].
The great functional resultants and the resultant consciousnesses of kamma—
thus there would be eighty-nine types of consciousness in this world,
or ninety-one types, or even one hundred and twenty-one.

The stream-entry path-consciousness, associated with the first jhāna, is considered to be endowed with initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), joy (pīti), happiness (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (cittassekaggatā).
The second [path-consciousness] is inferior to it by way of initial application; the third, however, is inferior by way of sustained application.
The fourth is inferior to [the third] because it lacks joy;

it is endowed with equanimity and one-pointedness. Together with the first, these five are considered the "unexcelled" (anuttara) jhānas, which abandon views, doubt, and attachment to rules and observances.
Likewise, the path-consciousness of the once-returner is also fivefold;
it is described as that which effects the non-recurrence of the triad of lust, hatred,
and delusion, and which eradicates the defects of sensual desire without remainder.
The third [set] is likewise fivefold, consisting of the wholesome states that are unsurpassed.

Furthermore, there are the five fetters pertaining to the higher realm (uddhambhāgiya): attachment to the fine-material realm, attachment to the immaterial realm, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance. These constitute the five in their entirety.
The supreme mind that effects the total eradication of the remaining fetters is the fourth unsurpassed path-consciousness, and it is fivefold.
There are exactly four fives regarding both the paths and the fruits.
And the remaining eighty-eight [factors] make one hundred and twenty-one.
Thus, for the eight supramundane [paths],
there is again a fivefold classification according to their respective suitability into jhāna-factors, path-factors, and enlightenment-factors.
"Foundational jhāna, jhāna by name, likewise jhāna by aspiration,
and insight leading to emergence— these determine [the type of] insight.
Thus ends the discussion on the inclusion of the actual forms within the analysis of consciousness.
The First Chapter.
The Second Chapter:
2. Miscellaneous Discourse.
There are twenty-one wholesome states, twelve unwholesome states,
thirty-six resultant states, and twenty functional consciousnesses. Among these,
fifty-four pertain to the sense-sphere, and fifteen to the fine-material sphere.
There are twelve types of consciousness that are appropriate for the sense-sphere, and eight that are unsurpassed (supramundane).
In the sense-sphere, there are twenty-three resultant states, twenty that are wholesome or unwholesome, and eleven that are functional; thus, in total, there are fifty-four.

The twenty-seven sublime (mahaggata) states consist of three sets of five in the fine-material realm— distinguished as meritorious, resultant, and functional— and four sets of four in the immaterial realm.
Furthermore, there are eight states by way of the jhānas pertaining to the four paths and their fruits.
When both are combined, there would be thirty-four supramundane states. Meritorious, resultant, and functional [states], as well as evil, exist in the sense-sphere and the sublime realms;
however, there is no evil in the functional category, nor do they exist in the supramundane.
Excluding those that are neither evil nor rootless, all the blameless states—
fifty-nine consciousnesses in total— are the results of merit, demerit, and the functional.
Thirty-three types of kamma-consciousness are entirely both meritorious and demeritorious.
Of these, thirty-six are resultant, twenty are functional, and none are both.
The five consciousnesses named after the eye-consciousness element and so forth, the five-door adverting consciousness,
and the two types of receiving consciousness.
The three mind-elements (manodhātu) and the seventy-six that follow are called the mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu);
thus, there are sevenfold divisions of elements. Both the mind-consciousness-element and the three mind-elements [are included therein].
Having performed mental consciousness— thus the six consciousnesses are enumerated:
adverting, seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting,
and touching, as well as receiving and investigating.
Advertence, impulsion, that which is called registration,
the life-continuum, death, and rebirth-linking— thus consciousness exists in fourteen ways.
Seven pairs, beginning with advertence, occur in due order.
There are three types of investigating consciousness and one type of determining consciousness.
All wholesome and unwholesome states, as well as results, excluding advertence,
and the fifty-five functional states— these are called "impulsions."
The two great resultant investigating consciousnesses,
known as "registration," arise eleven times when the object of the impulsion is sublime.
The two great resultant investigating consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity [arise]...
The cuti, sandhi, and bhavaṅga consciousnesses, along with nineteen other types of mind— namely, the javanas,
the two types of adverting, the determining, the two types of happiness, the two types of investigating,
the sublime consciousnesses, the great resultants, and the investigating accompanied by equanimity.
Sixty-eight and two, nine, eight, and two, respectively;
these are the bases for functions numbering one, two, three, four, and five. They are:
the material [result], the ripening [consciousness], the great ripening [consciousnesses], the mind-element, and investigation.
Nineteen [types of consciousness] produce materiality, but not the other two.
All [consciousnesses], excluding those of direct knowledge, as well as the javanas of absorption,
produce twenty-six types of materiality while projecting the postures.
Furthermore, the two types of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*),

the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabba*), the limited javanas (*paritta-javana*), the thirty-two [types of consciousness] that accomplish bodily intimation (*rūpa-viññatti*) and the postures (*iriyāpatha*), the five sense-consciousnesses, the formless-sphere resultants (*āruppa-vipāka*), and all moments of rebirth-linking (*sandhi*);
"Cuti" refers to one whose taints are exhausted; these sixteen [factors] have no function whatsoever.
The seventy-seven types of consciousness produce material phenomena in every way;
the fifty-eight types of consciousness project the postures.
The thirty-two [types of consciousness] together with the fourfold intimation arise from the mind;
however, they do not produce even one of the sixteen [kinds of material phenomena] as previously described.
But those [consciousnesses] accompanied by joy, being limited impulsion, [do produce them].
"Even producing" refers to the thirteen [mental states] that perform the four functions.
All this function has been explained as occurring in the five-aggregate plane;
however, in the formless plane, everything dependent upon form is not found.
But for those without perception, none of these [mental aggregates] are found;
for them, only the aggregate of form is called "selfhood" (attabhāva).
However, that which is accumulated by way of killing living beings, taking what is not given, and so forth...
Having given merit devoid of restlessness, one ripens seven results on the plane of the four lower realms;
but having given a gift during the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma,
even if accompanied by restlessness, one ripens them on the plane of the five aggregates.
Furthermore, wholesome kamma occurring in the sense-sphere through the distinctions of giving,
virtue, and so forth, when it is preeminent in the mind and possesses three roots, constitutes a fourfold set.
Having given a rebirth-linking with three roots in the sense-sphere, one is born in a happy destination.
There are sixteen types of kamma that ripen as merit; however, it is during the course of existence (*pavatta*) that such merit ripens.

Having given a gift that is at least three-rooted merit, or even the highest two-rooted merit, one attains a two-rooted rebirth-linking (*sandhi*) in a happy destination within the sense-sphere realm.
But in the course of existence (pavatta), excluding that which is associated with knowledge,
twelve types of meritorious resultant [kamma] ripen according to their respective suitability.
The lowest type of merit possessing two roots produces a rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) devoid of roots.
They give results in the human realm, as well as in the woeful states and among the asuras.
During the course of existence, however, they ripen as eight rootless resultants.
All four sets [of kamma] also ripen on the plane of the five-aggregate realm.
But merit consisting of mental development— whether sublime or supramundane—
yields its respective fruit according to the specific rule of its own plane.
The results of kamma performed that produce material form occur on the five-constituent plane.
The fruits of merit and demerit ripen in the formless and supramundane realms, and likewise in the fine-material and non-percipient realms.
The thirty-three types of wholesome and unwholesome kamma produce their results,
as appropriate, in both rebirth-linking and the course of existence.
Thus ends the miscellaneous discussion on the analysis of consciousness.
The second chapter.
The third chapter.
3. The Discourse on the Compendium of the Sense-Bases (Vīthisaṅgahakathā) The sense-bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body are fivefold;
together with the sensitive matter and the heart, these six are designated as the bases (vatthu).
The doors of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body are fivefold;
the mind-door is the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). These are the six doors of the cognitive process (cittavīthi).
Visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles are the five objects (gocara).
The designation of mental objects as objects, the sequence of objects at the six doors,
signs, destinations, and kamma— indeed, kamma itself as the range of experience—
and [the relationship] of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death, as appropriate.

For a being at the point of death, the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) into another existence occurs with respect to the object that has appeared at the six sense doors. That [rebirth-linking] lasts for a single moment of consciousness;
thereafter, it persists as long as life endures.
At the end, there is the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and death (cuti) occurs for a single moment.

Following a death with two roots or no root, there are the rebirth-linkings (sandhi) of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). Following a death with three roots in the sense-sphere, all types of rebirth-linkings may occur.
Following death in the fine-material sphere, there are rebirth-linkings accompanied by roots;
from the immaterial sphere or above, or in the sense-sphere, there may also be those with three roots.
