In a single birth, the rebirth-linking and the life-continuum are one and the same.
Cessation and its object likewise occur accordingly.
When the eye-sensitivity or other faculties are struck by an object such as a visible form,
the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is interrupted in the middle, and what is called a "cognitive process" (vīthi) proceeds.
Adverting, the fivefold sense-consciousness, receiving, investigating, determining, the sense-sphere javanas, and their object—
these seven are the summary of the stations of the mind associated with the five doors.
All fifty-four [types of consciousness] in detail and according to their specific forms—
namely, those called "advertence," "all-javana," and "that-object"—
are sixty-seven in number as specific forms of mental consciousness belonging to the mind-door.
When the object is desirable, the results of merit arise in every way;
when it is undesirable, the results of evil arise—this is the rule that has been proclaimed.
Even therein, when the object is extremely desirable, there occurs the "registration" (tadārammaṇa) and "investigation" (tīraṇa).
Accompanied by joy when the object is desirable, and experienced with equanimity when it is neutral;
when the object is limited or of very short duration,
the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) itself merely vibrates, and thus that [cognitive process] is rendered futile.
In the case of a limited object, the determining consciousness (voṭṭhabbana) occurs two or three times;
thereafter, there is a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and that [determining consciousness] is called "fruitless.
In the case of a great object, after the impulsion (javana) has run its course, [the same follows].
When it does not arise with that as its object, it is called "vain.
But when one roams within a vast range of existence, such as among those of exceedingly long life,
and it arises with that as its object, it is called "complete."
When the object is vast, there arises the corresponding objective condition (tadārammaṇa) at the five sense-doors and at the mind-door when the object is clear.
For beings of the sense-sphere, this occurs with respect to objects of the sense-sphere.
One should point to the registration (tadārammaṇa) as occurring only during the minor javanas.
Registration is desired when the javana is proceeding evenly and slowly,
neither too rapid nor too swift, and not excessively intense.
That object, accompanied by pleasure, occurs after the activity of equanimity;

it is not accompanied by equanimity, just as [a state] accompanied by pleasure does not arise from the activity of suffering. Likewise, a mind characterized by joy does not arise from mental distress.
Then there is the registration consciousness, or another [consciousness], or likewise the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) or death-consciousness (cuti).
Here, by way of attachment and so forth, unwholesome impulsion (javana) may arise;
however, when faith, wisdom, and so on are present, wholesome [impulsion] arises.
That very same [consciousness] in those free from lust is called "functional" (kriyā),
having reached a state of non-resultant [kamma], due to the complete exhaustion of the root of the round.
The remaining [consciousnesses]— whether sublime or supramundane— are absorption-javanas.

Twenty-six [mental states] may occur, as appropriate, in the cognitive process of absorption (appanāvīthi) for one who is performing the preliminary work (parikamma) upon the objective field of the kasiṇas and so forth,
with a well-concentrated mind through access concentration (upacārasamādhi).
Beyond the preliminary, access, conformity, and change-of-lineage [moments],
the fifth or fourth impulsion becomes absorption.
For worldlings and trainees, it arises from sense-sphere merit and the three roots.
From a three-rooted sense-sphere functional state, absorption arises for those free from lust.
Even therein, after a joyful state with swift speed,
there arises from a joyful state of the two [higher] grades a state associated with equanimity, endowed with equanimity and one-pointedness.
Five, six, or seven times there may be the impulsion of the protective charm (paritta-javana);
once or twice, it has that same object, as do the adverting consciousnesses and the rest.
However, at the first arising, the absorption-impulsion (appanā-javana) occurs only once.
Thereafter, for one who has attained mastery, it proceeds day and night. However,
at the moment of attainment, the fourth immaterial-sphere javana occurs either once or twice, and then consciousness ceases.
For one emerging from cessation, the two higher fruits, the five supernormal powers,
and likewise the paths, are considered to consist of a single moment of consciousness.
In the cognitive process of the path, there is either one, two, or three such moments of fruition.
At the moment of attainment, that [consciousness] also occurs throughout the day and night.
In the five sense-doors, the supramundane and the sublime [consciousnesses] are not found;
nor are they found in the mind-element dissociated from the cognitive process, or in the final five types of consciousness.
All paritta [consciousnesses] arise in the five sense doors;

in the mind door, there may be determining, registration, and impulsion. The cognitive process of the nose, tongue, and body consists of [the respective sense-door consciousnesses], registration, and [impulsion].
In the realm of form (rūpa), there are no such paths as the eye or ear;
all such paths exist in the realm of desire (kāma).
In the realm of form, three [mental] paths are declared.
In the formless realm, there is only one type of cognitive process; among those without perception, there is no cognitive process at all.
Seven types of cognitive processes occur in the sense-sphere, while six types occur in the fine-material realm.
In the formless realm, there are two: mind-door adverting consciousness and impulsion.
Thus ends the discourse on the summary of cognitive processes within the classification of consciousness.
The Third Chapter.
The Fourth Chapter:
4. Discussion on the Refinement of the Cognitive Series Initial adverting occurs before fifteen [consciousnesses] in the subsequent series.
There is a second adverting [consciousness] after the twenty-first.
From one [adverting], there is a fivefold sense-consciousness; from the five, there is reception;
and after the twenty-fifth, there is pleasant investigating.

The thirty-seventh consists of the two types of equanimity-investigation; after the two types of determining consciousness, which are of the same nature as those [preceding], come the sense-sphere impulsions.
After the two [types of path-consciousness], come the superknowledges; after three, come the mundane attainments.
The fruits of four and five [factors], plus two higher fruits—
these forty arise with pleasant ripening and two roots;
likewise, thirty-nine are associated with equanimity.
Seventy kamma-resultants in the sense sphere have happiness as their maturation and are associated with three roots;
from seventy-two, however, arise those accompanied by equanimity.
From fifty-nine, there arise resultants of the fine-material and immaterial realms.
Having thus calculated the "prior groupings" (pubba-saṅgaha) by subtracting one, two,
three, and so on, up to forty-eight from the total of sixty-two,
the wise and confident scholar should discern the number and other details of the "subsequent groupings" (para-saṅgaha).
One should illuminate ten types of consciousness from the five-door adverting [consciousness];
it is stated that forty-five arise from the remaining adverting [consciousness].
From the fivefold sense-consciousness, there is the unwholesome resultant receiving [consciousness].
From one with two roots, there arise one resultant consciousness, two types of receiving, and two types of investigating;
thus twelve resultants are born from a two-rooted desirable resultant.
From a three-rooted desirable resultant, twenty-one are obtained.
From the resultant consciousness of the fine-material sphere, at most nineteen [consciousnesses] arise;
from the ninefold material-sphere resultant, seven or six, respectively.
From the consciousness accompanied by aversion, however, only seven arise; from that accompanied by joy, thirteen are said to arise.
From those with two causes—evil and merit—one should develop twenty-one [types of consciousness].
From those with two causes in the sense-sphere and the functional, eighteen arise accompanied by equanimity;
seventeen accompanied by pleasure should be analyzed by the wise.
It is declared that from the three-rooted sense-sphere wholesome [consciousness], there are thirty-three accompanied by equanimity;
from the five-rooted sense-sphere wholesome, fifty-three accompanied by pleasure.
From the three-rooted sense-sphere functional, there are twenty-four accompanied by equanimity.
But being himself happy, the wise man should illuminate [the realms] up to the twenty-fifth.
He should explain the ten, the formless, the jhānas, the one, the eleven, the twelve, the thirteen, and the fifteen, in their proper order, including the formless attainments.
From the fruit, they say there are fourteen [factors]; from the path, however, its own fruit.
Thus, the wise one should enumerate the supreme inclusion, having understood the synthesis of what precedes and what follows. Beyond that—
One should indicate the combination of bases and paths as they occur.
Based on five bases, there are five consciousnesses in sequence;
based on thirty-three, however, there may be heart-consciousness and mind-consciousness.
The sense-sphere resultant mind-element, the smile-producing mind-consciousness,
the roots of hatred, the Path, and all four fine-material jhānas;
the ten remaining unwholesome states, sense-sphere wholesome states, and the great functional states.
The registration consciousness, the sense-sphere javanas, and the seven supramundane states—
these forty-two types of consciousness in the five-aggregate plane depend upon the heart-base; in the formless plane, they exist without a physical base.
The four immaterial resultant [consciousnesses] are entirely without support;
when divided in detail, they are eightfold, but in brief, they are threefold.
With support, there are thirty-three; without support, there are fourfold.
The remaining forty-two types of consciousness are both dependent and independent.
There are five types of cognitive absorption occurring sequentially within each single process;
these are known as the triad of mind-elements, which are said to be associated with the five sense-doors.
Furthermore, thirty-one types of consciousness— consisting of the two types of investigating consciousness accompanied by pleasure,
the protective consciousness, and the javanas— arise when occurring in the six cognitive processes.
Additionally, the eight great resultants and the two types of investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity [also arise].
They arise at the six doors, and ten [types] are released by way of the cognitive process (vīthi).
Due to the influence of death, rebirth-linking, and the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), there are nine great (mahaggata) processes that are free from the cognitive process.
Thus, the summary of the cognitive process is tenfold.
States of consciousness with one door, likewise those with five doors and six doors; those liberated from the six doors, and those liberated in every way.
Thirty-six, thirty-three, ten, and nine.
Having understood the convergence of the pathways and the appropriate range of objects,
one should enumerate them in order: the five sense-consciousnesses, the supramundane, and the sublime [consciousnesses],
excluding the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), total forty-five types of mental consciousness.
According to their occurrence, they have each a single object such as visible form;
however, the triad of mind-elements (manodhātu) range over all five objects.
The investigating consciousnesses, the great resultants, and the limited javanas [function in this way].
Adverting and direct-knowledge: these forty-three types arise. They occur with respect to six objects;
thus they are eightfold and again threefold.
There are consciousnesses with one object and those with five objects.
Briefly stated, there are forty-five mental states, and likewise three;
thus, how could they be sevenfold? [They are:
the sense-sphere resultant mind-element, the smile-producing mind, and the mind-element.
Twenty-five [kinds of consciousness] are considered to have limited objects, as appropriate.
Space cleared of the kasiṇa is the object of the first immaterial-sphere consciousness;
likewise, the non-existence of that very same space is the object of the third immaterial-sphere consciousness.
Having taken hold [of the formless], they proceed from there in sequence as the formless attainments;
the second and the fourth have the six sublime states as their object.
They are designated as "immeasurable," but when Nibbāna is their object, [they are called "boundless"].
The eight supramundane states are fixed by necessity for the yogi in the sections on the kasiṇas, the foulness,
and mindfulness of breathing.
For one who applies themselves to the sublime states (appamaññā) upon the counterpart sign,
fine-material jhāna arises with respect to the designation of beings.
In the case of the aforementioned sign, the rest are called "formless" (āruppa).
All twenty-one sublime (mahaggata) states,
excluding the direct knowledges (abhiññā), proceed as "indeterminate" (navattabba) when reckoned by way of designation (paṇṇatti).

Likewise, the impulsions dissociated from knowledge that are unwholesome, as well as those associated with the immeasurables—excluding the latter—number twenty in each of the three categories: the limited, the sublime, and the immaterial.
The wholesome kamma of the sense sphere with triple root-cause, and these five types of wholesome direct-knowledge, [are likewise twenty].
In all four [planes], they arise except for the two types of Arahantship.
The functional superknowledges (*kriyā-abhiññā*) and the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabba*)—these six are three-rooted in the desire realm of the functionals;
thus, the mental consciousnesses are established in seven ways in all places.
But as for the threefold [consciousness] whose range consists of one, four, and four sections respectively: there are sixty-three, twenty, and eleven in their respective order.
In the five doors, all five have only the present as their range.
The momentary [consciousness] is not to be described [as internal or external] in the mind-door as appropriate.
In the five doors, the objects are both internal and external;
in the mind-door, it is not to be described, and even the state of non-existence is found there.
In the five doors, each of the five [senses] has its own respective range;
yet all six objects become the range within the mind-door.
That which is apprehended in the five doors, as well as other ranges, [are taken up there].
It is taught that "determination proceeds at the mind-door.
Those possibilities belonging to the realm of sense-desire, whether past or present, are comprised within the six doors;
these objects of experience are likewise threefold.
Only the sign of the kamma, having appeared at the mind-door—
whether it be past and thus not to be described [as present], or included among mental objects— becomes the object;
and having taken that as an object according to the circumstances, the rebirth-linking consciousness and the sublime consciousnesses [arise].
At the beginning, in the middle of existence, and at the end, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) also proceeds.
Thus ends the discourse on the preliminary process within the analysis of consciousness.
The Fourth Chapter.
The Fifth Chapter:
5. Discussion on the Levels and the Person.
Hereafter I shall explain [the path] according to the distinctions between the levels and the person.
Now, how is the summary of all these states of consciousness given in order?
Hell, the animal realm, the hungry ghosts, and likewise the asuras—
these are considered the four planes of misery within the sense-sphere realm.
The Cātumahārājika, the Tāvatiṃsa,
and the Yāma; the Tusita, the Nimmānarati, and the Vasavatti—
these six divine worlds, together with the Mānusottara, constitute the sevenfold [heavenly realms].
The realms of sensual pleasure and the eleven planes of sensuality,
the Retinue of Brahmās, the Ministers of Brahmā,
and the Great Brahmās— these three constitute the planes of the first jhāna.
The Parittābhas, Appamāṇābhas, and likewise the Ābhassarās—
thus the plane of the second jhāna is shown to be threefold.
The Parittasubhas, Appamāṇasubhas, and Subhakiṇhakas;
These three are declared to be the planes of the third jhāna.
The Vehapphala, the Asañña, and the fivefold Suddhāvāsa— these seven, moreover, are the planes of the fourth jhāna.
The Aviha, the Atappa, the Sudassa, the Sudassī, and the Akaniṭṭha—
these five are proclaimed as the Suddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) realms.
Thus, the Brahma-worlds are said to be divided into sixteen types.
The abodes of the material Brahmās are the planes of the fine-material sphere;
and the immaterial Brahma-worlds, beginning with that named the base of infinite space, are the four planes of the immaterial sphere.
The supreme [states] are considered fourfold by way of the distinctions of stream-enterer and so forth;
thus, in total, there are thirty-five planes.
They arise in the four woeful states through the connection with the ripening of evil deeds.
Among the gods of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), they are born from great karmic fruits (mahāpāka).
However, those without roots (ahetuka) born of meritorious fruition are born from a rootless [rebirth-linking consciousness];
this applies to the terrestrial gods and humans, while others are born from great karmic fruits.
The resultant first jhāna is in the plane of the first jhāna;
the second and third are in the plane of the second jhāna.
The fourth is in the third, and the fifth is in the fourth.
And in the formless realms, the rebirth-linkings occur only in succession.
Having committed deeds such as the taking of life with evil minds at the doors of body, speech, and mind, those being born in the woeful planes [do so] through the formless realms alone.
Having performed giving, virtue, and meditation through the doors of body,
speech, and mind by means of sensual merits, one may be reborn in a happy destination within the sense-sphere realm.
These correspond respectively to the limited, intermediate, and sublime jhānas.
Having developed [the first four jhānas], yogis become threefold across the three planes;
they are born among the Vehapphala deities having likewise developed the fifth.
And by developing the state of fading away from perception, they are born in the plane of non-perception.
Non-returner individuals are born in the Pure Abodes;
and having developed the formless attainments, they are reborn in the formless realms in due order.
But having developed the supramundane [paths], immediately after each respective one, [they pass away].
At the very moment of attainment, the mind of fruition enters [the meditative state].
Beings who have passed away from the states of deprivation are born in the realm of sense-desire;
those who have passed away from a happy destination of sense-desire are born in all places.
Those who pass away from the form realm are born everywhere except in the states of deprivation;
those who pass away from the formless and the non-percipient realms are born in the sense-sphere happy destinies.
Likewise, those who pass away from the form realm are born there itself or in the higher realms.
Through the complete eradication of the root of the round, they become extinguished and free from taints.
Non-returners are reborn in the Pure Abodes;
those other than non-returners are born in the realm of sense-desire.

There are no noble ones (ariya) among the Brahmās born in the lower realms, nor anywhere else [except for those in the higher planes]. There are no noble persons at all among the non-percipient beings or in the states of misery (apāya).
Those established in the Vehapphala, Akaniṭṭha, and the Peak of Existence (bhavagga) [are noble ones].
But noble persons (ariyapuggala) are never born elsewhere;
those who have not yet reached the state of non-returning (anāgāmī), though free from passion, do not remain among the six classes of devas.
Even worldly practitioners (yogin) do not stay there for long.
They do not abide in the marks of a householder, being free from taints among human beings;
they abide in the state of renunciation, on the earth, and even in the state of a Brahmā.
Those fifty years—
For humans, that which is a single day and night is for him a month,
consisting of thirty nights.
Twelve months constitute a year; five hundred of those years would be the measure of the lifespan of the Cātumahārājika devas.
Furthermore, when those [five hundred] are multiplied by ninety thousand, that is the total.
By counting human beings in groups of four times ten million,
one hundred human years are made to constitute a single day; by that reckoning,
the lifespan among the Tāvatiṃsa devas is taught to be one thousand years.
Three koṭis and sixty-one hundred thousand more would be the total number of humans when combined with those in the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
Such is the measure of the lifespan of the gods, each higher than the last.
Having doubled it twice, one-fourth is declared;
by the count of humans there, there are fourteen koṭis and forty thousand more in the Yāma realm.
They illuminate the Tusita devas for fifty-seven koṭis and sixty-one hundred thousand years.
For the Nimmānarati devas, it is two hundred and thirty koṭis.
In total, for forty-four hundred thousand years,
nine hundred and twenty-one million, and sixty hundred thousand years more,
they dwelt among those who exercise power.
A third part of an eon, and half [an eon], in due order;
one eon, two, four, eight, and sixteen eons;
thirty-two and sixty-four eons in the nine Brahma-bhūmis.
The Vehapphala and the Asañña beings have a lifespan of five hundred aeons.
One thousand, two, four, eight, sixteen,
and thousands of aeons are specified for the Suddhāvāsa [deities].
Twenty thousand aeons, forty and sixty;
eighty-four thousand aeons—these are the lifespans in the formless realms respectively.
There is no fixed rule for the lifespan among humans on earth.
There is no counting the years spent in the four planes of misery.
There are two kinds of persons: the worldlings and the noble ones;
and the worldlings are further divided into three types based on their possession of the three roots and so forth.
Those established on the path and those established in the fruit—
these are the eight noble persons;
from the beginning, seven are trainees (sekkha).

The one beyond training (asekkha) and the other who has abandoned the defilements (arahant) are also found [in these realms]. However, among beings in the miserable destinies (duggati), only those without roots (ahetuka) are found;
whereas among those with minds in the fine-material and immaterial realms, only those with three roots (tihetuka) are found.
Among the deities of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), those devoid of roots (ahetuka) are excluded;
likewise among the fallen states (vinipāta), the asuras, and humans—these three [realms] are excluded.
Noble ones (ariya) are found only in those realms excluding the non-percipient beings (asañña) and the states of misery (apāya).
Ordinary worldlings (puthujjana) are found everywhere except in the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa).
Having excluded the Pure Abodes, the states of misery (apāya), and the three types of non-percipient existence (asaññibhava),
both stream-enterers (sotāpanna) and the other noble ones are found in all remaining places.
Thus, having understood the classification by way of all its divisions—
the grouping according to planes and persons— a wise person should discern how consciousnesses arise therein.
Thus ends the discussion on planes and persons within the Analysis of Consciousness.
The Fifth Chapter.
The Sixth Chapter:
6. Discussion on the Grounds, Individuals, and the Arising of Consciousness.
In the happy realms of sense-sphere existence, there are great results according to their respective merit;
there are also sublime results established according to the continuity [of rebirth].
The volitional acts of sense-sphere merit are dissociated from wrong views.
And including that accompanied by restlessness— thus there are fourteen in all. However, the investigating consciousness, the mind-element, and the eye, ear,
and mind [consciousnesses]— these ten types of consciousness arise everywhere except in the formless realm.
Associated with views, as well as conjoined with doubt—
these five arise everywhere except in the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa).
Likewise, the two rooted in hatred, the triad beginning with the nose, and the mind [arise in all planes].
Eight types of consciousness arise everywhere, excluding the sublime (mahaggata).
The fourth immaterial-sphere javana, the fruit of non-returning and so forth,
and the great functional (mahākiriya) consciousnesses arise in those excluded from the woeful planes— namely, thirteen types— excluding the woeful states.
Two each for the lower and upper realms of form, excluding the six apāyas;
The formless realms and the apāyas are excluded from the javanas of the fine-material realm.
The fruits of stream-entry and so forth occur in those pure of apāyas and free from the [lower] realms.
In the first [supramundane plane], which is unsurpassed and excludes the pure abodes and the formless realms,
the unsurpassed states are not included because they constitute the planes of existence (*avatthābhūmi*);
likewise, the single-aggregate plane and mere form are not included.
Those belonging to all planes and those belonging to every plane, excluding one, two, and three;
likewise the Pure Abodes, the Brahma-worlds, and the states of misery.
These five mental divisions consist of seventeen, fourteen, [ten, seven, and three].
Thirty-six, twenty-one, and one respectively;
they are eighteen, and again ninefold, then once more singlefold;
and by way of division, they are fourfold, threefold, and singlefold.
Furthermore, there are thirteen components that exist across several planes:
consciousnesses belonging to six, five, eleven, seven, and ten planes;
and those numbering twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three, twenty-four, and twenty-five.
Twenty-six and thirty-two [verses] would thus occur in their respective order.
Then four, and again four, one, eight, eight, and one;
four, eleven, two, two, seven, twenty-three, and fourteen.
The fifty-two [types of knowledge]— those of the Kriyā, Java, and Mahāpāka classes,
as well as the supramundane and the sublime— are not found in the four planes of misery,
nor among the gods of the sense-sphere, nor among humans on the six earths.
In the sensuous happy realms there are none; there are nine sublime resultants.
The great resultants rooted in hatred, the three beginning with the nose, and the mind—there are twenty that do not have immaterial rebirth as their result, in the fine-material plane.
The five types of resultant consciousness associated with doubt and wrong view are fourfold;
the five types of non-returner consciousness and those of the Pure Abodes are not found there.
Initial application, the path consciousnesses, and those accompanied by aversion or the immaterial sphere [are likewise excluded].
In the realm of form, which is free from the ripening of sensual desire, those forty-three do not exist for you.
Thirty-seven limited [faculties] are found in the woeful planes,
while eighty mental [faculties] are found, however, in the happy realms of sensuality.
In the form realm, there are sixty-nine [factors]; in the pure [form realm], fifty-five;
in the formless realm, forty-six; and in the non-percipient beings, none at all.
Thus, there are sixteen [realms] belonging to one, two, three, four, and five planes.
Ten, fifteen, thirty-four, and fourteen:
these are the consciousnesses obtained by those born in the woeful states who lack root-conditions,
excluding the great resultants and functional consciousnesses of swift speed, as well as the remaining limited consciousnesses.

For those with two roots and for those without roots, the remaining [results] pertaining to the sense-sphere and the mind-sphere are obtained, excluding the results of knowledge, ripening, functional, and impulsion.
For beings possessing three roots, in their various respective rebirths:

Therein, those beings reborn in various places receive whichever [faculties] are obtainable for them: for all those with three roots, for those in the mental plane, and for those in the woeful planes, thirty-seven are to be specified;
for the remainder, forty-one are to be specified.
For worldlings and for those in training, there are no impulsion-moments;
for those free from lust, there are no meritorious or demeritorious deeds in any way.
The five types of consciousness associated with doubt and wrong view do not exist for those in training.
The two roots of the two types of defilements do not exist for the non-returner.
Among the Noble Ones alone, each possesses their own unsurpassed state;
for one standing on the path, there is only their own path, and no other whatsoever in any way.
For both types of worldlings and for the two who stand in the fruit, respectively,
sixty-three and fifty-nine consciousnesses are obtained, owing to the occurrence of the third and fourth fruits.
There are fifty-seven types of consciousness, and thirty-three in every way.
Forty-four, fifty, and those reduced by two;
these arise among sense-desires, while forty-four proceed by way of the eye.
Forty-nine, thirty-nine, and likewise in order;
thirty-nine, and thirty-five among the material [phenomena].
Twenty-seven, twenty-three, and twenty-three, respectively.
They are also found among those in the formless realms, numbering eighteen in total.
There are four types of worldlings—those bound for the states of misery, those without root-cause, and so forth—and eight types of noble ones; thus, they exist by way of twelve [categories].
The sixfold divisions of the mind, as well as those belonging to a single person;
the wheels of four, five, six, seven, eight, and nine persons;
twenty-six, fourteen, thirteen, and two mental states.
Ten with seven more, and again seven with ten more.
Thus ends the discussion on planes, persons, and the occurrence of consciousness within the Analysis of Consciousness.
The Sixth Chapter.
The Seventh Chapter:
7. Discussion on the Arising of the Plane and the Person For those with two roots or without roots, absorption does not arise.
If there is no attainment of Arahantship, there is indeed no impulsion (javana) activity.
The fruition of knowledge does not occur because of the dullness of the root-linking (mūlasandhi);
it may or may not exist in a happy destination, having that [root-linking] as its object and being accompanied by two roots.
For beings possessing three root-conditions who are developing serenity and insight,
twenty-six kinds of absorption arise. For beings who are arahants,
there occur the functional consciousnesses of the impulsion stage.
According to the specific order of each stage, the fruits of knowledge are obtained.
Those subject to destruction by the first path are doubt and the associated views;
aversion is destroyed by the third alone, as is tainted karma by the final [path].
Therefore, those consciousnesses do not arise in them in any way whatsoever;
rather, when one is on the path, it is only the path that exists, and nothing else arises at all.
As for the rootless resultant states, they occur when the appropriate cognitive process is available.
Furthermore, for all [beings], these occur at all times as appropriate:
at the five doors and the mind door, two constant adverting consciousnesses,
along with limited merit and demerit, are obtained due to their rapid occurrence.
In the *kriyā* and *javana* moments, as well as in absorption (*appanā*), there is no cause for rebirth in the lower realms;
nor are there resultant states accompanied by roots, because of the connection [to the wholesome] through the state of being well-born.
Among the *brahmās*, there is no aversion, as it has been suppressed by meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
Because they are dispassionate toward the lower jhānas, those in the formless realms do not develop them.
Furthermore, the noble ones belonging to the formless planes have already seen the Truths;
therefore, this path does not exist there, and likewise, sitting is absent due to the absence of a body.
The Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsas) have already been reached; below them are the five "Unsurpassed" (Anuttara) states.
Because they have abandoned the seven types of evil, those [defilements] do not exist there.
Five-door consciousnesses do not exist where the doors are absent.
Having understood thus the possible and the impossible regarding persons and planes—
including those with roots and those that are resultant, as established according to their respective levels—
one should indicate the inclusion of consciousness therein by way of what is obtainable.

And the classification that has been indicated according to the distinctions of the wholesome and so forth, as well as by way of the distinctions of plane and so forth, and by way of basis, door, and object, as well as by way of plane and person— [that is now to be explained].
And from the arising of consciousnesses,
the mental factors are to be known according to their association.
Thus ends the discussion on the arising of planes and individuals within the analysis of consciousness.
This is the seventh chapter.
And the analysis of consciousness is completed.
The Eighth Chapter:
2. Analysis of Mental Factors 8.
Discussion on the Association of Mental Factors
Having thus understood the procedure for consciousness, by one who discerns the fifty-two [factors],
how are the mental states (dhammas) arisen in the mind to be known as mental concomitants (cetasika)?
Contact, feeling, perception, volition, and likewise one-pointedness;
Vitality, attention, and these seven universal factors:
initial application, sustained application, rapture, energy,
as well as desire and resolve— these six are known as the particular factors.
The miscellaneous [factors] proceed scattered among the results of merit and demerit,
as well as among appropriate activities and mental states.
They are faith, the faculty of mindfulness, and the two powers of moral shame and dread of blame.
Non-greed and non-hatred, wisdom and equanimity—
these eight are called the supreme states, the means for attaining the highest goal.
They are declared to be "the requisites," while the six pairs that follow are likewise so called.
Tranquility of body and mind, as well as buoyancy, plasticity, adaptability, proficiency, and rectitude;
the pair of illimitables known as compassion and sympathetic joy.
Right speech, right action, right livelihood, and the threefold abstinence—
these twenty-five factors arise, as appropriate, among those who are blameless,
free from evil, and devoid of roots of unwholesomeness.
Greed, hatred, and delusion;
conceit, views, and doubt;
sloth-and-torpor, and restlessness—
And likewise remorse makes ten.
Shamelessness, lack of moral dread, envy, and stinginess—
these are the fourteen blameworthy states, arising only among those that are blameworthy.
Thus, fifty-two mental factors (cetasika) have been established in four groups of four.
Now I shall explain their association and their classification.
Seven are universal, being common to all consciousness.
There is nowhere any dissociation from the mind for these eight [mental factors].
Initial application (vitakka) is excluded from the fivefold sense-consciousness and from the second [jhāna] and above.
Sustained application (vicāra) is likewise excluded from those same states and from the third [jhāna] and above.
In a state associated with joy, excluding the fourth jhāna and rapture;
energy arises excluding the first jhāna, resultant states, and rootless states.
Volition arises everywhere, excluding states of sheer delusion and rootless states.
Resolve (adhimokkha) occurs in all states except for doubt and the five types of sensory consciousness.
Excluding the miscellaneous factors, there are sixty-six, fifty-five, seventy-one, and sixteen, as well as twenty and eleven.
Fifty-five are with the mind, sixty-six are with initial application;
fifty-one are with sustained application, and likewise forty-nine are with rapture.
Seventy-three are with energy, and sixty-nine are with desire.
The seventy-eight mental states are said to be "accompanied by liberation.

Among these, excluding those that are unwholesome, rootless, and free from [the fetters], there are fifty-nine in which wisdom, the immeasurables, and abstinences are found; among those accompanied by faith, there are nineteen.
Briefly stated, wisdom arises in every way among the forty-seven types of beings who are excluded from those with two roots and those without roots.
It arises in the great functional, sense-sphere beautiful, fine-material jhāna, and immaterial jhāna consciousnesses.
In the eightfold distinctions of the immeasurables (appamaññā), excluding the fifth jhāna;
in all supramundane (lokuttara) states, it arises together with the three abstinences (virati);
in meritorious acts pertaining to the sense-sphere (kāma), it arises either collectively or separately according to what is possible.
In the five abstinences and the immeasurables, as appropriate,
only one arises at a time and not all together. Shamelessness,
lack of moral dread, delusion, and restlessness likewise.
Those called "shared with evil" are the four origins of evil:
greed among those things rooted in greed, and wrong view among those associated with wrong view;
conceit among those dissociated from wrong view; and neither wrong view nor conceit together.
Among those rooted in hatred, there are four: hatred itself, envy, stinginess, and remorse;
while doubt is found among those characterized by perplexity.
Along with these, sloth and torpor are included among the five factors accompanied by volitional formations.
Thus, there are fourteen blameworthy states, determined as such among the blameworthy:
conceit and sloth-and-torpor, either together or separately;
and envy, avarice, and worry, which are mutually separate from one another.
Thus ends the discussion on the association of mental factors within the analysis of mental factors.
The eighth chapter.
The ninth chapter.
9. Discourse on the Compendium of Mental Factors The seven universal factors, the six occasional factors,
and the twenty-five beginning with faith— these thirty-eight are combined together.
Among the merits of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), they are found in the first two [jhanas];
in the second, thirty-seven are found, excluding mere wisdom (paññā).
In the third, as previously stated, they are found excluding mere joy (pīti).
In the fourth [jhāna], there are thirty-six, excluding both wisdom and rapture.
In the great functional [kamma-formations], they are joined by omitting the abstinences;
thus, there are thirty-five, two sets of thirty-four, and thirty-three respectively.
Excluding the immeasurables (appamaññā), when applied to the great resultants (mahāvipāka),
there are thirty-three, thirty-two, thirty-two, and thirty-one respectively.
Having taken the immeasurables and likewise excluding the abstinences (virati);
In the first [moment], there are thirty-five [factors] in the mind of the fine-material sphere.
In the second, having excluded initial application (*vitakka*), and after that, sustained application (*vicāra*) in the third;
furthermore, in the fourth, joy (*pīti*) is excluded, and in the fifth, the immeasurables (*appamaññā*).
Of the types already mentioned, thirty-four are obtained in their respective order:
thirty-three, thirty-two, and thirty.
And those identical with the fifth [jhāna], excluding the immaterial-sphere mind, [are likewise obtained].
Excluding the immeasurables (appamaññā) but including the three abstinences (virati), there are thirty-six types of the path when the first jhāna is present in the mind,
taking into account the distinctions of the planes (bhūmi), objects (ārammaṇa), and the excellence of the factors (aṅga).
Having abandoned initial application in the second [jhāna], and sustained application after that;
having abandoned rapture in the fourth, and in the fifth as well, in every respect.
The thirty-five factors, of the kinds already described, follow in their respective order.
Thirty-four, thirty-three, and likewise another thirty-three—
thus the twenty-two-fold classification is included within the blameless states;
this is declared for the thirty-eight among the fifty-nine consciousnesses.
Having taken up all forms of abstinence and the immeasurables (appamaññā),
and having taken up each one individually, as well as having renounced them in every way—
thus there are seven types of merit regarding sensual pleasures, and likewise four types regarding the functional (kiriya).
The same synthesis should also be applied to the fourfold jhāna of the fine-material sphere.
By this method, the synthesis of faultless states of consciousness should be understood according to seventy-six divisions.
Thus, having understood in every way the determination of what is blameless,
the wise person should apply it to the inclusion of what is blameworthy.
There are seven common factors and six miscellaneous qualities.
There are these four evil asceticisms and seventeen such states.
There are nineteen formations in the first [category], namely greed and views;
in the second, greed and conceit, along with as many as have been mentioned.
In the third [jhāna], there are eighteen without rapture, due to greed and views;
in the fourth as well, there are that many without rapture, due to greed and conceit.
In the case of the [first] two resistances, there are likewise those without rapture, and similarly in the case of the [first] two formations.
Twenty [types of non-restraint] are obtained through hatred, worry, and stinginess;
they are stated as being twentyfold among those without volitional effort (*asaṅkhāra*) and fivefold among those with volitional effort (*sasaṅkhāra*).
With sloth and torpor, there are twenty-one; by the overcoming of the hindrances, there are twenty and twenty-two.
Having abandoned zeal and rapture, these are fifteen;
having abandoned liberation and doubt, and likewise having grasped [them] in one who is doubtful—
thus there are twelve groupings of twenty-seven states.
Among the twelve types of unwholesome consciousness,
the wise should discern them by setting aside six factors that lead to decline and grasping the others as appropriate;
thus, the thirty-four combinations therein should be understood by the intelligent.
Having understood the supreme inclusion among the twelve unwholesome [states],
how should the inclusion among the rootless consciousnesses be known in its proper order?
There are seven common factors and the miscellaneous factors, excluding desire.
In the consciousness arising from a smile, twelve factors are declared.
In the process of determining (voṭṭhabba), excluding joy, and in the investigation of pleasure,
the eleven factors as previously stated are taught in both cases.
In the triad of mind-elements (*manodhātu*) and the two pairs of equanimity and investigation (*upekkhā-tīraṇa*),
there are ten factors as previously stated, excluding energy (*vīriya*) and joy (*pīti*).
Seven factors are common to those arising from the fivefold sense-consciousness (*pañcaviññāṇa*).
Thus, in the rootless consciousnesses, the fivefold inclusion is established.
Having thus enumerated the mental factors within the consciousnesses,
a wise person may further enumerate them by including them together with the consciousness itself.
Regarding those thirty-eight which were mentioned, when combined with consciousness, they become thirty-nine;
in all such cases, one should apply the method of adding one.
Thus, twenty-two, ten, two, and five—each according to its proper place.
The factors of integration for associated states—this discourse is incomplete by one verse.
Applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), rapture (*pīti*), wisdom (*paññā*), as well as the immeasurables (*appamaññā*) and the abstinences (*virati*):
these nine factors [function] according to their respective roles.
In the case of blameless states, there are those to be grasped and those to be discarded;
feeling, however, turns them all as appropriate.
Desire, resolve, energy, and faith—these nineteen [mental factors] are present.
"Contact and the rest are exactly six," thus twenty-eight do not waver.
But thirteen are with fault, and six are in the mind without root-cause;
ten others do not waver, and fourteen and six arise.
Thus ends the discourse on the classification of mental factors within the analysis of mental factors.
The ninth chapter.
The tenth chapter.
10. The Discourse on Classification:
Arising together and ceasing together, having a single object and basis;
conjoined, co-nascent, associated, and co-existent.
These fifty-three mental states, associated as appropriate,
consist of consciousness and mental factors (citta-cetasika) of eighteen kinds.
They are established in one way, six ways, four ways, and seven ways.
By means of the classification of the arising of consciousness, these should be analyzed by one who discerns:
eight inseparable factors, when divided, become eighty-nine;
when all are combined together, they total seven hundred and twelve.
The investigating mind-element, the smile-producing and the determining [mind-elements], as well as the unwholesome, the wholesome of the sense sphere, the great resultants,
and the great functional [consciousnesses]; the states of the first jhāna, and those that are supramundane and sublime.
All fifty-five types of applied thought (vitakka) are analyzed;
those same [fifty-five] types of sustained thought (vicāra),
which constitute the second jhāna, together with eleven others, are thus explained as sixty-six.
Non-merit, merit of sense-sphere, great results, and great activities;
the four tetrads and the four [foundations of mindfulness];
coldness and the crossing over to happiness. The first and subsequent jhānas of the threefold system, supramundane and sublime.
Thus, in every way, there are fifty-one types of joy.
Together with the two kinds of cold-removing [joy] and those that are both blameworthy and blameless,
energy (vīriya) is likewise divided into seventy-three types.
Both with fault and without fault, excluding the two types of sheer delusion,
all these desires (chanda) amount to sixty-nine varieties. The investigating mental element (santīraṇa-manodhātu),
as well as the smile-producing and the determining [mental elements], are likewise [to be understood].
Blameworthy and blameless, excluding doubt—
thus the fifty-five types of resolve are divided;
when the miscellaneous factors are added, they total two hundred and ninety-eight.
There are fifty-nine [types], or nineteen through faith, and one thousand one hundred and twenty-one in total. Furthermore,
those associated with knowledge are twelvefold in the sense-sphere realm.
There are thirty-five wisdoms and forty-seven discourses.
There are four jhānas of the form realm, the sense-sphere merits, and the great functional states;
likewise, there are twenty-eight immeasurables, making fifty-six in total.
The supreme meritorious deeds of sense-sphere desire, together with the three abstinences, are divided sixteenfold; when combined, they total forty-eight.
Thus, the twenty-five types of non-prohibited [states] are associated in four ways.
In terms of their divisions, there are one thousand two hundred and seventy-two.
When the four types of evil ascetics are further divided into twelve,
they all amount to forty-eight when totaled together.
Greed is divided into eight ways; sloth and torpor, five ways;
views and conceit, four ways; and the various views, four ways.
The four beginning with hatred are twofold, and doubt is singlefold.
The blameworthy offenses are stated as sevenfold;
when divided, they are eighty-three. Thus, they are stated as eighteenfold;
and when further subdivided, they amount to two hundred and fifty-nine.
Having distinguished the five factors— applied thought, sustained thought,
rapture, happiness, and equanimity— by way of the different jhānas, the unsurpassed [state] should be grasped.
But elsewhere, in all other cases, there is no purpose for such a distinction.
Why are there exactly eight? Because they are characterized by non-distinction.
The first four jhānas—both supramundane and sublime—are each of ten kinds;
thus, when combined, they total forty-four.
Twenty-three with the fifth [jhāna] make sixty-seven when combined;
all absorption therein is explained as fifty-eight.
In brief, there are thirty-five types of supramundane and sublime [consciousness].
All twenty-six types of absorption (appanā) taught therein are explained as fivefold:
the supernormal powers (iddhividha), the divine ear (dibbasota), that called penetration of others' minds (cetopariya),
recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussati), and the divine eye (dibbacakkhu).
They call the knowledge of direct higher power (abhiññā-ñāṇa) the fifth [category] of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara);
it is divided into two kinds: the wholesome (kusala) and the functional (kriyā).
When these two are combined, there are the five mundane direct higher powers (pañcābhiññā).
The knowledge of the destruction of the taints and the six direct knowledges are proclaimed [as supramundane].
The ten mundane direct knowledges, having excluded wholesome action,
along with the seventy-seven meditative absorptions and the sixty-eight attainments, [constitute the mundane].
Seventy-seven types of consciousness, and fifty-four in every way;
when the derivative states of consciousness are added, there may be one hundred and thirty-one.
Thus ends the exposition on the classification of mental factors.
The Tenth Chapter.
The Eleventh Chapter:
11. A Discourse on the Nature of the Aggregates.
The discourse is eighteenfold according to the inclusion of all things by way of their intrinsic nature,
commonality, and particularity as appropriate, and further by way of the removal of craving.
There are also the five aggregates of contact, and others such as the jhānas and the faculties.
The mundane heap consisting of the paths of action caused by the strength of the Path,
the six blameless factors beginning with serenity for one possessed of mindfulness,
the pair of concurrent calm and insight, and likewise the access concentrations.
Contact, feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness itself—
these five phenomena are declared to be the aggregate of the fivefold contact.
Applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, and likewise one-pointedness;
Pleasure, pain, and equanimity—these are the names of the seven factors of jhāna.
The faculty of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are said to be fourfold; then there is the mind and the five types of feeling.
The life-faculty is one, and the [faculties] beginning with the eye are sevenfold;
thus, twenty-two faculties are named, while sixteen factors are taught.
In the first path, there is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
The faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*) occurs in the middle, and the faculty of one who has already known (*aññātāvindriya*) at the end.
These three faculties also exist in those consciousnesses that are supreme in wisdom;
in the remaining types of consciousness associated with the three roots, only the single faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*) is recognized.
The faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, as well as the faculty of mental joy, the faculty of mental grief, and equanimity—
thus the discourse on feeling is fivefold.
The life-faculty is single, while it is twofold according to the division of the material and the immaterial.
The faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, femininity, and masculinity;
therein also the life-faculty—these eight are not included here.
Therefore, one should designate only fifteen as material faculties.
Right view, intention, effort, the three abstinences,
right mindfulness, and concentration— these nine path factors, together with wrong view,
constitute twelve when divided according to their nature.
Right and wrong intention, effort, and concentration;
the pair of world-protectors, and furthermore, moral shame and dread of blame;
the pair of lack of moral shame and lack of dread of blame, which destroys the world.
And the five qualities beginning with faith are called the factors of power;
they are unshakable by their opposites, whether by way of the dark or the bright side.
These six causes are within the collection of causes.
The triads beginning with greed and non-greed,
along with delusion, doubt, and restlessness—
these are said to be eightfold therein.
Wrong view and covetousness, ill will, and the three abstentions;
right view, non-covetousness, and non-ill will, along with volition—
these ten courses of action are stated here as abstention and volition.
The "Destruction of the World Guardians" and the "World Couplets" are stated as being twofold.
The six groups (rāsi) are faultless, consisting of pairs such as tranquility (passaddhi) and so forth;
mindfulness (sati) and clear comprehension (sampajañña) constitute the "Couplet of Assistance."
The pair called "Conjoined Joy" consists of serenity and insight;
exertion and non-distraction are declared as the "Serenity Pair.
Those states which have been described by their own nature within the arising of consciousness by the Tathāgata—
Excluding those [already mentioned], the remaining ones are called the "Yevāpanaka" (the rest).
They are: desire, resolve, equanimity, restlessness, and attention—these five are called the "Apaññaka" (unspecified) factors.
Conceit and sloth-torpor, envy and stinginess,
remorse and the non-illimitables, as well as the three abstinences—
these eleven are called "indefinite" (aniyata), according to their respective application.
And therefore, all the remaining factors are declared to be "fixed.
Since some do not belong to any group and some are "indefinite," only sixteen factors are taught as "associated with the [four] foundations."

The remaining thirty-seven [factors], however, are indicated in their own form throughout all types of consciousness-arising, as appropriate in each instance. In the cases of the Unsurpassed and the Exalted states,
they are taught by name as abstinences and non-delusions.
Likewise, in the supreme states of consciousness, the threefold abstinence is fixed.
Mind, applied thought,
faith, conscience, shame, and the two powers;
Non-greed and non-hatred,
greed, hatred, and wrong view;
lack of moral shame and lack of moral dread.
Restlessness and the three abstinences—
these sixteen are taught, as appropriate, in two places.
Feeling is shown in three places, energy and mindfulness in four,
concentration and wisdom in six, and [faith] in seven places. These twenty-one factors,
together with their case endings, are thus enumerated.
The remaining thirty-two states are all likewise unclassified.
Thus ends the discussion on the nature of the groups within the analysis of mental factors.
This is the eleventh chapter.
The Twelfth Chapter: 12.
Discussion on the Determination of the Aggregates.
Therein, there are six groups of consciousness and seven elements of consciousness.
Contact consists of visual contact and so forth; it is sixfold and also sevenfold.
Furthermore, feeling, perception, and volition are each divided into six and seven types by way of their distinctions, such as those born of visual contact and the rest.
Within the arising of consciousness, all phenomena— namely the aggregates,
bases, elements, and nutriments— are included as appropriate within this heap of the fivefold contact-group; therefore, there is the discernment of name.
And this fundamental collection is called the "All-Inclusive.
Within the collection of jhānas there are five factors according to their sevenfold classification;
as for the faculties, there are twenty-two, but sixteen according to their nature as phenomena (dhamma).
The nine factors of the path are divided into twelve types;
therein, the six causes were taught for the sake of those who are anxious and agitated.
Furthermore, ten courses of action were taught as six factors.
The remaining forty-four factors are common to all ten dhammas.
Among them, wisdom is of ten kinds, feeling is established as ninefold,
concentration is sevenfold, and energy is fivefold.
Mindfulness is divided into four types, while applied thought is considered to be threefold;
consciousness and the other [mental factors] are twofold, and there are fifteen that arise together.
All the remaining thirty-two phenomena, moreover, each occur in only one way.
Excluding these [two] faculties of form, how are the divisions eightfold?
Contact, volition, perception, sustained application, rapture, and life—these six pairs are blameless; [the others] are blameworthy, delusive, and wavering.
And the miscellaneous factors (yevāpanaka-dhammā), excluding the abstinences and restlessness—these twelve as well. Thus, each [set] in the group of thirty-two is of one kind.
Consciousness is the mind-faculty (manindriya); consciousness is the faith-faculty (saddhindriya) and the power (bala).
In the *Bala* [chapter], those pertaining to the mundane are stated, as well as two pairs of mundane [factors]—
the two pairs beginning with greed and non-greed—
and four [factors] in the category of causes.
Wrong view is included among the factors of the path and also among the five courses of action;
it is taught as one of the "miscellaneous" factors within the group of abstentions and the rest.
In the factors of the path, fifteen are established in two ways.
Applied thought (vitakka) is threefold in the jhānas and the paths, but ninefold [in the factors of enlightenment].
Feeling (vedanā) is likewise [threefold] in the root-group, as well as in the jhānas and the faculties.
In the group of faculties and the path, in the triad of powers and the back,
mindfulness is fourfold in that very place, and energy is fivefold.
Concentration is said to be sevenfold in the factors of jhāna and in those same places.
Right there, wisdom is tenfold regarding the causes and the paths of action.
It is established as tenfold, ninefold, sevenfold, fivefold, fourfold,
threefold, twofold, sixfold, singlefold— fifteen ways in total— and thirty-twofold, respectively.
There are eight concise divisions, and the terms may be tenfold;
there are exactly fifty-three categories of phenomena and eighteen groups.
Thus, in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, in the determination of phenomena (*dhammavavatthāna*).
In the section on the analysis of the arising of consciousness, there is a compendium of the method of enumeration:
eighty-four terms are taught according to their specific forms,
and sixteen are taught under the name "Yevāpanaka" (the Miscellaneous) as appropriate.
Therein, the names of the fixed [verses] consist of exactly eleven words;
ninety-nine such fixed verses are stated according to their possible occurrences.
In this regard, the unconfused words are in every way exactly fifty-three.
But it should be illustrated by way of the mind and mental factors.
Thus has been explained the determination of the aggregates by way of the categories of phenomena that are analyzed;
[this concludes] the determination of the groups of mind and mental factors according to their order.
Thus ends the discourse on the determination of groups within the analysis of mental factors.
The twelfth chapter.
The thirteenth chapter.
13. Discourse on the Combination of Groups (Rāsiyogakathā) Thus, having understood the sequence of groups,
the wise man should explain the combinations of those very groups as they occur within the arising of states of consciousness.
In the first two types of consciousness belonging to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), all groups (*rāsi*) are present according to their possible occurrence. How so?
There is the group of the fivefold contact (*phassa-pañcaka-rāsi*) and the group of the fivefold jhāna (*jhāna-pañcaka-rāsi*).
The group of eight on the faculties, the group of five on the paths,
the group of seven on the powers, the triads on roots and courses of kamma,
the remaining ten groups, and the dyads beginning with the world-protectors.
The miscellaneous set of nine, excluding fixed restlessness,
the two illimitables, and the three abstinences—
thus these seventeen have been taught according to their specific forms.
The miscellaneous group and the eighteen obtainable factors;
fifty-six terms are taught here according to their form,
while thirty dhammas occur therein according to their form.
Including those that are included [in the aggregates], there are fifty-five terms;
furthermore, through their possible combinations, there are thirty-nine states.
Therein, twelve states are taught with their detailed classifications.
But all the remaining [bases] are called "unanalyzed" (*avibhattika*).
They consist of groups of one, two, three, four, six, seven, and eight,
as well as twenty-seven, one hundred and one, and two and one, respectively.
But thirty-four factors are fixed by way of co-occurrence;
the discourse on the fivefold fixity is according to their possible occurrence.
Therein, in the case of the unfixed, having grasped all [factors] and having abandoned [others];
Having taken each separately, the wise one should apply them seven times in a sequence of leagues (*yojana*):
forty-nine in one instance, thirty-four in the next according to order, and five times he should apply thirty-five. Thus says the wise one.
The *rāsa* (groupings) and the word-pairs here, the analysis of different meanings,
those that possess similar forms, the inclusion (*āpanaka*), the determined and the undetermined,
as well as the distinction in the method of application, the enumeration, and the established system of compendium;
Observing here and there by means of available inference,
one who has abandoned rapture and dwells in equanimity regarding that which is devoid of knowledge,
turns away from feeling— both sensual pleasures and the remaining types of merit.
One should apply [the factors] to the Great Action, having abandoned the threefold abstinence;
and having set aside the immeasurables, one should then apply them to the Great Fruit.
Having abandoned reasoning and so forth in due order, the threefold abstinence applies everywhere.
In the fifth [chapter], having abandoned the immeasurables, one should apply them to the form realm;
having abandoned the immeasurables, one should apply them to the unsurpassed jhānas according to their order;
and taking up the supramundane faculties as well as the threefold abstinence.
Forty-four jhānas are described as associated with pleasure;
twenty-three are associated with equanimity; and in the fifth jhāna, they are entirely absent.
The immeasurables and the abstinences are found among the meritorious deeds of the sense sphere.
The immeasurables (appamaññā) occur in the fourfold material jhānas and the great functional (mahākiriya) states.
The three abstinences (virati) arise everywhere in the supramundane (lokuttara) states.
Both [the first] two [abstinences] do not exist in the immaterial (ārūpa) states or in the fifth great resultant (mahāvipāka).
The three types of thought are wisdom, and the five indeterminate factors are unstable;
the remaining factors, through the power of the Buddha's teaching, never waver at any time.
Furthermore, herein, the twenty-two-fold inclusion pertains to the blameless.
"By way of each pair and each dyad, and also by way of the fivefold jhāna—
having thus understood how the formation of groups arises among those things that are blameless,
the wise person should likewise understand how groups are formed even among those things that are blameworthy."
In the first [category] among those rooted in greed, there is the aggregate of the fivefold contact,
the aggregate of the fivefold jhāna, and likewise the pentad of faculties,
the tetrad of path-factors, and the dyads of root-conditions and courses of kamma.
The "Destruction of the World" heap, the "Tranquility" [heap], and the "Tranquility" dyad;
excluding "Equanimity toward the Middle," there are four [factors] known as the "Inclusive" (yevāpanaka). Thus, eleven heaps are found therein.
In this [work], thirty-two phrases have been taught according to their essential form;
with the inclusion of the *yevāpanaka* (residual) factors, they become exactly thirty-six.
Herein, there are twenty-four possible unconfounded phrases.
And those called "with analysis" (savibhattika)—these nine factors have been explained.
Furthermore, they are fixed according to their positions:
one, two, three, four, six, eleven, six, one, and again one, respectively.
Here, there are no indeterminate factors (aniyata) nor those termed "included" (yevāpanaka);
therefore, no distinction in the method of application exists therein.
Pride (māna), sloth-and-torpor (thinamiddha), envy (issā), and avarice (macchariya) likewise [are not found].
"Remorse" is considered to be among the blameworthy; the six [factors] are regarded as indeterminate.
"Conceit" is found among the five dissociated from views that are accompanied by volitional formations;
"sloth and torpor" belong to the remaining three; and the two types of "aversion" are associated with the rest.
Thus, these eight are faulty, while twenty-eight are faultless;
all thirty-six mental states are factors that lead to the indeterminate.
One is associated with them as appropriate, by one, two, three, or five at a time.
Two, twenty-two, three, and nine respectively—
according to this stated sequence, one should apply the available factors to other blameworthy actions as well, in their proper order.
In the [three] rooted in greed, one takes greed and hatred; in the pair rooted in aversion, hatred;
in the roots of delusion, doubt and restlessness—having thus grasped the heap of causes.
In that which is dissociated from views, having abandoned view, one takes joy and equanimity.
The wise person, while transforming feeling, likewise transforms the root of hatred,
the courses of action, views, rapture, and desire, becoming free from delusion.
Having abandoned both doubt and resolve, one should apply the groups [of factors].
But when the mind has attained stability, there is indeed one-pointedness of mind.
Those who are in doubt have indeed fallen away from the five factors beginning with the faculties.

Having thus understood these in twelve ways, one should understand how they are included even among those states that are blameworthy and even among those that are rootless, according to their occurrence.
Among the eighteen rootless [consciousnesses], in the fivefold sense-consciousness and the mental consciousness,
there are the pentads of contact, as well as the dyad of jhāna factors and the triad of faculties;
these are known as the "inclusion" (yevāpanaka) factors.
Regarding "a single act of attention," there may be four groups.
They remain unconfused in their respective meanings; among them, two are with analysis:
the single, the pair, and the triad, making six; and then once again, the single.
In the triad of mind-elements and in the rootless rebirth-linking pairs, however,
applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are additional in the aggregate of jhāna.
In the pleasant investigating consciousness and in the second adverting, however, joy (*pīti*) is additional.
Energy and concentration are found in the group of faculties.
In the [mental] smile, joy, energy, and the others are predominant;
as are the secondary factors (yevāpana) and resolve, in all states except for the fivefold sense-consciousness.
There are twenty-two [types of] yokes regarding the blameless, twelve others regarding the blameworthy,
and five regarding the cause.
This concludes the discourse on the application of groups within the analysis of mental factors.
The thirteenth chapter.
The Fourteenth Chapter: 14.
The Discourse on the Arising of the Aggregates.
There are nine eva-yeva-paññattis and eighteen aggregates (rāsi).
Twenty-nine are combined with "na," ten and two are with case-endings.
In the sections on one, two, three, four, six, seven, eight, nine, and ten,
there are twenty-seven, seven, one, two, one, and again one.
The "just-so" factors (*dasevāyūpanakā*), the eleven groups (*ekādasa-rāsī*),
the twenty-eight mixed types (*aṭṭhavīsatī-sambhinnā*), and the ten with their subdivisions (*daseva savibhattikā*).
Furthermore, those fixed by position as single, pairs, triads, tetrads, and sextets;
There are eighteen single factors, and one alone is the evil factor.
There are two "evenly distributed" (yevāpanaka) factors, and four types of groups;
among these, thirteen are unmixed, while three are with subdivisions.
In the cases of one, two, and three [factors], there are ten, two, and one [types of consciousness] that are rootless;
thus is the determination of the yokes regarding the blameless and the blamable rootless states.
There are also seven [types] for the blamable, while for the blameless there is the illuminator [the path].
In the rootless [consciousness], there are no fourteen types of attachment, such as to the Path and so forth.
However, wholesome [states] do not exist in unwholesome [consciousness], nor do unwholesome states exist in wholesome or indeterminate [consciousness];
and neither exists at all in the rootless arising of consciousness.
But those that are blameworthy [should be applied] to the blameworthy, and those that are blameless to the blameless;
however, the common miscellaneous factors are to be taken in all cases.
One should point them out among the sixty-seven types of consciousness within the fivefold jhāna.
Through the distinction of jhāna factors and their association, there is a classification of groups here and there.
Likewise, among those excluding the four and the nine, there is that produced by knowledge and rapture.
One should point out a twenty-fourfold division within the limited (paritta) states, categorized in four ways.
In the manifestation of the immeasurables for those with lust and those free from lust,
compassion and appreciative joy arise as great meritorious actions regarding sense-sphere objects. Reaching both access and absorption,
they have beings as their domain and consist in the happiness [of others].
Therefore, they are not found in the fifth formless attainment, in the great kamma-results, or in the unsurpassed [Nibbāna].
They are found in the states where the preliminary stages (parikamma) and so forth occur— namely, stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, and equanimity—
because the jhānas have equal results, and they are obtained in those states which possess such results.
Abstention from sensual pleasures and from merit is found among those still possessed of lust, because of the possibility of transgression;
it is found in both the attainment [of the path] and in formal undertaking.
This is due to its function of cutting off the volition of misconduct through whichever door it enters.
Because they have an equal fruition on the path and are fixed in their result,
all five aggregates— though distinct in their mode of occurrence and object—
may or may not exist separately even when occurring in the mundane realm.
Evil results are obtained from evil deeds; beings [experience] seven, six, and one [result] respectively;
those with form experience both; the eight fixed [results] and the six others;
and the common [results] are everywhere, as are the miscellaneous ones already mentioned.
In that context, there is no one-pointedness (ekaggatā) for one who is doubtful regarding the faculties and so forth.
Even though desire (chanda) and resolve (adhimokkha) are present, they are excluded from the eleven [factors].
Restlessness (uddhacca) is excluded from the eleven, while equanimity (majjhatta) is excluded from the faultless ones.
In all cases there is attention (*manasikāra*);
others [are] three, two, and two; in the eight, twenty-eight, four, five, and two, respectively.
Here, by way of the aggregate, the triad of abstentions from restlessness is included.
In other instances it has case endings, but here it is without case endings.
Therefore, among the arising of states of consciousness, this [term] is both with and without case endings;
thus the wise person should correctly observe what is possible and what is impossible.
Thus ends the discourse on the arising of the groups within the analysis of mental factors.
The fourteenth chapter.
The fifteenth chapter.
15. The Discourse on the Compendium of Categories Thirty-three, thirty-two, thirty-one, and thirty;
And twenty-nine and thirty-two less one—these are the thirty blameless qualities.
In the case of the blameworthy, there are ten factors, with additions of six, five, and four;
in the case of the root-conditions, however, there are eleven, ten, nine, and sevenfold.
Thus, the sections are divided fourteenfold according to their specific forms.
The arising of consciousness (cittuppāda), as classified and combined by them, follows this sequence:
twenty-five consisting of three and eight, ten and five more than nine,
and eighteen— these seven groups, along with the others, are faultless (anavajja).
Two, four, six, one, two, five,
then ten others; [these are] with fault,
with root-cause, and so forth.
There are fourteen sections:
nine, six, four, four, five, five, seven, nine, two, two, and likewise one; these are the groupings of the "Included" (yevāpanaka) factors.
But those associated with them are thirty-two in number, consisting of minds:
two, two, two, three, one, two, eight, and ten respectively,
from thirty-seven down to thirty-one, excluding the faultless.
In the *Tikaṭṭhaka* and following [chapters], seven groups of fixed aggregates are established.
Among the evil [states], there are twenty, nineteen, eighteen, and sixteen;
they are established in four ways in two [chapters], and in four ways in four [chapters], and in two ways in four [chapters].
In the groups of one, two, five, and ten, and in those with two kinds of roots,
there are respectively fifteen, two, one, ten, and eight factors. Five, two, two, eleven,
and five sections are fixed and established.
Those [factors] were thus combined: twenty [in total], consisting of two pairs of triads and single units.

In the past and future, in the two types of non-meritorious [kamma], in the fruition of sense-sphere [kamma], and in the rootless; in the fifth [jhāna], in the immaterial [spheres], and in the supramundane—there is no occurrence of the indeterminate.
Among those with thirty-six mental states, the indeterminate [attainments] are obtained or not;
however, the remaining fifty-three are all associated with the determinate.
Having categorized them as determinate and indeterminate, they are thus obtained in both ways.
Both types [of consciousness] are associated with the threefold [mental factors] according to their respective nature;
thus, by following what has been stated, one should understand that the mental states are indeed conjoined with them.
Thereafter, one should further analyze the method that encompasses all [factors].
The forty-ninefold, up to the thirtyfold;
the ninefold regarding blameless states, and those mental states associated with them.
Then the two, four, ten, and furthermore the ten increased by three and five.
Twenty-three, seven in sequence, two, and another fifteen;
two, two, three, two, two, one; sixteen among those with fault;
nineteen, twenty, and then twenty-one, twenty-two, and twenty-three.
In the rootless [consciousness], there are eight; in the [two] with one or two roots, ten and twelve respectively;
in the [two] with ten, five, two, and one, there are nineteen [factors] in total.
This is the compendium of phenomena according to how they occur.
It can indeed be understood by the wise in the manner already described.
Thus ends the discussion on the grouping of aggregates within the analysis of mental factors.
This is the fifteenth chapter.
The Sixteenth Chapter:
16. Discussion on the Arising of Consciousness.
Having thus understood the determination of phenomena within the arisings of consciousness;
Now, the classification and grouping of the arising of states of consciousness should be understood according to feeling, nutriment, cause, predominance,
jhāna, faculty, path, power, and the inclusion of the "mere" (yevāpanaka) factors.
In that context, three feelings are taught— pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant— according to their specific distinctions in experience and purpose.
Furthermore, there are pleasure, pain, mental joy, and mental grief.
Thus, from the classification of the five faculties, there is the faculty of equanimity alone.
For in the pair of body-consciousnesses, the feelings receive the names of pleasure and pain, but not of joy and grief.
But elsewhere, in all cases, pleasant and painful feelings receive the names of joy and grief respectively.
And neutral feeling, which is neither painful nor pleasant, receives the name of equanimity.
Among the fifty-five types of consciousness, and those others that have been explained:
the pair of body-consciousnesses are associated with the faculties of pleasure and pain;
the two types of mind-consciousness associated with aversion are associated with the faculty of mental displeasure.
The eighteen limited (paritta) states,
beginning with the fourfold jhāna and associated with the faculty of mental joy, constitute sixty-two types of consciousness. Furthermore,
there are thirty-two limited states, with twenty-three having jhāna as the fifth factor.
Fifty-five mental states are associated with the equanimity faculty. Among them,
sixty-three are associated with pleasure, three are associated with pain,
and fifty-five are associated with neither-pain-nor-pleasure and are characterized by equanimity.

The form consisting of the eightfold nutritive essence (*oja*), feeling, the mind at the moment of rebirth-linking, and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)—these are taught as the "nutriments" (*āhāra*) because they bring [existence] forth in succession.
The nutriments are: physical food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*), contact (*phassa*), volition (*sañcetanā*), and likewise...
The four [formless aggregates] beginning with consciousness, as well as the supports and the origins;
in all instances of the arising of consciousness,
there are three material nutriments.
Edible food sustains the body in the realm of desire;
non-greed and non-hatred likewise sustain it.
And non-delusion is another;
greed, hatred, and delusion—
these six factors have been taught as roots.
Wholesome and unwholesome roots, and three indeterminate ones—
therein they are ninefold and twelvefold according to the distinction between resultant and functional states. Then, by way of the distinction of planes, there are fifteen therein.
There are forty-four types [of consciousness] divided into meritorious,
resultant, and functional; however, in the investigating mind-element, the fivefold sense-consciousnesses,
