the mental element, the determining consciousness, and the smile-producing consciousness, no root (hetu) is found.
In those rooted in greed,
both greed and delusion are found;
in the two rooted in aversion, hatred and delusion are found.
Delusion alone is present in the state of bewilderment.
In those states dissociated from knowledge,
there may be the dyad beginning with non-greed.
Then, in all the remaining cases,
there are also those with the three roots of non-greed and so forth. There are forty-seven [consciousnesses] with three roots and thirty-two with two roots.
Twenty-two [types of consciousness] have two roots, and eighteen are rootless.
Desire, consciousness, energy, and investigation—
these fourfold co-nascent dominant states may be called "dominants" as previously described.
Making that which is to be taken as an object (yamālambaṃ) predominant, the mental states (nāmadhammā) proceed;
that object is thus described by the name "predominant object-condition" (ārammaṇādhipa).
Among those possessing the three roots, one [root] is predominant in all four [types of consciousness], as appropriate.
In the two-rooted [kamma], it arises without the predominance of inquiry (vīmaṃsādhipati).
In the supramundane, in meritorious deeds of the sense-sphere,
in the three-rooted great functional [kamma], and in the unwholesome rooted in greed, the predominance of the object (ārammaṇādhipa) is obtained.
And therein, regarding the sense-sphere, the indeterminate [resultants] are obtained even when they are available;
but in the sublime and the supramundane, they are strictly determinate, as appropriate. [This applies] to the functional, the double-rooted, and the impingent.
There is no predominance of the object in the case of kamma-result that is rooted in delusion,
nor in any worldly [kamma-result].
Those associated with both predominants, those possessing innate predominance,
those whose intention is fixed in both, and those whose innate predominance is unfixed;
and those dissociated from both— thus are the mental states therein fivefold.
Eight, eighteen, twenty, six, and thirty-seven respectively;
those associated with five predominants, those associated with four predominants,
those joined with three kinds of predominance, and those that are entirely liberated.
Sixteen, then thirty-two, six, and then thirty-seven respectively—
thus they are described as fourfold. Furthermore,
those associated with the predominance of investigation and those possessing the concomitant predominance.
Associated with objects and predominants, as well as entirely dissociated from them—
thirty-four, fifty-two, twenty-eight, and thirty-seven respectively;
thus they should be explained in four ways.
Those who have attained [insight] through the predominance of the co-nascent (sahajā) possess fifty-two [types of knowledge] in every way;
those who have attained it through the predominance of the object (ālambana), as well as those who have attained both predominances, possess twenty-eight in total.
All of them together, including those with predominance, amount to exactly fifty-two.
All the remaining thirty-seven factors are entirely without a dominant influence (*adhipa*).
Having thus understood the fourfold classification by way of feeling and so forth,
one should also analyze them by way of jhāna, faculty, path, and power.
The first jhāna has applied thought as its lower limit; the mind-faculty has the mind as its upper limit;
the path-factor has the cause as its upper limit; and the power has energy as its last.
Since these are naturally absent in the state without applied thought, therefore no jhāna exists there.
And as there is no path-factor or power in the rootless, nor virility in the absence of energy;
so here, the eight material faculties are in no way included.
Likewise, concentration is not included among the factors of the path, the faculties, or the powers in one who is full of doubt.
In the case of sensual pleasures and meritorious deeds, there is no fixed determination; likewise, abstinences are not over-exalted.
Wisdom is distinguished by its presence in the unsurpassed consciousnesses and by the three faculties.
The remaining factors are to be understood according to the sequence already stated, as they occur in the attainments of jhāna and so forth.
The types of consciousness arising in succession should be understood according to their association with these [factors].
Those associated with joy in the sense-sphere, the supramundane,
and the sublime, as well as the first-jhāna consciousness, are considered to possess five jhāna factors.
Associated with equanimity regarding suffering, excluding the five types of sensory consciousness,
and belonging to the second jhāna, they would possess four jhāna factors.
Associated with the three jhāna factors, they belong to the mind of the third jhāna.
In the fourth and fifth formless attainments, there is the association with two jhāna factors.
In the pair of fivefold sensory consciousnesses, there is no jhāna factor whatsoever.
Thus, by way of the classification of jhānas, the mental states are established as fivefold.
Twenty-nine, thirty-seven, eleven more, thirty-four,
and ten respectively for the courtesans;
in all supramundane states, nine faculties are said to occur.
Among all those with three roots, one should extract [the factors] in eight ways regarding the mundane;
among those dissociated from knowledge, one should extract them in seven ways;
and regarding merit, one should explain [the factors] in five ways, including cold and the removal of thirst.
In those associated with doubt, one should specify four ways;
three faculties are mentioned, while the remaining ones exist in the rootless mind.
There are eight, thirty-nine, twelve, or thirteen [types].
One and sixteen—thus, in this regard, the compendium is sixfold.
The first is considered the unsurpassed jhāna possessing eight path-factors;
the remaining jhāna is called unsurpassed and possesses seven path-factors.
The first mundane jhāna, likewise the three-rooted [consciousness] regarding sense-desires,
and those called the fivefold path-factors— these are the types of consciousness that have been explained.
The remaining sublime jhānas and those associated with wrong view [are also included].
They are considered to be dissociated from knowledge and associated with the four path-factors.
Likewise, those associated with the two roots of hatred and with restlessness,
as well as those dissociated from views, are conjoined with three path-factors.
Associated with doubt, the path described as having two factors,
and that which is neither path nor root— thus the summary therein is sevenfold.
Eight, thirty-two, ten, and five more besides.
Tālīsa (42) [factors] decrease by seven, and another [set] by one, eight, and ten.
However, there are only seven powers (balas) in all cases where the consciousness is associated with three roots (tihetuka);
in those dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇa), six powers are indicated.
The wholesome states are fourfold, while those associated with doubt are threefold;
that which is based on the two powers is to be understood as firm, while the rest is said to be weak.
In this regard, the compendium is sixfold, and there are forty-seven others.
Twelve, eleven, two, and sixteen respectively;
thus five, six, seven, and six sections stand in their proper order.
All twenty-four are explained according to the factors of jhāna and so forth.
Thus ends the discourse on the arising of consciousness within the analysis of mental factors.
The sixteenth chapter.
The seventeenth chapter.
17. Discussion on the Compendium of Views The states beginning with zeal,
as well as the categories such as the aggregates and so forth, have been taught under the name "Miscellaneous" (yevāpanaka) according to their respective fitness.
In this context, the factors such as desire (chanda) have already been analyzed as appropriate;
now, the aggregates (khandha) and so forth, as well as their origins (sambhava), should be understood.
Feeling (vedanā) is the aggregate of feeling, consisting of that born of eye-contact and the rest.
Perception and the aggregate of perception are thus declared to be sixfold.
The remaining mental factors are considered to be the aggregate of formations.
And the six groups of consciousness are designated as the aggregate of consciousness.
The aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) alone, together with the four formless aggregates that are dissociated from it— these are declared to be the five aggregates (pañcakkhandhā). Furthermore,
that which is called the mind-base (manāyatana) is simply consciousness (citta), as are the others.
The seven consciousness elements, beginning with the eye-consciousness element;
all mental factors (cetasika-dhammas), which are comprised within the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana);
and the element of mental objects (dhammadhātu)—these fifty-two [factors] are called such in every respect.
Subtle forms and Nibbāna are to be understood here [as the objects];
gross forms consist of the ten bases and elements.
Those termed the sense bases of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body;
The sense bases of visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects—
these twelve sense bases all become eighteen elements.
With the exception of Nibbāna, there is no conceptual designation (paṇṇatti) among the three [categories of aggregates, bases, and elements].
The sections beginning with nutriment are exactly as described previously;
thus, this summary of the mixed categories should be understood by the discerning one.
Even among the twelve unwholesome states, fourteen are likewise established.
Now, the inclusion of those things that are blameworthy is being set forth.
The taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance—these four taints have been stated;
three of these are explained according to their specific nature.
The taints (āsava) are so called in the sense of being taints;
likewise, the floods (ogha) are so called because they carry away;
and they are called yokes (yoga) because they yoke.
These four have been taught:
sensual desire, existence, aversion, and conceit; as well as views, doubt, adherence to rites and rituals, and attachment to existence.
Envy, stinginess, and ignorance—these are the ten fetters;
eight of these factors are explained in their specific forms in the Abhidhamma.
Having abandoned envy and stinginess, one should there cultivate pride and arrogance.

Having pierced through the two-fold craving for existence—namely, that for the fine-material and the immaterial—the ten fetters are thus declared: five belonging to the lower realm and five belonging to the higher realm;
yet in the Sutta, seven are mentioned according to their specific forms.
There are four fetters of the mind (dhamma-ganthas), three of which are defined by their own nature:
the bodily fetter of covetousness, ill will is declared [the second],
and the adherence to rules and observances is likewise the other bodily fetter.
Adherence to the view that "this alone is the truth"—
thus is view analyzed. Sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, and furthermore,
restlessness and remorse, as well as doubt and ignorance— these are the eight.
The phenomena called hindrances are taught as sixfold;
wrong view alone, however, is called "misapprehension.
There are four kinds of clinging, known as clinging to sensual pleasures and so forth.
The clinging to views, to rules and observances, and to the doctrine of self—
these two, driven by greed and views, are taught by the Great Seer as threefold:
namely, views, rules and observances, and the doctrine of self.
Greed, hatred, and delusion,
conceit, views, and doubt;
as well as sloth and restlessness—
Likewise, the pair of world-destructions.
Thus the bases of defilement have been explained as "defilements";
these ten are indeed identical both collectively and individually hereafter.
Sensual lust and aversion, conceit, views, and doubt;
craving for existence and ignorance—these are considered the six underlying tendencies of beings.
(620) They are also graspings, fetters, conceptual proliferations, and imaginings.
Craving, conceit, and views; views, craving, and the supports.
Adherence is one, while the supports are two; the conceivings are three.
The taints, floods, yokes, and ties, as well as the two kinds of clinging.
The eight hindrances have been stated, and the discourse on the seven underlying tendencies;
the fetters and the defilements stand further on as ten.
These groups of one, two, three, six, seven, eight, and ten are to be understood according to their respective order.
Phenomena exist according to their own nature within the groups as previously described.
Sensual lust and lust for existence, the taint of sensuality and the taint of existence,
lust for the fine-material realm and lust for the immaterial realm— thus is greed analyzed.
Adherence to "this is the truth," as well as views and rules-and-vows, the doctrine of self, and misapprehension—thus is view described.
View is of fifteen kinds; therein, eighteen types of greed are found.
The remaining sixty-two [views] are equal to their respective groups.
In the eleven origins, views and greed are established;
ignorance is said to be in seven, while aversion is in five.
Pride and doubt are extracted in four instances;
sloth is found in three and two. These eight are categorized with their specific divisions.
Envy, avarice, remorse, torpor, and world-destruction—
The factors of the analysis of the aggregates (khandha-vibhaṅga) are fourteen,
unmixed. However, in those [factors] dissociated from views, the attachment to form, the attachment to the formless,
the taint of sensuality, and the taint of existence are as previously stated.
Having thus understood this summary of what is blameworthy,
the wise person should further discern the compendium of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma),
in which the perversions of perception, mind, and view occur respectively.
"Pure, pleasant, permanent, and self"— thus it abides in twelve ways. Therein,
as one revolves through the body, feelings, mind, and mental phenomena,
[the opposite]— impurity, suffering, impermanence, and non-self— is established.
For the sake of abandoning the perversions as previously described,
the four foundations of mindfulness— beginning with the contemplation of the body— are distinguished according to their respective objects and functions, and they arise accordingly.
Thus has this one right mindfulness been taught by the Great Seer:
for the abandoning of evil that has arisen and for the non-arising of that which has not yet arisen;
or else, for the production and growth of that which has not yet arisen and that which has already arisen.
The effort of one who strives consists in the application to what is to be done and the analysis [of that task];
thus were the four right strivings (sammappadhāna) spoken of by the Great Seer.
Furthermore, zeal, energy, mind, and investigation were taught by the One Such (Tādī).
The four bases of psychic power (iddhipāda) are analyzed as the four predominants (adhipa).
The faculty of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration,
and the faculty of wisdom— these five alone are included in the summary of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya).
In terms of faculties and non-faculties, and in terms of powers,
they are thus divided and analyzed into two groups by the Great Seer:
mindfulness and investigation of phenomena, as well as energy and joy.
Tranquility, concentration, and equanimity—
these seven factors of enlightenment are taught by the Tathāgata according to their intrinsic nature as one awakens;
they are distinguished by way of body and mind, having made tranquility a single factor.
Right view, intention, effort, the threefold abstinence,
right mindfulness, and concentration— this is considered the eightfold path.
Thus, in brief there are seven [factors], but in detail, thirty-seven.
Having made one [factor] into tranquility, there are fourteen that are unmixed.
Energy is said to be ninefold across five of the six groups;
mindfulness is eightfold, while the remaining factors belong to the group of identical terms.
Wisdom and concentration are analyzed in five ways;
faith is analyzed in two ways—thus these five are with analysis.
The remaining nine are without analysis; furthermore, there are desire and consciousness.
Rapture, tranquility, and equanimity, intention, and the threefold abstinence—
all these factors conducive to enlightenment mentioned above arise in their entirety, as appropriate, within the supramundane states.
In the preliminary stage, as appropriate, they are found among worldly qualities;
and at the time of the development of penetration, during the practice of the sixfold purification.
Thus, these factors conducive to enlightenment include both mixed and faulty qualities.
In the group of miscellaneous factors, they exist according to their possibility.
However, the courses of action arise in all respects within both merit and demerit;
likewise, there are paths of good conduct as well as paths of bad conduct.
In that context, regarding the place of the courses of action,
non-covetousness and the others are said to exist by way of access, whether in resultant states or in functional states.
Thus ends the discussion on the inclusion of views within the analysis of mental factors.
The Seventeenth Chapter.
The analysis of mental factors is thus completed in every respect.
The Eighteenth Chapter.
3. Analysis of Form 18.
Discourse on Form:
Thus, fifty-three mental phenomena have been explained.
Now, the twenty-eightfold category called "matter" (rūpa) is explained.
It is fourfold: earth, water, fire, and air;
and fivefold: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
Visible form, sound, odor, and taste, and four others besides:
the female and male faculties, life, and the heart-base;
as well as the two types of intimation—bodily and vocal.
The space element is [the cause] of material form; lightness, malleability,
wieldiness, integration, continuity, aging,
impermanence, and physical nutriment are likewise entirely [causes] of that [form].
This material form is of twenty-eight kinds according to its nature;
one should discern its individual essence through the analysis of its characteristics.
The earth element has the characteristic of supporting and is characterized by hardness.
The water element has the characteristic of cohesion and the characteristic of trickling.
The fire element has the characteristic of ripening and the characteristic of heat.
The air element has the characteristic of motion and the characteristic of distension.
Though inseparable in all respects, they possess unmixed characteristics and are specifically defined by the predominance of their respective constituent factors.
Mutually supporting one another, they serve as the support for the remaining types of matter.
Thus, within the fourfold groups, the great primary elements proceed.
In the eye, which is the eye as an aggregate and is covered by seven layers of membranes,
that which is called "translucent essence" (pasāda) resides in the center of the black circle.
That clarity of the eye by which one perceives forms—
this is limited and subtle, comparable to the head of a louse.
The ear, resonating within the ear-canal...
Likewise, that which is covered with copper-colored hair and has the appearance of a finger-piercing hole is declared to be the *pasāda*.
The nose is situated within the nostrils at the tip of the nose;
the tongue is in the middle of the tongue, which resembles the shape of a blue lotus.
Thus, these four [faculties] are each established in their respective locations.
"Appropriated by the sensitivity of the body" refers to "all [the primary elements]" respectively.
Or, it refers to those elements that are susceptible to impact by visible forms and so forth, as appropriate;
or indeed, to those elements that have become the kamma-source for the desire to see and so forth.
The material phenomena (rūpa) characterized by clarity depend upon the primary elements (bhūta);
they are described as being like the moisture within a layer of cotton.
All five are protected by the life-faculty (jīvita) and are surrounded by [the objects] such as visible form (rūpa).
The two daughters and the two sons live within the sheath.
Form is the appearance of the elements, and sound is likewise their resonance;
smell is the smelling therein, and taste is the state of being tasted.
The tangible consists of the three primary elements (bhūta), excluding the water element;
sound therein is indeterminate, while the others coexist with it.
However, they are characterized respectively by the quality of resistance to the eye and so forth.
Only five are considered the objects of the fivefold consciousness process.
Femininity is taught as the female state, the condition of being female;
likewise, masculinity is the male state, known by the name of the masculine faculty.
That twofold [maintenance] is found everywhere in the body, whether it be non-clung-to (anupādinnaka);
it consists of that which is distinct from other aggregates and that which functions within a distinct continuity.
It has the characteristic of maintaining those material phenomena born of karma.
The materiality of the life-faculty is called "vitality" (āyu).
Likewise, for the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element,
the heart-based physical basis (vatthurūpa) has the characteristic of being their support.
In the middle of the heart-cavity, within half a *pasata* of blood,
the material form derived from the primary elements functions like the eye and other faculties.
The space element has the characteristic of delimiting material forms.
It is called the "limit" of various groups of material forms.
Mind is the condition for conascent material phenomena, as well as for the body’s acts of going and so forth, and for its stiffening, supporting, and moving.
This is a modification of the air element, termed bodily intimation;
however, some say it consists of the primary elements with the air element predominant.
Likewise, that which is mind-originated occurs during the manifestation of vocal sound.
But it is a condition for the impact upon the appropriated material body.
This is a modification of the earth element, termed "vocal intimation";
however, some say it belongs to the primary elements in which the earth element predominates.
Both of these serve as the doors for bodily and verbal action respectively;
they are characterized by the nature of change due to contact.
One makes known what has been thought through the body and through speech.
Because it is itself made known, it is designated as "intimation" (viññatti).
Furthermore, lightness (lahutā) of material phenomena has the characteristic of non-slowness;
and plasticity (mudutā) of material phenomena has the characteristic of softness.
The wieldiness of material phenomena has the characteristic of being ready for application;
disrespect and rigidity are, respectively, its opposites.
Having obtained suitable food and drink and the excellence of the mind, [it arises].
When matter occurs as light, soft, and wieldy, then for that matter occurring in such a way,
these three qualities— lightness and so forth—
which are distinguished by their mode of occurrence, exist together with it.
Conducive to penetration, helpful to practice, and possessing specific modes,
the perfection of form was indeed proclaimed by the Great Seer.
What is called the accumulation of form has the characteristic of being an accumulation of form.
The continuity of material form is explained as having the characteristic of occurrence.
Material form arises repeatedly through accumulated form;
as the yogi observes its mode of accumulation, birth is grasped by him.
Because it arises in the manner of continuous succession, it is seen as "birth" from the perspective of one who observes it;
at that time, however, birth is grasped by him as having the aspect of continuity.
Thus, the nature of birth is divided into two kinds according to the distinction of mental application (*ābhoga*).
By way of being apprehended as a self, or simply as that which is born,
matter fills up the secluded space in the sense of filling it;
and because it leads from non-existence to renewed existence, its occurrence is called "continuity."
Thus, O you who possess the excellence of all modes,
the illuminator of birth and form divided that birth-and-form into two types.
Aging is the departure of youth, characterized by the ripening of forms.
Impermanence is non-attainment, characterized by disintegration.
Thus, the characteristic-form (lakkhaṇa-rūpa) is threefold according to its different times;
among the phenomena that are essential form (sabhāva-rūpa-dhamma), it is distinguished by its respective time.
"That by which form is characterized as having a distinct aspect at every moment—
for the purpose of the method of insight— that, the Tathāgata has thus declared,
is material food."
That which is characterized by water must be sustained;
food, possessing sense faculties,
is the protector of the material body.
Thus, with their delimitations, their variations, and their specific characteristics,
they have been explained as taught in their respective places according to what was appropriate, by the One who is Such (Tādī), out of compassion, for the sake of penetrating their functions.
Material phenomena, together with their own form, are twenty-eight in all.
Having established one birth [moment], there, within the continuity of accumulation,
it should be pointed out that twenty-seven material phenomena come to be.
Having classified the tangible as consisting of twenty-six elements— namely, the three primary elements (bhūtattaya) and the twenty-three derived elements—
and having likewise taken both types of tangibles (the primary and the derived),
one who is confident should thus analyze the material phenomena as being twenty-five-fold.
"Similarity," "the compendium of names," "intrinsic nature," and "specific characteristic.
Thus ends the discussion on similarity in the analysis of matter.
This is the eighteenth chapter.
The Nineteenth Chapter:
19. Discussion on the Classification.
Now, these twenty-eight kinds of material phenomena (rūpa) shall be explained according to their respective categories.
The discerning one should analyze [matter] through the distinctions of the primary elements, visible forms, and so forth.
This primary matter, beginning with earth and the rest, is fourfold;
the other, derived matter, is twenty-fourfold.
The fivefold form, beginning with the eye, is considered internal;
the remaining twenty-three types are called external.
Form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects—these seven are each fivefold.
The objects of the five sensitivities are called the five objective bases (ārammaṇa).
The remaining twenty-onefold [classification] is comprised within the objective base of mental phenomena (dhammārammaṇa);
it is to be cognized by mind-consciousness and is the domain of the mind-door.
The fivefold [faculties] consist of the serene ones (the faculties) and their objects; both types of [material] existence are likewise fivefold.
All twelve, by way of their own nature, constitute ten bases and ten elements.
Furthermore, all this matter is considered to be with resistance.
That which is gross is called "near";
the rest is called "non-reactive," namely the base of mental phenomena and the element of mental phenomena.
And that which is subtle is form; thus form is established in sixteen ways.
The twenty-two kinds of material phenomena consist of: the sixfold base-materiality (vatthurūpa), the sensitive organs, and the heart;
while the remaining non-base-materiality (avatthurūpa) is of twenty-two types.
Furthermore, the sensitive organs and the intimation (viññatti) constitute the sevenfold door-materiality (dvārarūpa).
The remaining doorless material phenomena, though twenty-onefold, consist of eight types as faculties:
the five sensitivities, the pair of sex-faculties, and life.
The other material phenomena are twentyfold and are non-faculties.
Color, odor, flavor, and nutritive essence—these eightfold [factors] are inseparable material phenomena (*avinibbhoga-rūpa*);
the others, however, are twentyfold as separable (*vinibbhoga*).
The inseparable material phenomena are sound, the bases, and the faculties.
The eighteen kinds of derived matter are to be understood as "matter that is matter.
Furthermore, space is the delimitation; intimation, lightness, and so forth are the modes of change;
the characteristics and the [four] essentials such as integration are the primary qualities of matter.
Even though it is non-produced in ten ways and does not exist as an ultimate reality,
because it is made of form, it is called "form" (rūpa).
Only the sense-sphere of form (rūpāyatana) is declared to be visible.
But the non-indicative is of another kind, being twenty-sevenfold.
Furthermore, that which is born of kamma is either clung-to or not clung-to;
likewise, that which is born of consciousness, born of temperature, and born of nutriment are each threefold.
The eye-element is enumerated as the basis for eye-contact;
its remaining [factors] are not the basis, but would be twenty-sevenfold.
Likewise, there are two kinds based on the bases for ear-contact and so forth.
And one should analyze it in three ways according to its occurrence:
visible form with color and resistance,
invisible [form] which is otherwise, and coarse form with resistance.
Non-indicative matter, the rest which is non-reacting,
and the sixteenfold— all matter should be understood as being of three kinds.
Furthermore, the pair consisting of the eye and the ear is called "grasper by non-arrival."
The three beginning with the nose are said to be "graspers of what has been reached" (sampattagāhaka).
Therefore, the remaining twenty-three types are "non-graspers" (agāhaka);
none of them are at all called "possessing an object" (sārammaṇa) in the sense of grasping.
Based on internal form, and likewise based on external form;
and that which is not based on external form—thus it would also be threefold.
Internal [form] is clung-to, and external is likewise another.
And "not clung-to" (anupādinnaka), and so forth by way of such categories as these:
visible form is the seen, sound is the heard, the three beginning with odor are the sensed (muta), and the rest are the cognized (viññāta);
thus it is fourfold by way of the mind (mano).
Materiality, materiality, delimitation, change, and characteristic are in order;
eighteen, one, five, and four—thus it is.
There is both the door and the basis, but the basis is not the door itself.
One should designate [them] as "not the door," "only the basis," and "neither.
Furthermore, it is taught that there are exactly four types: derived (upādā), not clung-to (anupādinna), likewise not clung-to (anupādinnaka), and neither derived (nopādā) which is twofold.
Materiality with resistance and grasping, likewise materiality without resistance and not grasping—
thus, from the beginning, there are four types, including the two kinds that are neither.
There is materiality born of one [cause] and eleven, and the ninefold heart-faculty.
That which is born of kamma, that which is born of consciousness, and likewise the two kinds of intimation—sound is thus born of consciousness and temperature;
therefore, one kind of material phenomenon is considered to be doubly born.
The triad beginning with lightness is triple-born, being produced from consciousness, temperature, and nutriment.
The nine inseparable from space, those arising from the four causes such as karma,
and then the characteristic materiality— thus materiality is fivefold.
The nine inseparable from space are the nine bases and faculties.
The eighteenfold material form, born of kamma, exists as a composite.
Sound, space, the non-separables, the intimation-forms, and lightness and so forth—
these fifteen kinds of material form are declared to be mind-born.
The inseparable from sound and space, and the triad beginning with lightness;
these are the thirteen kinds of material phenomena that exist as produced by temperature.
The inseparable from delimitation, and also the triad beginning with lightness;
Thus, the matter born of nutriment is established in twelve ways.
Birth, aging, and death do not arise from anywhere;
thus, it is also fivefold according to the classification of the birth of matter.
Twenty-five kinds of kamma, established in the realms of sense and form,
produce kamma-born matter in the two existences of sense-sphere and fine-material realms.
The fivefold sensory consciousnesses, the immaterial resultant states, and all moments of rebirth-linking [are likewise].
"Death [occurs] for one whose taints are exhausted"— these sixteen [types of consciousness] one should avoid.
The remaining seventy-five types of consciousness arise from these mental states and produce mind-born matter in the five-aggregate plane.
Material form born of temperature arises from the fire element in both realms; however,
in the sense-sphere plane, that which is born of nutriment is produced by food, and likewise,
that which is born of itself is produced by kamma at every moment.
At the moment of the arising of consciousness, and immediately following that arising,

materiality produced by temperature arises in thirteen ways: the four primary elements, the seven derived materials beginning with visible form, and also the triad of lightness and so forth, due to their inseparability from delimitation.
At rebirth-linking as well as during the course of existence, the karma-born [materiality] produces materiality;
the remaining types [of materiality] produce it during the course of existence, but not at rebirth-linking.
In a continuity bound to the sense faculties, all three types—karma-born and the rest—also [arise].
Matter is produced by the mind and by the external [elements] as appropriate.
Thus, kamma and the others produce matter according to their respective functions;
they also serve as conditions for the arising of the remaining types of matter.
"Thus, it elucidates therein the classification of matter, the distinctions of its types, their origins,
and the various categories of matter such as the generative cause and so forth.
Thus ends the exposition on the classifications within the analysis of matter.
The Nineteenth Chapter.
The Twentieth Chapter:
20. The Discourse on Groups.
Thus, in the manner described, all matter (rūpa) taken together—
according to the system of co-arising— is said to be of twenty-one kinds.
[These are] karma, consciousness, temperature, and nutriment-produced, respectively.
There are nine, four, and two groups, making twenty-one.
By joining the life-faculty and the inseparable material phenomena respectively with the eye and the other [senses],
eight decads are explained.
The fourfold decads of eye, ear, nose, and tongue;
likewise, the other three decads consisting of the body, femininity, masculinity, and the physical basis;
and the ninefold [decad] of material phenomena inseparable from life.
In these [groups], nine groups born of kamma have been declared.

These are the inseparable material phenomena (*avinibbhoga-rūpa*). Then there is another, the pure octad (*suddha-aṭṭhaka*), and the body-intimation nonad (*kāya-viññatti-navaka*) together with body-intimation.
The decad of vocal intimation, because it occurs together with sound;
the undecad beginning with lightness, because the three [qualities] arise together.
Together with bodily intimation and the qualities beginning with lightness, there would be a duodecad.
Likewise, there is a group of thirteen consisting of vocal intimation, lightness,
and so forth. Thus, six groups originating from consciousness have been explained,
including the various modes and transformations of material form as appropriate.
The first is the pure octad; with sound, there is a nonad;
with lightness and so forth, an undecad; and with the three beginning with lightness, a decad.
With sound and the qualities beginning with lightness, likewise there is a dodecad.
The groups born of the seasons are enumerated as fourfold:
first, the pure octad; next, the nutriment-born; then the elevenfold group beginning with lightness;
thus, these two are considered to be born of nutritive essence (*ojā*).
Because they have the characteristic of delimiting groups (kalāpa),
the wise say that space and the [other] characteristics are not members of a group.
Therein, there are respectively eighty-nine and sixty-three [factors].
The twenty-nine derived [material qualities] and those components of the groups (kalāpa):
the characteristic and the unmanifest material qualities, occurring here and there within the groups, are five each; thus, there are three hundred and sixteen material qualities.
By including what has not yet been grasped, one should develop twenty-five [types of form] under the heading of "the twenty-eightfold division of form.
Having established the three primary elements as the tangible, one should include the subsidence and continuity [of matter].
Or, having made it a single category, one may exclude the heart from that [list].
For in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, within the section on matter (*rūpakaṇḍa*), this "base-matter" (*vatthurūpa*) is not explicitly indicated; however, it is taught in the *Paṭṭhāna*.
Two groups of nine sounds,
and three pure groups of eight;
two pairs produced from the mind and from heat.
One is nutriment-born,
and five are born of those [three]; nine are born of kamma— thus,
by way of materiality and form, these fourteen groups are taught.
Having grouped together the tenfold [set] itself, there is the ninefold life-faculty therein;
or, having made the single tenfold set of mental states the basis, likewise without [the others].
Sound is only two, born from mind; three are their originators.
There are seven pure octads and ten decads born of kamma.
The wise declare that therein matter is of ninety-six kinds;
by including what has not yet been mentioned, it becomes eighteenfold.
Of those very same groups (kalāpa), there are seven,
six, five, four, three, two, and single [factors] as appropriate.

The method of unity and diversity, and another, the method of non-action;

for those who are constantly oppressed by aging, death, sorrow, and so forth, ignorance arises from the constant emergence of the taints (āsava).
With ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be just as before;
thus, the beginningless wheel of existence is bound together without interruption.
It has craving and ignorance as its hub, and aging and death as its rim.
The teaching is adorned with the profound method of the fourfold compendium,
consisting of the remaining aspects and so forth as its axle-pin, yoked to the chariot of the three realms of existence;
it possesses three halves, three wheels, and likewise three joints as its axle-pins.
The wise proclaim "the stability of phenomena" (dhammaṭṭhiti) as specific conditionality (idappaccayatā), which is analyzed into twenty modes and subsumed under twelve modes.
This is dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) by way of its name, "the mode of conditions."
In brief and in detail, through its various modes of differentiation,
it generates the arising of ignorance and the rest within the dependently originated [process],
and it brings about their cessation in every respect through the cessation of ignorance and the rest.
Some say that saṃsāra proceeds solely by way of conditions and the phenomena arisen from conditions; they thus grasp at conditions.
This is according to the analysis of the great treatise, the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* (The Book of the Connected Discourses).
Some discern the twenty-four requisites.
Thus, the discernment of conditions in their various modes is to be understood as the definition of conditioned mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa).
Knowledge of specific conditionality, the vision of the mode of conditions,
and what is called the knowledge and vision of the stability of phenomena as they truly are—
these purify doubt and defilement regarding the distinctions of the three periods of time.
"The overcoming of doubt is called purification.
Thus ends the discussion on the purification by overcoming doubt within the analysis of Nibbāna.
This concludes the twenty-fourth chapter.
The Twenty-fifth Chapter: 25.
The Discourse on the Growth of Insight Purification of Virtue, Mind, and View; and Purification by Overcoming Doubt.
First, one should contemplate them by way of groups; thereafter, one should proceed further.
Contemplation by way of groups, the vision of rise and fall, the knowledge of dissolution, the knowledge of fear, and likewise the knowledge of disadvantage and disenchantment.
The knowledge of desire for deliverance, contemplation of reflection,
equanimity towards formations, and conformity— these ten successive knowledges established in this order are declared to be insight.
Having reached the three characteristics, [the mind] proceeds toward formations.
Therefore, one should first contemplate the three characteristics according to groups;
having contemplated them, [one should contemplate] the aggregates, bases, and elements of the past and so forth.
"Impermanent are they in the sense of destruction; the aggregates are suffering in the sense of fear;
non-self are they in the sense of being coreless"—thus one should constantly reflect.
As he was thus comprehending, the three characteristics became manifest to him.
Then, regarding formations— from the perspective of the moment,
the continuity, and the duration— the yogi contemplates therein the arising and the passing away of present phenomena by means of the fivefold division of wisdom.
Likewise, the arising and cessation of ignorance, craving, and kamma are shown;
as well as the origin and cessation of the five aggregates.
Furthermore, [the origin] of matter is shown through nutriment, and that of the three [mental aggregates] through contact and name-and-form.
"All these forty [factors] combined with consciousness—
when one sees here the characteristic of arising and the characteristic of dissolution,"
And by way of their momentary arising and passing away,
these amount to fifty-five.
Thus, by way of the aggregates, these arisings and vanishings have been analyzed.
These [characteristics] should be applied accordingly according to the divisions of the sense bases and so forth.
As that yogi thus contemplates both arising and passing away,
formations become manifest to him, and the three characteristics emerge.
And they see the factors conducive to enlightenment in particular; from that,
the secondary defilements arise.
The bases for the secondary defilements:
illumination, rapture, tranquility, resolution, exertion, pleasure,
knowledge, establishment, equanimity, and attachment.
Through the graspings of craving, conceit, and views—
these three— he relishes them, exalts himself, and clings to them as "mine," thereby defiling himself.
Unskilled, he thinks, "I have attained the Path, the Fruit, and Nibbāna."
One who conceives "I am awakening to insight" is an overestimator (adhimānika) and thus fails to attain it.
These [factors] such as the Path do not exist from the standpoint of the objective basis for the grasping of craving and so forth.
Craving, conceit, and views are secondary defilements that act as obstacles.
The vision of the arising and passing away of the aggregates is indeed ancient;
because it has the three characteristics as its object, the Path becomes a condition for Nibbāna.

Thus, for one who purifies both the path and what is not the path, there is accomplished the purification known as the knowledge and vision of the path and the non-path. Likewise, there is another purification:
the vision of the arising and passing away [of formations].
Beginning with that which is called the knowledge and vision of the way,
the wise person subsequently proceeds— just as before— to the end of purification from defilement and distraction, by means of the vision of arising and passing away.
Thus, for one training in the sequence of knowledge that contemplates arising and passing away,
insight soon reaches maturity.
When one sets aside the conventional expression "arising" and resolves upon "passing away" alone, [insight becomes fully developed].
Through attachment to arising and delusion, one persists in destruction alone.
Therefore, like the stream of a waterfall, like the water obstructing the Ganges,
like grass being torn asunder, or like a flame [extinguished], such is the course of practice.
As conditioned phenomena fall away, pass away, and break up, the knowledge that perceives this is called "contemplation of dissolution.
Following that, for one who sees them as fearful,
there is "contemplation of fear" through the insight, "They are fearful."
The knowledge of contemplation of danger is "contemplation of danger.
For the yogi who is disenchanted, there is the contemplation of disenchantment;
then, for one who desires to be liberated, there is the knowledge of the desire for liberation.
If it were permanent, it would not cease; if it were pleasant, it would not afflict you.
If the self were to abide and persist, then in its absence, those things would not be so for you.
Thus, desiring to be thoroughly liberated, one should practice accordingly.
The knowledge of contemplation by reflection is said to have arisen.
Having thoroughly reflected upon the three characteristics in the formations,
one likewise contemplates those formations once they have been fully understood.
"Formations are indeed impermanent, suffering, and non-self, and there is nothing else besides them;
neither a self nor anything belonging to a self—neither 'I' nor 'mine.
Therefore, one should remain equanimous toward that, having emerged from delight and lust."
One contemplates formations with equanimity by way of their state of not being self or belonging to self.
This knowledge is called "equanimity regarding formations.
That which is joined with emergence from that state is called "adaptation" (anuloma).
For one who has thoroughly understood conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) and well mastered the three characteristics,
while maintaining equanimity toward those very same things, insight (*vipassanā*) reaches its culmination.
It continues to proceed for some time, taking conditioned phenomena as its object.
Like a bird watching the shore until it sees the further bank,
when one perceives Nibbāna, one has then grasped emergence.
That which leads to emergence is called "conformity."
"Thus, for one who is purified by these two purifications and is practicing insight,
it is said that he fulfills the way of insight.
Thus ends the discussion on the growth of insight within the analysis of Nibbāna.
The Twenty-fifth Chapter. The Twenty-sixth Chapter:
26. Discussion on Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way to Liberation (Vuṭṭhāna-visuddhi-kathā).
When one has practiced in this way, insight reaches its culmination;
then, at that time, there arises what is called "insight leading to emergence.
Beyond the preliminary, access, conformity, and change-of-lineage [moments], it proceeds further.
From that comes the Path, then the Fruit, and from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) comes the reviewing consciousness.
Having had as its object the preliminary, access, conformity, and path— designated as the "sphere"—
the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) arises with Nibbāna as its object.
Whether it be the fourth, the fifth, or even the sixth as appropriate,
that path-moment consciousness enters into nibbāna only once.
Thereafter, three, two, or one fruition consciousnesses follow in due order.
In the cognitive process of emerging from the path that leads to the cessation of the remainder of the path,
there is then a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
Having cut that off, there occurs the reviewing consciousness.
The three [knowledges] are fivefold,
according to their respective application.
For one necessarily reviews the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna.
He reviews the lower defilements and the remainder, or he does not.
Then, again, practicing insight into formations as before,
he enters successively into the remaining paths and fruits.
In this context, the fruits of Nibbāna and insight (vipassanā) pertaining to the path are spoken of:
namely, emptiness (suññatā), the signless (animitta), and likewise the desireless (appaṇihita). For one contemplates by means of what are known as emptiness-insight and the others.
Thus they are divided into three kinds as being the doors to liberation (vimokkhamukha).
By way of the names "emptiness" (suññatā) and so forth, the liberations (vimokkha) are considered to be threefold:
the paths leading to the fruit of Nibbāna and the attainments (samāpatti) of concentration (samādhi).
The noble person who has reached that very first stage is called a "stream-enterer" (sotāpanna), one for whom there are at most seven more births.
And he who has reached the second stage is named a "once-returner" (sakadāgāmin).
Having come to this world for just a single time, he becomes human.
Having reached the third stage, he is called a Non-returner (anāgāmī);
because he does not return from the Brahma-world to be reborn here in the sense-sphere realm.
Having attained the fourth stage, the Arahant, the supreme person, extinguishes the fire of suffering in this very life; thus it is said.
Such are the noble persons who dwell in the state of the path and its fruit.
In two ways and four ways, there are eight [types] when divided.
However, by way of the division of those liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*) and so forth;
These seven are analyzed according to their respective application: namely,
emergence from impermanence through the burden of faith, and likewise from suffering.
"Because wisdom is not-self, the wise proclaim this.
One who follows by faith at the beginning, one liberated by faith in the middle,
and one liberated by wisdom alone at the end— therefore, one may be 'burdened with faith'."
At the beginning, there is the follower by dhamma; above that, the one who has attained vision;
at the end, there is only the one liberated by wisdom, as well as the one whose vehicle is wisdom.
Furthermore, there are those whose vehicle is serenity, and those for whom the formless is the supreme support.
Those who follow the method of insight (vipassanāyānika) and all those who are dry-insight practitioners (sukkhavipassaka)—
by way of the distinction between those who take up the burden and those who have laid it down— there are five types in every respect;
likewise, those who use the formless attainments as a basis for insight are also twofold from the outset.
In the middle of the six stages, one is classified as a "body-witness" (kāyasakkhī);
established in Arahantship, one is "liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutto).
Thus, from the distinction between those who have undertaken the yoke of the vehicle and those who have emerged from it—
The stages of the paths and their fruits, and the seven noble persons therein;
and therein, the unsurpassed knowledge that penetrates the truths,
purifying the underlying tendencies of the defilements through their complete eradication.
Emergence is described by way of the analysis of the four paths;
it is likewise called the purification of knowledge and vision.
Furthermore, the path thoroughly understands suffering pertaining to the three planes.
He abandons, as appropriate, both craving and its origin;
he realizes cessation and the unsurpassed truth of the path.
Having descended into the course of cultivation, he is said to "cultivate."
The state of wrong views, doubt, and the entirety of mere rules and observances;
that which leads to the states of deprivation, and the triad beginning with lust and hatred;
and the defilements associated therewith—[all these are abandoned] by the abandoning of their co-nascent factors.
The path of stream-entry, belonging to the first stage, abandons [the defilements];
it also abandons those associated with them, such as lust and hatred, though in their gross form.
The path of once-returning, belonging to the second stage, abandons these in their gross form.
The path of the non-returner abandons without remainder sensual lust and ill will,
along with those states associated with them that arise from them;
as well as the pentad consisting of lust for the fine-material and immaterial realms, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance.
The supreme path abandons the defilements entirely, as well as those remaining.
Thus, the Buddhas proclaim the knowledge of the path— the seventh stage of purification— which penetrates the truths and brings about the fruit of the destruction of the defilements.
Thus, by means of these six purifications, for the sake of complete purity,
that which is to be attained on the seventh stage is called Nibbāna—
the supreme refuge that brings about the destruction of defilements and the transcendence of saṃsāra.
The further shore is fearless and free from all conditioned phenomena.
By means of the subduing of pride and the removal of thirst,
it is shown to be the antidote to the defilements, to saṃsāra, and to conditioned formations.
It is ageless, deathless, absolutely unarisen, unconditioned, supreme, without volitional formations, infinite, and incomparable.
It is the ultimate goal, beyond analogy, peace, and peerless bliss.
The truth of cessation is Nibbāna, the state that is exclusively the deathless.
It is twofold according to its conventional designations:
the element of Nibbāna with residue remaining and likewise the other, the element of Nibbāna without residue remaining.
Emptiness, the signless, and likewise the desireless—
these three are also classified according to the absence of grasping at a self and so forth,
and according to their opposition to the defilements, to saṃsāra, and to formations.
It is described in many ways through its distinctions,
such as the destruction of existence (bhavakkhaya) and so forth. Thus, this deathless Dhamma—
supramundane and timeless— is designated as “Nibbāna” because it transcends speech due to the absence of speech.
Thus ends the discussion on purification by emergence within the analysis of Nibbāna.
This is the twenty-sixth chapter.
And the analysis of Nibbāna is completed in every respect.
The Twenty-Seventh Chapter:
5. Analysis of Designation, Section 27:
Exposition of Classifications.
Mind, mental factors, matter, and even Nibbāna have been analyzed;
therefore, they are now also called "designations" (paññatti) as appropriate.
And this [designation] is divided into the categories of designation of meaning (atthapaññatti) and designation of name (nāmapaññatti).
Description is twofold: there, it is the description of the meaning (atthapaññatti).

It arises from the aggregation of the constituents of a being, from its configuration, from its combination, from its transformation, from its conceptualization, from its manifestation, from its mode, from its conventional expression, and from its adherence.
Meanings established by convention as they occur are contrived and designated as "names"; thus they are described as "descriptions" (paññatti).
For meanings are twofold: ultimate meanings (paramattha) and descriptive meanings (paññatta).
In that context, there are ultimate meanings, which are real in their actual sense and possess their own specific characteristics.
There are also conceptual meanings, which— due to their lack of a nature possessing reality and specific characteristics—
are grasped otherwise and constructed by depending on this or that basis.

Therefore, there are designations by way of the derived (upādāpaññatti) and designations by way of meaning (atthapaññatti); these are merely names for that which is to be designated, and they are the meanings designated in every respect.
As for the ultimate realities (paramattha) as previously stated—the mind, mental factors, and so forth—
Things such as woman, man, bed, chair, and cloth are designated.
That by which they are spoken of is "name" (nāma); because it designates, it is called "designation" (paññatti).
And that designation is therefore considered to be "conceptual designation" (nāmapaññatti).
It is analyzed as *saṅkhā*, *samaññā*, *paññatti*, and *vohāra*; thus it is described as the fourfold "designation of that which is to be designated.
Following that are *nāma*, *nāmakamma*, and furthermore *nāmadheyya*.
"Etymological analysis (nirutti) and phrasing (byañjana) are called expression (abhilāpa)," thus they are classified.
"Designation by name (nāmapaññatti) is called name," thus designation (paññatti) is made twofold.
Furthermore, "all phenomena (dhammā) are the path of designation," thus they are classified.
In this context, there are two kinds of ultimate designations (*paramatthapaññatti*);
they are indeed paths of designation (*paññattipatha*), while the ultimates themselves possess their own specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*).
Designation and the object of designation exist merely as that which is to be designated.
And it is a "path of description" because it is the state of being a path for the description of names.
Although a name is indeed something that must be described by something [else],
nevertheless, in this context, it is described simply as "description."
The phenomena to be described, those already described among them,
the paths of description that are to be desired, and the diversity of descriptions— thus,
according to what has been stated, it is explained in the manner of the Commentary.
Having adopted this method, even here the designation (paññatti) is made twofold.
Within that too, there are ultimate realities (paramattha), which possess the characteristic of being truly established;
and there are things that are mere designations, known as "designation of objects" (atthapaññatti).
That which makes them known and is called "conceptual designation" (nāmapaññatti)—
thus, in this path of descriptive names, it is made threefold because of its knowability.
And there, that which is called ultimate truth (paramatthasacca) is indeed the ultimate itself.
For they are non-deceptive because they possess a nature that accords with reality.
Conventional truth consists of the two types of designation, because they are non-deceptive in their worldly common usage, intention, and conventional application.
Thus these two truths were declared by the Supreme Person.
Therefore, one who understands names may employ either of them in conventional discourse.
Thus ends the detailed explanation regarding the classification of designations.
The Twenty-Seventh Chapter.
The Twenty-Eighth Chapter: 28.
Discussion on the Designation of Meaning.
And therein, it is designated as the aggregates occurring in succession;
it is bound up with the specific manifestations of intimation and the faculties;
it possesses its own characteristic marks, and is divided into various classes such as gods, spirits, and humans.
This is called a "conceptual designation of a being" (sattapaññatti), and it is this that is conventionally regarded as a "being.
It exists by way of the aggregates and the sense bases,
in dependence upon the three rounds of existence.
"This one is the doer or the feeler,
who wanders from existence to existence.
Therefore, that person who has entered into saṃsāra is called a 'being' (satta)."
Another woman conceives the notion, "This is a man. Yet this being,
consisting of the aggregates and so forth, is not said to be something other [than them],
because a being existing apart from the aggregates and so forth simply does not exist.
These aggregates belong only to the aggregates; it is not called a "being.

This is because, apart from the conventional designation of "aggregates," no other designation for it is possible. Thus, although there is a difference between the aggregates and the person, in actual fact they are one.
And because the conventional usage of "specific" (visesa) is observed there,
this person is called a "being" (satta), and it is said that he is "born" (jāyati) and "grows old" (jiyyati);
and because he "dies" (mīyati), this process of his is termed "saṃsāra."
The dead person is not identical [to the living one], because of the conventional designation of the dissolution of the aggregates;

nor is he another, because of the conventional designation of the absence of a break in the continuity. Thus, neither difference nor identity [applies] to the person, because it is merely a conventional designation.
Neither annihilation nor permanence [apply]; therefore, the person does not exist.
Thus, this so-called "person" or "being" who performs the wandering in saṃsāra is declared to be a designation based upon the aggregates and so forth.
Therefore, it should be understood by the discerning that the designation "sentient being" (sattapaññatti),
which consists of a person and is bound to the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), is merely a name.
This applies both to the internal parts, such as hair and so forth, and to the external ones.

Earth, mountains, rocks, grass, trees, creepers, and so forth, which are conceptually constructed as the differentiation of the manifestation of the collection of primary elements— taking these [elements] as their basis,
they are called "conceptual designations based on a collection" (sambhāra-paññatti).

That which is conceptually constructed from the aggregation and differentiation of the primary elements is known as "conceptualization of shape" (saṇṭhāna-paññatti), such as pillars, jars, and so forth.
That which is conceptually constructed from the specific combination of the primary elements—
That which is called a "designation for a collection" (saṅghātapaññatti) is considered to be such things as a chariot or a house.
That which is fashioned through the transformation of specific combinations of primary elements is considered a "designation for a transformation" (pariṇāmapaññatti), such as curd-rice and the like.
Thus, internal and external phenomena, produced from a collection of conditions, exist as a continuous flow;
established by convention, designation is fivefold.
It is designated as such according to the conceptualization and mental application that arise in various ways.
"Concepts based on mental determination" (vikappa-paññatti) refer to [notions] such as time,
direction, and so forth. "Concepts based on appearance" (upaṭṭhāna-paññatti) are considered to be those such as the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta),
which are determined by relying upon this or that specific characteristic (nimitta).
Even a mere specific mode (ākāra), when conceptualized as a distinct entity,
is called a "conceptualization of mode" (ākāra-paññatti), such as intimation (viññatti),
lightness (lahutā), and so forth. These are designated through conventional usage by resorting to various respective causes.
What is called conventional designation refers to things such as the Kathina-offense and so forth.
That which is a fool is my self;
he shall become "I" and "mine."
Furthermore, [views] such as "the self is eternal, stable,
and permanent" arise in every way even in the absence of any grounds for such conventional designations.
The designation of dogmatic adherence refers to that which is fabricated by the followers of other sects.
Thus, in this way, the meanings established through the world,
the dispensation, the sectarian tenets, the continuum, and pure convention are fivefold.
This designation of meaning (*atthapaññatti*) is twofold, according to its continuity of occurrence and its distinction by way of utterance; it is explained in ten ways.
Thus, regarding the meanings designated in the manner described, the wise—
It is with reference to mere conceptual designation that people employ conventional expressions as they do.
But others— both fools and unskilled followers of other sects—
having run away from mere designation, grasp at things as if they were ultimate reality.
People who grasp things in such a manner,
seized by ignorance and adhering to what is false, increase their bondage to existence.
Therefore, one who is wise regarding both kinds of meaning—
"In the ultimate designations, one should characterize the analysis.
Thus ends the discussion on the designation of meaning within the analysis of designations.
This is the twenty-eighth chapter.
The Twenty-Ninth Chapter:
Discussion on Designation by Name (Nāmapaññatti-kathā) Designation by name is based upon the application of conventional usage, linguistic expression, and social convention.
The contemplation of the meanings and words as they have been described has been completed.
This is the designation by name (*nāma-paññatti*), which is distinct from both meaning and word;
it is characterized by a mode of knowability based on a convention bound to those two.
That which is grasped by the cognitive process arising within the range of the sound of a name,
and by the mind-door process arising immediately after that occurrence— namely, the sound of beds,
chairs, and so forth, by means of the ear-consciousness process.
Having heard that [sound] and having reflected upon it by way of the mental-door process,
the name produced by convention is then grasped through reflection; thereafter,
the meanings of the name-designations are grasped according to their occurrence.
For in this regard, reflection is intended to be fourfold or threefold, according to the categories of names, meanings, designations, and ultimate realities. Indeed,
by one who describes the path of the Aṭṭhakathā in this manner, it has been shown.
"The method [is determined] by the teacher"—thus has this classification been explained.
Others, however, have described it thus: "There is no other intimation (viññatti) whatsoever;
rather, it is sound itself, accompanied by a modification, that is the designation of a name (nāmapaññatti)."
Although this name exists in many ways by virtue of its nature as a designation (paññatti), according to the intention of the etymologists (neruttika) and others, it may be divided into two types.
First, the roots and their forms within the conventional designations (saññā), and thereafter, the suffixes.
Having applied vowel-insertions and other grammatical refinements established by the rules of phonology (saddalakkhaṇa),
they utter a nominal derivative (neruttika) as a word formed according to whim—
a mere product of desire, devoid of both phonetic integrity and semantic meaning.
It is of three kinds: *anvatthaka*, *kādimañcopacārima*, and so forth;
it depends upon the meaning of its etymological derivation (*nibbacana*). Among these, that which is expressed according to its literal meaning is called *anvattha*.
That which is based on an arbitrary convention is called *kādimañcopacārima*.
The designation of a thing as being what it has not yet become is called "becoming that.
Likewise, there are names based on commonality, names based on qualities, and conventional names;
thus, there are four kinds of names, including those for beings of spontaneous birth.
There are three types of names: those agreed upon by the great multitude, those that correspond to the actual fact, and likewise those of a similar nature;
among these, there are names such as "Moon" (Canda) given at birth, names given according to one's whim, names based on circumstances, and furthermore, names derived from omens.
Name is of five kinds: derivative, conventional, arbitrary, according to seniority, and such as "calf" or "ox";
furthermore, there are situational names, indicative names, and those based on qualities such as virtue or wisdom.
The indicative designation is that which is seen through a sign, such as "the man with the staff" or "the man with the umbrella.

The conventional designation is that which has become current through a mere resemblance, such as "ox" or "buffalo. There are three types: the designation of the existent, the designation of the non-existent, and the designation mixed with both.
Conceptual designation by way of analysis is indeed sixfold therein.
"Designation of what exists" (vijjamānapaññatti) is that which indicates an existing object;
it refers to the aggregates, bases, elements, the five faculties, and so forth.
That which is called a "designation of what does not exist" (avijjamāna-paññatti) refers, in the ultimate sense, to things such as beds that do not exist;
it is explained as a designation of a thing (attha-paññatti).
That which is called a "designation of what does not exist by means of what exists" (vijjamānena avijjamāna-paññatti);
One who possesses the threefold knowledge, the six supernormal powers, and is virtuous and wise—
[these are examples of] designations for what actually exists applied to what does not exist:
such as "female form," "female sound," and "female mind," and so forth.
That which exists is designated by the name "existent designation," such as eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and so forth.
That which does not exist is designated by the name "non-existent designation."
"A khattiya’s son, a brahmin’s son," and so forth—
following these stated examples, the wise one should discern the nature,
the object, and the classification of designations by name (*nāmapaññatti*).

Thus, the ultimate realities (paramattha) as previously described are fourfold, and conceptual designations (paññatti) are twofold; therefore, the objects of knowledge (ñeyyattha) are considered to be sixfold.
Thus ends the discussion on the designation of names within the analysis of conceptual designations.
The Twenty-Ninth Chapter.
The analysis of the categories of designation is thus completed in every respect.
The Concluding Discourse.
Born into a noble family in the excellent kingdom of Kañcīvara, in the preeminent city of Kāverī,
by the Elder Anuruddha, who was highly learned and possessed of wisdom, and whose fame was unceasing;
While residing in the city named Tambapaṇṇi in the province of Tambapaṇṇi, he—
being distinguished among the Saṅgha and requested by them— composed this work,
free from confusion, based on the method of recitation of the Mahāvihāra dwellers.
"By him, the knower of the ultimate meaning, this treatise was composed, which elucidates the ultimate meaning and is a definitive exposition of the ultimate.
Thus [ends] what was composed by the teacher Anuruddha.
The *Paramatthavinicchaya* is completed.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
The *Saccasaṅkhepa*.
Prologue to the Work:
Having paid homage to the Supreme One of the Three Worlds, who has reached the further shore of the ocean of the knowable;
to the Dhamma that brings about the cessation of existence; and to the Saṅgha, an ocean of virtues.

Relying upon the tradition of the ancient masters, which is not inconsistent with the true meaning, I shall expound this compendium of truth for the benefit of the practitioner who strives for welfare. 1.
The First Chapter.
The summary of form,
the truths, and the two— ultimate reality and conventional designation— are found therein.
That truth which is to be known by way of stiffness and so forth is the ultimate truth.
Conventional reality (sammuti) should be understood as specific arrangements and so forth;
it is declared to be "truth" because it is established through the conventions of entities and linguistic designations, owing to its being such [in that context].
Ultimate reality (paramattha) here consists of the five aggregates together with Nibbāna, insofar as they are a "heap" (rāsi).
The meaning of "aggregate" (khandha) has been explained through its classification as past and so forth when used in compounds. However,
in the case of feeling and the other [aggregates], the word "aggregate" is used by way of conventional usage (ruḷhi) even for equanimity (upekkhā),
just as the term "ocean" is applied to a single part of the ocean.
Therein, matter arises from cold and so forth; it consists of earth, water, fire, and air.
These elements have the functions of solidity, cohesion, heating, and motion.
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, light, and sound—
Odor, flavor, and the female faculty; the male faculty, the physical basis, and vitality.
The elements, birth, aging, and dissolution; lightness of matter, as well as malleability and wieldiness;
and bodily and vocal intimation—these are derived from the primary elements.
The sensitive materiality of the eye and so forth, produced by kamma rooted in the desire to see and so on,
has as its objects visible forms, sounds, and so forth, which are the domains of visual cognition and the rest.
Nutritive essence is the cause of maintenance, while femininity, masculinity, and so forth are the causes of gender characteristics.
The two states [of mind and matter] are like the body [to its parts]: pervasive, yet not co-existent.
The support and the basis for the two elements [of consciousness and mind-objects] is like water for lotuses and the like at the moment of their subsistence, providing sustenance born of karma.
Space is the delimitation of forms;
then the triad beginning with birth, the production of form, maturation, and disintegration, respectively.
The triad beginning with lightness is indeed the sequence of the qualities of forms.
Non-blindness and non-stiffness, as well as adaptability to bodily action—
these are the modifications of the wind born of the mind that produces forward movement and so forth;
they constitute the cause for the postures of the body and the like, which is bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti).
Through a mind that effects vocal expression, there arises the alteration of the primary elements of earth;
this is the cause for the impact of vocal intimation and the appropriated [body].
All such matter is indeterminate (avyākata), dissociated [from consciousness], and rootless (ahetuka).
According to the method, it is of one kind: "without an object" and "limited" (paritta), etc.
The internal [bases] are the five sensitive organs beginning with the eye;
these same [five] are the bases by way of their physical locations (vatthu), while they are the doors together with the intimation (viññatti).
The remainder consists of twenty-two, twenty-one, and twenty [factors], as well as the external,
the basis for lack of confidence, and that which is without doors, in their respective order.
There are five types of confidence, the state of existence, the faculties, the non-faculties, and the rest.
From the beginning up to the *vināpa*, the tastes are coarse and not otherwise.
That which consists of the eight inseparable factors—color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence—is the primary element (*bhūta*);
however, one should designate the other as that which is separable.
From the eighteen [bases], visible forms are produced, but the others are not;
however, tangible objects—excluding the [subtle] element—are primary elements in the sense-sphere, but the others are not.
That which is associated with the trainee and with resistance, and that which is associated with the non-trainee and with resistance, are excluded from the pair.

That [matter] is threefold: coarse, fine, and the other (intermediate). It is also threefold according to whether it is born of kamma, not born of kamma, or neither born of kamma nor not born of kamma;
likewise, it is threefold by way of being mind-born, temperature-born, and so forth.
The seen, the heard, the sensed, and indeed the cognized by the mind—each one of these, as well as all five together, may occur in twenty ways.
The heart is the basis; intimation is the door; and the pentad beginning with the eye is the gateway.
The base and the door, and the remaining [factors]; the base and the door may not exist [in certain cases].
Derived materiality consists of the elements, delimitation, and characteristics;
the triad beginning with birth is materiality, as is alteration such as lightness and so forth.
Just as the characteristic of conditioned phenomena is itself conditioned,

so too are matter such as delimitation and the rest, because they do not transcend their respective origins. Herein, by way of the conditions of kamma, consciousness, heat, and nutriment, [matter arises].
How does the occurrence of matter proceed, and how is it categorized into aggregates?
That which is born of karma is the sense-base together with the faculties; intimation is born of consciousness; sound is born of both.
The triad of lightness and so forth is produced by the fire of consciousness and by the air-element.

The eightfold birth and space, the fourfold decay and destruction—neither of these two has ever arisen from anywhere, for they are merely the breaking up of what was previously produced. Even in the case of birth, there is no state of being born from anywhere;
such is the method of the discourse on "Is" and "Is-not."
Because of the absence of its characteristic mark, there is no finality when that [life-force] exists.
Nine and seven aggregates are to be understood as being produced by karma, consciousness, fire, and water;
four and two are with life, and two are without life.
The eightfold [group] by way of life-faculty, the ninefold by way of the bases of existence;
the five decads beginning with the eye—these are the nine groups born of kamma.
There is also a decad consisting of the pure octad conjoined with intimation.
By the term "pure" (suddha), there is one group of nine; by "lightness" (*lahutā*) and so forth, there is one group of ten.
By "intimation" (*viññatti*) and "lightness" and so forth, there are again twelve and thirteen;
thus, it should be understood that there are seven or six groups born of consciousness (*cittaja*).
The pure octad, the sound nonad, the single decads beginning with lightness;
the four "spokes" consisting of sound together with lightness and the others;
the nine beginning with the pure octad and lightness and the others; and the two [decads] beginning with the nutriment-born. These are the nine.
Seven, four, and two—these are twenty dyads.
Three eights and four nines; nine tens, three twos, and one one;
ten by one, and [ten] by two and by three.
Furthermore, here, the various classifications of form should be understood according to the predominance of each of the four elements: that born of kamma, mind, fire, and nutriment.
From hair to the brain, there are twenty [types] consisting of earth and the other [elements].
Those [qualities] excluding bile and so forth are the watery element, consisting of twelve aspects.
That by which there is heating, that by which there is digestion, as well as burning,
and that by which there is the ripening of white and other [substances)— this is the section on the fourfold fire element.
The upward-moving, the downward-moving, the stomach-remnant, the trunk-section, the limb-joint,
and what is known as inhalation— these six parts are dependent on the wind.
The feces, urine, excrement, and the stomach are the four [parts] born of the elements.
Kamma, heat, fire, and mind—these six are of a single birth (ekaja).
Sweat, snot, and saliva arise from the heart and the stomach;
these thirty-two parts are of double birth (dvijā), while the remaining ones are of fourfold birth (catubbhava).
In the four beginning with Ekajaṭṭhī, there are the fourfold sets born of the seasons (utu),
the ninefold set of vitality (jīvita), and the eightfold set of mental existence (cittabhava) should be placed first.
Among the twice-born (dvija), there are two eightfold sets each for mind (mano) and heat (tejo).
In each of the elements of earth, water, fire, and air, there are three [kinds of matter] each.
