Through the eight fires of the koṭis of ages, there arise eight [types of matter] from kamma;
likewise, there are eight vitalities. Thus, these are the eight fourfold existences.
In the remaining twenty-four [bases], there are three sets of fourfold and eightfold [groups];
and in each one, the groups of mind-born, fire-born, and kamma-born should be understood.
Therein, the kamma-born may also consist of the tenfold [material qualities], which are called the bodily existence-group.
In each of the twenty-four factors, there are two each.
Furthermore, the five beginning with the eye and ear constitute ten units (dasakas) of locations;
the ninefold units are designated as sound, and there are two [others]—thus it is according to the groupings (kalāpa).
There are fifty-three, ten, one, and one hundred and nine;
there may be tens, nines, and eights in succession.
Five hundred [factors] regarding the body pertain to the trainee (sekha), and that [number] proceeds to a thousand.
Form exists when the faculties are complete, being produced through the differentiation of the elements.
However, at the arising of consciousness, there may be causes for form such as karma and so forth.
Yet, in the textual tradition, there is no stability of consciousness, nor is there the production of form at the moment of its dissolution.
Because it is stated, “change [occurs] while it stands,” the moment of standing is indeed implied.
If one asks, “Does it exist?”—standing there is spoken of by way of continuity.
Alternatively, the action occurs during three moments: at the moment of the mere arising of consciousness;
When one has departed from one's own place, there are indeed three causes for form:
at the moment of a better rebirth, they consist of the body,
the state of existence, and the basis.
For one who possesses existence (bhāvin), there are ten [mental factors];
without existence, there would be two.
Beyond that, those born from the fire of karma and the mind are the aggregates (piṇḍika).
The two types of nutriment-born [matter] and those born of the moment of speech uttered previously—matter arises from these four conditions:
nutriment, the eye-decad and so forth, and time. Thus, matter proceeds in combination.

That materiality, which has a lifespan of seventeen moments of consciousness— excluding the characteristics of intimation— continues from its arising until death, bringing about the fruits such as aging.
It does not arise from kamma during the seventeen moments of dissolution after its production.
From that [craving], rebirth arises; through its destruction, death occurs.
Death may occur through the exhaustion of both lifespan and karma, or through external intervention, or for some through the cutting off of the karma that sustains life.
For one who is of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*), there are seven sets of ten [faculties] born of karma (*kammaja*).
In the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), these exist prior to those born of the fire of existence (*bhavangaja*).
This applies to the humans of the first eon (*ādikappa*), to those in the woeful states (*apāya*), and to the blind.
For one who is deaf, six [factors] would exist from the very beginning, as would the others.
In that same case, for one who is both blind and deaf, five are non-existent;
this should be understood here according to the logical principle, whether there are five or even four.
"For one who lacks the triad beginning with the eye, there are only four [factors]"—
having examined this statement, it should be understood by the wise.
There is the life-decad in relation to visible forms, and the three heptads beginning with the eye.
Five [bases] arise from the four primary elements and mind; six [bases] arise for those possessing perception. There are five types of determinations, such as the elements, etc.;
in the textual tradition, there is no production of smell or taste therein, because the primary elements do not function when the tangible is absent.
There is no state of being "solid" or "hot" apart from the functions of the elements and so forth,
because they are perceived through those very functions, such as odor and the rest.
Just as in the case of visible form, there is resistance and so on, and therein lies its nature of being "formed."
The striking together [of the elements] and the production of sound must be accepted as being causes for other purposes as well;
this is to be desired exclusively in this way, because it does not contradict the reading.
Alternatively, by means of those [terms], the decads, nonads, and octads are to be understood.
In the sensual existence, all form [is present]; in the fine-material existence, nineteen;
for the non-percipient beings, ten; and for the Brahmās, excluding those born of odour and taste.
Thus ends the summary of form in the *Saccasaṅkhepa*.
The First Chapter. 2.
The Second Chapter:
A Summary of the Three Aggregates.
Feeling is the experience [of an object] in three ways: as pleasure, pain, and equanimity.
Its characteristic is the experiencing of the desirable, the undesirable, and that which is intermediate between them.
Feeling consists of bodily and mental pain, pleasure, and equanimity.
One [type] is purely mental, due to the distinction of the five sense-faculties.
Whether it be perception (*saññā*) or mindfulness (*sati*), it is the basis for binding;
that [binding] occurs in six ways, by way of the perceptions born from contact arising at the six doors.
Volitional formations are volition,
contact, attention, vitality, and stability;
they are also reasoning, wandering, and effort.
Rapture is the factor of resolution through desire.
Faith, mindfulness, moral shame, moral dread, generosity, loving-kindness, and wisdom;
again, equanimity and tranquility—these two are according to body and mind.
Lightness, plasticity, wieldiness, proficiency, and likewise rectitude;
compassion, gladness, restraint of wrong speech, and restraint of action and livelihood;
greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as wrong view and restlessness.
Lack of moral shame, lack of moral dread, and doubt;
conceit, envy, and avarice; remorse, sloth and torpor—thus these fifty are designated as the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha).
Activity is volition, contact is the act of touching and there the meeting;
attention is the maintenance of life, concentration is non-distraction.
Application is the place of rubbing, while investigation is the movement of reasoning.
Vigor is energy; rapture is refreshment; desire is the wish to act.
Resolve is certainty; faith is clarity;
mindfulness is the state of remembering.
Shame is indeed disgust for evil;
moral dread is fear of it.
Non-attachment, lack of harshness, generosity, loving-kindness, and wisdom—
Equanimity is understanding things as they truly are; its characteristic is evenness.
It dispels the six pairs: [the states of] body and mind, passion and pride, dullness and rigidity, unwieldiness, illness, and crookedness.
These are, respectively, the opposites of restlessness and so forth, of dullness and so forth, and of views and so forth;
as well as the opposites of the remaining factors, of lack of faith and so forth, and of deceit and so forth.
Compassion, sympathetic joy, and gladness are for those who desire the removal of suffering.
The threefold abstinence is the cessation of verbal misconduct and the rest.
Greed, hatred, and delusion are the fuel of craving,
violence, and intoxication.
Gradually, wrong view and false grasp arise;
agitation is considered wavering.
Lack of shame is non-modesty, and lack of dread is heedlessness.
Doubt is indeed perplexity; pride has the characteristic of loftiness.
Envy consists in resentment toward the prosperity of others and in concealment [of one's own].
The torment of envy and avarice,
the grieving over what has been done and left undone,
and the contraction of the mind through sloth, which is its lack of functional fitness;
A wise person should understand the characteristic and the method of these [mental factors] in this way, including torpor.
The seven beginning with feeling and ending with concentration are known as "universal";
those beginning with reasoning and ending with resolve are called the "particulars."
When faith and the others cease, there are twenty-five states without conflict (araṇā);
with greed, torpor, and so forth, there are fourteen states with conflict (saraṇā).
Envy, stinginess, remorse, and hatred pertain to the sensual realm, as do compassion and gladness.
In the sense-sphere and fine-material spheres, the remaining forty-six [mental factors] are born of the three elements.
They consist of: zeal, resolve, equanimity, attention, and the five beginning with faith;
the five beginning with compassion; the six beginning with conceit; and the sixteen occasionals (yevāpanaka).
The five beginning with greed are fixed; among them, eleven are not otherwise.
Shamelessness, lack of moral dread, and the pair that destroys the world—these two, along with delusion and restlessness, are the four universal unwholesome roots.
The pair of World-Guardians has been explained, as well as those named Moral Shame (hiri) and Moral Dread (ottappa).

The factors of jhāna consist of the contemplation of the object, applied thought (vitakka), sustained thought (vicāra), rapture (pīti), and one-pointedness (ekaggatā); these seven are indeed comprised within the three modes of consciousness.
Faith, mindfulness, concentration, energy, and wisdom are the destroyers of the world;
these nine are the powers of one who is unshakable.
Herein, having made the five beginning with faith the life-force, one should apply the intellect fourfold.
With the feelings, these [factors] become two groups of seven, because the faculties do not exercise sovereignty over them.
These, together with the mind and the material faculties, are all termed "faculties";
twenty-two in total, when the two pairs are each counted as one.
The views, one-pointedness, reasoning, mindfulness, and abstinences are the paths;
by dividing the first four into two each for the sake of deliverance, they become twelve.
Contact and volition likewise...
In this context, there are only two [types of nutriment] by way of their function as nourishment; or alternatively, there are four nutriments, including mental volition.
The triad of greed and the rest is declared to be the root of evil in the sense of being a cause;
it is likewise [the root] of the wholesome and the indeterminate.
Likewise, the triad beginning with non-greed,
as well as wrong view, greed, and hatred, are the paths to the miserable states;
their opposites are the paths to the happy states— thus six paths are established.
The six pairs beginning with serenity are called "pairs" because they occur in dyads;
mindfulness and wisdom are called "aids" because of their state of being great aids;
and they are called "yokes" because they carry one across the floods.
Reaching as far as the peak of existence by means of yoga,
yet hearing [the teachings] with taints and views—
there the deluded one would be bewildered, greedy for the two.
Through firm grasping at views, there is clinging (upādāna) therein in three ways;
through the fault of views, these are the knots (gantha), and from the perspective of being knots, views are twofold.
From the five hindrances (āvaraṇa), there arise sensual desire, doubt, and the fault of asceticism (tapas).
Torpor and drowsiness are included under delusion, or else there are six hindrances here.
Having made "arisen from distress" one [hindrance], torpor and drowsiness are spoken of as a single factor because of their common nutriment, their function, and a trace of their opposite.
Delusion regarding views, quarrels, disputes, blindness, doubt,
and arrogance— these ten, along with the destruction of the world and the pair [of views], [are the ten fetters].
Defilements (kilesa) are so called because they defile the mind.
Greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, doubt, and stinginess are the fetters (saṃyojana);
having pierced through them by means of vision, one is freed from the two kinds of bonds.
Those views— delusion, conceit, doubt, hatred, and greed—
are declared in the Sutta to be tenfold by dividing greed into three ways.
Therein, view, greed, delusion, conceit, hatred, and doubt are each twofold.
Having thus explained greed, these underlying tendencies (anusaya) have been set forth.
View itself is to be known as misapprehension (parāmāsa);
such, in brief, is the meaning of the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), stated according to what has been taught.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Summary of the Three Aggregates," in the *Saccasaṅkhepa*. 3.
The Third Chapter.
The Exposition of the Occurrence of Consciousness: Consciousness grasps its object; it is twofold according to whether it is matured or unmatured.
First is the wholesome and unwholesome; the latter is considered the indeterminate.
In that regard, wholesome [consciousness] may be fourfold according to the planes beginning with the sense-sphere:
eight, five, four, and four respectively. How so?

One [type] is associated with joy and accompanied by volition; one is associated with equanimity and accompanied by volition; one is associated with joy and unaccompanied by volition; and one is associated with equanimity and unaccompanied by volition.
With volitional effort, one-pointed, likewise inferior, and two types of wisdom;
likewise associated with equanimity and wisdom, and deficient in wisdom—thus eightfold;
herein, the merit of the sense-sphere is analyzed according to feeling and so forth.
Generosity, virtue, and meditation;
the giving of merit, rejoicing [in others' merit], service, and honoring [the Sangha];
teaching, hearing, and the excellence of view—having become one in these, whether based on a physical object or not;
For those born from wombs lacking doors and so forth, there arises— whether at the appropriate time or otherwise— a cognition that is devoid of purity and lacks discernment,
taking as its object one among the various distinctions such as the destinies and the like, or the limited objects of the three times.
Among the sense-spheres, the five beginning with visible form constitute the five sense-spheres;
the remainder—both material and immaterial—as well as concepts, constitute the sixth sense-sphere.
Therein, having bestowed the excellent three-rooted connection associated with knowledge;
Subsequently, there are two types of cooked food (*pākānaṃ*) during the course of the eightfold [path];
among those very same [types], having given the inferior [type] as a junction (*sandhi*) consisting of two roots (*duhetuka*),
one gives twelve [types] of cooked food during the course [of the path], excluding that which is conjoined with wisdom (*dhīyutaṃ*).
Thus, when wisdom is lacking, the result is inferior both in its connection [to the cause] and in its manifestation;
yet even when it is inferior in both respects, it ripens precisely because the cause was deficient.
This [kamma], which bestows existence and enjoyments, ripens only within the happy realms of sensual desire.

Even when form has vanished, the mind continues to evolve accordingly. The mind is conjoined with applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), zest (*pīti*), happiness (*sukha*), and one-pointedness (*ekagga*);

the first [jhāna] consists of these, while the subsequent three are characterized by the progressive removal of applied thought and so forth, and the fading away of zest and so forth, along with happiness and so forth.
Equanimity and one-pointedness constitute the formless [attainments] as factors;
however, the aggregate of form is fivefold from the perspective of its object.
Having observed the impurity within...
The three beginning with loving-kindness are to be observed;
first, the four and the five [kasinas],
as well as the earth-kasina and so forth.
In the fourfold range of the mind regarding emptiness, by gradually transcending [the lower realms],
there arises fourfold merit pertaining to the formless [attainments].
Directed toward stainless peace, that [merit] comes to be through application to the path.
Furthermore, by way of the fourfold division of the foundational jhānas, there are twenty [types of insight].
The first dispels views and doubt; the next attenuates the faults of sensual desire;
the one following that eradicates them; and the last destroys the remainder.
Thus, on these three planes, merit consisting of mental development (bhāvanāmaya) arises:
based on the first object, it arises through both [generosity and virtue]; based on the second, through both as well;
and based on the third, from the beginning.
The remaining ones exist either supported or unsupported; therein,
the first two establish their own existence.

One may accomplish unsurpassed peace through the higher knowledges (abhiññā), yet not by mere aspiration, because that is the fruit arising from jhāna, and because the giving of the fruit is impossible [otherwise].
There is no karma that yields fruit in another existence; it is not within the domain of material maturation (rūpa-vipāka).
It has its own sphere of activity and nothing else; this is its impossibility.
Evil is exclusively of the nature of desire; furthermore, it is twofold by way of cause, and threefold by way of root, arising through the power of greed, hatred, and delusion.
One associated with joy and views is without volitional formation (*asaṅkhāra*);
one with volitional formation (*sasaṅkhāra*) is likewise single. Two inferior views are the same.
So too are those associated with equanimity and views, as well as those dissociated from views.
Thus, the eight [types of] craving rooted in greed are associated with views regarding feeling and so forth.
The other [type], rooted in hatred, is accompanied by suffering and fault;
that rooted in delusion is also accompanied by equanimity. That which is associated with doubt and restlessness is twofold.
In that regard, two [factors] depend upon a basis, while the others depend either on a basis or not;
how could they be associated with killing and so forth?
Harshness, killing, and ill-will [arise] from hatred, while [covetousness arises] from greed.
Wrong view and sexual misconduct [are abandoned] by two [factors]; the remaining courses of action are [abandoned] by both.
He provides a connection in all four miserable states through his conduct everywhere;
his entire range of experience ripens, except for that which is stainless.
The indeterminate is twofold: fruition and functional; therein, the first is twofold by way of plane.
Herein, the fruition of the sense sphere is fourfold, and it is twofold by way of the fruition of merit and so forth.
The fruition of merit is twofold—by way of cause and with-cause—thus making two sets of eight.
The five kinds of knowledge are rootless; they consist of both grasping and investigation.
Therein, body-consciousness is accompanied by pleasure, while investigation is accompanied by joy.
The remaining six are accompanied by equanimity; like the wholesome, they are all with roots.
Only through the processes of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, the object of that [life-continuum], and death does the rest of this [existence] arise;
it should be understood according to the method previously stated.
For those who fall from the human state into the lower realms, the investigation of the limits of the beginning, such as rebirth-linking, and so forth, [is to be applied].
It arises through another kamma, whether with a cause or without a cause.
Born of evil, born of merit, or caused by both— such as the bank, and so forth—
bodily consciousness accompanied by suffering has these as its undesirable objects.
Those [consciousnesses] have the agreeable as their domain;
among them, two are the initial investigation of the two objects. Five have five objects, while the other two have all objects. They have limited spheres;
the five beginning with receiving have visible forms and so forth as their objects therein.
The remaining [types of] results are only present; six [types of] results belong to the three time periods.

I shall state that the results of both material and immaterial kamma are entirely similar, except for their own specific function, such as the foundation consciousness, and the triad of their respective functions.
Even though they have attained the peerless fruition, they have not yet completely exhausted their own kamma.
For they have abandoned that gateway to liberation in two ways on the path and three ways in the fruition.
Their activity is of three kinds due to the absence of defilement.
In that context, [the states] belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmika) arise from the planes (bhūmi);
they are twofold as "with cause" and "with root-cause" (hetu-sahetu),
and thus how are they threefold with respect to the root-cause (hetu)?
They are preceded by attention and preceded by laughter, accompanied by equanimity and pleasure, and accompanied by equanimity;
they belong to the five sense-sphere realms and have all [six] objects as their domain.
They possess causes, both material and immaterial, and are endowed with their own wisdom.
Just as a creeper that has been cut does not bear fruit from its flowers,
so too for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*),
the two types of non-cultivated offenses do not bear fruit even while they are occurring, being like fruit from a useless flower.
Thirty-two, two, six, four, and five respectively;
merit, demerit, fruit, and functional [consciousness]—thus it is of eighty-nine kinds.
The life-continuum, the adverting, the fivefold [process of] seeing and so forth;
The death-consciousness has as its object the apex of javanas that have arisen and been arrested at the six sense doors. Thus, by way of their functions and occurrences,
how shall the occurrence of consciousness at the six doors be briefly described for these twenty-seven types?
For one with lust for sense-pleasures, at the moment of death, the sign of kamma and so forth appears to the mind alone; for others, it is the range of kamma.
Taking that which has appeared as its object, the impulsion occurs five times.
Then, from that very object, there occurs a falling away (cuti) either by way of speed,

for those bound for the states of loss, through ignorance, craving, and volitional formations arising together with it— [factors] which obscure the danger of sense objects and cause one to bend and cast oneself down.
When those [defilements] have been abandoned, there remains the concealing and the bowing down of the rest;
however, the formations that are swift here become exclusively wholesome.
When the three functions have thus been performed within the sphere illuminated by karma, [the path arises].
Depending on a corresponding basis that has arisen together with it, or not depending on it there,
a corresponding rebirth-linking may occur, having abandoned the interval between lives;
for how could rebirth-linking occur in a distant place without that interval?
In this very way, due to the causes such as karma and craving,
the mind may become distant from the preceding consciousness,
just as an island or an echo [is distinct from its source]. There is no perception for one passing away, nor is there a sign, nor is there a "falling away" (cuti) itself.
What is the sign of connection above? Even a condition is immediately proximate.
Now, death in a previous existence is the connection for birth in the sense-sphere realm;
because there is no interval between other minds, it serves as the immediately preceding cause.
Kamma performed in another existence finds its opportunity therefrom;
by that very means, the connection is established when the range of objects has been presented.
Because he was unable to bring about the total fading away of the mind, [the process continues].
Therefore, for one who still possesses latent tendencies (*anusaya*), there may be a renewed arising in existence.
At the five sense-doors, the reconnection (*sandhi*) may occur even without [a new] kamma, within the range of two [objects];
it is called "reconnection" because it connects existence, and it is the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) by virtue of being a factor of that [existence].
In that very way, there is falling away from that [state] due to the passing away from that object;
thus, within a single continuity, there are the distinctions of arising and duration.
For when another object has come into the range of a different state of consciousness, [there is falling away].
The number of causes for the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is two instances of vibration when another object is impinged;
it is like the analogy of pebbles, wherein the shaking of one thing supported by another occurs through their being bound together as one.
Excluding the activity of the mind-element, there occurs once in that existence;
then seeing and so forth, which have their respective doors as their range, followed by apprehension;
then investigation from that, and then registration once from that.
The impulsion occurs seven times regarding the sense-sphere objects, corresponding to them.
From that, the pair of registration moments arises. From that, there is a great interval to the life-continuum.
From the impulsion, the determining consciousness arises regarding the great object; for the small object, it is the others, namely, the mind-door adverting consciousness.
But regarding the limited (paritta) object of adverting, they say that its occurrence lasts for two or three moments, like a flash of lightning; for it is not subject to repetition in the texts.
Furthermore, here there is a restriction of the mind, just as there is a restriction of karma and so forth.
Having shown [the nature of] the object by means of similes such as the mango, one should clarify it well.
Then, from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), there may arise an intrusion through the mind-door or other doors;
but when the desired object called "sensual" has become manifest, [consciousness arises] from that.
For those with sensual desire, however, that [consciousness] becomes the object; from that, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) may arise.
When [the object] is not manifest and is limited, the life-continuum arises immediately after the impulsion (javana).
Whether [the object] is unmanifest or manifest, limited or unlimited;
But when the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) has already flowed for a Brahmā within the fourfold range,
if it then flows directed toward a sublime object associated with hatred,
would the life-continuum not cease because of that contradiction? How could there be a connection with pleasure?
There is investigation by equanimity; how could there be fault in what is limited?
There is no restriction without fault, because the fruit arises from the path.
All [consciousnesses] are sublime and stainless; they may arise immediately after the change-of-lineage consciousness.
Cessation, the arising of the fruit, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and the impulsion (javana) and so forth; those with causes,
those subject to taints, results (pāka), the two types of investigation, and the two types of equanimity— these,
along with the junctions and the life-continuum, and death, total nineteen.
Two each for adverting and so forth, three ending with apprehension,
one for investigation, and that which is named "determining.
There are eight great resultant consciousnesses of the sense sphere and three for investigation.
These eleven are known as the registration-minds.
All wholesome and unwholesome states, as well as functional states excluding the two types of initial application (āvajja),
and the fifty-five fruits— these constitute the impulsion consciousnesses.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Saccasaṅkhepa*, titled "The Exposition of the Occurrence of Consciousness. 4.
The Fourth Chapter.

Now, for the sake of the swift progress of practitioners, a concise summary of the method concerning the miscellaneous aspects of the aggregate of consciousness is stated according to the "one-fold" and other methods:
all grasping of objects is of a single kind, namely, the mind.
Eighty-one [factors] pertain to the three planes; that includes the mundane and the sutta.
The remaining eight are supramundane. The "Unsurpassed" is considered twofold.
There are seven types of causes: the world-ripening cause, the functional cause, and the single cause.
Thirty [mental factors] are without predominance (anadhipati); together with predominance, the remaining ones are also twofold.
One who possesses wisdom is endowed with desire, consciousness, energy, and investigation;
one devoid of investigation is endowed with only one, being lacking in knowledge.
Limited, measureless, and exalted— these three, six, nine, and eight respectively.
Two are fivefold consciousness, and three are the mind-elements.
Furthermore, the seventy-six types of consciousness are threefold by way of the element of mental knowledge.
These consist of nine types of sublime consciousness with a single object that are not direct knowledges,
five types of pure consciousness, and the fivefold sense-consciousness.
The mind-element has five objects; it is born of the sense-sphere and possesses direct knowledge.
The remainder has six objects, numbering forty-three in total.
These include the two types of sense-sphere resultant and unwholesome consciousness, the first path, and the first two functional consciousnesses.
All these material phenomena (rūpa) are not [included] in the immaterial states; thus they total forty-three.
Excluding matter, there would be four types of immaterial resultant consciousness;
the remaining forty-two exist in both ways [as resultant and functional].
According to the fourfold classification by way of being without cause,
having one cause, two causes, or three causes, there would be eighteen, two, twenty-two,
and forty-seven [types of consciousness] respectively. In the sense-sphere, all impulsion consciousnesses, as well as the two types of direct knowledge, are capable of being mastered.
In the case of the material paths of action, there are four groups of eight consisting of the volitions that produce intimation.
The remaining twenty-six are impulsive moments that perform the material paths of action.
Excluding two of the five [sets of] ten, these are the fruits of the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere.
These nineteen types of formative acts have an initial activity;
the remaining fourteen have a broken continuity, and three have no continuity at all.
Among those, starting from the five that have a single function, there are those with a single function.
The impulsion consists of two or five consciousnesses; the mind-element occurs sixty-eight times.
The determining consciousness has two functions and so forth; the "pleasant shore" occurs in the sublime states.
The resultants are those of the sense-sphere and the great resultants; the remaining ones are the "shores," respectively.
Seeing, hearing, what is seen, what is heard, and what is smelled and so forth;
what is touched, and the triad of mind-elements—these are the seen, the heard, and the touched.
What is seen, heard, touched, and cognized, along with the supernormal knowledges and the rest of the objects of desire.
One should likewise set forth the sixfold [classification] according to the object cognized.
However, by way of the seven consciousness-elements, it becomes sevenfold.
Now, the sequence of the method immediately following that will be stated.
In the sense-sphere, there are two types of merit at the beginning;
in the fine-material sphere, there is infinite merit; the producer thereof is the unsurpassed and infinite;
and the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is the first observation. From the second pair, there is the observation of the limit; from the third pair, the life-continuum.
These are infinite, stainless, equanimous, and sublime.
In all instances, they occur by themselves as fifty-three, thirty-seven, and thirty-three;
these, however, arise from merit within the fine-material realm.
And those which ripen there, together with the ten that ripen in the realm of sense-desire through the application of wisdom;
and those from the merit of the formless realms; and again, its own ripening itself.
And those that ripen below from within [the higher realms], and these final ones are the fruit of the third [path].
By means of one, two, or five [factors], the Path produces its own respective fruit.
Like the "end-maker," "desire," and "the beautiful" [root-conditions],
the seven [defilements]— along with the two types of hatred— are themselves dependent upon the sense-sphere life-continuum (kāmabhavaṅga).
By means of the great manifest causes, all connections are blameworthy;
by the remaining types of sensual death, the sensual connections are blameworthy.
Sensual death, the investigative consciousness, and one who personally delights in pleasure [are also included].
Two [types of ignorance] involve both concealment and investigation; the others involve only investigation.
Each one conceals its own respective object through the five and two types of consciousness.
Those associated with the ripening of form are blameworthy, excluding those at the moment of rebirth-linking and those that have roots as their object.
From the beginning among those with formless ripening, there are those with desire-realm ripening that possess three roots;
including those with ultimate faultlessness and those with formless ripening, these last nine arise.
From the second [moment] onwards, those same [nine] arise, excluding the lower ripening.
The resultants with three roots and the two types of ripening, together with [the rootless] itself— these are fourteen.
The fivefold pairs beginning with the functional, the smiling consciousnesses, and the same excluding the formless— these ten, along with the life-continuum associated with knowledge,
constitute the ten [types of consciousness] from the point of view of registration.

In the sense-sphere, there are impulsions and life-continuum; in the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere, there is also [the life-continuum] itself. There are nine and five [types of consciousness] from the perspective of the wholesome and so forth, and the two types of functional [consciousness].
In the fine-material sphere, there is the life-continuum itself, the mind-element, and also the functional [consciousness] with a single root.
And "that which gives rise to" (tappādaka) and "the most excellent" (antima)—these twenty-two are the third [category].
These too are ripening (pāka), self-existent (sayañjata), intermediate (majjha), and sublime (mahaggata);
as for "functional" (kiriya), there are twenty, by means of the remaining two dyads.
Including "already arisen" and "itself," there are thus fourteen types of impulsion (kriyā-javā).
Excluding their object (tadārammaṇa), one should apply this according to the method of the *Paṭṭhāna*.
Now, pleasant [volition] has a pleasant [result], and the remainder likewise has a remainder as its result.
I shall explain their respective objects according to the method of the commentaries.
All sublime functional states there are equal to their own corresponding merits;
they differ only in that the final fruit is the ultimate limit.
The phenomena immediately following this have been declared as being "so many";
now, by means of these [same factors], this method (naya) is further explained:
by two [factors] come the sense-sphere states; by three, the fine-material and immaterial; but by four, [the supramundane].
Two paths have six [factors] each, with the two fruits and so forth; the remaining two, however, have seven.
From one [factor], ten [paths] arise through five [faculties];
concealment and the investigation of pleasure are grasped from their own [set] by means of desire, aversion, action, and the lack of speed.
In the sense-sphere, there are thirty-three consciousnesses that cross to the further shore:
those with impulsion devoid of functional result, those with that as their object, and those accompanied by doubt.
Two [of these] are from the "black" category of sense-sphere merit and happiness-crossing.
The great resultants are final, as are those following death from the formless realms.
Excluding two of these, there are thirty-seven;
from these thirty-five, the second pair of rebirth-linkings arises.
These seven, beginning with the "Ferry of Happiness" (Sukhatīra), arise from action as well as from birth.
The remaining four should be known as obtainable through the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
All [these] are devoid of the Path (maggavajja) and possess the faculties of the sense-sphere, happiness, and the "Ferry."
"Cutī" refers to the nine [types of] kamma; thus he indicates the third pair.
By means of these [nine], which are free from fault, there are seventy-one [types of kamma];
the other two pairs are without form and without ripening, being those with no cause and with two causes.

With sixty-three [factors], excluding the arising of materiality (*rūpa*), there are [the paths] with laughter as the object of transgression (*hāsāvajja*) and in the [first] impulsion (*java*). However, in the second and subsequent impulsions, there are eight and six [factors] respectively, along with those same [sixty-three] plus the wholesome roots (*sādhupāka*).
And by themselves, there are the second and subsequent [paths].
In the lower realms, they arise with one fewer [consciousness] at each successive level.
Including the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) of the blissful plane itself, there are twenty-one;
however, for the others, excluding the formless life-continuum, there are nineteen, including the final faultless consciousness.
Now, the method (naya), which consists of what has just been stated, is manifold;
its occurrence, according to the various classifications such as the individual (puggala) and so forth, is now being described.
Indeed, in an ordinary person (puthujjana), views and doubts arise.
The seven pure trainees (sekkha) belong to the infinite [stream], while the rest belong to the finite.
Nineteen types of action are of limited purity and are blameless;
the remaining wholesome and unwholesome types belong to trainees and worldlings (puthujjana).
The other two blameless [paths of action] and the three ripened [paths of action] are with-outflows (*sāsrava*);
thus there may be five types from the sevenfold division.
In the sense-sphere, there are sixteen; the triad beginning with the nose, the faulty, and the great-fruited [paths of action].
In the realms of form and formlessness, there are twenty-five types of consciousness that mature together.
The remaining ones are maturations of the sense-sphere. The first path and the two initial functions belong to the first birth;
in the realm of form, there are twenty-two types of impulsion, while the rest are of threefold birth within the three realms.
In detail, across the planes, one should know the beautiful and the ugly of the sense-sphere,
excluding laughter, the rootless, and those leading to the states of misery—
these are thirty-seven. Excluding those ripening in the sublime, there are eighty remaining in the rest of the sense-sphere.
The eye, ear, and mind elements, investigation, and determining; each [is] deficient in passion, energy, and speed respectively;
maturation occurs in the ignoble realm of form;
fifty-five and sixty [types of consciousness] arise in the three [planes] beginning with Parittābha.
In the case of those associated with doubt and wrong view, excluding the first five pure [factors],
those same fifty-five arise in the pure stages (*suddhabhūmi*).
One's own [stage] has the speed of a weak horse, like the sound of a single axle on the first path.
Maturity and investigating consciousness—these would be forty-three in the immaterial realm. These are the non-guilty [consciousnesses] of the lower and lower realms;
they are maturity and each of their own respective types.
In the second [jhanas] and so forth,
two by two are subtracted from each;
in the formless [attainments], one from each, and likewise in the first three of the fine-material [attainments].
In the first triad there is one [resultant], and two in the second triad.
However, the final material resultant occurs in the six [realms] beginning with the Vehapphala;
whereas the great resultants occur only in the happy destinies of the sense sphere.
The three [types of] lust in the sense-sphere, as well as the two types of aversion;
among the seventeen [factors], the first is stainless in the case of pride and the rest.
Among those excluding the noble ones and the miserable states, there are the four fruits beginning with the fruit of stream-entry.
In all realms except for the woeful states and the formless realm, there is laughter, the form-sphere, and wholesome kamma.
Excluding the three woeful states and the upper realms, there is space-infinity and wholesome kamma.
Likewise, excluding the two woeful states and the upper realms, there is consciousness-infinity and wholesome kamma.
In all planes, excluding the Peak of Existence and the woeful states, there are the spheres of Nothingness and the Beautiful-Karma;
in the pure [planes], they are associated with views and doubt, except for those on all planes.
And the three final [attainments] are stainless.
Subhakriya and Mahakriya—
these thirteen do not fall into the states of woe.
In the formless realm, there is the mind-element; seeing accompanied by investigation;
in the sensual realm, union with the undesirable; for Brahmās, the fruit born of evil;
the determining [consciousness], sense-sphere merit, and that which is deficient in view yet possessed of pride.
These fourteen types of consciousness arise in thirty planes.
Two faculties [arise] in those with no root-cause, excluding the two extremes;
three in those with doubt or other non-root-cause evil states; and four in thirteen [other] states.
Seven [factors] are stainless when one lacks the six knowledges and possesses the [remaining] latent tendencies;
forty are thus lost. This is to be known according to the classification of the faculties.
Two powers are [lost] in the two pairs of non-causes; three, however, are [lost] in doubt.
In the six types of consciousness rooted in the remaining two roots (greed and delusion), there are four of the ten powers.
However, among the seventy-nine types of consciousness associated with wisdom, seven [of the powers] are present.
For the remaining ones are weak; thus, the power of energy is the [predominant] strength.
There are two and five factors of non-jhāna, for they are factors of that [jhāna] only when they are present.
In jhāna, when joy is absent, there are two in the stainless (anāgāmi) first jhāna;
in the third, three in the speckled (sāmala); likewise four in the second.
In the sensual-sphere jhānas and those without rapture, there are five factors each; in the remaining ones, four.
There are two paths in the case of doubt and views; in the remaining unwholesome states, three.
In the second and subsequent pure jhānas, there are two roots, and in other cases, one.
Four or five [consciousnesses] have the first jhāna as their desire-root cause;
seven have the second jhāna and so forth as their root cause; eight have the remaining [jhānas] as their root cause.
For, from the end of the causes of the path, there is that which is not a path-factor and is without root-cause.
There is no path-component associated with the faculty of equanimity, nor with the five [faculties] beginning with faith.

One who possesses equanimity toward merit regarding a pleasant object has an agreeable object; one who possesses it regarding an intermediate or disagreeable object has an intermediate or disagreeable object, respectively. However, when the range of objects is the opposite of that, the same applies to the opposite case.
That object is [associated] with two faults, but not because it is made pleasant;
for when all that is beautiful and ugly has vanished, it is called an "object" by way of its function.
Or rather, it is an "object" by way of its function, yet one is not happy through equanimity toward it.
"One [consciousness] and the other"—this one should clearly observe.
Through the karma that provides the connection, there is the determination of the impulsion (*javana*) during the occurrence that takes that as its object;
this is due to the karma itself, and not from any other karma.
Those mental factors which were mentioned in relation to the mind—
those shall now be stated briefly as two and five.
All seven [mental factors] arise everywhere.
Through reasoning, investigation, and resolve, those same [seven] arise as ten.
[They arise] in the fivefold mind-element and in the fivefold pleasant investigation.
These [five hindrances] are predominant in laughter; and with exertion, they are predominant in two ways.
In the case of distraction (*voṭṭhabbana*), these same [hindrances] are present, ten in number, excluding joy (*pīti*).
They are shared by those who commit evil, and are associated with three or five types of restlessness.
Those associated with doubt (*kaṅkhā*) are likewise these same [eighteen], but with inferior resolve (*hīna-nicchaya*).
Those free from doubt (*kaṅkhā-vajja*), however, are these same [eighteen] with resolve accompanied by hatred (*sadosa-chanda*).
In the case of the seven [types of] misconduct (*dūse*), there are [sixteen]; but in the two cases involving greed (*lobha*), there are seventeen.
Those [first two] are faulty with regard to harm and accompanied by greed;
in the subsequent pairs beginning with the third, they are respectively characterized by the addition of wrong view and the pair of rapture.
Twenty-two [mental factors] arise in the fourth jhāna and so forth,
in the fine-material and immaterial realms, excluding the access concentration of joy, from the beginning up to the thirtieth [factor].
In the case of the first two jhānas, which possess rapture and applied thought, one or two [factors] are abandoned respectively; in the third and those following,
those same [remaining factors] persist.
Fifty-two [factors] are added [to the previous totals].
In these two [sets] beginning with "desire," in the second and subsequent pairs,
they should respectively be understood as excluding wisdom, rapture, and both wisdom and rapture.
In the jhānas, the immaterial states, and the abstinences are already mentioned;
therein, speak of these [volitions] as being fixed in their result, since they occur in all instances.
In the case of sense-sphere meritorious deeds, each one—
For among those not fixed [in destiny],
there are the abstinences, compassion, joy, and the pleasant and beautiful kamma pertaining to the sense-sphere.
Some say that even in the intermediate [state], in wholesome kamma accompanied by roots,
and in each of the pleasant jhānas, there are indeed compassion and gladness. In that [intermediate state],
sloth-and-torpor occurs with volitional effort, as do the two inferior views.
Or, with pride (*māna*), there are three; when deprived of the remaining views, there is one.
Envy (*issā*), avarice (*macchariya*), and worry (*kukkucca*) occur separately in the two [categories] associated with hatred (*dosa*).
Within that [latter category], there may be three together with sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*).
Thus have been stated here all these mental factors (cetasika) in their entirety.
Now, regarding this same number therein, this method (naya) is being explained.
Among those sixty-three, there are pleasure, pain, and equanimity as the three feelings (vedanā).
In fifty-five types of consciousness, regarding existence by way of faculties:
it should be understood that in each single instance among sixty-one [types], there are two [faculties]; in two instances, five;
and in fifty [instances], the pentad of faculties beginning with pleasure.
There are one hundred and ten [factors]; from that, energy is determined.
From that, five are inferior; from that, the faculty of concentration is indicated.
Desire is nineteen less than one hundred; furthermore, there are faith and the others.
There are nine hundred deficient thoughts that are faulty through lack of knowledge.
There is practice in seventy-nine [thoughts], non-arising in sixty-six,
joy in fifty-five, and it may exist in fifty-one.
In the sixth and twentieth [jhānas], there would be abstinences; or else, compassion and gladness.
With the eight types of mind accompanied by equanimity, there would be twenty-eight.
Shamelessness, lack of fear of wrongdoing, delusion, and restlessness—these twelve alone;
Greed occurs in eight types of consciousness; dullness and torpor, however, in five.
Conceit and wrong view occur in four;
likewise, hatred, envy, stinginess, and remorse occur in two types of mind.
In one case there is doubt; thus it should be understood according to what has been stated.
Furthermore, the method of non-occurrence can be known by the wise.
This same method should be understood regarding the aggregates beginning with feeling.
The aggregates should be understood as being of various kinds—
such as "one" and so forth— due to their lack of separation from the power of conjunction.
They are to be known respectively as a mass of foam, a bubble, a mirage, a plantain tree, and an illusion.
Because they are alike in being subject to crushing, in being unendurable, in being momentary, in being beautiful, in being alluring, and in being deceptive, they are brought together as the same.
Those with taints are the aggregates of clinging; those without taints are simply aggregates.
Therein, because they are the basis of suffering, the aggregates are suffering and a burden;
because they are phenomena such as impermanent, they are like murderers and full of danger;
and because they lack the nature of happiness, they are like a woman with a raised sword.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Summary of the Miscellaneous Aspects of the Aggregate of Consciousness," in the *Saccasaṅkhepa*. 5.
The Fifth Chapter.
The description of Nibbāna illustrates the destruction of lust and the other defilements; Nibbāna has the characteristic of peace,
serving as a refuge for one scorched by the suffering and heat of saṃsāra.
The mere exhaustion [of defilements] is not Nibbāna, because it is described as being "profound" and so forth;
for non-existence is never described as being "profound" or similar qualities, just as one does not describe the hair on a tortoise.
What is called "exhaustion" (khaya) is the Path; because this [Nibbāna] has reached that state, it is called "exhaustion."
Arahatta is stable because it is devoid of arising and passing away.
For knowledge does not take either the conditioned or conventional reality as its object;
rather, one must cut off the stains from that basis and seek the unconditioned.
One who desires to attain that peace should undertake the sixfold purification;
however, one seeking welfare must accomplish the purification of knowledge and vision.
Therein, the purification of virtue is fourfold, consisting of volition and the other factors.
But concentration accompanied by access is called "purity of mind.
Having accomplished these two purities, one should define name as "bending" and form as "being broken," and determine that there is no self or other such basis therein.
Just as fire exists when there is a meeting of fuel, a flint, and heat— even if it was previously absent—
so too does the mind arise upon the encounter of the sense base, the object, and other conditions.
Just as a lame person and a blind person are each individually incapable of traveling, [yet together they may succeed].
Just as those who are joined proceed, so too do the activities called "name-and-form.
The view that there is a self or anything else other than name-and-form is called "purification of view" because it purifies wrong view.
In the beginning, that pair [of name-and-form] arises through ignorance, craving, clinging, and kamma;
during the course of existence, form arises from kamma and so forth, while name arises from the bases and so forth.
Since this is always, everywhere, and for all beings, it is not identical [in every respect].
One does not see another self as a permanent cause without a reason.
Thus one investigates with the wisdom by which [one understands] conditions;
because of having seen [this], that purity is called "crossing over doubt."
Having fully understood through the full understanding of what is to be known,
he strives with unwavering resolve; ever diligent for the sake of purification,
by means of the full understanding called "investigation," he groups the aggregates together according to the three times and other such categories into clusters.
"Impermanent, suffering, and non-self"—thus one first contemplates with insight.
The aggregates are impermanent in the sense of destruction; they are indeed suffering in the sense of terror; they are non-self in the sense of being coreless.
Thus one should see them again and again.

One should thoroughly investigate [the aggregates] by means of the forty aspects beginning with impermanence, in order to make the characteristics clear and to understand the aggregates in their entirety.
Even if this is not accomplished, one whose faculties are sharpened in nine ways—
One should correctly practice insight into both the material and immaterial realms by means of two sets of seven:
through the taking up and laying down of material form, its progression toward youth and old age, its correct cultivation,
its birth and so forth, and also through its nature as a manifestation of phenomena.
One should see that name arises from the collection, from the moment, and from action;
and one should see the emergence of form from the causes of ignorance, craving, and kamma, as well as from the removal of views, conceit, and attachment.
Without nutriment, there would be the triad of feeling together with contacts;
but without those very [contacts], there would be name-and-form and so forth, even without contact.
"Mind, indeed, according to each respective destruction of its cause, undergoes that very [destruction]. Thus,
through the arising and passing away of causes, as well as through the momentary arising and passing away;"
Thus, in fifty ways, one should observe arising and passing away again.
For the yogi who has thus begun the observation of arising and passing away,
the secondary defilements become manifest, both in terms of their intrinsic nature and their causes.
These are: light, non-distraction, serenity, happiness, equanimity, mindfulness, zest, resolution, and attachment—these ten are thus described.
And they are thirtyfold by way of craving, views, haughtiness, and grasping.
When that [consciousness] had arisen and was flickering, the fool saw a path where there was no path.
Now, insight has entered the right way; he is wise.
He thus sees: "This is not the path, because it is a basis for grasping."
When one sees the secondary defilements as being under the sway of impermanence and so forth, and subject to arising and falling away,
that vision which has entered the cognitive process is called the "path.
That wisdom which stands thus, having discerned what is the path and what is not the path, is [the path].
The fifth purity would consist of the discernment of what is the path and what is not the path.
Since the accomplishment of purity begins with the full understanding termed "abandoning," one should now exert oneself in the final stage,
which consists of the full understanding termed "investigation."
That person becomes a possessor of new knowledge; for one who is striving, there arise here nine [factors] beginning with purification, effort, and emergence.
Furthermore, they are so called because of their continuity, their density, and their concealment.
The characteristics do not become apparent; insight is defiled.
Therefore, investigate further from that point, once again observing arising and passing away.
By means of that, seeing impermanence and so forth, one attains supreme proficiency.

When, having turned [the mind] back, one contemplates by way of arising, stability, and so forth, the knowledge stands still at the very moment of dissolution; then there may be the "cognition of dissolution.
When, for one contemplating dissolution in this way, the threefold existence (tibhava) appears [as such],...
Just as fear arises from lions and other beasts, there may be occasions when danger is encountered.
When one stands upon that which is fraught with peril— like a house on fire with its structural elements ablaze—
at such times, the contemplation of danger (ādīnavānupassanā) will be attained.
When one has seen the danger in volitional formations and so forth, and no longer delights in states of existence and the like,
then, having attained such an intelligence, there may arise the vision of disenchantment.
When your knowledge desires to be liberated from all conditioned things, O ornament of all beings...
And just as fish and other creatures caught by nets and such are then released, so too,
when one perceives conditioned phenomena as foul, impermanent, suffering, and non-self,
one becomes eager to abandon them; this is the contemplation of reflective discernment (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā*).
Herein, for the sake of proficiency in the operation of all-knowledge,
there are the similes of the fisherman’s perception of a snake and the fisherman and the crab.
Emptiness regarding self and what belongs to self is twofold, as expressed by the passage beginning, "I am nowhere," and so forth.
Seeing it intensely in four ways, six ways, and many ways—
having crossed over the whirlpool and grasped the fire—
the intellect perceives the conditioned as a mere film.
Just as one who is burdened by the body regards its faults,
so does he maintain equanimity toward it. Thus,
even toward that which is full of peril, the mind remains fixed upon its true characteristics.
Just as the sea-bird does not reach the shore even though it is within sight,
so too this insight that has reached the peak through the knowledge of equanimity towards formations is called "leading to emergence" and "conformable."
Having reached the gateway to liberation, one accomplishes the seven types of persons;
and by means of the various classifications such as the factors of jhāna, the bases, and so forth, that [insight] proceeds.
For if there is emergence from the contemplation of impermanence for a given yogi, [then insight arises].
Through the abundance of the liberation of the mind, one becomes possessed of the faculty of sharp faith.
If that [liberation] occurs through the aspects of suffering and non-self, then those [faculties] arise in succession:
through the abundance of tranquility and bliss, one becomes possessed of the faculties of sharp concentration and equanimity.
The state of being devoted to wisdom is indicated by what has been declared as emergence;
the state of being devoted to faith [is indicated] by the rest through their respective inclinations.
There may be two types of those who follow by faith: those with sharp faith and those with calm.
In the first and middle positions, there are six who are liberated by faith (*saddhā-vimutta*).
From the other [positions], starting with the follower of Dhamma (*dhammānusārī*), there are those who have attained vision (*diṭṭhippatta*) in infinite numbers.
Among those liberated by wisdom (*paññā-vimutta*), both types—those with and without jhāna—are found at the end.
For one of sharp faith, even though it is included [in the category of those with dull faculties], it is impelled by the state of being liberated through faith (*saddhāvimutta*);
for one of middling [faculties], it is described in the *Visuddhimagga* as a body-witness (*kāyasakkhin*) among the eight types.
However, that which was stated in the discourse on liberation concerns one who possesses sharp wisdom (*tikkhapañña*).
For this state of having attained vision (diṭṭhipattatta) does not exist among the Abhidhammikas.

If all those [who have attained the fruits] were to obtain the eight liberations while being in the middle of the six [dhyānas], they would be body-witnesses (kāyasakkhī); at the end [of the path], they would be those liberated both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta).
In the path's course, there are indeed four, three, or two conforming [factors],
according to whether the faculties are dull, medium, sharp, or very sharp.
In the *Visuddhimagga*, all four are entirely prohibited.
Thus it has been stated because it is so explained in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.
Even if there is a slight fault in proximity to the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), because of the stability of the path of purification,
the ascetic thus attains purity through the knowledge and vision of the way (*paṭipadāñāṇadassana*).
Just as the preliminary consciousness (āvajjana) is to the Path,
so too is the change-of-lineage (gotrabhu) produced by those two— namely, the sixth and seventh purifications— having taken up peace in the interval between them.
Thereafter, the Path arises, which severs the three fetters (saṃyojana).
When fruits [of the path] arise one, two, or three, having thus transcended what was previously stated,
for one who develops [the path] in that way, there occurs the thinning of lust and hatred;
the second fruit from that is the Once-returner, the possessor of that fruit.
For one who meditates thus, there arises that which destroys lust and hatred;
from that, the third fruit arises, and by virtue of that fruit, one is a Non-returner (*anāgāmī*).
For one who meditates thus, there arises that which destroys the remaining defilements.
The fourth is the fruit thereof: the Arahant, established in that fruit.
Having performed his task, with the cutting off of existence, he is worthy of offerings through the destruction of the substrata of being;
like a lamp, he goes to Nibbāna, which is known as the end of all suffering.
Thus would purity, known as knowledge and vision, be established.
To this extent, the truth of the ultimate sense has been stated in brief.
Since it is said that conventional truth consists of things such as "beings" which are not real entities, [the ultimate truth is what remains].
It cannot be obtained like a firebrand’s circle, for that [circle] exists without the forms and so forth [that produce it].
However, without departing from the form and so forth in their respective ways,
there occurs both the designation and the apprehension in those very same ways.
"It can be obtained through conceptualization; since it is not false in that regard, they say it is 'unspoken as a basis' because it is not explicitly stated in the *Paritta* and other such texts.
This 'being' is a continuity of aggregates, possessing both evil and virtuous friends."
Having grasped [the elements] as a unity, the wise here employ conventional designations.
Since the person is not distinct from earth and the other elements,
the apprehension of a "person" would exist merely as a basis for wrong view.

Having taken this as the object, those who know [the matter] have stated that it is a "designation of the non-existent" (avijjamāna-paññatti) by means of such words as "conch" and so forth. However, because its object is form and so on,
which do exist, it is a "designation of the existent" (vijjamāna-paññatti).
If you wish to understand the designation of the body well, listen to the truth as it is spoken.
For sound, along with its indicative modifications, pertains to the two truths;
it is called a "designation" (paññatti) because it makes something known—thus it has been stated by those who know that.
"Having the present and so forth as its object, this is the knowledge of the analytical knowledge of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa)";
this is appropriate only in this way, and not otherwise. [If it were otherwise,] then for all things, such as sound, the denotable, and the concept, [the same would apply].
Because it is to be made known, there is the inclusion of the categories of designations.
When it is said, "All phenomena that are designations," this is how it should be taught;
and likewise for the act of making known and the bases for what is to be made known.
If it is argued that this enumeration was made for the purpose of making the classification known,
then it should not be treated as separate, since it is included within the path of the formal definitions (paññatti).
For it is made known by means of the four terms beginning with "formal definition" (paññatti).
"Because they are designated by others," so the teachers have said. Since form and the rest must be designated in dependence [upon other factors],
the first is therefore the designation-in-dependence-on-the-non-existent (*avijjamānupādāyapaññatti*).
Immediately after the continuum of auditory consciousness,
by means of a mind-door consciousness that has acquired its birth and grasped the previously learned convention,
they designate the seven horses and so forth by means of that [consciousness] which has grasped them.
Thus it is a designation by name, and it is designated as "the second.
The comprehension of the meaning through the awakening to a name other than the sound is to be praised according to the previous method, because it accomplishes what is difficult to achieve.
That is a designation for what exists, as is the state of non-existence;
by means of what exists, there is that which does not exist, and its opposite.
By means of what does not exist, there is that which exists, and its opposite.
Thus, among those [types of volition], there are six kinds; the first consists of those beginning with "thought" (mati).
A sentient being, one endowed with faith, a human being, a man, Seniya, and mental volition (manocetanā); [these are the six].
Thus these should be understood according to their order, beginning with the second;
having known them thus by way of their characteristics.
The two truths are not to be confused;
however, conventional usage should be employed by the wise, and not otherwise.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Description of Nibbāna," in the Summary of Truths.
The *Saccasaṅkhepa* is completed.
